translations.text: "It is a good rule for everyone who begins a discourse or a task to begin from God and to bring it to completion in God, as Gregory the Theologian says: 'Let God be the beginning and the end of your every deed and word.' Now therefore we too loudly proclaim the worship of God and the orthodox confession of the faith, upon which the Church of Christ is founded, and which grows day by day and increases more than the cedars of Lebanon. Upon this foundation of the holy Gospel of Christ and of his life-giving commandments we, all the orthodox believers, stand firm, and thus we decree and declare: that just as it is written above concerning keeping unshaken the true faith which the holy apostles preached and the God-clothed Fathers taught us, so also may the rules and canons established by them be firm and unshaken."

Of our holy and blessed father John Chrysostom, archbishop of Constantinople, the Commentary on the Gospel of John. Chapter 1. On Saint John the Evangelist and Theologian. When the athletes of this world see some newly arrived athlete from a foreign land,
valiant and renowned, at once everyone gathers to see his skill and his fighting, and they bring him forward into their midst,
and vast multitudes watch his feats, and their whole mind is there.
And again, if some marvelous performer arrives, in the same way the people gather together, leave all their business, and go up to a high place to see his skills and his performances.
So too again among philosophers: if some renowned foreign philosopher comes, they do likewise; for they all gather, and watch him, and listen to the words of his wisdom, and test him with many words.

But if such a thing happens in the case of men who are philosophers of this world, and performers, and fighters, and if many hasten in this way, with great desire and zeal, to see them and to hear their words,

how much more does it behoove you to hear, with much eagerness and desire, the words not of a performer and carnal philosopher, but of a man speaking from heaven, who cries out and utters a voice more brilliant than the sun;
for his voice has seized and filled the whole world and has reached its ends, not because of its loudness, but because he moves his tongue by divine grace;

and this is the marvel, that at such a height of his voice it is not irksome or unseemly, but is more desirable and sweeter than all sweetness, and delights the soul and mind far more than those devilish songs of the singers of this world, which the devil has sown among men. But this voice is sweet and beautiful,
and besides this it is awesome and all-holy, and it is full of so great a mystery and a bestower of good things,
that those who receive it with desire and keep it in their hearts are no longer men of earth,
but are raised above all the affairs of this world and are transformed into the order of angels; and as though they were dwelling in the heavens, so they live upon the earth. For that son of thunder,
The beloved of Christ, the pillar of the churches of all the world,
who holds the keys of heaven, who drank the cup of Christ and was baptized with his baptism, who leaned on the breast of the King with great boldness,
he now comes among us to speak, not in the manner

of the performers of the world, adorned in face and covered on the head, who go up onto the place of performance and play with their feet, adorned in golden clothing; rather, this blessed one enters among us clothed in a garment
whose beauty the eyes cannot withstand, for he is clothed with Christ, and his feet are shod with the readiness of the gospel of peace, and he is girded with a belt, not of purple leather
wrought with gold, but woven of truth and bound about his loins with purity.

In this way he comes in to show himself to us, not with duplicity or deceit, for none of these things is in him; but with an open face he tells us the open truth, not so as to be one thing and to appear to us as another in word and appearance and voice,

nor does he need an instrument for the singing of his song, a ten-stringed harp or a two-stringed lyre, but he does everything with his tongue, whose voice is sweeter than any harp or lyre. The place of his song is the whole of heaven, and his theater is the world, and his spectators and hearers are all the angels, and those men who are angels or who desire to become angels. For only such as these are able to hear him well and to carry it out in deed; for his hearer ought to be such a one as carries out those words in deed, but whoever does not carry them out in deed does not know what he is hearing. Rather, they hear as little children hear, not knowing what they are hearing; they are turned toward the delight and luxury of the world, as children are toward play, and though these too hear these words, they are able to understand nothing, since they have enslaved themselves to the making of clay and brick, which is sin.

But before this apostle the heavenly powers stand amazed at the beauty of his soul and the wisdom of his mind and the goodness of his virtues, by which he made himself beloved to Christ and received the grace of the Holy Spirit. For like a well-tuned lyre, golden and adorned with precious stone, sending forth golden sounds, so he prepared his soul and gave it to the Holy Spirit, that the Spirit might speak through him. And therefore it is no longer that fisherman, nor the son of Zebedee, who plays this lyre, but the Holy Spirit, who knows all the depths of the things of God; and therefore we no longer hear anything human from him, but everything he says comes from the mysteries of the Holy Spirit and from the depths of the divine mysteries, which even the angels did not know before this, for they too learned these mysteries together with us through the words of John. And the apostle Paul indicates this when he says: "so that the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the principalities and powers through the church." If principalities and powers and cherubim and seraphim learned all this through the church, it is evident that they too listen with great eagerness to the voice of John.

For this too is no small honor given to us, that the angels have learned together with us what they did not know. And that they learned not only with us but also through us—what more shall I say about this? We who were such that it is not fitting now to say who we were or of what sort, have attained such honor. Therefore let us all lend our hearing in silence, not today only but always, for it is always good to hear these words. For if we are always eager to hear the words of a king—what he said, or what he did, or what he is planning—from which there is no benefit to us, shall we not hasten all the more to hear those words that God speaks, words desirable and longed for and of great benefit to us? For everything that God says, this man, who is his beloved friend, has told us well;

and what is more, he has God himself, the King of all, speaking within him. And what he received from the Father, he gave to this man as a mystery, for he himself says: "You are my friends, for everything that I heard from the Father I have told you." And now, just as, if we saw someone appearing from heaven in the air of the heavens and telling us in detail everything that happens in the heavens, we would all hasten to hear him, so let us do now. For this lofty and great man speaks to us from heaven, as much as he speaks to us, for he is not of this world, as the Lord says: "You are not of this world." Rather, he has that Spirit, the Comforter, speaking within him, who reaches every place, who knows the things of God as the spirit of a man knows his own things.
That Spirit of holiness, the Spirit of truth, the upright Spirit, the chief guide who leads up to heaven, the giver of other eyes, spiritual and clear-sighted,
who shows things to come as though they had already been done, who makes people living in the flesh worthy to see the things of heaven.
Therefore let us keep great stillness; let no one be negligent, let no one be sleepy, let no one among those who come in here be defiled,
but let us lift ourselves up to heaven, for he speaks these words in the heavens to those whose citizenship is in the heavens. But if we remain on earth in our minds,
we will gain no benefit from these words, for the words of John are not addressed to all those who do not wish to come out of a foul life.
For thunder frightens hearts, but his voice disturbs none of the believers,
but rather calms all tumult and disturbance, wherever it reaches; it terrifies only the demons and those who serve them.
Therefore let us listen quietly, so that in this way we may see how he frightens the demons; let us quiet every outward bearing, and still more that of the mind.
For what is the benefit of silence of the mouth when the soul is in tumult and disturbance?
It is this I seek, the quiet of mind and soul, and it is those ears I ask for, for this singer of ours is of such a kind.

Therefore let there be found [?] no desire for riches, or for empty glory, or the tyranny of anger, or evil lusts, or the turmoil of the other passions; for if the ears are not cleansed of all these evil things,
they will not be able to hear these words as they ought, or to understand them in the way that befits these incomprehensible mysteries.
For if no one can learn the cymbal and the lute unless he nails his whole mind to it, how will you be able to listen to these divine mysteries with slackness? For this reason Christ the Lord said:
"Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not cast pearls before swine."
He gave these words the name of pearls, although they are far more precious than pearls;

but he likened them to a pearl because among us nothing is more precious than that thing. For the same reason Scripture often compares the sweetness of God's words to honey. It is not that the likeness of honey is the measure of their sweetness, but that among us nothing is sweeter than honey.
If this is not so, hear what the prophet says, showing the surpassing excellence of these words:

"They are more to be desired than gold and much precious carbuncle, and they are sweeter than honey from the comb." But this is so for those whose minds see clearly. For this reason he also added: "Your servant will keep them," and in another place he said:
"Your words are sweeter to my palate than honey."
And again he says: "More than honey to my mouth," for his mind was sound. Therefore let us too not approach these words weak in soul,

but let us heal our souls and listen in this way. For this is why I have said these many words and have not yet spoken any of the words themselves: so that each of you may drive out every form of weakness and, as those entering heaven, may come in thus, pure of every passion and care.
For if you do not thoroughly cleanse your souls in this way, you will gain nothing from this. And let no one say: "How can I do this thing in an instant?"

What is worse than robbery? Yet see how that robber attained virtue in an instant and was shown to be an inhabitant of paradise. He did not use days, nor even half a day, but the twinkling of an eye. For it is possible to change in an instant and to make oneself gold instead of clay, since this matter rests with our own will: either to change, or to stand fast in evil.

It is written: "If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land." Do you see how the will alone is needed, and earnestness of soul along with the will, and that the will alone is of no profit unless there is earnestness as well? For everyone wishes to ascend to heaven, but the will must be shown by deeds. Merchants, for example, wish to grow rich, yet they do not stop at merely wishing but also act: they prepare a ship, cross seas, borrow gold at interest, travel to a foreign land, and endure many waves. In the same way we too must show our will, for we too are sailing on a sea, one that carries us not from land to land but from earth up to heaven. Therefore let us make our mind a good pilot, give it obedient sailors, and prepare a sturdy ship, so that it may neither be sunk by the cares of the world nor be swept about by the wind of arrogance, but may be secure from being swept away, and light as well.

And if our ship is of this kind, and the pilot and sailors are like this, we shall sail well, and we shall bring to ourselves the Son of God, that true pilot, who will not let our ship sink; but even if myriads of winds should blow, he will rebuke both the winds and the sea and make a great calm. So then, prepare yourselves in this way and come to church tomorrow, and in this way we shall tell you the words of the great John and sow them among you. But do not be a road, nor a rock, nor thorny ground, but be good and fruitful soil, so that we too may zealously sow the seeds, if we see that the ground is clean. But if it is stony and thorny and hard, forgive me, for I cannot labor in vain, since it is foolishness to sow seed in barren ground.

Whoever comes to this table must not sit at the tables of the devil, for what fellowship is there between righteousness and lawlessness? Or will you, who listen to the words of John, and through him of the Holy Spirit, afterward go off again to listen to the words of harlots and to converse with them?

How can you listen with purity to these words, you who wallow in such mire? Behold, I tell all of you in advance: let no one who shares a meal at this table corrupt his soul with evil sins. For you who have been baptized know how many promises you made to us, and not to us, but rather to Christ, when he was baptizing you.
Did you not renounce the devil and all his works?
Therefore there is reason to fear that someone may trample on that promise, and so become deserving of many torments and fall away from those mysteries.

Do you not see that the kings of the earth share their secrets not with offenders but with friends? Now an apostle has come from heaven, from God, to us, and will you instead of him listen to devilish words? How many torments does such a deed deserve? For just as it is not right to sit at the table of the demons, so neither is it right to listen to devilish words, nor to come in filthy garments to this splendid table, filled with myriads of good things, which God himself has laid.

For so great is its power that in an instant it lifts us up to heaven, if only we listen to it with a pure mind. For it is impossible that one who listens in this way to the words of God should remain in the lowliness of this world; rather, he becomes winged and reaches the dwelling place of heaven and attains those treasures of good things, which may we all be worthy to attain by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 2
This saying: "In the beginning was the Word." If John were going to speak to us and relate his own sayings, it would be well for us to speak also of his family, his upbringing, and his homeland.
Since, however, it is not he, but God who speaks to human nature through his mouth, it is now not necessary to speak of this.
And yet, even so, it is not unnecessary; rather, it is very necessary.
For when you learn who he was, and from where, and of what sort, and then hear his voice and see such wisdom,
then you will know well that these words are not his, but belong to that divine power which stirred his soul.
Let us see, then, where he is from. For he is from a very small village and a contemptible land, which produced nothing good,
for the scribes denounced Galilee and said: "See, for no prophet has arisen from Galilee."
And that true Israelite also said: "Can anything good come from Nazareth?"
And this blessed man was from such a land, and of a poor father, a fisherman; they lived on a small lake and mended nets, which is itself also a sign of poverty;
and in this state Christ called him together with his brother. As for education, what need is there even to speak of it?
For great lack of learning accompanies this very craft of fishing; for when would one who was constantly at fishing have learned anything of letters?
And so this fisherman, who lived on lakes and among fish, had come from Bethsaida of Galilee, the son of a poor father.

And he was very poor and wholly uneducated, one who had neither learned letters before nor learned them afterward, once he had followed Christ. Let us see what he says, or about what matters. Does he perhaps say something contemptible, about fishing and the affairs of the world? For these are the words of fishermen. Yet he said not one of these things, nor have we heard anything of the kind from him; rather, we have heard from him heavenly words, which no one anywhere knew before him. For he has now come to tell us such lofty teachings, as if truly from the treasuries of the Holy Spirit, as though he had only now come from heaven; and what is more, not even all those who are in the heavens knew these things, as we said above. Now then, are these the words of a fisherman?
Or did the eloquent rhetors ever say anything of the kind, or the philosophers and sages?

Far from it! For this is not a matter for human nature: to philosophize in this way about that incorruptible and blessed nature, and about the powers standing around it, about immortality and eternal life, about the nature of mortal bodies that are in the end to be made immortal, about torment and the eternal tribunal and the judgments to come, about words and deeds and thoughts, and what man is, or what the world is, or what truly is a man, and what it is for someone to think

that he is a man when he is not, or what wickedness is and what virtue is. For some of these things the philosophers Plato and Pythagoras investigated, and I do not even mention those other philosophers; but since these chiefs of theirs have shown themselves to be such, what would you say about the others?

For these men became laughable and contemptible, like little children: they wished to write down words of teaching, and they set every abomination before them, and about the soul they said... But how shall I tell you of that vanity of theirs, how many blasphemies they uttered?
For they said that the soul of man becomes gnats and flies and thorn bushes, and they blasphemed God. And not only is this laughable in them, but this as well:
that, like those tossed about on the sea, they cannot stand firm on a single statement, but turn now this way and now that because of their erring minds.
But this fisherman is not so; rather, he says everything firmly and, like one established on a rock,
is shaken from no direction, for he became a seer of invisible things and had the King of all speaking within him. And therefore nothing human was with him, but everything was divine.
But they are like a man who has never been admitted before the king, but lives out in the villages, and who wished to speak about the affairs of the palace.
In the same way they went astray, since they wished to speak about invisible things, and so in their error they oppose one another,
and not only one another, but themselves as well.

But this unlearned man, by the grace of the Most High, spoke all truth; for even though the pagans laugh at us ten thousand times for his lack of learning, we are still not ashamed to say that he was unlearned,
and the more his lack of learning is made evident, the more our cause shines forth.
When that barbarian and unlearned man speaks such words
as no one among men has ever understood, and not only speaks them but also persuades all who hear his words, which is a sign of divine grace, who would not marvel at the power dwelling in him?
For this blessed one took possession of the whole world through the Gospel, while in the flesh he dwelt in Asia,
where formerly that pagan school of philosophy was; and while there this blessed one made the demons tremble and dispelled their darkness,
and he overthrew the chiefs of their cities, and in spirit he went to that country where it is fitting that he and those like him should dwell.
For everything of the pagans has been dissolved and has passed away, but everything of his shines;
for since this man and those other fishermen and apostles appeared, from then on everything of Plato and Pythagoras has passed away, and many do not even know their name,

Those who were powerful and rich and practiced sorcery of every kind, who taught people nothing good but every evil. For this reason their memory has dried up and passed away entirely, rightly and fittingly, whereas the words of this man shine and are known among the Egyptians and Indians and Persians and Ethiopians and barbarians, and many other nations have translated his words into their own languages, and through this unlearned man barbarous and foolish people have learned great wisdom.

For this reason I would rightly say that the whole world became a theater for him, because his zeal was not for the adornment of words, but only that he might teach people virtue and true faith and raise them up from earth to heaven.

For this reason he did not hide the power of his words in darkness, as they did; for because their words were evil, they wanted to conceal them by that difficulty of language, but this man's teachings shine more than the sun. For this reason his voice has gone out into all the earth and his words to the ends of the world, because he did not do their devilish deeds, but made his speech so easy that it is understood even by small children, because his words are true and useful for all, and the facts bear witness to them; and he drew the whole world to himself, and by his word he set us free from all evils. For this reason we find death easier than separation from his teachings.

And from all this it is evident that there is nothing human about him, but everything is from God, having come to us through his Holy Spirit; and here there is no vain abundance of words and useless composition, but the invincible power of true faith and a treasury of countless good things.
But the sayings of those vain philosophers are like tombs, adorned outside and full of stench within.

If you take away the composition of the words, you will see there a great stench of deeds and countless abomination, and especially when they speak about the soul, and honor it beyond measure, and then turn around and revile it,
for such is the snare of the devil, that he no longer allows one to stand within measure, but either exalts beyond measure,
or humbles beyond measure those who obey him.
But let us leave the filthiness of their deeds, for even what we have said about them was unnecessary, except that you might recognize that filthiness of theirs,
but now let us begin to speak of these words of ours, which were sent down to us from heaven, and among which there is nothing human. So now come, and let us bring those words into our midst,
concerning which I entreated you before and entreat you now also, that you listen well to what, then, is the beginning of these words of the Evangelist.
Gospel: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."
Commentary: Do you see this boldness and great authority? How he proclaimed the truth neither doubtfully nor hesitantly, but with decisive statement?

For this is the task of a good teacher, that he not be weak and doubtful about his own word. For if one who teaches others himself needs confirmation from another, he is not a teacher but a disciple. And if someone should say:
"Why did he leave aside that first cause and immediately begin to speak about the second cause?"
But let us leave aside talk of first and second, for this matter is not ours, since God is above number and the nature of times.
Therefore let us leave this aside as well; and we confess the Father unbegotten and the Son begotten of the Father.

But if that speaker should say to us: "Yes, it is so, but why did he leave aside the Father and speak about the Son?" we say that it is for this reason: because the Father was known by all, although not as Father but as God, whereas the only-begotten Son was still unknown in the world. And therefore he rightly began, at the very beginning of his discourse, to teach the knowledge of the Son to those untaught people.

And again, understand this too: that he did not keep silent about the Father in these words either. And see this spiritual arrangement: for he saw that people honored God before all else and held him preeminent over all. Therefore he made the beginning of his discourse in this way, and speaks of him beforehand as God. For this reason he designates him "Word": since he was going to teach us that this Word is the only-begotten Son of God, so that no one should imagine a birth involving passion, he therefore removed that evil suspicion beforehand by this name "Word," for he indicated both the birth of the Son from the Father and its freedom from passion.

Do you see that, as I said, he did not keep silent about the Father either in these words spoken about the Son? And if these illustrations are not sufficient to state everything plainly, do not be astonished, for our discourse is about God, of whom no one is able either to speak or to conceive as is fitting. For this reason he too nowhere mentions the name of essence in this way, for it is not even possible to say what the essence of God is; rather, everywhere he shows him to us through his works. For the one whom he here called "Word," you will see a little later how he calls him "Light," and that Light he in turn calls "Life." Yet he did not give him this name for this reason alone, but also for this: since he was going to speak to us about the Father, as he says: "All that I have heard from the Father I have told you."

But he names him Light and Life, the one who has granted us the light of understanding and the life that comes from him. And one name is by no means enough to teach us about God, nor two or three; rather, it is good if through many names we may learn some small thing about him. So he called him Word, in order to indicate that impassible birth. Do you see that I was not speaking idly when I said that this evangelist speaks to us from heaven? Do you see where, at the very beginning, he has lifted up the soul and mind of his hearers? For he lifted it up above all visible things and carried it beyond earth and sea and heaven; he lifted it up above the angels, above the cherubim and seraphim, above the thrones and principalities and powers, and set it above all creation. But when he had lifted it up to such a height, was he perhaps able to bring that ascent to an end there? Far from it! Rather, it is as when someone takes up a man standing on the seashore, who sees cities and groves and harbors, and brings him into the heart of the sea to show him higher things, and leads him out from the stench and raises him up greatly, yet he finds no end to the sights of that sea, but the man's mind sinks into those endless sights.

So too did this evangelist. For he has raised us above all created things and led us toward the ages that are above them, and he has left our sight lifted up and has given us no end to that height, for indeed there is no end. For the mind goes up to "the beginning," and then it seeks what is first, and then it finds that word "was," and wherever this may go, the mind runs ahead of it, and thought can nowhere come to a stop, but it gazes upward and nowhere finds a place to stand; then it grows weary and turns back here. For this word, "In the beginning was," is nothing other than an indication of eternal being. Have you seen the true philosophy and the divine words? For he shows us the true God, before whom there is no one,
for he is the King, the Creator of all, and all come after him, and he alone is before all ages.
Instruction 1: On reverence in church. I wished to say many other words, but lest your mind should grow weary, I therefore wish to teach you some small thing for your benefit and then fall silent,
for I know many who become thus faint-hearted because of the abundance of these divine words; but this happens when the soul is weighed down by the many burdens of the world.
As the eye, when it is clean, sees well and does not quickly grow weak in discerning tiny objects,
but if some illness comes upon the eyes from the head and a blood-like darkness spreads over the pupil, they cannot easily see even bulky bodies,
so it is with the soul: when it is pure and free of passion, it sees well wherever it wishes,
but when it is muddied by many passions and ruins its virtue, then it can no longer look toward even a single lofty matter, but it quickly grows weary and falls,
and it abandons virtue and no longer undertakes it with desire.
But may you not be like this; rather, rouse your minds, so that you may not hear in this way,

as the unbelieving Jews heard from Paul, for he said to them: "The word is long and hard to interpret." It was not that the word itself was so, but that they had become slack in hearing, for the negligent and slack person quickly grows weary, and a little seems much to him, and what is easy seems hard. But may no one here be like that,
but cast aside every worldly care, and so listen attentively to these words.
For when the desire of the passions is in a person, he is no longer able to find the desire for divine words, for one soul is not sufficient to acquire many desires,
but one harms the other and destroys it.
For when a man has one son, all his love is directed toward him; if he then has another as well, his love toward the first weakens and is divided toward the second.

And if, where this is the tyranny of nature and both those beloved ones are his own, it is so even here, what then shall we say of voluntary desires, and especially when those desires are opposed to one another, as spiritual desire and passion are opposed to one another? Do you not know, brothers, that when we come in here, we enter heaven?
I do not speak of places, but of power and mind, for it is possible, while being on earth, to be in the heavens and to experience their good things.

Now therefore let no one bring earthly things into heaven; let no one of those standing here be concerned about worldly matters and his own house, for when you go back there, you ought to speak of the benefit received here, and not to recall here the affairs conducted there.

For this is why we come into this holy place: that we may wash away the stains of sins. If, on the contrary, we remain here within the same defilement, it is better not to come in here at all. So let no one in church be concerned with worldly matters; rather, in the world remember the things of the church. Let this be held in honor above all, for this belongs to the soul and that to the body; and moreover the divine words spoken here are of benefit to both soul and body. Therefore it is fitting that this be our inward occupation and all the rest be external. For this is of benefit both in this life and in the next, whereas the passions are harmful both here and there, for this house is a place of healing, which teaches us not only about the age to come but also about this present life, how we should conduct ourselves, and so that whatever wound comes upon us from outside, we may be healed of it here.

But if we do not listen to the words of the Holy Spirit, not only will we fail to be healed of our wounds, but we will incur others besides. Rather, let us listen eagerly to the word of the Scriptures, which by the grace of God reveals everything to us. And we are able, if we wish, with little labor to know their meaning, so that we may teach others as well; for great is this apostle whose words we are reading, and he speaks of lofty and great matters more than others do. So let us not listen carelessly, for this is why I tell you these things little by little, so that you may be able to learn everything easily and not forget it. Let us fear, then, lest we become liable under that saying which declares: "If I had not come and spoken to them, they would have no sin." For what is the benefit of hearing, if you go away knowing nothing, as though you had not heard?

So give us good ground for sowing, so that we may become diligent in the sowing. Whoever has thorns, let him kindle among them that fire of the Spirit. Whoever has a heart that is hard and resistant, let him enrich it and make it soft by that same fire. Whoever is by the road and is trampled by all the passions, let him enter a more inward place and not be open to plunder by everyone, so that your fields may flourish. And if we strive in this way, then though not in an instant, yet little by little we shall be freed from all the passions. Let us take care, then, that it not be said of us as well: "Their ears are those of a deaf asp." And is not one who does not listen to the words of God worse than wild beasts and cattle? And if a man is one who pleases God, then how does one who does not listen at all to the words about pleasing him differ from the beasts? See then how evil it is that Christ wishes
to change us from men into angels, and we have changed ourselves from men into beasts. For slavery to the belly, being ruled by the love of money, anger and hatred: all this does not belong to man,

but to a beast, and it is even worse than the beasts, for each of them has one passion or another, and that by nature. But when a man destroys his own mind and falls away from the divine way of life, he is caught up no longer in one passion but in all of them. He comes to resemble not one beast, but becomes more wicked than all of them, and he no longer has mercy,

for he entered into evil willingly. Yet in this one matter may nothing of the kind be heard, for we are confident of better things concerning you, and for this reason we warn you all the more, so that we may all reach the summit of the virtues and obtain those eternal good things, which may we all be worthy to obtain by the grace and love for mankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom glory befits the Father together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
Chapter 3
This saying: "In the beginning was the Word." Commentary:
There is no longer any need to speak about listening attentively, for you have fulfilled my teaching in deed,
you who became so eager to gather and hear my words that you even pressed against one another, gathering here and listening well, and did not depart until you had completed that spiritual assembly.
And all this is a sign of the fervor that your souls have.
But for this reason I beseech you to remain in this same zeal and not to slacken, and not only here in the church, but also when you go home:

do not cease, each of you, to speak to your neighbor about what you hear here, and make this good seed grow without ceasing. Come to this holy temple, and do not make the excuse that your affairs leave you no leisure.

For it is a wicked thing if, when you go out to the horse-racing ground, there is no lack of leisure, but when you are to come here, every lack of leisure comes upon you. And how will God not be angered at this?

No, brothers, not so! Rather, hasten to come here yourselves and bring your children as well, for the age of little ones is especially able to receive teachings because of the softness of their nature, just as soft wax takes a seal well; and also for this reason, that their age is the time of becoming settled either in good or in evil.

And if someone is diligent even now to keep them back from evil and lead them into good, virtue will become a nature to them, and they will no longer wish to turn away from good, since habit draws them toward virtue, and they will become more honorable than old men. For it is impossible to hear such an apostle as this and not have the mind enlightened, whether it be a man, or a woman, or a child, who listens to his words and delights in this table. For if men tame wild beasts and teach them whatever they wish,

will they not all the more bring men to virtue by teaching, men who are rational and intelligent and have gentleness by nature? Whereas those have wildness by nature, and moreover those are the arts of men, but these are the words of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, then, gather all of you to this place of healing, and listen to the words of the Holy Spirit, and write them on your minds, so that when the devil sees the law of God written on the soul, he can no longer approach it. For where royal letters are written, not on some perishable material, but on a God-loving soul by the Holy Spirit, there the devil cannot even look, but flees from afar. For nothing is so terrifying to him as a mind that is trained in divine matters and a soul that is always in this training. For no affliction of this world can distress such a person, nor can any good thing make him exult,
but in every stirring of the waves he will find great calm, for all turmoil comes upon us not from the nature of things, but from the weakness of our mind.

For if it came from things themselves, what people would be like this, since we all sail on one sea? But if we wish it, no great wave will come upon us, since some people are able to remain in calm. It is not the sea that causes the drowning, but we drown ourselves willingly. Yet I do not know how I arrived at the wisdom of these words; but forgive me, for I am afraid that your zeal may slacken, and for this reason I have prolonged my teaching. If I had trusted in your fervor, these words would not have been needed.
But now it is time to enter upon what lies before us, and do not grow weary, for today we have a battle before us against the enemies of the truth,
who strive to diminish the glory of the only-begotten Son of God, and rather that of their own selves,
for his glory stands forever, just as it is, and it suffers no harm from their blaspheming tongue,
but the mouths of those who wish to diminish him are filled with abuse,
and they say: "The Son is not co-beginningless with the Father." But you, listen to the word of the Gospel:
Gospel: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."
Commentary: Understand, then, that he first said:
"In the beginning was the Word," in order to indicate the beginninglessness of the Son, and then the second saying:
"and the Word was with God,"
reveals his begetting from the Father. For since this is what is proper to God above all else, beginninglessness and endlessness,
for this reason he said this first, and then, so that no one, hearing the saying:
"In the beginning was," should understand the Son to be unbegotten, he immediately healed the matter and said:
"the Word was with God."
And again, so that when someone hears this "Word," he should not reckon it to be something dispersed into the air, or something conceived in the heart, for this reason he added and said:
"the Word was God," yet not unbegotten, but begotten before the ages, timelessly and without beginning, as the Lord said:
"I am with the Father and the Father is with me," and again he said:
"I have been with you for so long, and do you not know me, Philip? Whoever has seen me has seen my Father," and:
"As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills," and:
"As the Father knows me, I also know the Father.
And I and the Father are one."
And in every place he shows his inseparability from the Father.
And he shows his authority through those words, when he said to the leper: "I will it; be cleansed," and: "I say to you, demon, come out of him," and again:
"You have heard that it was said to those of old, 'Do not kill,' but I say to you: Whoever is angry with his brother without cause is liable to Gehenna,"

and he says and does many such things in order to reveal his own authority, for even a single one of these sayings is enough to reveal his authority, if only one understands those words and is not wholly without understanding.
Instruction 3, on vainglory. But vainglory is an evil thing, and it blinds the mind of those overcome by it even to things that are plain, and those who know what is true and good,
And vainglory does not allow them to confess, for this happened also to the Jews, who denied the Son of God not out of ignorance but for the sake of human glory, for the Evangelist says:
"They believed in him, but they were afraid that they would be cast out of the synagogue," and for this reason they gave their life over to perdition,
for it is impossible that anyone who desired and loved the glory of this world should also find the glory that comes from God.
For this reason the Lord also said: "How can you believe, you who receive glory from men and do not seek the glory of the only-begotten God?"
For this evil passion is a drunkenness, and it nails the soul conquered by it to earth and clay and does not allow it to lift its eyes toward that true light,

but always keeps it buried in the mire and makes it a slave of all, for it is for the sake of men that one puts on beautiful and splendid garments, to display them to men and for no other reason. Now, is there anything worse than this passion? For merely so that others may praise him, a man takes upon himself so many evils.
Do you want to know its power?
The words spoken by Christ are sufficient, but ask, if you wish, one of the citizens who make great expenditures on adornments: "Why do they spend so much gold?"
And they will tell you nothing else but: "To please the people."

And again, if you ask: "And what sort of people is it that praises that deed?" they will tell you nothing else, if they speak the truth, but this: "Foolish men, lovers of this passing age, tossed about in the sea of the world." But the one who is the slave of such people, than whom is he not more pitiable?

Yet as for those who are in the world, although their condition is evil when they are engaged in this business, and very evil, still worse is the condition of those who have withdrawn from this world and are sick with this same disease. For when they incur harm to the soul for the sake of human glory, what could be worse than this?
And some even treat their own faith with contempt for the sake of human glory.

And although the other passions are harmful, they nevertheless hold some desire and pleasure, even if for a short and passing time, for even the lover of money and the drunkard and the fornicator have some harmful taste of enjoyment. But those taken captive by this passion of vainglory live a bitter life, for their wish is never fulfilled, since they want glory from everyone and do not attain it. For this reason that desire is called not glory but vainglory, for that thing is empty in which nothing good is found; its outward form appears good, but its inside is all filth, full of abomination. But from where is this so brutish passion born, in which there is no enjoyment at all?

From where then is it born, if not from a base and world-loving soul and mind? For a soul enslaved to the glory of the world is base and small and wretched, and is unable to understand anything good. For the one who would not undertake a single labor to please God, yet makes every effort to please men, how could he understand what is good and a divine matter,
Or what is the profit, even if people do have it?
Do not, I beg you, do not seek such works of vanity as these, for this passion of pride has turned everything upside down; it has given birth to greed, envy, slanders, and evil schemes.
It stirs people up to fight against the innocent, and the one mastered by this passion no longer knows friendship, nor is any shame found in him,
but he has cast every good thing out of his soul, and he is at war with everyone, unstable and unloving.

And the passion of anger, even though it too is a tyrannical evil, is nevertheless not constant, but arises only when something is found to inflame it; but the passion of vainglory is perpetual, and there is no time

when it would not be found, unless there is a mind to restrain it; rather, it is always present, and it not only makes us sin, but even when we do something good, it snatches that away from us as well.
For if the apostle Paul classes greed as idolatry, then what must its root, its mother and its source, which is vainglory, be?
For no name can even be found worthy of its wickedness. Let us therefore be watchful, beloved, and let us strip off this evil garment and tear it apart,
and cast it away, and let us become clothed with that true nobility, and let us understand the honor which God has given us.

Let us therefore despise this vain glory of the world, for nothing is as blameworthy and vain as this passion, and nothing is so full of contempt; and we can understand this in many ways, if we wish: that the love of worldly glory is a disgrace, while true glory is to despise it, and in every way to serve God and to please him. For he will love us when we please him alone. Or what need have we of many onlookers, since the one who bestows the reward is watching us? Or is it not wicked that slaves of worldly men do everything to please their own masters and show themselves to no one else, even if there are great and glorious men, but are eager for one thing only, to win the favor of their own masters? And we, who have such a Lord, gracious and good, do not strive in this way to please him, but look for others to witness our good deeds, who are able to benefit us in nothing, but rather to harm us.

Do not, I beg you; but let us show our deed to him from whom our reward is given, and let us call on him to praise us and to be the witness of our good deed. Let nothing of ours be for human eyes to look at. For even if we also desire this glory, it will be given to us when we seek only what is from God. For the Lord says: "Those who glorify me I will glorify." And just as when we despise wealth for God's sake, then we become rich, for the Lord says: "Seek the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you," so too with glory: when it is not harmful to us, then God gives it to us. And it is not harmful when it has no mastery over us and does not command us as slaves, but obeys us as masters.

For this is why God does not wish us to desire it: so that it may not master us. And if we set this right, then he will give it to us generously. For who is more illustrious than Paul, who says: "I do not seek glory from men, neither from you nor from others"? Or who is richer than he who has nothing and yet has everything? For, as I said, when these things cannot master us, then they become our slaves. And if we desire glory, let us flee from glory, so that in this way we may be able to fulfill the law of God and attain both glory here and that eternal glory, which may we all be worthy to attain, by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 4

This saying: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." Teachers do not recount a great deal of learning all at once to children newly come to be taught, nor do they lay heavy burdens of learning upon them,
but they teach them little by little and tell them one lesson many times,

so that in this way the lessons may enter well into their minds, and so that they may not be frightened at the very start by the great amount of learning and begin to grow negligent. And I too, for this same reason, wish not to make the burden heavy for you.
And therefore little by little I take up the words of teaching and teach you, and I sow them in your souls.

Therefore I think it right to undertake to speak on these same words, not in order to repeat what I have already said, but in order to complete what we have left unfinished. Come, then, and let us turn our discourse back to the beginning.
Gospel: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."

Commentary: Why is it that all the other evangelists began by speaking of the Lord's incarnation? For Matthew says: "The book of the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ, the son of David," and Luke makes the beginning of his account concern the Baptist and the Mother of God, and Mark too occupies himself with similar words about the incarnation. So why is it that Matthew begins in this way, whereas John said only a little about the incarnation, and that afterward, namely: "The Word became flesh"? And he passed over all the rest, the conception, the birth, the upbringing, and at once began to speak of that beginningless birth?

But what the reason for this is, behold, I will tell you. All the other evangelists composed their account about the incarnation, and there was a fear that some people dull of mind might stop at these words and understand nothing of that divine birth, which is what happened to Paul of Samosata. Therefore he rightly made the beginning of his discourse from that beginningless birth, so as to deliver people from this error,
for Matthew began from King Herod, and Luke from Tiberius Caesar, and Mark from John the Baptist;
but this one left all this behind and ascended above all time and the ages, so as to lead people's minds up there, to that "In the beginning," and he nowhere allowed them to stop.
Nor did he set a boundary, as Matthew did: Herod and Tiberius and John;
But neither did this one, when he began to speak of his ineffable birth, pass over in complete silence the matters of the incarnation.

Nor did these, when they began to speak of the incarnation, pass over in complete silence that beginningless birth. For one Spirit was the giver of their speech; therefore Matthew, Mark and Luke, and this blessed one as well, displayed great unity.
But you, beloved, when you hear "Word," no longer listen to those who say that he is created, nor to those
who call him simply a word in this way; for many are the words of God, which even the angels carry out,
but not one of those words is God, for all of them are prophecies and commands. For this is the custom of Scripture: it is accustomed to speak thus of the laws and commands of God, as it is written:
"Mighty in strength, who do his words." But this Word is a personal, hypostatic being, come forth from the Father himself without suffering.
For, as I said above, he signifies this by the term "Word," and just as the saying:
"In the beginning was the Word" shows the beginningless one, so also the saying "The Word was with God" signifies co-existence and shared beginninglessness.

And lest perhaps, when you hear "In the beginning was the Word," even though you understand the Son to be beginningless, you should say, "The Father is older by some amount of time, by a longer age," and in this way assign a beginning to the Only-begotten.
Therefore he added and said: "The Word was in the beginning with God"; thus he is beginningless just as the Father is,
for the Father has never existed without this beginningless Word, but God was always with God, in distinct person.
But if anyone should say: "And how does he say, 'He was in the world, and the world was made through him'?"
How was he in the world, if he was with God? But understand that he was both with God and in the world. For neither the Father nor the Son is ever circumscribed in one place,
for "just as there is no end of his glory and no number of his understanding," so also there is no temporal beginning of his essence.

You have heard that "In the beginning God made heaven and earth." What do you understand as prior to this beginning? Do you not understand this, that they were made before all visible things? So also, when you hear concerning the Only-begotten that:
"In the beginning he was," understand this, that he is before all ages and all things invisible and visible.

But if again anyone should say this: "And how is it possible that he should be Son and yet not be younger than the Father? For whatever is from someone, it is evident that it is later than the one from whom it is."

What then shall we say about this? Only this we say: that all these are the ways of human affairs. And whoever seeks this, let him seek also what is worse than this; and these words ought not even to be received by the ear. For our discourse now concerns God, and not the affairs of human nature, except for the reassurance of the weak. Therefore let us say: "Tell me, does the radiance of the sun come forth from the sun, or from somewhere else?" And of the radiance that comes forth from the sun we do not say that it is later and not equal to the sun itself in its origin, for it is not even possible that the sun should ever have existed anywhere without radiance. But if it is so with these visible bodies, and that which [comes forth] is not inferior to that from which it is, why do you disbelieve if that invisible and ineffable nature is so, as befitted its essence?

For this reason Paul also called him thus, in order to show both his being from him and his co-beginninglessness. And what did he say? "Were not all the ages made by him, and all times?" For this is known to all, unless someone is entirely bereft of understanding; and since all the ages and times were made by him, it is evident that there was no time
by which the Son would be later than the Father; for since all times were made by the Son, where then was that time to be found which was before him?

Far from it! But since there is no time by which the Son would be later than the Father, it is evident that he is co-beginningless with the Father. And "first" and "last" — these words indicate times, and apart from ages and times no one can use these words; but the Son is above times and ages. And since this is so, there is no laterness anywhere.

But if you speak of a beginning of the Son, you have surely spoken of one for the Father as well, for the Lord says: "Whoever does not honor the Son, neither does he honor the Father." For every person who investigates such matters does not attain the truth but goes astray, for human minds are easily led into error. But let us say this to our opponents: "What is that saying of the prophet, who said:
'Before me there was no other God, and after me there shall be none'?"

For if the Son is later than the Father, how does he say, "After me there shall be none"? Shall we then utterly despise the essence of the Only-begotten? For either dare to say this, or believe in the Godhead — Father, Son and Holy Spirit, equal, beginningless — a Trinity in one Godhead. Or how has it been said that "All things were made through him," if the Son is later than the Father? For if time and age had existed anywhere before him, how could that which existed before him have been made through him? Do you see to what audacity the audacity of those who say such things leads?

For why did the evangelist not say that he was made from nothing, as Paul says concerning created things: "who calls the things that are not as things that are," but instead said, "From the beginning he was"? For this is the opposite of that — and rightly so!

For God is neither created, nor does he have anything older than himself; rather, these are the words of the pagans. But tell me this as well: is not the Creator incomparably higher than created things? Indeed, you cannot say that he is not far higher than them and incomparable with them. But if he has a beginning as they do, where is his incomparability and his superiority over created things? Or what is the saying: "I am the first and I am the last.
And before me there has been no other God"?
For if the Son is not without beginning, then surely he does not have the nature of the Father, for the Father is without beginning.
And if he does not have the nature of the Father, then surely he is another God.
If he is not without beginning together with the Father, how did he say:
"His life is without limit"?

For if he has a beginning, even though his life is unending, it is still not without limit, for what is without limit must be without limit in both directions, as Paul the apostle says: "Having neither beginning of days nor end of life," by which he signified his beginninglessness and his endlessness. For just as he has no end, so also he has no beginning.
And there is neither an end here nor a beginning there. Or how was there a time when he who is eternal life did not exist?
For life must be such that it exists always, without beginning and without end. It must be so, just as indeed it is.
But if there was once a time when he did not exist, how is he the life of all, when he himself once did not exist?

But the speakers of vanity say: And how did John say, "In the beginning he was," and did not say, "He was without beginning"? O vain and worthless one, you heard "beginning," and did you not hear this:

"The Word was in the beginning; he was always, and never [?], and there has never been a time when he was not"? Or when the prophet says of the Father, "From age to age you are," what did he say: is he perhaps assigning him a limit? Far from it!
Rather, he was signifying beginninglessness and endlessness. So understand this in the same way as well: he does not set a limit to him, nor did he say:
"He had a beginning," but "In the beginning he was," so that by this word "was" you might understand his beginninglessness, for he says: "The Word was with God, and the Word was God."

And so that no one might think that the divinity of the Son is inferior, for this reason he added and spoke of those works by which the perfection of his divinity is made known: that this one was in the beginning with God, so that you might know his beginninglessness, that the Father has never been without the Son,
but in the beginning he was God, the Son with God the Father. And then he went on to proclaim his creatorship,

saying: "All things were made through him, and without him not one thing was made of all that was made," which is indicative of his true divinity, just as the Father too, through the prophets, always points to this as a sign of his own divinity.
And the prophets always proclaim this in opposition to the idols: "The gods who did not make heaven and earth shall perish," and again he says: "With my hand I stretched out the heaven."
And since it is indicative of divinity, for this reason he brings forward creatorship in every place.

But the evangelist was not content with this alone; he also designates him as Life and Light. If he was always with the Father, and has created all things and holds them, and he enlightens all, who could be so darkened and wretched as to say that he is lesser than the Father and later than him? Do not mix created things with the Creator, so that we too may not hear it said: "They served the creature and not the Creator."

Instruction 4. We ought always to give thanks to the Lord. Concerning wrath [?]. Let us never cast ourselves into such a curse as this, for it was for this reason that the Son of God came to us, to redeem us from this curse. For this reason he put on the form of a slave, to set us free from this slavery; for this reason he endured spitting and blows to the face and a death of dishonor. Let us not, then, make all of that void [?], nor turn back to our former lawlessness, for this is worse and more dreadful than anything, and more evil even than idolatry, when we lower the Creator of all to the level of created things, as far as we are able. For he is not harmed [?] by our reasoning, as it is written: "You yourself are the same, and your years will not fail." But by such actions we make ourselves partners of the devil.

Rather, let us glorify him as we have learned from the fathers; let us glorify him both by faith and by deeds. For if our deeds are evil, there is no benefit from faith. Therefore let us order ourselves according to the will of God, and let us be far from all filth and injustice and greed, as strangers and pilgrims and passers-through of this world. If anyone has possessions and great riches, let him use them as a pilgrim would, who after a short time must part from them all, whether he wishes to or not.

And if evil comes upon anyone from another person, let him not be implacably angered. For the apostle has not granted us even a single day for being angry, as he says: "Let the sun not go dark upon your anger." For it is a great thing if even in that one hour in which we become angry we do no evil; but if night also finds us in wrath, that evil grows all the more,
for just as fire flares up all the more, when at leisure we begin to practice evil.

And for this reason he commands that we quench that fire before it flares up. For the passion of wrath is fierce, and sharper than new [?]. Therefore we need great earnestness to quench it, and not to allow its flame to rise to the height of heaven.

For this disease becomes the cause of many evils: it has overturned many houses from their foundations, and has made kinsmen and friends murderers of one another, and has wrought immeasurable evils in short spaces of time.
Let us not, then, brothers, leave this beast unbridled, but let us discipline it with muzzle and bridle, which is the fear of the eternal judgment.
When a friend distresses you, or one of your servants angers you, remember your sins, which you have committed against God,

And understand that by gentleness toward him you will please your God as well and lighten your debts, for it is written: "Forgive, and you will be forgiven." And then consider further: if at some time you have resisted this passion and have overcome it,

and again, if at some time you have been overcome by it, call both of those times to mind, and in this way you will find great benefit. And consider when you have been pleased with yourself: when you were overcome, or when you overcame that passion.
Do we not blame ourselves for growing angry, and are we not ashamed, and does our own mind not reprove us without any reproof from others, and do we not deeply regret it? But when we overcome wrath,
then we are joyful and glad. Yet victory at such a time does not consist in insulting in return for insult and striking in return for a blow,
for this is not victory but a wretched defeat. Rather, victory is when we patiently pass through such things and endure both insult and blows,
for this is what insult [?] is: not doing evil, but enduring evil.

Therefore do not say: "I too will insult in return for insult and take revenge, so that this person may not be able to despise me." For you are not contemptible when you endure, but when you pay back in kind.
And if anyone despises you at the very time when you endure, do not look at him, but understand
that he is foolish; and do not seek to please the foolish, but strive to please the wise and prudent.

Or why do you give occasion [?] to these small and lowly people? But it is not of the evil time [?] that one should praise you for patience. And whom God praises, what need does he have of human praise?
For human praise often becomes harmful and has no benefit at all,
but praise from God is desirable and far from all harm, and it gives great benefit to the one praised, if we seek it earnestly.
Do you wish to know how evil anger is? Go out into the streets, find men fighting one another, and observe them.
For within yourself you cannot properly observe that ugliness while your mind is darkened and drunken. But when it is pure of the passion,

Then understand your own case from another's: look at the crowds standing around there and at those in their midst who are behaving so indecently. When anger boils up in your breast, fire burns in the face and eyes, the face is swollen, the hands flail about in disorder, and the feet are thrown here and there disgracefully. Such a person is in no way different from one possessed by a demon, or from wild asses that bite and kick with their feet. Truly an angry man is an indecent sight. Then, after those many evils, when they go away by themselves and come to their senses, still greater pain and great shame come upon them, as they remember those who stood there and saw their indecency. They are ashamed before everyone, both friends and enemies: before friends as those who reproach such conduct, and before enemies as those who rejoice at their misfortune. And if they have also inflicted wounds on one another, the shame and disgrace are all the greater, since fear of death also arises from those wounds. They curse the whole affair that caused their trouble and blame the demons. The more foolish even make an evil hour the cause. But it does not come from an evil hour, for no hour anywhere is evil. Nor does it come from the devil, but from their own mind.

For they bring the demons upon themselves. And if you say, "What am I to do, since the heart burns when another insults me?", it is for this very reason that I too marvel at those who overcome this evil beast. If only we are willing, we are able to overcome it. Why do we not become angry when those in authority harm us? Because fear restrains it. Or when we insult our slaves, how is it that they bear everything in silence?

Because they too have that bond of fear. But will you not fear God and consider his wrath? Is it not shameful if we endure countless hardships for the sake of men, yet for the fear of God we show not a single act of reverence? And what mercy shall we find from God? Brothers, may God not be more despised in our eyes than men! Or did this saying seem astonishing to you, and did you shudder? But I do not want you to be frightened by a word, but by deeds, so that when you are struck on the cheek, you not only bear it patiently but also turn the other side. This is God's commandment. But we not only fail to turn the other side, we even retaliate for the blow, and it seems a disgrace to us if we do not act so. And the evil is this: when we have been defeated, we think that we have won.
And when we have been thrown down by the devil, and countless wounds come upon us from the devil, we think that we are strong.
Therefore I implore you, let us learn the form of true victory and practice it: for patient endurance of evil is what wins the crown.

And if we wish to be crowned by God, let us keep the law he has laid down and bear everything with long-suffering, so that we may attain those eternal good things by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
Chapter 5
This saying: "All things were made through him."
1:3. Commentary: When the prophet Moses began to speak about creation, he began by speaking of visible things and enumerated them at great length, for he says:
"In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth," and then he says:
"There was light," and the second heaven, and the natures of the stars, and the kinds of each of the living creatures, and everything else, so that I need not speak of them one by one.

But the Evangelist spoke of all this briefly, in a single phrase, and he did well in this, for the things mentioned earlier were known to all, and because he intended to speak of higher matters, not of created things but of the Creator of all. And for this reason that other one made his whole discourse about visible things,
for he has said nothing about the heavenly powers. But since this one was ascending to the Creator himself,
he therefore rightly passed over all of that and made everything known in a single phrase, when he said: Gospel: All things came to be through him (1:3).
Commentary: And so that you may not suppose that he speaks only of what Moses also has spoken of, he therefore added and said:
"Without him not one thing came to be of all that came to be." That is to say, of created things, whether invisible or visible,
all came to be through him and nothing has come into being anywhere without the Son, for here the sentence must be divided at this phrase: "of all that came to be,"
so that we no longer join it to the phrase that follows it,
but here make the end of the sentence and then begin again:
Gospel: With him was life.

Commentary: And this saying means the following: Without him nothing has been made of all the created things that came to be. Do you see how with this one phrase he indicated everything, for he said: "Without him not one thing came to be of all that came to be."
By this he indicated all things visible and invisible, but he set the Holy Spirit apart when he said: "Without him not one thing came to be," so that no one might say:
"If not one thing came to be without him, then surely the Holy Spirit too has been made by him."
For this reason he added: "of all that came to be," as if to say: "I am speaking of created things: not one thing came to be without him of all that came to be."
But the Holy Spirit is not among the things made,
but is creator just as the Son is, and through him all things came to be,
as many as came to be, whether invisible and incorporeal or dwelling in the heavens.
Do you see this good and unerring teaching? For he spoke of the created things of which Moses had spoken, and then he mentioned the invisible things as well,
but he set the Holy Spirit apart from them all.
In the same way Paul, filled with this grace, said:

"Through him all things came to be," and so that no one could join the Holy Spirit with all those things, he therefore added: "whether thrones or dominions, whether principalities and authorities." For all this signifies this same saying: "All things came to be through him and without him not one thing came to be of all that came to be."
But so that no one may say about this saying, "All things came to be through him," that:

"He speaks of miracles and not of the work of creation," for the other evangelists spoke of miracles. He added further below and said: "He was in the world, and the world was made through him." But now, in this place, having said something about the work of creation, namely: "All things were made through him, and without him not one thing was made of all that was made," he immediately added: "In him was life," so that no one might become unbelieving and say: "How were all these things made through him?" For this reason he said: "In him was life."

For just as, however much you draw up out of an abyss, you take nothing away from that abyss, so too with the creative work of the Only-begotten: however much you believe to have been created by him, and [?], that:
"without him not one thing was made," so that I may take a closer image, the one that he too used. For this reason I will speak of light, of which he too spoke, saying: "It was light."
So then, just as, however many myriads a light has illumined, nothing is taken away from its brightness,
so too God, both before creation and after creation, is one and undiminished, and nothing is lacking to him, nor does anything go out from his fullness, nor does he grow weak in making and creating.

Rather, even if he should wish to create myriads of other heavens and earths such as these are, his power is sufficient to create all of this, and over all of this he remains undiminished. And his power is sufficient not only to create all this,
but also to hold it and keep it unharmed, for this name of "life" that stands here signifies not only creation but also that providential ordering
by which it subsists. It also sets before us the teaching of the resurrection, and it begins these wonderful good tidings:
for when life came to us, the power of death was undone, and since light has shone forth,
there is darkness no longer, but life abides always among us, and death is not able to overcome it.
And for this reason, what is said of the Father is truly said of the Son as well, that "through him we live and move and abide," as Paul the apostle also says:
"Through him all things were created, and all things subsist through him." For this reason he is also called root and foundation.

But when you hear: "In him was life," do not understand this as of something joined together from two things, for further below he says of the Father as well: "As the Father has life in himself, so too he has given to the Son to have life."
But just as you do not say of the Father on the basis of these words: "He is twofold," so do not say it of the Son either, for in another place it is written:
"God is light," and again it says: "He dwells in unapproachable light."
All this has been said, however, not so that we should understand mixture and twofoldness concerning him, but so that little by little we may advance to that height of theology.

For since no one could so easily understand how his life is in essence, he therefore first spoke that lowly word and afterward leads up to the height. For the one who said, "He gave to him to have life," also says again, "I am the life," and, "I am the light." And what kind of light is it? For it is not visible in this way, but is an invisible illuminator of the soul.

And since Christ was going to say, "No one comes to me unless the Father brings him to me," the Evangelist therefore said here beforehand that he is the light that illuminates, so that if you hear some such thing about the Father as well, you should not say, "This belongs only to the Father," but that it belongs also to the Son. For he says, "All that the Father has is mine." So he first taught us about his being Creator, and then he also speaks of those spiritual good things that he granted us by his coming; and the Evangelist indicated this in a single phrase and said:
Gospel: That life was the light of men.

Commentary: He did not say "the light of the Jews," but "of all men," for the Gentiles too came to this understanding, and this light is common to all and shared by all. But why did he not speak of angels as well and say, "That life was the light of angels and men," but spoke only of men? For this reason: because his discourse now concerns this nature, and it was to these that he came to announce good tidings.
Gospel: And that light shines in the darkness. 1:5.

Commentary: He calls both death and error "darkness" [? the text reads "light"]. For this visible light does not shine in darkness, but shines apart from darkness, and when darkness comes, it too is darkened. But the preaching of Christ shone forth in the midst of the darkness of error and dispelled it. And when he came to death, he dispelled that too, and overcame it so completely that he brought up even those who were held captive in it. And since neither death nor error could overcome him, but he shines in every place by his own power, he therefore says, "The darkness did not overtake it." For it is invincible, and it does not take up its dwelling in souls that do not wish to be enlightened.

Teaching 5, that sin is darkness, and on the eternal judgment. But if he has not enlightened everyone, do not be surprised at this, for he enlightens no one by force; rather, God desires our enlightenment by our own will. Therefore do not shut the doors against this light, and it will enter into you, for the light comes through faith, and when it has come forth from there, it brilliantly illumines those who receive it. And if you show it a good life, then it will remain with you forever. For the Lord says: "Whoever loves me will keep my commandments, and I and the Father will come and make our dwelling with him." So just as you cannot see the brightness of the sun unless you open your eyes, so too it is impossible to see this light without opening the eyes of the soul. How, then, are they opened? Only by the cleansing of the soul from the filth of the passions, for sin is darkness, and a deep darkness. This is evident from its being done secretly and obscurely, for "everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light," and "it is evil to speak of things done in secret."

And just as in the dark no one can recognize either enemy or friend, but is ignorant of everyone, so it is also when one commits sin. For the greedy man sees neither friend nor enemy, and the envious man sees even his own people as enemies, and the doer of every sin differs in no way from drunkards or madmen. And just as in the dark we perceive wood and lead and iron and gold and silver and precious stone all as one, when the light that distinguishes them is absent, so too the one whose life is defiled does not know the light of virginity, nor the beauty of wisdom.
And as I said, in the dark, even if there are precious stones, they do not appear, not because their nature is such, but because those who look at them cannot perceive them.
And this is not the only evil that befalls those who are in sins, but also this: that they are always in fear, and,
just as some who walk in pitch darkness are afraid even if there is no one to frighten them, so too the doers of sin cannot be without fear,
but they are afraid of everyone and tremble, and they suspect everyone, for their own nature reproves them, and therefore fear surrounds them on every side.
Let us therefore flee from such an evil life, brothers, for after this evil life comes death, a deathless death, if we remain like this.
For there is no end to those future torments, and even in this life those who pursue vain things differ in no way from madmen,
for they gather perishable wealth and take their pleasure in harmful pleasures, and they do not recognize that madness until they have departed from it.
Therefore it is necessary to be awake and alert, as the apostle Paul commands, for:

Whoever is wakeful and watchful, even if he is seized by sin, still does not fall completely, but the one who is asleep and maddened does not perceive how he has been seized by it. Therefore let us not sleep,
for this time is not of the night but of the day, and "let us walk decently, as in the daytime."

For nothing is more shameful than sin; understand this not only of spiritual shame but of bodily shame as well. When people caught in some sin are led to judgment before the rulers, how shameful and disgraced they are! They swear falsely and lie, and they are shameful. Yet we are ashamed to put on a garment the wrong way round, and if we see someone else dressed like this, we despise him as a fool, but we feel no shame at living in sin. Tell me, then: what is more loathsome than a fornicating man and going in to a woman, or what is more blameworthy than an envious person and an evil-speaker? And what is this, that we consider going about naked more shameful than such deeds? For no one ever goes naked willingly.
Nothing that happens unwillingly is so shameful. But every person who commits sin does so willingly, and that is worse and more loathsome.

And if someone were to enter the assembly of the angels, then he would understand the loathsomeness of sin. But why do I speak of the assembly of the angels? For even in royal palaces, if someone brings in a harlot, or gets drunk with wine, or does anything of the kind, or does some such evil, he is sentenced to the ultimate penalty. And if such a thing is loathsome in royal palaces, what will it be before the King of all? Shall we not be sentenced to the ultimate penalty if we dare anything of this kind? Therefore I beseech you, let us show purity in our life, for we have a King who sees everything, and nothing is hidden from him.
