Let us then draw his light upon us, so that he may enlighten us forever, and that we may attain those eternal good things by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong glory and might, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
Chapter 6
The text: "There was a man sent from God, whose name was John."
Commentary: At the beginning of the discourse he spoke about the Word of God briefly and powerfully, and now, proceeding in due order, he has come also to the herald of the Word, his namesake John.
But when you hear that he "was sent from God," do not take anything he said to be merely human, for he says nothing of his own, but everything is from the one who sent him.
Gospel: "He came as a witness, to bear witness about the light."
Commentary: Perhaps someone will say: "What is this? Does a servant bear witness to the King?"

But when you see him not only receiving witness from a servant, but also coming to that servant and being baptized by him like other people, will you not be even more amazed? Yet do not be troubled at this; rather, marvel at his unfathomable goodness. If anyone is still troubled at this, let him say to that person too what he said to John: "Permit it now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness." And if someone is troubled even more, let him say to that person too what he said to the Jews: "I do not receive testimony from men." For it was not that he needed John's testimony and that John was sent by God for this reason; that would be wicked blasphemy.
And if someone says: "Then how does the evangelist say, 'so that all might believe through him'?"

And the Lord himself says: "There is another who testifies concerning me, and I know that his testimony is true." And he was referring to John. But understand this saying, for at one time the Lord said: "I do not accept testimony from men"; and again at another time he said: "There is another who testifies concerning me." And so that the unintelligent might not say:
"He contradicts his own words," he therefore immediately healed that doubt, for he said: "I say this for your sake, so that you may be saved," as if he were saying:
"Since I am God and the Son of God, and consubstantial with that incorruptible nature,
I need testimony from no one; even if no one testifies concerning me, my essence will lack nothing.
But since I seek the salvation of many, for this reason I have come down to this humility, even to the point of entrusting testimony concerning me to men."
For all this was done because of the weakness of the Jews [?] and their wretchedness, so that they might easily believe; but even so they did not believe.

For just as he clothed himself in flesh, so that all might not perish from the power of his divinity, so also he sent a man as a witness to him, so that those men might listen more easily to a voice of their own. Otherwise,
what need had he of that man's testimony? For it would have been enough for him to reveal the power of his divinity,

and all would have been terrified. But he did not do this, as I said, so that all those who could not look upon that light of his, which eyes cannot withstand, might not perish. And for this reason he both clothed himself in flesh and entrusted the testimony concerning himself to one of his servants,
for he sought in every way the salvation of men and did not look to his own honor, but to the means by which he might be more fully accepted by men and might benefit them, as he himself also said:
"I say this for your sake, so that you may be saved."
And when the evangelist said, "He came to testify concerning the light," he immediately added and said: "so that all might believe through him." As if he were saying:

"Do not suppose that John came for this reason, to add anything to the King, but so that men might believe the more, since they were unable to see his divinity." And for this reason, to dispel this suspicion as well, he added and said:
Gospel: "He himself was not the light"

Commentary: But if he were not saying these words to dispel this suspicion, why was it necessary to say this in this place? For since he said, "He was sent to bear witness to the light," why does he then say, "He himself was not the light"? Yet he did not say these words in vain. Rather, since among us the one who testifies is reckoned greater and more trustworthy than the one to whom he testifies, he wished that no one should imagine the same about John. Therefore he guards against this from the very beginning, wipes away this evil suspicion, and tears it out by the root. He shows who the witness is and who it is that is witnessed to, what kind of difference there is between the witness and the one witnessed to, and how the one witnessed to is superior to the witness. And since he has done this and has shown that incomparable superiority of his, from then on he begins to speak without fear; having torn out every word that the foolish might find doubtful, he thus began the word of teaching without hindrance.

Moral Teaching 6: That orthodoxy is of no profit if our deeds are evil. Let us therefore pray to God that, together with understanding of the divine words and right faith, we may also have good deeds and a holy and radiant way of life. For if we do not have good deeds, there is no profit from these things. Even if we have faith and understanding of all the Scriptures, yet are bereft of good deeds, nothing can keep us from going into the fire of Gehenna, to torment in the unquenchable furnace. And just as those who do good will rise to the resurrection of life, so those who do evil will rise to the resurrection of judgment, for endless torment. For all these reasons, then, let us strive not to lose and make void the profit that we have gained through right faith; and not through evil deeds, but through good deeds, let us strive to become worthy of seeing Christ, for nothing is like this blessedness. May we all, then, be worthy to attain good deeds, so that we may do everything to the glory of God, to whom be glory, with the only-begotten Son and the all-holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
Chapter 7
This saying:
"The true light was, which enlightens every person coming into the world."
Commentary: For this reason, O spiritual children, we set the delight of the holy Scriptures before you little by little, and do not tell you everything at once,
so that you may be able to keep what has been said well and easily. For whoever is building a wall, and lays another stone on top before he has made the first one firm,
builds a useless wall. But whoever secures the stones laid first and only then lays another makes the building firm and unshakable by laying it slowly and well.
So let us too imitate such builders and build up your souls in this way, for we are afraid
that while what was built first is not yet firm, we may bring another depth of words upon it, and the mind may be unable to bear it all. What, then, is this that we read today?
Gospel: "The true light was, which enlightens every person coming into the world."

Interpretation: For since he had earlier said concerning John that "He came to bear witness to the light," and that "now he was sent," lest anyone hearing this should say, because of the recentness of the witness, that "the one witnessed to is likewise [recent]," for this reason he raised his discourse above all times, to his existence, which has no end anywhere, nor beginning. Yet in spite of all this those who fight against the Godhead say: "How is it possible for a Son to be without beginning?" O wretched one, I speak to you about God, and you say, "How can this be?" and you neither fear nor tremble. And if someone should ask you, "How will the life of these our bodies be endless and incorruptible in that age?" or, "How are souls immortal?" you rebuke him as a fool, because he has taken up a matter that is not possible for the human mind, and in which only belief is required and not investigation.

And if we say of the Creator of soul and body, "He is without beginning," is the manner of that matter demanded of us? And who would say that this is not the act of a deranged mind? You have heard: "He was the true light."
Why then do you struggle in vain to ascend in your mind above that boundless life, which is impossible to attain?

Why do you seek the unsearchable? Why do you pursue the incomprehensible? Why do you investigate what cannot be investigated? Examine the source of the light of the sun: you cannot, and yet you are not troubled, nor do you chafe at that inability.

How then have you become so bold beyond these things, and so daring [?] about incomprehensible and unsearchable matters? When John, the son of thunder, who has the spiritual trumpet, heard from the Holy Spirit that "He was the true light,"
he sought nothing further; but you, who from the grace that he had,
are farther off than the earth is from heaven, wish to ascend above his measure. For this reason you fall altogether and cannot understand even a little.
For such is the devil's device. He leads a person out of the boundary set by God,

whoever submits to him, and urges him on toward what is higher; and then, when he has deceived him by such a hope and estranged him from the grace of God, from then on not only does he not lift him up to some higher good (for how could the devil do this!)
but he does not even allow us to return to those former things, where we were living without error, but turns us hither and thither, led astray, having no place anywhere to stand.
So he also did to Adam, when he was in paradise,
for he deceived him with the hope of greater honor and understanding, and separated him even from what he had,
for not only did he fail to become equal to God, as the devil promised him, but he was also given over to the tyranny of death; and not only did he not find greater understanding,
but what he had, that too he lost by seeking more, for shame and the disgrace of nakedness then came upon him.
Before this he had been free of such shame. And these countless passions sprang up from that time on; may they not come upon us!
Let us obey the Lord and abide as he commanded us, and let us seek nothing more,
so that we may not fall away even from these good things that have been given to us, as happened to those
who sought a beginning for that Life which has no beginning, and lost everything, and
did not attain what they were seeking, since it is impossible, and fell away from orthodoxy.
But let us not alter those eternal boundaries which our holy fathers set,
but let us obey the spiritual law, and when we hear that "He was the true Light," let us seek nothing further, for it is not even possible to ascend higher than this word.

For if his birth had been like that of a man, there would have been some separation between the begetter and the begotten; but since he begot him ineffably and as befits God, it is so [that there is none].

Leave aside "earlier" and "later," for these are names belonging to time, whereas the Son is the creator of all the ages. Again that speaker of evil says: "And if it is as you say, then surely he is not a Father, but the Son is the Father's equal, a brother."

You who have been blinded by the darkness of folly, why do you say this? For if we were saying that "the Father and the Son have both alike sprung up from some other root," then your argument would have a place. But since we flee from this lawlessness and say that "the Father is without beginning and unbegotten, and the Son likewise is without beginning, begotten of the Father," for what reason do you still speak this lawless word?

For he is the radiance, and by nature a radiance is understood together with that to which the radiance belongs. It is for this reason that Paul gave him this name, so that you might not imagine any separation between the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. This is what this word signifies; and the phrase that follows refutes the argument of the lawless. Do not imagine, because you have heard "radiance," that he is lacking in his own hypostasis, for this is lawlessness and a doctrine of the heresy of the followers of Sabellius and Marcellus. We do not speak so; rather, with his own distinct hypostasis he is united by nature. For this reason, having said "the radiance of glory," he immediately added: "and the image of his power." For he showed the individuality of the hypostasis and the unity of nature with him whose image he is. For it is not possible, as I have said, to set forth the divine faith with a single word; rather, one must be content if we gather many words and select from each what is fitting, and so are able to attain a worthy glorification of God.
But I say "worthy" according to our capacity, for if anyone supposes that he is truly singing praise to God as God deserves, he is in error.

Homily 7. That we should not scrutinize the words of the faith, but should believe the words of the holy Scriptures without inquiry. But now, we who know all this, let us remain firm in the faith that was handed down to us from the beginning by those who were eyewitnesses and servants of the word, and let us not inquire into anything beyond it. For two evils come upon those who are sick with this disease: first, that they do not find what they seek but labor in vain; and second, that they anger God, because they seek to undo the law he has laid down. And how great a wrath this matter arouses there is no need for us to say, for you yourselves know.

Therefore I beg you, let us tremble at his words, so that he may thus protect us without ceasing, for he says: "To whom shall I look, but to the humble and quiet, and those who tremble at my words?" Let us abandon all inquiry and break our hearts; let us mourn for our sins, as Christ commanded us. Let us call to mind all our sins and hasten to blot them out, for God has given us many ways for this purpose.

As he says: "Tell your sins first, that you may be justified." And again he says: "I will tell you my lawlessness, and you forgave all the ungodliness of my heart." For the confession and remembrance of our sins helps us not a little to blot them out. And there is yet another remedy for blotting them out: that we hold no grudge against anyone who has sinned against us, but forgive. Do you wish me to tell you a third as well? Hear the prophet Daniel, what he says: "Blot out your sins by almsgiving, and your iniquities by mercy to the poor." And there is yet another way of blotting them out: abundance of prayer and tireless supplication to God give us the consolation of forgiveness; and fasting, when it is accompanied by mercy toward others, quenches the blaze of God's wrath,
"for water quenches a blazing fire, and by almsgiving sins are cleansed." Let us therefore walk in all these ways,
for if we make our journey in them, we will not only wash away our past sins,

but we will also fence ourselves against those to come, and will give the devil no room to fight against us and to cast us into that wicked and vain inquiry. For this too comes about when a person has no work of virtue to do but is idle. But let us strive to please God, so that we may labor for this short time and afterward delight forever in the good things of heaven, by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 8
This saying: "There was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into the world" (1:9). Interpretation:
Nothing prevents us from undertaking today as well the inquiry into the same words, since earlier we were not able to deal thoroughly with all those words.
Where, then, are those who say of him: "He is not true God, for here he is called true light, while in another place he is also called truth itself and life itself"? But that matter,
when we have reached its proper place, then we will examine it.
For now, however, it is good to say this to your love: if he enlightens every man coming into the world, how have so many remained unenlightened?

For not all have known the faith of Christ, so how then does he enlighten every man? But understand that he enlightens everyone, as far as it depends on him; he strives in every way to enlighten, and he would enlighten all.
If some, by their own will, have blinded the eyes of their mind and have not wished to receive the radiance of that light,
their darkening does not come from that light, but from their own wickedness, they who by their own will have deprived themselves of that gift.
For that grace has been poured out over all, and it turns away neither Jew, nor Gentile, nor barbarian, nor free man, nor slave,
neither man, nor woman, neither youth, nor old man, but receives all equally and calls them with one honor.
But those who have not wished to receive such a gift, let them blame themselves,

for by their own will they have brought such blindness upon themselves. When the way has been prepared for all and there is no one to prevent entry there, and some by their own will remain outside, such people perish from nothing else but their own wickedness.
Gospel: "He was in the world."

Commentary: He was in the world, but not as one equal in time with the world, far from it! For this is why he added and said: "And the world was made through him," so that by this word he might lead you to understand the beginninglessness of the Only-Begotten.
And when you hear that "all this is his creation," even if you were senseless and an opponent of the glory of God, you would unwillingly confess that the Creator is before all created things.
For this reason I always marvel at the madness of Paul of Samosata, how he dared such opposition to so clear a truth and by his own will destroyed himself along with the demons.

For it was not that he was ignorant of the truth, far from it! Rather, he knew the truth very well, and by his own will he came to love lawlessness, and the same thing happened to him as to the Jews: for they knew well that he is the only-begotten Son of God, but for the sake of pleasing men and rulers they did not confess it.

In the same way this wretched man knew everything, but to please a certain woman he gave himself over to the devil. For evil is the tyranny of vainglory, and it blinds the eyes even of wise men if they are not careful. For if the taking of a bribe blinds a man, would not vainglory also blind him, which is far worse than that? For this reason the Lord also said to the Jews: "How can you believe, who receive glory from men and do not seek the glory of the only God?"
Gospel:
"And the world did not know him."

Interpretation: By "the world" in this place he means the untaught and foolish people, those who are corrupt and turned toward earthly affairs. But the friends of God and all the marvelous men knew him even before his incarnation. Concerning the patriarch, Christ himself says: "Abraham your father rejoiced that he would see my day, and he saw it and was glad." And concerning David, again, he rebuked the Jews and said: "David in the Spirit calls him Lord and says: 'The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand.'" And again in many places he mentions Moses to them. And again, concerning all the other prophets, the apostle Peter says: "From Samuel onward all the prophets knew Christ and proclaimed his coming." And to Jacob and to his father, as also to his grandfather, he thus appeared and spoke, and he promised to give them many good things, which he also fulfilled.

But as he himself again said: "Many prophets desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it." Why then? Could it be that they did not receive understanding and did not know him? Yes, they knew him very well indeed, and I will demonstrate this matter from this very saying. Some say: "They did not know him, for he says: 'Many desired to see what you see.'" It is evident, then, that since they desired to see, they surely knew of his coming to men.

For if they had not known, they would not have desired to see either, since no one thinks of a thing he does not know, nor does he long for it. So it is evident that they knew the Son of God and said: "He is to come to men." But when he says, "They did not see or hear what you now see and hear," that saying concerned his incarnation. For they both heard his voice and saw him, but not incarnate in this way, not living among men, nor present on earth so openly. And for this reason he himself did not say:
"They desired to see me," but rather: "what you now see."
And although they had not seen his incarnation, yet they knew that it was to take place, and they desired to see it and believed in it, though they had not seen it. But when the pagans say to us:
"What was Christ doing during all those many former ages, that he did not stretch out a helping hand to the human race,
and why did he come only at the last to seek our salvation, while for so many ages we were left neglected?"

To this let us answer them that even before this he was in the world and governed his creatures and was known by all who were worthy. But if, because at that time not all knew him, but only the holy and those pleasing to God, you make this a charge against him,
then lay the charge against him now as well, for even now not all know him.
But just as now no one, on account of the unbelievers,
refuses to credit what concerns the believers, so too concerning those former times doubt is not fitting, for he was known by all believing people. But if anyone should say:
"And why did not all listen to him?" I too will say:
"And why do not all listen to him even now?"
And some were saying, "All created things exist of themselves," and some attribute the governance of the whole world to demons;
but we do not look to those who are unbelievers.
For this too is madness, if we should imitate madmen. For no one calls the sun harmful to the eyes, even though it does harm certain weak eyes;
and no one calls honey bitter, even though it seems bitter to certain sick people.
Shall we then say something evil about God, because certain people say it? And who in command of his senses, who was not driven mad and possessed by a demon, would do this?
For the world did not know him, but those of whom the world was not worthy, they knew him.

For the evangelist did not say simply, "They did not know him," but "The world did not know him"; that is, people nailed to the affairs of the world and lovers of the world did not know him. For Christ too gives such people this same designation and says, "Righteous Father, the world too has not known you." And indeed not him alone, but the Father too the world did not know, in the way that we have said,
for nothing so darkens the mind as preoccupation with the affairs of the world and love of them.

Teaching 8. On love of riches. But you who know all this, separate yourselves from fleshly affairs, for many evils come upon us through them, since there is no person who would not love the affairs of this world or would strive for the kingdom [?]; but without doubt whoever has turned to these things falls away because of them. For no one can "serve God and mammon," but must love the one and hate the other. And those who have overcome love of money have loved God as is right, but those who were overcome by it have fallen. For the soul overcome by love of money is easily overcome by all the passions that anger God, since it is the slave of everything that loves evil.

But be watchful and rise up and understand whose servants we are, and let us glorify his dominion alone. Let us weep and mourn for those former times in which we served mammon. Let us cast off from us its heavy yoke and take up the sweet and light yoke of Christ, for he commands us nothing of the kind that mammon commands. For mammon tells us to be enemies of everyone, whereas the Lord instead enjoins love on us. Mammon buries us in clay and mud, for gold is clay and mud, whereas Christ lifts us above the material things of earthly affairs and commands us to care for the treasure of the heavens. Mammon both here consumes our life with toil and anxiety and there makes us liable to the unquenchable fire, whereas the Lord gives us a reward even for a single drink of cold water, without fail and indeed many times over. How then is it not madness, in place of such a good Lord, to serve so wicked a tyrant, who gives us no profit either here or there, but rather torment and affliction in both places to those who obey him? For the greater part of those going to hell go there because of this: they loved gold and did not have mercy on the poor. So that this may not come upon us too, let us scatter it and give it to the poor,
Let us free our souls from the cares of this world and from the torments of the next,

and let us treasure up righteousness in heaven; instead of gold on earth, let us gather unfailing treasures, which will go with us to heaven, lend us a hand in affliction, and make the Judge merciful toward us. May we all be worthy to stand before him with boldness and to attain the eternal good things that are given to those who love him, by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ,
with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
Chapter 9
This saying: "He came to his own, and his own did not receive him."
Commentary: If you remember the earlier words, let us diligently build up what is still lacking, as people who have prospered and succeeded,
for if you remember what was said before, you will also learn everything well, and you will not cause us much labor,
because whoever loses what he has already learned always needs a teacher and will never become learned.
But whoever keeps what he has learned and in this way receives the word will soon become a teacher instead of a pupil, and not for himself alone,
but he will benefit others as well, as is now the case with this assembly, which loves learning and keeps its teaching well.
But come now, let us deposit that divine silver in the treasuries of your souls, and let us make a profit from these words read today, as the grace of the Holy Spirit may grant us,
for the Evangelist spoke about those earlier times, saying, "The world did not know him," and then in his account he came to the times of the preaching and says:
Gospel: "He came to his own, and his own did not receive him."

Commentary: By "his own" in this place he means the Jews, as the chosen people, and he also means all people, as those created by him. And just as above he said in amazement that the world which was made by him did not know its Creator,
so also here he spoke in amazement about the lack of understanding of the Jews and of those many others,
saying that he came to his own and "his own did not receive him."
And not only this, but all the prophets also marveled at this matter and spoke in the same way, and likewise the apostle Paul says the same thing in amazement.
For the prophets said:
"A people whom I did not know served me; with the obedience of the ear they heard me. Foreign sons lied to me; sons of foreign seed were startled and limped away from their places," and again:
"Those to whom nothing had been told about him shall see him, and those who had not heard of him shall understand."
And the apostle Paul says: "What shall we say? That the Gentiles, who did not pursue righteousness, found righteousness,
and Israel pursued righteousness and did not attain the law of righteousness."

And is it not astonishing how those who had been brought up in the books of the prophets, who daily heard about Christ from Moses and from the other prophets, and who daily saw Christ himself performing those miracles,

And he taught only them, and he did not permit the disciples to go to the Gentiles or to enter a city of the Samaritans, nor did he himself do this, but he always said: "I have been sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel." And despite all this they so blinded their eyes and stopped their ears that they did not come to faith in Christ at all. But the Gentiles had nothing of this kind;

they had never heard divine words, nor had they seen such things even in a dream, but they were always occupied with fables and wickedness, in the service of false gods, of wood and stone, which were lawlessly worshipped. And yet such people suddenly appeared in such splendor, as if they had come out of heaven. How and from where this came about, hear from Paul, for that blessed man investigated this matter closely, found its cause, and taught it to us. Hear him, then, as he states the cause of this blindness of theirs and cries out: "They were ignorant of the righteousness of God and sought to establish their own will, and they did not submit to the righteousness of God, and for this reason all this befell them." And again, in another place, the same man explains this statement and says: "What then shall we say? That the Gentiles, who did not seek righteousness, have attained righteousness first, but the righteousness that comes from faith. And Israel pursued the law of righteousness and did not attain the law of righteousness. Why? Because it was not from faith, for they stumbled on the stone of stumbling." And what he is saying here is this:
unbelief became for them the cause of such great evils, and arrogance gave birth to unbelief, for since they had previously been more honored than the Gentiles,
because they knew God, and on account of the other things the Apostle speaks of.

But after the coming of Christ they saw that both, Jews and Gentiles alike, were held in equal honor and that they had no advantage beyond circumcision; for this reason they were wounded by arrogance and could not bear the Master's love for mankind and his incomprehensible goodness.
And this befell them from no other source than from hatred of mankind and arrogance.
What harm does it do you, O you most foolish of all people?

What harm does the good done to others do you? Or are your own good things diminished by the kindness shown to others? Truly wickedness is blind and is unable to understand anything good, for their heart was wounded.
For because others too became sharers in their good things, they ran themselves through with a sword and became estranged from God's love for mankind. As the Lord says: "Friend, I do you no wrong.
But I wish to give to this man also, just as to you." And in fact they are not even worthy of these words,
for that laborer, though he grumbled, at least had something to say on account of his labor through the whole day, and his hardship and sweat.
But these had nothing of the kind, only negligence and wickedness and countless sins, by which they too had sinned against God, just like the Gentiles; and for this reason the Apostle says:
"There is no distinction between Jew and Gentile, for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, but they are justified freely by his grace."
And again he says: "Those who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law," that is, they will receive a worse judgment, since both reason and the law convict them,
and not for this reason only, but also because through them the name of God was blasphemed among the Gentiles, as the prophet says.

For this reason also, when the apostle was speaking of the deeds of the Gentiles, he immediately began to speak of their lawlessness as well: that they both turned away from the faith and became doers of evil deeds, as all the prophets said concerning their wickedness.

And then he says: "We know that whatever the law says, it says to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be stopped, for all have sinned." Now therefore why do you still exalt yourself, O Jew? For that senseless mouth of yours and that boldness of yours have been stopped, and you are liable to judgment. For even if you had done good and had not gone astray, even then you ought not to have grieved over the salvation of others, and this is the mark of a wicked mind, all the more so when mercy on them did not come through any hardship of yours. For if the salvation of others harmed your good things, then you would have had an argument, although that too would be senseless. But if no greater good is given to you by the torment of others, and you are not harmed by their salvation, why do you thus bring evil upon your own head because others receive freely, without payment?

And as I said, even if you were a doer of good, you still ought not to grieve over another's good. But since you too have sinned and done evil, and yet you still grumble over the good of others and think that you alone are worthy of all grace, this is not a matter of envy only, but you have that root of all evils, pride, concerning which the wise man says: "The beginning of sin is pride," and its mother and source and root.

Instruction 9. Because of pride the first-created man thus fell from that blessed life. And again the devil too, who deceived him, fell in this same way from that great height. For this reason the wicked one knew the power of that sin, that it is able to cast down even from heaven. Therefore he fought against Adam in the same way and threw him down, for he made him puffed up by that talk of being equal to God, and thus threw him down and brought him down to the depths of hell.

For nothing so estranges a person from God and hands him over to the Gehenna of fire as the tyranny of pride, for when it is with us, our whole life is impure, whether we practice virginity, or fasting, or prayer, or almsgiving,
or anything else, for "everyone who is high of heart is impure and abominable before the Lord."

Let us therefore quench our pride, if we wish to be holy and to be freed from the judgment that awaits the devil, as Paul says: "Not a new convert, so that he may not be puffed up and fall into the judgment and snare of the devil." Rather, be saved from this lawless thing. If we understand our nature and remember the multitude of our sins, the bitterness of the torments to come, and the vanity of the affairs of this world, for it is in no way better than the grass and the flowers of the field, and withers more easily,

if we ponder all this and imitate the virtues of the saints, the devil will never be able to strike us down with pride. And may the God of the humble, the good and gentle one, grant both us and you a contrite and humble heart, so that in this way we may be able to succeed in the other virtues as well and to glorify our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and for ever and ever, amen.
Chapter 10
This saying: "He came to his own, and his own did not receive him."
Commentary: God is a lover of humankind and a benefactor, beloved, and he seeks every means by which we might be adorned with virtue,
and for this reason he brings no one to virtue by force and against their will, but draws them to himself by doing good and by their own free will. For this reason too, when he came,
some received him and some did not,
for he does not wish to enslave anyone against their will, but seeks those who are willing, who would thank him
for having received them. For human beings need service from others, and for this reason they make many their servants even against their will.
But God needs nothing from anyone; he does everything for the sake of our salvation, and for this reason he has given us authority over this matter, and he draws no one to himself by force;
he seeks what is better for us, and to bring someone against their will is altogether the same as not going to them at all. But some say:
"And why does he hand over to judgment those who did not obey him?

Or why did he promise Gehenna to those who do not keep his commandments?" But listen: the Lord always has mercy on us; even if we disobey him, he does not withdraw from us, and when we flee he pursues us, in order to turn us back.
But since some have become disobedient to his goodness and have counted it as nothing, for this reason he brings upon them that second course, punishment, which is bitter.
Yet it too is good, once that first means has been despised, for lawgivers and judges also inflict many harsh penalties on offenders,
and still we do not hate them but rather honor them, though they need nothing from us, and often they do not even know who will benefit from their judgment.
And in all this they care for the good order of our life and honor the virtuous, while restraining from evil the wicked, who also harm the peace of others.

Now if we praise these people for this, should we not all the more love God for his so great beneficence, God whose depth of dispensations and of the goodness he has toward us is beyond comprehension?
But those whom he hands over to torment, he hands over for this reason: because they have shown themselves wicked and ungrateful.
And understand it in this way: that "he came to his own" not because he needed anything, for, as I said, God needs nothing from anyone else, but he came for the benefit of those who were his own.

And on top of all this, his own did not receive him who had come for their benefit, but drove him away, and not only this, but they led him out of the vineyard and killed him. And on top of all this he still did not shut the door of repentance to them, but granted them, even after such great evils, that if they wished, they might wash away all their sins through faith in him and become equal to those who had done nothing of the kind, and be beloved to him. And so that you may know that I do not say this in vain, look at blessed Paul, about whom I cry out loudly, for after the crucifixion of Christ he persecuted him and was an accomplice in the death of his martyr; and since he turned and repented, he therefore immediately became a partner of the chief apostles themselves and was shown to be a teacher and instructor of the whole world, he who was formerly a blasphemer and a persecutor, as that blessed man himself proclaims the gospel with joy, and he was not ashamed of it.
For this reason he also says at one point,
that:

"I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the churches of God"; and again he says: "Jesus came to save sinners, of whom I am the first"; and further he says: "You have heard of my way of life in Judaism, that I persecuted the churches of God." For it is as though he repays Christ by showing forth his goodness, in that he shows that he saved in this way such an enemy and fighter as he was, and he boldly proclaims the war that he formerly waged against Christ, and after this he gave to all who despaired the hope of salvation, for he says:
"Christ also did this for this reason, that in me too he might show his surpassing goodness, as a pattern for those who would come to repentance."
But let us return to that first saying, which the evangelist speaks:
Gospel: "He came to his own, and his own did not receive him."

Commentary: From where did he come, he who is everywhere and has filled all things? What place did he empty of himself, he who holds all things in his hand? But understand that he has emptied no place at all, for how could this be? Rather, he did this by coming to us; for although he was always in the world, the world did not know him, and for this reason he was not considered to have come, since it did not know him; but at last he revealed himself, when he put on our nature and this flesh. And for this reason he calls such a manifestation and disclosure a coming. And see how the disciple is not ashamed to speak of that dishonor done to his teacher, that "they did not receive him," and he says everything with boldness. And this too is no small sign of his love of truth; and again, even if he had been ashamed,
the shame belonged to those who showed contempt and not to the one who was held in contempt,
for he appeared all the more glorious, in that despite all this he had mercy on them, while they were shown to all to be foul and defiled,
Him who had come to do them such good things they turned away as if he were an enemy, and they fell short of the portion that was given to those who received him.
Gospel: "But as many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God."
Commentary: Why do you not tell us, O blessed one, also about the torments to which those who do not receive him are given over, but instead said this:
"They were his own, and when he came to his own they did not receive him." He did not say what judgment comes upon them in return for this, or to what torment they were given over,
for then fear would have come upon them all the more, and the harshness of their heart would have been bent. But this blessed one says,
and what could be greater than this torment: that it had been prepared for them to become children of God, and they did not become so,
but of their own will cast themselves out from such an honor?

However, this will not be their only torment; the unquenchable fire will also receive them, as he reveals further on. But here he now speaks of the incomprehensible good things for those who receive him, and he shows them all in a few words, for he says:
Gospel: "But as many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God."
Commentary: He deemed all worthy of this honor: slaves and free, pagans or barbarians, learned and unlearned, women or men,
or children, or the old, the rich or the poor: all have been made worthy of this honor and have received this power.
For faith and the grace of the Holy Spirit scrape away the disorder of worldly affairs, bring all together, and transform them into one royal likeness.
What could be worthy of this grace? For an earthly king, who is made from that same earth

from which we also come, and who returns to it just as we do, will not enroll in his armies his equals, men who are his fellow servants of God, who share his same nature and are often even better in their deeds, if they are slaves.
But the only-begotten Son of God did not disdain tax collectors and sinners, and many who were bodily deficient in their limbs he brought into the assembly of children.
Such is the power of faith in him; such is the abundance of his grace.
And just as fire, when it receives earth from the veins from which gold comes, makes it into gold in place of earth.

So likewise, and even more so, baptism, by that washing, changes us from clay into gold. For at that time the Holy Spirit enters our souls like fire, burns away the image of the earthly one, and makes the image of the heavenly one brilliantly renewed, and makes it shine as if from a furnace. But why did he not say, "He made them children of God," but rather, "He gave them power to become children of God"? Understand that he indicates this: that we need great diligence, so that we may keep untouched and undefiled the image that is imprinted upon us in baptism. And he also shows us that no one can take this power from us unless we ourselves destroy it. And if those who receive authority over certain matters from men have power over them, how much more would those have it who receive honor from God! For if they do nothing unworthy of such honor, we shall be stronger than all, since he who has given us this honor is stronger and better than all.

And again, the Evangelist wishes to make us understand that this grace is not given idly in this way to everyone, but to those who strive to receive it. For it is within their power, he says, to be children of God; for if they do not seek it first, that grace does not come upon them. Just as he shows in every place that he brings no one by compulsion, but seeks those who are willing, so too he has made it clear here: even in these great good things, one part is God's, the giving of grace, and one part is man's, the showing of faith and constant diligence in the times that follow. For baptism and believing alone are not enough to preserve our purity; rather, if we wish to keep its brilliance, we must display good works. For that spiritual birth and the cleansing from all previously committed sins are given to us through baptism, but that we should remain after this in that same purity and no longer defile ourselves, this lies under our own power. And for this reason he reminded us of the manner of this birth, and brought into the discussion the account of fleshly birth as well, and from it showed the superiority of this one, and said:
The Gospel:
"who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God"

Interpretation: Now he said this so that we may see the worthlessness of that first birth, which comes about from blood and by the will of the flesh, and may then understand the height and honor of this second birth, which comes about by grace, and so may recognize its greatness and height and the honor and gift of our Begetter, and may show great diligence. For there is cause for fear, if we defile this fine garment of ours by later sins and are cast out of the bridal chamber like the five foolish virgins and like the man who did not have a wedding garment. For he too was one of the guests, and he too had been called, but since he did an unseemly thing, hear with what pitiable sentence, worthy of many tears, he was condemned: when he came to sit at that splendid table, not only was he kept from it, but, bound hand and foot as well, he was cast into the outer darkness, into eternal weeping and gnashing of teeth.
Homily 10, that holy baptism will be of no benefit to us who remain in evil deeds. Let us not, then, suppose, beloved,
that faith alone will be enough for our salvation if we do not do good works, but come to that blessed wedding clothed in an unworthy garment.
What befell that wretched man will befall us too, for it is an evil thing
if God and King does not consider it beneath him to call worthless and pitiable people to his table, and we become so senseless
that even at so great an honor we feel no shame and do not turn to what is better, but even after the calling remain in such wickedness.
It was not for this that he called us to that awesome mystery of holy communion,
that we should come with our former wickedness,
but so that we should strip off wickedness and put on what those called by the King ought to put on.
But if we are unworthy of that calling, this does not come from him who calls but from our own wickedness. For it is not he who drives us out of that wondrous assembly of the called,
but we ourselves drive ourselves out,

For he did everything that he needed to do: he adorned the wedding and prepared the table, sent out those who issue the invitations, received those who came, and showed them every honor. But we have insulted him himself, and all those who had come there, and that great wedding, with defiled garments, which are impure deeds. And for this reason we are justly cast out, for it was for the honor of that wedding and for the rest of those gathered there that he cast out those shameless and foul ones. For if he had left there the one clothed in a stained garment, that man would have been insulting the others. But may such a thing not befall any of us! For this reason all this has been written before it comes to pass, so that we may be chastened and take heed by hearing it, so that we may not fall into those evil deeds and bitter torments, but may go with a shining garment to that wedding, of which may we all be made worthy by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, for to him belong glory and might, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 11
This passage: And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.
Interpretation: I ask one thing of all of you, before we have yet begun on these words of the Gospel,
and do not be disobedient to me in this request, for I am not asking anything burdensome, nor for my own benefit, but for yours.
For this is my request: that on every Sabbath on which I read and interpret the words of the Gospel to you,

you should, on the day before, each take them up and read them through on your own, and search out the meaning of those words: which word is easy to understand, and which needs much searching and is difficult;
and that you should take note of all this and so come to listen,

for from this practice no small benefit will come both to you and to us, and we will not have great labor in making the meaning of the words clear to you, when you too have first taken pains and you too understand readily.
For many now come who do not even know the words of the Gospel, yet they want to learn all at once both the words and their meaning, which we expound.
And this is impossible, for how could they learn in this short time, and especially since they listen only superficially?

But if anyone pleads the cares of the world as an excuse, those other activities accuse them: when there is singing, all are found to be at leisure, yet for the work of God they have no leisure, so that they cannot spare even one hour. And does this not deserve myriad torments?

But some also plead another excuse, saying, "We do not have books." To the rich there is no need to say anything about this; but to the poor let us say: how is it that each of you has all his other implements, which bring no benefit to the soul?

And those useless things they acquire with eagerness, yet the true benefits of the soul, which are books, do they not seek? But if someone should be so poor that he cannot acquire a book, it is possible, by coming to church continually, to learn everything. Only let us not come carelessly, and as if discharging a debt, and with the body alone, but let us come with the mind also and with the whole soul to learn the words of the Gospel. Now, then, I shall speak the words which that pipe of theology cries out:
Gospel:
"And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us."

Commentary: First he said: "They were born of God, those who received him, and they became children of God." And therefore he now states here the cause of that incomprehensible honor, which is the incarnation of the Word and his putting on the form of a servant.
For he who is the Son of God became the son of man, in order to make human beings children of God.
For when one who is exalted comes to one who is lowly, he suffers no harm to his own glory, but he raises the lowly one up to himself, as the Lord also did.
For he did not diminish his own nature by that descent, but us, who sat in darkness and in the shadows of death, he raised up and led to that incomprehensible glory.
For even a king, if he speaks kindly with some poor man, does himself no harm, but makes the other honored.

And if, in this worthless human nature, a great man suffers no harm from associating with a poor man, how could that incorruptible and untouchable nature be harmed, whose honor is not something acquired, as a man's is,
nor something that comes and passes away again, but all that is his is unshakable and firm forever.
And therefore, when you hear that "the Word became flesh," do not be troubled.
It does not mean that he changed the essence of his nature into flesh, for even to think of this is dreadful, but his nature remains as it was, and he also put on the form of a servant.

But the evangelist said "became flesh" in order to stop the mouths of the heretics who say, "His taking on flesh was some kind of illusion." And it was to stop the mouth of their blasphemy from the very beginning that he said "became flesh." He is not indicating a change of his nature,

for not even demons devise this, nor madmen and those who have gone out of their minds. Rather, this theologian apostle signifies the truth of his taking on flesh, while the nature of his divinity is altogether unchangeable, as the apostle says: "All will grow old like garments, and like clothing you will change them, and they will be changed. But you yourself are the same, and your years will not fail."

For his nature is above all change, and may their blasphemy turn back on their own heads, those who say, "His nature became flesh." So that you may know that the evangelist said this phrase "became flesh" only in order to confirm that his taking on flesh was real, listen to his next words, how he scrapes away every evil doubt and purifies his statement, saying:
Gospel: "And dwelt among us."

Interpretation: It is as if he were saying: "Let no one imagine anything evil from the word that I spoke, namely 'he became flesh,' for I did not speak of a change of that unchangeable nature, but of a dwelling among us. And what dwells is not the same as that in which it dwells; rather, one thing dwells in another. And in this way God dwelt among us.

Otherwise, it would no longer be called dwelling. And when I said that one thing dwells in another, I said it concerning the nature [?] of the Godhead, for by the union of the Incarnation the Word of God and the flesh that he put on are one. It was not a mixing or a fusion that took place, nor an annihilation of the essences, but a certain inexpressible and incomprehensible unity; and how it came about, he alone knows. And as to what his dwelling among us is, hear the prophet, who says: "I will raise up the fallen tent of David,"

for truly our nature had fallen with an incurable fall, and raising it up belonged to that firm and mighty hand. No one else had the power to raise it up except that mighty hand which also created it, which came to its aid from heaven and raised it up by that birth of water and the Spirit.

And behold that awesome and incomprehensible mystery, which dwells forever in this tent: for he put on our flesh, not in order to abandon it again, but in order to keep it with himself for ever. For if this were not so, he would not have seated it upon the royal throne, nor, clothed in it, would he be worshipped by all the hosts of heaven, the angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, principalities and powers. What mind can conceive, or what tongue can tell, the greatness of the honor with which he has honored our nature? Or what angel or archangel is able to conceive of this deed?

No one is able to comprehend it, neither any of those in heaven nor anyone on earth, for so great are the works of the Lord and so incomprehensible his benefactions that they surpass not only the speech of humans but even the understanding of angels.

Teaching 11, on virtue. Therefore let us too now fall silent from speech of this kind. And this I command and implore you: that you hasten to make such good returns to that Good One, returns which will be of profit to us; that is, that we take good care of our souls. For this too comes from his love for humanity: that he needs nothing from us and seeks only our own good, and he counts it as a repayment for his own benefits when we care for our souls.

Therefore it is a matter of great senselessness that, since he so desires our salvation, we should not do good according to our ability, so as to attain those countless good things. For all this, then, let us offer thanks to God, the lover of humanity, not in word only but rather in deed, so that those eternal good things may be given to us. May we all be worthy to attain them by the grace and love for humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and unto the ages of ages. Amen.
Chapter 12
This saying:
"And we beheld his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten,
from the Father, full of grace and truth."
Commentary: Perhaps our earlier words seemed burdensome to you, because we reproached you for negligence? But if I were burdening you for some purpose of my own, you would have grounds for complaint.
Since, then, I do everything for your own good, why should there be any resentment? Why should you not rather thank me for the love that I have toward you?

For I am afraid that I may labor and teach you while you do not listen, and that you may become liable to judgment. For this reason I press you constantly, so that you may listen with all your heart and become worthy of those good things of heaven.
But come, let us begin today also to speak about the Gospel, passage by passage, for it says:
Gospel: "We beheld his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten, from the Father, full of grace and truth."
Commentary: How could we have beheld it, had he not appeared in this body like our own?
For if Moses, who was himself a man, could not be looked upon in the face, and that righteous man needed a veil so that others could look at his face, then surely,
how could we have been able to see the power of the Godhead, that light
which even the heavenly powers cannot bear to look upon? How could we, who are of earth and clay, have been able to look at it?
For this reason he dwelt among us, so that everyone who wishes might be able to see him and converse with him.
But what is this saying of his: "Glory as of the Only-begotten, from the Father"? For many of the prophets were glorified,
such as Moses himself, and then Elijah and Elisha, of whom one was taken up by a chariot of fire, while chariots of fire stood around the other.

And then again Daniel was glorified, and the three youths, and many others who performed signs and were glorified. And again, angels also appeared to people and revealed to them the light of their own glory.
And not only angels, but the cherubim also appeared to the prophets in great glory, and the seraphim likewise.
But the evangelist lifts us up above all of this, passes beyond that splendor of created beings, and leads us to the very head of all good things, for he says:
"Not of a prophet, nor of an angel, nor of an archangel, nor of those supreme powers, the seraphim and cherubim, nor of any other created nature,

if indeed there is anywhere another, higher nature, but it is that of the King himself and of the only-begotten Son of God himself. And we have seen the glory of the Lord of all. Now this phrase, "as of the only-begotten": the "as" in this place is not one of likeness or of comparison, but of confirmation and certainty, as if he were saying: "We have seen such glory as was fitting and proper for the only-begotten Son of God, the King of all, to have." And again, there is such a custom among men, and I will not refrain from speaking of that too. Listen to which custom I mean. Some people often see a king adorned with all kinds of adornment and with precious stones. And when they recount his glory to others, they tell of the beauty of his garments, the loveliness of the precious stones, and the glory of his throne. And when they have said all this and much more of the kind, and still cannot fully show his glory in words, they then say:

"Why should we say much? He was such as a king truly is." And by that phrase they do not mean to show that he was like a king, but that he truly was a king. So too the evangelist said, "as of the only-begotten," to make us understand his great glory, which cannot be expressed by the tongue. For all the other prophets did everything by command, but he, as King, did everything with authority. For this reason also the people marveled at how he taught with authority. For angels too appeared in glory on earth, as in the case of Daniel, David and Moses, but they did everything as servants of the King, whereas he did so as King, the ruler of all. And he did all this while appearing in a lowly form, in humility. Yet even so, created things recognized their Creator, and a star from heaven summoned the magi to worship him, and the host of angels.

Every place where he came to be [?] was filled with his dispensations, and all creatures announced the great mystery to one another: angels to the shepherds, the shepherds to the people of the city, Gabriel to Mary and Elizabeth, and in the temple Anna and Simeon. And not these alone, but even the infant who had not yet come into the light, the citizen of the desert and namesake of this evangelist, John, preached in his mother's womb, when he leapt in his mother's womb at the sight of the Mother of God.

And all rejoiced in that hope, and all this took place at his birth. But when he had grown up, there were again still higher deeds. For it was no longer a star and heaven, nor angels and archangels, nor Gabriel and Michael, but the Father himself bore witness from heaven, and the Spirit, the Comforter, came flying down from heaven and remained upon him.
Truly it was because of all this that he said: "We have seen his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father," for after this it was no longer shepherds and a star,
but the very voice of the deeds themselves proclaimed him, for the report of his work was at once heard throughout all Syria.
Then the earth too became [?], for the King of the heavens had come openly, and all were crying out: "The King of the heavens has come,"
And the demons fled, and their ruler trembled; death was pursued,
then it became wholly invisible, and the tombs released the dead, and demons were driven out of the demon-possessed, and the diseases of the sick were healed,
and there were truly wondrous deeds, which the prophets longed to see and did not see,

for then you would have seen eyes made from earth so that they could see, and that desirable thing which all would have longed to see: how God at first created Adam from the earth, he showed all of this in a single moment on the highest member of the body, and he joined those paralyzed limbs to the whole body.
Dead hands moved, paralyzed feet at once [?], stopped-up ears were opened, and the tongue bound by muteness cried out loudly,
for as a skilled master builder renews a house grown old over a long time, so he clothed himself in human nature,
so he strengthened its shattered members, joined together those that were loosened, and raised up those that had wholly fallen.
But what can anyone say about that creation of the soul, which was far more wondrous than the creation of the body?
For even the healing of the body is great, but that of the soul is far higher,
by as much as the soul is higher than the body. And it is wondrous not only in that the soul is above the body, but also in this, that bodies are changed in whatever direction the Creator wishes,
whereas the soul was created its own master and has the power to incline in whatever direction it wishes, whether toward good or toward evil,
and God brings no one to virtue by force, for what is done by force is not virtue; rather, one must come to virtue willingly.
And for this reason its healing is more difficult,

but that too went forward well, and he not only turned souls from evil but also led them up to the very summit of the virtues. A tax collector became an apostle, a persecutor and blasphemer became a preacher to the whole world, magi became teachers of the Jews, a robber became a citizen of paradise, a harlot shone with faith, that Samaritan woman, also a harlot, became the converter of her city, and the Canaanite woman by faith drove the demon out of her daughter. And others, worse than these, entered the company of kings, and everything was changed at once, the sufferings of bodies and the pains of souls, and they came to the health of virtue.

And not two or three, or ten or a hundred people, but great cities and nations were converted to this. What can anyone say about his great wisdom, about the heavenly rules of virtue, about the orderly life of the angelic host? For he taught us such a life, he laid down such laws for us, he made known to us such a way of citizenship, that if we fulfill his commandments, we may become equal to the angels and like God according to our capacity, even though we may be lower than all people. So the evangelist gathered together all these wonders, those of bodies and of the soul and of material things, the commands and that incomprehensible gift, the laws and way of citizenship higher than the heavens, those eternal promises and his sufferings, and on account of all this he cried out this wondrous saying:

"We beheld his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth," for we marvel at him not only because of the wonders, but also because of the sufferings: how he was nailed to the cross and scourged, and struck on the cheek, and spat upon by those for whom so many good things had been done. For even concerning those things which are thought to be, as it were, beloved [?], this same word is fitting, since he himself called this deed great. For those deeds were not only of love and mercy, but also of incomprehensible power, for then death was being undone and the curse blotted out, demons were being wounded and brought to nothing and driven away, and the handwriting of sin was being nailed to the cross. And since he was working these miracles invisibly, for this reason he also displayed some visible ones.
And when they crucified him, he, nailed upon the wood, showed that he is truly the only-begotten Son of God and King of all creatures,

for while that blessed body was still upon the cross, the sun turned away its light, and the earth was shaking, and the dead were rising, and the rock was opening. And from the sealed tomb that dead one, crucified and buried, arose, and he filled the disciples with power and sent them into all the world as healers of human nature and teachers of the angelic life, to destroy the power of demons, and as proclaimers of the immortality of souls and of eternal life and of those eternal, unending good things which are beyond the grasp of the mind. All this, then, and more than this the blessed one considered, things that he did not even tell because of their multitude, for the world could not contain them; and because of all this he cried out: "We beheld his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth."

Homily 12, on living well and on the eternal judgment. But we who have been made worthy of so many and such great sights and hearings, and have seen so many good things, must also show deeds worthy of the faith, so that we may also attain the eternal good things,
for this is why our Lord Jesus Christ came: that we might see not only the glory here, but also the eternal glory.
For this reason he says: "I desire that where I am, these also may be, that they may behold my glory,"
for if his glory here became so radiant, what can anyone say of the glory to come?
That glory will be revealed not on this perishable earth, nor during our existence in these mortal bodies, but in that unending life, and with such radiance as no one can express in words.

O thrice blessed, and many times blessed, are those who have been made worthy to see his glory! Concerning it the prophet says: "Let the ungodly be destroyed, that he may not see the glory of God." But may none of us be destroyed.
O Lord, Lord, may no one be left without seeing that glory! For if we are not made worthy to see it, it is fitting for us too to say:
"It would have been better if we had never been born."
And why do we live, or why do we go on with our lives, if we fall short of that glory and cannot see our King?

For if those who cannot see this light of the sun live a bitter life, what then will become of those who have been deprived of that glory? For here this alone is the affliction, that they do not see the light; but there it is not so, nor is this alone the torment, but it is more bitter by as much as that sun is incomparably more brilliant than this sun. And there is this as well: those who have been deprived of that light do not go only into darkness, but eternal burning in the fire also comes upon them, and gnashing of teeth.

Let us not, then, fall into that eternal torment through this small faintheartedness, but let us wake up and strive, so that we may attain that rest and escape that river of fire which flows with a terrible roar before that glorious throne. For whoever falls in there once, no one will any longer rescue him from it, neither father, nor mother, nor brothers, as the prophets themselves cry out. For David says: "A brother cannot redeem; will a man redeem?" And Ezekiel said even more than this: "If Noah, Job and Daniel should stand, they could not save their sons and daughters." For there we have only one help, from our good deeds, and whoever does not have that help will find nothing else. Let us therefore remember this always and purify ourselves, so that we may see the Lord with boldness and attain those eternal good things, by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
Chapter 13
The text: "John testified about him, cried out and said: 'This is he of whom I said: He who comes after me was before me, for he is prior to me.'"
Interpretation: Are we perhaps striving in vain? Are we perhaps sowing on stones, or on the road, or among thorns?
For I am very much afraid that our labor may prove useless and fruitless. And I say this not because that fruitlessness would do me any harm, but for the sake of your love,
for our labor is not like that of those who work the land, who, if their seeds do not bring forth fruit, have nothing from which they might be fed.
But we are not like that; rather, whether the ground is fruitful or unfruitful, once we have sown, we will receive the reward of our labor from the Lord,
for each will receive his own reward according to his own labor, as it is written,

that: "You, son of man, testify to this people, whether they will listen and whether they will understand." Yet although this is so, and our toil is not without reward, still, when we see that your affairs are not prospering, we sigh just as those same laborers do, for such is the compassion of a teacher and father. For God also said to Moses: "I will blot out this people and make you a great nation."

But that blessed man did not accept it, but chose to perish with them or to live with them, those who had once been entrusted to him. Such a one ought to be the leader of souls. And I say all this so that we may take care to do good deeds,
so that in this way they might be able to reach even the depth of understanding, for the passions darken the eyes of the soul and throw the mind into confusion. But listen to what we have read today:
Gospel: "John bore witness concerning him, cried out and said: 'This is he who comes after me, who was before me, for he is prior to me.'"
Commentary: This evangelist mentions John and his testimony many times,
and he does this not in vain but with great wisdom,
for all the Jews held him in great wonder, and Josephus too says that "that war came about over his death," and sets forth great praises of him,
and since he was greatly esteemed by everyone, the evangelist mentions his testimony,
for the other evangelists bring forward the ancient prophets, as Matthew brought forward Isaiah and Jeremiah and Hosea concerning his birth,
but this evangelist brought forward the new and great testimony of the Baptist, who also baptized him and preached him.
Yet he does not bring him forward as a witness in order to make the King credible through servants,
but he stoops down to the weakness of human beings; just as, if he had not put on the form of a servant, this preaching would not have been accepted,
so likewise, if he had not spoken to people through servants, many of the Jews would not have believed,
for the testimony from heaven occurred once and twice, but only the worthy were able to hear it,
whereas John's testimony occurred many times, and those who could not hear the testimony from heaven,
they heard the testimony of John.
And for this reason he says: "John bore witness concerning him, cried out," and spoke boldly, and fearlessly preached his coming. And listen to the preaching as well:
Gospel: "This is he of whom I said: 'He who comes after me was before me, for he is prior to me.'"
Commentary: This testimony is veiled and contains words of humility, for he did not say:
"This is the only-begotten and beloved Son of God," but rather, "This is he of whom I said: 'He who comes after me was before me.'"

For just as birds do not teach their nestlings to fly all at once, but make them fly little by little and bring them back again to the nest, until they have fully learned to fly, and then lead them out of the nest altogether, so too the blessed John does not lead the Jews up to the height of understanding all at once, but for now only raises them up from the earth and teaches them that Christ is higher and more exalted than he.

For even this was no small thing, to convince them that he was more exalted than John, that wondrous man to whom everyone was running, he who had not been made manifest and who had not yet performed a single miracle.

And for now he wished only to convince them of this, that the one witnessed to is more exalted than the witness, and the one who came last than the one who came first. And see how wisely he does everything, for he points him out not only once he has been made manifest but even before his manifestation, as Matthew says: "He said to those coming to him: 'I baptize you with water, but after me comes one mightier than I, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie.'"
And he did this before his coming so that, when he came, they might readily believe in him,
since their minds would have been prepared beforehand,

For if he had not heard about the Lord at all, and they had seen him suddenly and only then heard about him, they would not have believed, because of the lowliness of his appearance and his great humility; for Christ had such humility that Samaritans and tax collectors and prostitutes approached him boldly. And as I said, if John had spoken about him only at the time when he came, they would not have believed in him. But the forerunner prepared their minds beforehand, so that when he came, they might believe in him.
But what does this saying mean: "He was before me"?

This means that he was radiant and honored. And do not think, he says, that because I came first to preach I was superior, for I am far inferior, and so inferior that I am not worthy even to be counted as his servant. And it is not that he was after me
and by some kind of advancement came to be before me; rather, he was always before me and superior.

And he was also indicating that glory which is now renowned throughout the world concerning Christ: that although he came after me, yet he was always before me and glorious, and on earth too his glory became great after a little while. But if someone should say, "If he was indicating that glory of his which was going to become renowned in the world, how can he speak of it as something past?"

Then understand it this way: this is the custom of the prophets. For Isaiah too, when he spoke of his passion, proclaimed what had not yet happened as though it had happened: "Like a sheep he was led to slaughter," and he did not say, "He will be led." And David did not say, "They will pierce my hands and my feet," but "They pierced," as of something already done. And concerning the betrayer, who had not yet done it, he spoke as of something done: "He who ate bread with me has lifted up his heel against me." And again he says: "They gave me gall for my food, and for my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink." And you will find many such passages in Scripture, which speak of what has not yet happened as though it had happened.

You desire that teaching on mercy, so that we might bring in other examples as well, but these that have been spoken are enough, so that you may not grow weary of listening. Therefore let us bring our discourse to its conclusion. And the end must be made with thanksgiving to God; and God loves thanksgiving not in word only, but rather in deed, for he says: "Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father in heaven."

For nothing is more radiant than good works, as it is written: "The paths of the righteous shine like light." And they give light not for themselves only, but also to enlighten others. Therefore I beseech you, let us not let the oil of our lamps run short, so that their light may grow strong; for this oil is always good, since he says: "I desire mercy and not sacrifice." For this is the sacrifice of praise, which is not used up and does not perish, but always shines to the glory of God. Therefore, then, I beseech you, beloved,

Let us offer such a sacrifice as this upon these altars, for it is more honorable than fasting and prayer and many other virtues, since God loves such a sacrifice. But let it not be made from greed, nor from stolen wealth, for God hates that kind and turns his face away from it. Therefore let us strive not to anger him instead of delighting him.
And if Cain was punished because he offered what was inferior to God, what shall we do if we perform our almsgiving from greed?

Therefore I beseech you that we not do charitable works from possessions gained by seizure. If one blesses us and another curses us, what profit is there except useless labor? But if we take care and strive in everything to fulfill the will of God, we will be able to attain those eternal good things by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
Chapter 14
This saying: "And from his fullness we have all received grace from grace."

Commentary: First let us say that John wished to resolve the question of those who were going to ask how it was that the Lord came later to preach and yet became superior to him and more radiant than he.
For this reason he said, "He was before me," and this is one reason. But he also gave a second reason, which he now states:
Gospel: "And from his fullness we have all received grace in place of grace.
For the law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Christ Jesus."

Commentary: So someone may say, "What is this saying, in which he says, 'From his fullness we have all received grace in place of grace'?" And let us come to the first phrase. For he speaks in this way:
He does not have his grace as a gift, but he himself is the source and himself the root of all good things, himself life,
himself light, himself truth. And he has not kept the abundance of good things enclosed within himself alone, but spreads it out to others as well and satisfies everyone.

And after he has filled everyone, he still remains in fullness, and nothing is lost from the abundance of his graces; rather, he continually pours forth and satisfies everyone, and he remains in his own perfection. But what I have is given,
for I have received it from the Spirit, and it is small compared with the whole, and like a single drop beside the sea, the great abyss,
it is nothing. Indeed, even this is a poor comparison for this matter. For a drop
that someone has taken out of the sea, though it is small and of no account, nevertheless is taken away from the sea itself, even if no one can perceive the loss,
but concerning this source no one can say any such thing. However much anyone fills himself from it, it remains in its own fullness and nothing whatever is lost from it. For this reason it is fitting
