that we turn instead to another illustration. Although it too is weak and cannot reveal what we are seeking, it is nevertheless better able than the first to convey the force of this matter, more so than that first one. For let us consider a source of fire,
And then let us consider that from that fire tens of thousands of candles were being lit, and not only one myriad, but many.

Does not that fire remain in the same fullness as it was before? Even after the lighting of the candles, it is evident to all that it remains in the same fullness. Now if such a thing happens with these material and transient bodies, which are diminished by what is taken from them, so that after giving to others the fire suffers no harm but remains in its own fullness, will this not happen all the more with that incorruptible and incorporeal nature? For where matter is present and a corruptible and indivisible body, and it is not divided, how much more, when the discourse concerns a power, and that power which is given to us from the immaterial essence, will nothing of the kind occur? For this reason John said, "From his fullness we have received." This saying is not the Forerunner's but the Evangelist's. And this saying amounts to the following: "Do not suppose that we, who were with him for a long time, and saw him with our eyes, and served him with our hands, would speak of him out of favor and testify in vain.

Far from it! For John too, who had not yet seen him anywhere and before that time had not been with him, but saw him only when he was baptizing and cried out, 'He was before me,' received all of that from the fountain; and of our twelve, and three hundred, and five hundred, and three thousand, and five thousand, and those many myriads who turned from among the Jews and the Gentiles, and who are turning even now, and who shall be hereafter, all of us receive from his fullness." And what did we receive? Grace in place of grace. Which in place of which? The new in place of the old. For just as there is righteousness and righteousness, for it says, "According to the righteousness of the law he became blameless"; and again there is faith and faith, for it says, "From faith to faith"; and there is sonship and sonship, for it says, "Those to whom there is not sonship and adoption"; and there is glory and glory, for it says, "If that which was passing away came with glory, will not the true be all the more glorious?"; and there is law and law, for it says, "The law of the Spirit of life has set me free"; and there is service and service, for it says:
"Serve by the Spirit of God"; and there is covenant and covenant, for it says, "And I made with you a new covenant, not as the one I made with your fathers";
and sanctification and sanctification, and baptism and baptism,

and sacrifice and sacrifice, and temple and temple, and circumcision and circumcision, so also there is grace and grace. But those were types and shadows, whereas all these are truth, and they resemble those in name only and not in substance, even in the case of types and shadows.
And whatever is drawn with white paint or with black is in every case called a man, and again, that which is depicted with paints of various colors,
that too is called a man, but the true man is the one who is united of soul and body.

Likewise, then, do not suppose that the realities are just the same, in keeping with the likeness of the types; but neither should you imagine that they are completely foreign to one another. For if something is a type, it is not foreign to the truth, and since it is a shadow, it is inferior to the truth. What, then, is the difference between them? Do you wish me to speak, on one or two matters, about the old and the new, and how great a difference there is between them, so that you may understand
that the former were teachings for children, while the latter are for great men and philosophers,

and that these were given as to angels, while those were given as to men? Where, then, do you wish us to make the beginning of the discourse? If you wish, let us begin by speaking about the inquiry [? perhaps "sonship"].

What, then, is the difference between this and that? Understand that the one was an honor in word only, while the other is in deed. And concerning the former it says: "I said, 'You are indeed gods, and all of you sons of the Most High.'"
But concerning the latter it says: "They were born of God." How, or in what manner?
By the washing of second birth and the renewal of the Holy Spirit.

And even after that name of sonship they still had the spirit of slavery. While they were in slavery they were honored with that name, but we have become free, and moreover we have received the honor not in name but in deed. Paul indicated this when he said:
"We have not received the spirit of slavery again to fear, but we have received the spirit of adoption, by which we cry out, 'Abba, Father.'" For we were born from heaven and have settled in it.
And thus we were called sons. And again, if we examine the form of holiness, what this one is and what that one is, you will find a great difference here too.
For they, when they did not serve idols and did not fornicate or commit adultery,
were then called holy. But we first attain this gift through the coming of the Holy Spirit, and then through a way of life far surpassing that of the Jews. Hear what Scripture says about them:
"Do not be afraid, and do not sanctify your children, for you are a holy people."
And it is evident that their holiness consisted merely in not touching idols, but our holiness is not like this. For Scripture says about it: "That she may be holy in spirit and in body."

And again it says: "Seek peace and what is good, and practice holiness in the fear of God, for without it no one will see the Lord"; and again it says: "Practice holiness in the fear of God." Do you see that this is holiness: that its root and source should be within us?

For the mere name of holiness is not enough if the reality of it is not present. For this name of holiness does not show that all who are called by it are one and the same, since God too is called holy, yet not in the way that we are.

For this reason also, when the prophet heard this voice from the seraphim, listen to what he said: "O wretched me, for I am a man and have unclean lips, and I dwell among a people who have unclean lips." He who said this was holy and great, but if we examine ourselves against the holiness of heaven, we are found to be unclean. For holy are the angels, and holy are the archangels, and holy are the cherubim and seraphim, but there is a difference between their holiness and our holiness. And again, it would be possible for us to begin examining that superiority by means of other matters as well, but so that my discourse may not be prolonged, I will leave much of this to you, so that you may examine for yourselves the difference in those other matters. For it says: "Give occasion to the wise man, and he will be wiser."

I have given the occasion; now you bring the good work to its completion. And it is good for us to proceed to what remains lacking. For when the Evangelist said, "From his fullness we have all received," he immediately added, "and grace for grace." For the Jews were saved by grace, as it is written: "Not because of your righteousness, but because of your fathers I chose you." And those who had no help from their own virtue were given honor by the grace of God. We too are all saved by grace, but not in the same way as they were, for far higher and more exalted things have been given to us. For not only has forgiveness of sins been given to us, since this was given to them as well, but there have also been given to us holiness and righteousness and adoption and the grace of the Holy Spirit. A far surpassing grace has been given to us through the Holy Spirit, that is, boldness of speech, which has been given to us through reconciliation with God.

And by this grace we have also become beloved of God, no longer as slaves but as sons and friends. For this reason he says, "grace for grace." But those matters of the law too were bestowed on us by grace, as was being brought from non-being into being. It is not that we had first done something good and this was given to us as a reward for it, we who did not exist at all and so could not have done any good. Rather, everything has been given to us by the goodness of God: not only our coming from non-being into being, but also this, that as soon as we were born, we learned what ought to be done and what ought not to be done. And the law of these matters was planted in our mind, and the Creator established within us that tribunal of conscience; and this is the work of great grace.

And again, after this grace, see another grace: since we corrupted the natural law, another law, a written one, was then given to us. And after all this he renewed us by that second law of renewal. For the first too was a matter of mercy and grace. Hear what David says: "The Lord performed acts of mercy and his judgments for all the oppressed. He showed his ways to Moses and to the sons of Israel—the commandments of God." And again he says: "The Lord is sweet and upright. Therefore he gives law to sinners in the way of mercy." So then, the giving of the law was a matter of acceptance and grace. For this reason he says: "grace in place of grace," in order to show the magnificence of those latter things. For this reason too he adds and says:
Gospel:
"For the law was given to us from Moses, but grace and truth came through Christ Jesus."
Commentary: See how little by little both John the Baptist and the Evangelist lead the minds of their hearers up to a higher understanding,
since they first calmed their minds with lowly words. For he showed him to be superior to himself, and incomparably superior, and he proclaimed and said: "Mightier than I," and: "who was before me."
But this one made him superior to that one, yet this was below the dignity of the Only-begotten, for he made the comparison not with John, but with the one
whom the Jews held to be greater, that is, Moses. For he said: "The law was given from Moses, but grace and truth came about through Jesus Christ."

And see his wisdom: he made a distinction not of persons but of deeds, so that when the deeds appear far higher, then all may understand that Christ is far superior to Moses. For when deeds bear witness,
in which there is no pretext at all

for anyone to say that someone speaks out of friendship or enmity, then the truth of the deeds becomes beyond doubt even to those without understanding. For this reason their testimony is beyond doubt.
But see how wisely he makes that distinction, for he shows this greatness not by word, but by the truth of the deeds.
He set grace and truth in place of the law, and he set "came about" in place of "was given." And the difference between these is great, for giving belongs to a servant, who has received from another.
But this statement, "grace and truth came about," is the act of a king, who by his authority forgives sins and displays his gift.
For this reason he also said: "Your sins are forgiven you." And again he says: "So that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins."

And he said to the paralytic: "Rise, take up your bed and walk!" Do you see how grace comes about through him? But understand the truth as well, for this deed shows forth grace, as do the matter of the thief, the gift of baptism, the grace of the Spirit bestowed by him, and many other things.

And again, we may understand the truth if we look at the types, for the things that were to be fulfilled in this new law were prefigured beforehand in the types of the old, and when he came, Christ fulfilled them in deed.

But if you wish, let us also look a little at the types, for it is not possible to speak of them all at once; rather, from a few let us understand everything. And if you wish, let us speak about the Passion.
See, then, what the type says: "Take the lamb and slaughter it!"
"And they did all that he told them." But Christ did not command that it be done in this way; rather, he himself became the sacrifice and offered himself to the Father.

Do you see how the type came about through Moses? But the truth was given to us through Jesus Christ. Again, on Mount Sinai, in the battle with Amalek, so that the people of Israel might prevail, Moses stretched out his hands for this purpose, and Aaron and Hur, standing on this side and that, held them up. But when Christ came, he himself stretched out his hands on the cross. Do you see how the type was shown, but the truth was fulfilled? Again, the Law said: "Cursed be everyone who does not abide by what is written in this book." But what does Christ say? "Come to me, all who are weary and heavy-laden, and I will give you rest." And he came under the curse for our sake.

Homily 14. On living virtuously; the distinction between the graces given to us and to the Jews. Since, then, such great graces and the truth have been given to us, I beseech you, brothers, let us not grow slack because of the greatness of the gift. For the greater the honor given to us, the greater the virtue we owe. For one who has received a small benefit, even if he shows only small good works in return, does not deserve great blame.

But one who has ascended to the height of honor and then leads a worthless and slack life deserves great judgment. But may nothing of the sort befall you! For I trust in the Lord that you have lifted your souls up to heaven and have been made far from the earth; although you are in the world, you do not do the deeds of the world. Yet even so we will not cease to entreat you. For in battles it is not those who have fallen and fled, but those who are eager in the fight and run to and fro, whom everyone encourages and urges back into battle, since there the hope of recovery for the fallen and the fugitives is not great. But here, not only for those of you who are doing well, but also for those who have fallen, if they are willing, there is hope of good. For this reason let us strive in every way, with entreaty, reproach, teaching and praise, so that by every means we may win your salvation, leaving undone nothing that is possible for us.

And therefore let us not grow weary of these teachings. For although we know your zeal, teaching is not useless, so that you may be still more on your guard. For these teachings are not spoken to you alone, but also to us who teach you: these same teachings have been spoken and are spoken to us as well, for we too need teaching and consolation. Although these words are spoken by us, nothing prevents these words from applying to us as well, for the word of teaching corrects and converts those guilty of sin and puts on their guard those who have not yet fallen. For neither are we pure of sins; rather, this healing is common to all and the medicines have been set before us all, but justification is not common to all, but depends on the disposition of those who receive.

For whoever is willing to make good use of those spiritual medicines, his wounds will be healed; but whoever does not accept that spiritual medicine, his wound will remain unhealed and he will be handed over to a worse judgment. Let us therefore not be grieved at the healing of our wounds, nor be ashamed, even if that medicine of teaching seems bitter to our palate; rather, let us rejoice, for in the end very sweet fruit will be given to us in every respect, if only we strive to come, pure of those wounds that the teeth of sin have inflicted on us, to that eternal kingdom, so that we may be made worthy to see the face of the Lord and not be handed over to those merciless torturers [?] "I saw the Lord sitting on high thrones." And John bears witness to him and says: "Isaiah said this when he saw his glory," and he was speaking about him. Or what shall we say about Ezekiel?

For did he too not see him seated upon the cherubim? Or what are we to understand about Daniel, who says: "The Ancient of Days was sitting"? And again, what shall we call to mind about Moses, who said:

"Show me your glory"? And Jacob even received his name from this, for he was called Israel, which means "one who sees God." And many others also saw him. How then does John say: "No one has ever seen God"? Rather, he indicates this: that all those things were done by divine dispensation, and not that anyone has seen his natural essence; they were various visions granted by dispensation. For if they had seen the nature of the Godhead, it would not have been described by each of them in a different form, for that nature is simple, without form, uncompounded and uncircumscribed, and it neither sits, nor stands, nor walks.
For all these things belong to material bodies, but how he is, he alone knows.

And he indicates this through the prophet who says: "I multiplied visions, and in the hands of the prophets I took on likeness"; that is to say: "By dispensation I showed myself to you in different ways, and I did not reveal myself as I am." For since his only-begotten Son was going to appear in true flesh,
for this reason he made the prophets worthy to see him, each as he was able; but as God is, not only have the prophets not seen him,
but neither have angels and archangels seen him. But if you ask them about his nature,

You will hear nothing about him except this: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, and among men good will." And if you should wish to learn the mystery of the holy essence from the cherubim or the seraphim in turn, you will hear: "Heaven and earth are full of his glory." And if you ask the higher [?] powers, you will hear only his praise from all of them, for that is their work.

But they cannot see him; only the Son and the Holy Spirit see him, for no created nature at all could be able to see the Uncreated One. For if we are unable to see openly the nature of bodiless beings, who are themselves created,
and this has been shown many times through the angels, then how could anyone see that bodiless, uncreated nature?
For this reason Paul also says: "Whom no one has seen, nor is able to see." But what do you say: does this belong only to the Father and not to the Son? Listen to the same Paul, who says:
"He is the image of the invisible God." And the image of the invisible is itself invisible; if it were not, how could it truly be his image? For this reason he also says:
"Who was manifested in the flesh," for that manifestation was of the flesh and not of the nature of the divinity.

And so that you may know that he is invisible not only to men but also to angels, the great Paul, when he said, "God was manifested in the flesh," immediately added, "he appeared to angels." From this it is evident that he appeared to the angels as well at the time when he put on flesh.
But before this they could not see him, for that nature was invisible to them too.
If, then, someone should say: "And how does the Lord say: 'Do not despise even one of these little ones.
I tell you that their angels always see the face of my Father in heaven'?" But what does this saying mean:
does God have a face, and is he circumscribed in the heavens? Yet who could be so mad as to devise this? So what does this saying mean? For just as the one who says:
"Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God," speaks of that seeing of the mind which is possible for us, and of the understanding of God,

so too we understand concerning the angels that, because of the purity and wakefulness of their natures, they always see God by nature according to their capacity, and not that they see the nature of the divinity as it is.
For this reason Christ also says: "No one knows the Father except the Son." What then, are we all ignorant of him? May it not be so!
Rather, no one knows him in the way the Son does. For just as many have seen him according to their capacity, yet no one has seen the essence of God's nature,
so too many of us know God, but what his essence is, no one knows except the Only-begotten, who was born of him.

For by "knowing" he here means true [?] and knowledge, such as the Father has concerning the Son, for he says: "As the Father knows me, I also know the Father." For this reason, see also with what force the evangelist speaks.
For when he said, "No one has ever seen God," he did not say that the Son saw and declared him, but he says: "He who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him."
For sitting in the bosom is far superior to seeing,
for as to one who looks upon the edges, that he should understand everything — how could this be? It is impossible. But he who is in the bosom knows everything well.
And so that you may not say, "Although he knows more than all, yet he does not know how he is," the Evangelist therefore said:
"He is sitting in the bosom," and Christ himself said, "As the Father knows me, I also know him."
Ask, then, that opponent: "Does the Father know the Son?"
And if he is not completely mad, he will say, "He knows him well, and as he is."
And then from this statement prove to him that the Son too surely knows him well, and just as he is, for he himself said:
"As the Father knows me, I also know the Father," and again he says, "No one has seen God except him who is from God."

And for this reason, as I said, the Evangelist too mentions the bosom, and by this one word he shows everything: that the only-begottenness of that kinship is great, and that the knowledge of the Father and the Son is unchanging.

And their authority is equal, for if it were not so, would he be in his bosom, which is the condition of a beloved and equal son? And thus it is evident that he knows him perfectly, and is his equal and fellow counselor. Do you wish to understand also his being without beginning and without end?
Listen: Moses speaks concerning the Father, for when he asked,
"If the Hebrews ask me, 'Who has sent you?' what shall I answer?" God said to him:

"Say, 'He who is has sent me.'" Now as for what this word is, it signifies eternal being, being without beginning and being truly; and that "being from the beginning" signifies the same, for it signifies eternal being. And John uses this same word here to show that the Son is in the bosom of the Father without beginning and without end, as if he were saying: So that you may not suppose, because of your weakness, that he is some one of those made sons of God by grace, therefore hear this name of only-begottenness, set apart from all. And if you are still without understanding about this too, I will bring in a human expression as well in speaking of God, such as "He is in the bosom of the Father," only to free you from lack of understanding and from imagining lowly things. Do you see the love for humankind and the goodness of the Master, that he takes upon himself unbefitting names, only so that you may lift up your eyes and gain understanding through grace, and are you still bent down? Tell me, why has this coarse and bodily word "bosom" been mentioned in this place — so that we might understand God in a bodily way?

Far from it! Why, then, has this been said? So that we might understand what? Is it not evident that it was for nothing else than that we might understand the equality and the beginninglessness of the Son with the Father?

"He has declared him," it says. What did he declare? Only this, that "no one has ever seen God" and that "God is one"? But the other prophets said this too: Moses cries out, "The Lord your God, the Lord is one," and Isaiah says, "Before me there was no God, and after me there is none." What more, then, have we learned from the Son, who is in the bosom of the Father? First of all, these very words were spoken by his own power. And further, we have received from him far better and higher teaching: first, that God is spirit and that those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth; and that the sight of God is impossible and no one knows him except the Son; and that "he is the Father of the only-begotten Son"; and whatever else he said about him.

Now "declaring" signifies a clear and powerful act, which he performed and carried through not only toward the Jews but toward the whole world. For not even all the Jews listened to the prophets, whereas the whole world heard and believed the only-begotten Son of God. So "declaring" in this place signifies that manifest and firm teaching. For this reason he is also called "Word" and "Angel of Great Counsel." Since, then, we have received such great honor and a more perfect teaching, for God has spoken to us not through the prophets but through the Son himself, we ought therefore to show a way of life far higher and worthy of that honor. For it is a wicked thing if he himself humbled himself so far that he spoke to us no longer through servants but through his own self, while we show no life at all higher than that of former times. For those of former times had Moses as their teacher, but we have the King of Moses.

Homily 15, on love. Bless us, O Lord. Let us then show a way of life worthy of such honor, and let us have no fellowship with the earth; for this is why the teaching of this way of life was brought to us from heaven, so that we might follow the teaching of that Teacher as far as our strength allows.
And the imitation of him comes about in this way: that we seek not at all what is our own, but also what is our neighbor's, as Christ did.
And when a person seeks not what is his own but what is his neighbor's, then he is seeking what is his own,
for all that is our neighbor's is ours, since we are one body and members of one another. Let no one, then, say:
"That person is no friend of mine, nor a relative; how should I love him as I love my own?"
For consider: even if he is not a friend and a relative, he is still a human being of your own nature and a servant of the same King to whom you belong,
and a fellow inhabitant with you, for we all dwell in one world. And since he shares in your faith, see, he is also your member; for what friendship creates such close kinship as that unity of faith?
And for this reason we ought to love one another not merely as relatives and friends,
but as a member loves a member, for there is no greater form of love than this. Just as, then, you cannot say:
"Where does this kinship and closeness come from that you have toward your own self?"
For this saying is laughable; likewise it is not right to say this about a brother either, for all the baptized are one body. Let us not, then, disregard one another.

For no one disregards his own body and limbs, but pampers and cherishes them. For this reason God has given us one house, this world, and has divided everything among us in common; he makes one sun shine on us all, and has spread one roof over us, the sky, and given one dwelling, the earth, and one table of life, the table of the offering. He has given to all one form of birth, holy baptism; and the kingdom of the Father is one for all, and we all drink from one cup. It is not that more is given to the rich and less to the poor, but he has called all equally. So he has divided everything bodily among us equally, and the spiritual equally. Where, then, does this disorder come from? Only from the greed of the rich and from their arrogance. But let this be no more, brothers. Let these fleshly affairs not divide us, who are spiritually one, for everything fleshly is a shadow, and weaker than a shadow. Rather let us firmly keep the bond of love, and none of the passions will be able to break in to divide us from such unity. May we all be worthy to attain to it by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and unto the ages of ages, amen.
Chapter 16
The saying: "And this is the testimony of John, when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him: 'Who are you?'"
Interpretation: Envy is an evil thing, beloved; it is evil for the envious, and not for those whom they envy!
And first of all it harms them, like a deadly venom settled in their souls,
and if anywhere it should harm those against whom the envy is directed as well, the harm is slight, and [?] the benefit is greater than the harm.
Now I have said all this concerning the envy of the Jews, for those who went out from the cities to John and were baptized,
those same people, after their baptism, as though they regretted the deed, send to John and ask him: "Who are you?"
Truly, you offspring of vipers, evil and adulterous generation, do you ask and inquire closely after baptism?
For how did you go out to him? And how did you confess your sins?

How were you baptized? How did you ask what you should do, since you did not know where he came from? For all that conduct of yours was like that of brute beasts. But blessed John said none of this to them, nor did he reproach them, but answered with gentleness, so that he might all the more expose their wickedness. For John had testified to Christ many times, and when he baptized he said to everyone: "I baptize you with water, but he who comes after me, mightier than I, he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit." But they, since they always loved what is human and vain, did not want to submit to Christ, but rather held John in great esteem, while of Christ they said: "He is the carpenter's son";
and: "He is from Nazareth," which they held in contempt;
And that "He eats with tax collectors and sinners," he who was doing this in order to draw them to himself,
and because he did not wear a garment of camel's hair and a belt of leather. And all this those wretched men did not understand, but held Christ in contempt.
But when John was continually sending them to him, this matter seemed shameful to them, and they wished rather to have John as their teacher,
but they did not dare to say this openly; instead they sent to him not contemptible men,
but priests and Levites,
to ask him: "Who are you?"
For he was not an unknown man; even his birth became known to all, so that they were saying: "What then will this child be?"
When he came to the Jordan, everyone went out to him, and so it is evident

that they were not ignorant of who he was, but were questioning him for the reason I stated earlier. Hear, then, how the blessed John answered according to their thought and not according to their words.
For he did not say at once: "I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness," but first he removed that suspicion of theirs; for when they asked him: "Who are you?"
he confessed and did not deny, and he confessed: "I am not the Christ."
But they began to ask another question: "Are you Elijah?" And he said: "I am not," for they were also awaiting the coming of Elijah, as is written in another place.
And again they asked him: "Are you that prophet?" And he said to them: "I am not."
Yet he was a prophet; why then did he deny it? Because he saw their thoughts, and they had heard from Moses:
"The Lord God will raise up a prophet like me. Listen to him!"

For that one was Christ. Therefore they did not say to him: "Are you a prophet?", as one among the other prophets, but they said this: "Are you that prophet, the one of whom Moses spoke?" Therefore he said: "I am not" — not "I am not a prophet," but "I am not that prophet of whom Moses spoke." Then they said to him: "Tell us who you are, so that we may give an answer to those who sent us."
Do you see how they press him? But he with gentleness dispels every evil suspicion, and only then says of himself who he is. And he said to them:

Gospel: "'I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Make straight the ways of the Lord, as the prophet Isaiah said.' Those who had been sent were from among the Pharisees, and they questioned him and said to him: 'Why do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor one of the prophets?'"

Commentary: Do you see that I was not speaking idly when I said that they wanted to make him say, "I am the Christ"? It was for this reason that they were questioning him, and they did not say it to him openly. But once he had said to them:

"I am not the Christ," they then wished to conceal their own guile, and they spoke to him of Elijah and of that prophet. And when he told them: "I am not," they then abandoned that line of talk and revealed their crafty mind, and said: "Why do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor that prophet?"

For since they could not make him say by enticement what was not so, they then chose to press him in the manner of an accusation, so that he might say what was not so, but they could not. Yet he did not become angry, nor did he say, "Are you imposing a law on me?" Rather, he again brought forward a word of wisdom and sweetness and said:

Gospel: "I baptize you with water, but among you stands one whom you do not know, who is to come after me, the straps of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie." What then will the Jews say now? For behold,
they have prepared an unpardonable judgment against their own selves,
for they considered John trustworthy, and so truly
that had he been testifying not only to another,
but even about himself, one could say that they would have believed him. For we believe those who speak about themselves only when we hold them to be speakers of great truth.
And since they held John to be so trustworthy, why did they not believe his testimony,
which he gave concerning Christ? And they sent to him men of such distinction, priests and Levites,
and he confessed before all: "I am not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor that prophet," and he showed the supremacy of Christ;
and that "my baptism is small, but his is great and lofty."
And he brought forward the prophecy of Isaiah, which calls him Lord and John a servant.
And on top of all this, was it not right to believe in and worship the one to whom he testified and to confess him as God? "But among you stands," he says, "one whom you do not know."
For it appears that the Lord was mingled among the people, as he was always one who sought humility. And he says [?] this repeatedly: "He comes after me," as if he were saying:
"Do not suppose that all my power lies in this baptism. And if it were so perfect,
another would not be coming after me to give another, higher baptism. Rather, this baptism is his forerunner and preparation and image."
Gospel: "He was before me."

Interpretation: This means, "He is more honorable and higher than I." And he wished to show that he spoke of this supremacy in the sense that "he is not superior by only a little, but by so much that I am not even counted among the lowest of his servants," for the untying of sandals signifies this.

Homily 16: On pride, wealth and almsgiving. If John was not worthy to loose the strap of his sandals, John, than whom no one greater has arisen among those born of women, where shall we place ourselves? If he who was greater than the whole world said, "I am not worthy to be counted even among the last of his servants," what shall we say, we who are full of countless evils, who fall so far short of his virtue that heaven is not so far from earth? He said, "I am not worthy to loose the strap of his sandals," but those enemies of the truth dared to say, "We know him as he himself knows himself." What is greater than this pride, or more evil? Well did a certain wise man say, "The beginning of pride is ignorance of God." The devil would not have fallen from heaven had he not been seized by this disease; it was this that cast him down into Gehenna. This has become the cause of countless evils, this which alone is able to destroy all virtue, for what is exalted before men is abominable before God.

It is surely not fornication alone that defiles a man, but this as well. For fornication, though it is evil, has the desire of the flesh as its cause. But pride has no cause at all; it is an evil disease of the soul, born of lack of understanding. For nothing is more evil than a proud man, even if he is very rich; nothing is more foolish than he is, even if he has learned all the wisdom of men and possesses all power. For if a person who boasts about virtue and ascetic struggle loses all his reward, what shall I say of one who boasts about dreams and shadows, which is what the glory of this world is? For he is like a man who is dying of hunger and poverty, and who, if he somewhere sees some pleasant dream, exalts himself over it.

Wretched man, your soul is full of countless diseases, and you, because you have gold and silver, hold your mind higher than the clouds on that account. But that wealth is not yours, and if you do not believe me, look at the facts themselves. And if you are still drunk and do not understand from what has befallen others, wait a little, and from what befalls you yourself you will learn that all this profits you nothing, when death comes and you are not master of even a single hour, but against your will you leave everything behind, and perhaps those whom you would not wish,
they will carry it off. For many have not even been able to say a word, but,
so that this may not come upon us as well,
therefore, while we are still alive, let us send all that is ours ahead to that city, so that there we may find it all.
For there, there is no longer any fear of loss, neither from death nor from any other trial, but each one will delight forever in his own wealth.

Let us, then, transfer our wealth from here to there, for we have no need of caravans [?], or camels, or ships for this transfer. Rather, this business is done well through the poor, through the weak, the lame and the blind: they will carry it all from here to there, and they will bring us in, to the Merciful One, into the kingdom of heaven. May we all be worthy to attain it by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and unto the ages of ages, amen.
Chapter 17
Text: "This took place in Bethabara, beyond the Jordan, where John the Baptist was. The next day he saw Jesus coming to him and said:
'Behold the Lamb of God, who has taken away the sins of the world.'"
Commentary: A great boast is godly boldness, fearlessness before people, and that we should count everything as nothing compared with the confession of Christ.
And so great is this thing, as the only-begotten Son of God declares: "Whoever confesses me before men, I will confess him before my Father."
And this exchange is not equal, for if you confess him, you confess on earth, but he in heaven; and you before men, but he before his Father and the angels as well.
Such was the great John, for he counted everything as nothing and openly preached Christ.

For this reason the Evangelist also stated the place, to show his great boldness: that he preached not in a house or in a hidden place, but at the Jordan, in the midst of all the people who were being baptized. For it was there that he preached that great proclamation of Christ, saying: "I am not worthy to untie the strap of his sandals." This is why the Evangelist says:
"This took place in Bethabara, beyond the Jordan."
Gospel: "The next day he saw Jesus coming to him and said: Behold the Lamb of God, who has taken away the sins of the world."

Commentary: The Evangelists divided the periods of time among themselves. For Matthew shortened the account of the things done before John's arrest and speaks of those that came after it, whereas John dwells mostly on the things done before his arrest.
And he, in turn, passed over in silence the things done after John's coming from the wilderness and immediately spoke of the prison:
"When Jesus heard of John's arrest, he departed to the wilderness."
But John speaks of the things done after John's coming down from the wilderness, and after recounting those things he said:
"John had not yet been thrown into prison." But why did Jesus now come to him, not just once, but even twice?

For Matthew gave the reason for his coming, namely baptism, but John speaks of a coming even after the baptism. Why, then, did he come? Only for this reason: since he had been baptized by him along with the other crowds, it was so that no one would imagine that he was being baptized like one of the others, for the confession of sins. This is why he came to him a second time, to give that wonderful herald occasion to preach about him, and he did indeed preach: "Behold the Lamb of God, who has taken away the sins of the world." For how could he who takes away the sins of the world have sin himself?
But the saying:
"Behold, the Lamb of God," he said for the sake of the many who had been seeking him for a long time; he pointed him out and said to them:
"Behold, the one you were seeking: this is the Lamb of God."
He called him a lamb in order to remind the Jews of that prophecy of Isaiah and that figure given by Moses, so that from the type he might make them understand the truth.
That lamb took away no one's sins,
but this one has delivered the whole world from destruction and from the wrath of God.
Gospel: "This is he of whom I said: 'After me comes a man who was before me.'"
Commentary: Do you see how he explains "having been before him"? For when he had said, "who took away the sins of the world," he then added, "he was before me," in order to show
that this is what his precedence is: the taking away of the sins of the world and baptism with the Holy Spirit.
For I was able to do nothing else but to preach him and to perform this washing with water,
but he has the power to sanctify all people and to give the grace of the Comforter.
"This one was before me, for he is before me": that is, far greater and more glorious. Let all who have accepted the heresy of Paul of Samosata be ashamed, for they oppose such clear truth.
Gospel: "I did not know him."
Commentary: He makes his testimony beyond doubt, showing that there is nothing of human affection in it, but that it came about from divine revelation. For
how could one who did not know him speak falsely about him in order to please him? For this reason he says:
Gospel: "I did not know him, but so that he might be revealed to Israel, for this reason I came baptizing with water."
Commentary: For this one had no need of baptism, he says, nor do I baptize the people for any other reason than to preach Christ to them.
What then, could the preaching not have taken place without baptism?

It could not, for if there had been no baptism, the people would not have gathered to hear that preaching. For they did not go out in order to hear the preaching, but they went out to receive baptism and to confess, and when they came, they heard his preaching about Christ.
Gospel: "And John testified and said: 'I saw the Spirit of God descending from heaven like a dove and remaining upon him.'"

Commentary: He makes clear that he recognized him through the Holy Spirit. And again, so that no one may imagine that the descent of the Holy Spirit was needful for him, as it is needful for us, hear how he resolves this doubt as well and shows that the descent of the Spirit took place for the sake of preaching Christ. For he said:
Gospel: "I did not know him, but he who sent me to baptize with water said to me: 'He on whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he it is who will baptize with the Holy Spirit.'"

Commentary: Do you see that this was the work of the Holy Spirit, to reveal Christ? For John's testimony too was beyond doubt, yet he wished to make it still more credible. For this reason he referred it back to God and the Holy Spirit, since he had testified to so great and marvelous a thing, one that could astonish many: that he alone takes away the sins of the whole world, and that the height of that gift is sufficient as a ransom for so great a multitude.

For this reason he brings forward such undoubted testimony. And its purpose is this: to show that he is the Son of God and does not need baptism, and that the descent of the Holy Spirit took place only in order to make Christ known. For it was impossible for the Holy Spirit to be given by John, and those baptized by him show this, who said, "We have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit." And it is clear that Christ did not need baptism, but rather that baptism needed the power of Christ. For this alone was lacking, the chief of all good things: that the one baptized should be made worthy of the Holy Spirit. And Christ added this receiving of the Holy Spirit by his coming.
Gospel: "And John testified and said: I saw the Spirit of God descending from heaven like a dove, and it remained upon him.
I did not know him, but the one who sent me to baptize with water said to me:
'The one on whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, he is the one who will baptize with the Holy Spirit.' And I saw and testified that this is the Son of God."

Commentary: Again and again he says this word: "I did not know him." But why does he say this? Because he was his kinsman according to the flesh, as it is written: "Behold, Elizabeth your kinswoman has also conceived a son." And so that no one might say that he glorifies him because of his kinship, he says, "I did not know him." For he also lived always in the deserts, away from his father's house, and so his word was fulfilled. But if he did not know him before the descent of the Holy Spirit, how was it that before the baptism he tried to prevent him and said to him, "I need baptism from you"? For this is a sign of great knowledge. But he had not known him long before,
but God revealed him to him at the time when he sent him to baptize at the Jordan.

But before that he did not know him, for those wonders that took place in Christ's infancy, such as the one concerning the Magi and others of the kind, had happened long before, when John too was an infant, and much time had passed until the time of the baptism. For if he had known him, he would not have said, "I did not know him." And from this it is clear that those signs which certain people write down, calling them "the Childhood of Christ," are fables and lies told by certain vain men. For if he had performed signs from his very infancy,
John would not have been ignorant of him, nor would the people have needed another to preach about him. But now he says, "For this reason I came to baptize,"
so that he might be made manifest to Israel; for at that time God revealed this to him concerning him, and sent him to the Jordan to baptize and to preach.

For this reason also, before the descent of the Spirit, he said to the people: "After me comes a man who was before me." And for this reason too, to confirm his testimony, the Father also testified by a voice to the Son, and the Holy Spirit came down, so that he might confirm that voice as referring to Christ. For since John was baptizing and Christ was being baptized, so that none of those standing there might say:
"That voice was about John," for this reason the Holy Spirit came upon the Lord, so that he might set that doubt right.
And so it is evident that when he says, "I did not know him," he is speaking of former times and not of the time close to the baptism; otherwise,
how could he have said to him, "I need to be baptized by you?"
Now some say: "And how is it that the Jews did not believe, since not John alone saw the Holy Spirit come upon the Lord in the form of a dove, but they did also?"
Understand that for such visions spiritual eyes are needed and not bodily eyes only, so that people may not regard the event as something strange [?].
For they saw the miracles that Christ performed, and how he merely touched the blind and the lame and all the other sick, and immediately healed them.

And they were so drunk with envy that they strove to discredit all of this; would they then have cast off their unbelief through the mere coming of the Holy Spirit? But some say: "Not all of them even saw it, but only John and others who were in faith."
For although it was possible to see that descent of the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove with the bodily eye, yet it was by no means necessary that it be seen by all,
just as the prophet Zechariah also, and Daniel and Ezekiel and Moses, saw many things with the visible eye,
and no one else saw them; and not all the disciples saw the Lord's Transfiguration, nor the Resurrection either.
Gospel: "And I saw and have testified that this is the Son of God."
Commentary: For he had called him by way of announcement [?], and said that he was going to baptize with the Holy Spirit, but only now did he call him the Son of God,
for after the baptism the other evangelists no longer report any word of John, but begin on the miracles of Christ,

from which it is evident that they passed over all this and more than this in silence. And this same evangelist indicates this at the end of his account, that he has passed over many things in silence. For they were so far from falsehood that whatever is matter for reproach and contempt, all of them state with one voice, whereas of the miracles and praises, some are told by one or another of them, and some all four passed over in silence. I have not said this in vain, but on account of the wickedness of the pagans. For this is sufficient as a mark of the truth of the apostles, that they say nothing wondrous about him on their own account; and you should have this argument too against the opposition of the unbelievers.

Homily 17, that we ought to know the words of the faith well, and be careful about them; for it is an evil thing that a physician should labor over his own craft, and likewise a carpenter or a mason and every craftsman, while a Christian does not know the words of his own faith.

For their ignorance causes loss of money, but the ignorance of these causes spiritual loss. Yet we are in such wretchedness, for they are so zealous for their own craft, while we despise this, which is the cause of our life, as though it were nothing. So this state of affairs does not allow the pagans to abandon their error, for when they adorn and proclaim their error and falsehood with many words, while we, the servants of truth, cannot even open our mouths, how will they not say:

"Their law is surely very weak"? How will they not blaspheme Christ? And we are the cause of that blasphemy, we who do not wish to be vigilant in the words of life, but treat all such things as foreign to us and care for earthly things. And if someone disparages singers and horses, many speak countless praises of them, but if the conversation turns to Christianity, they fall silent and begin to scratch their heads, and so they go away mocked. And how is this matter not worthy of much wrath, if you have learned the praise of bards better than that of Christ? And if you are extolling that loathsome business, you find countless words, but do you not know how to praise the miracles of Christ, which saved the whole world? For we believe in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, the resurrection of the dead and eternal life. Now if one of the pagans asks you: "Who is this Father? Or who is the Son? Or who is the Holy Spirit? How is it that you speak of three gods, and yet you accuse us of polytheism?" what will you say, or what will you answer, and how will you refute his argument?

And if you are silent and he goes on to pose another question: "What is the resurrection of the dead? Shall we rise with this same body, or with another? And if we rise with this same one, why is its dissolution necessary?"

What will you say to all this? And again, if he says: "Why did Christ come only now and not many ages earlier? Or did he wish to receive human beings only now, and were we disregarded during all those earlier ages?" and if he brings up many other questions. For it is not good to state many questions at once and to be silent about their solutions, lest the unlearned be harmed all the more, and what has been said is enough to rouse you. For if they ask you this, and you cannot give even one word in answer, will you deserve only a small judgment, when you become the cause of such great error for those who sit in darkness? I would wish, if I had the time,
to bring forward the entire book of a certain wicked pagan philosopher,
which he has written against us, so that we might in this way be roused.
For if they have been so eager to speak evil of us, what do we deserve, when we cannot even withstand their words? Do you not hear what the Apostle says:
"Be ready to give an answer to all who ask of you an account of your hope"?
And again he says: "Let the word of Christ dwell richly among you." But what do the foolish say? "It is written that:

"the simple soul is blessed" and "he who walks in simplicity walks in hope." For this is the cause of all evils: that many use even the testimony of the Scriptures for what is not good. For Scripture does not bless the untaught and the foolish, but him in whom there is no wickedness. Otherwise, if it were as they say, that saying would be vain which says:

"Be wise as serpents and innocent as doves." But we, who have accomplished not a single good thing, how can we say this: "We are simple"? We who are more wretched than all, accusers of one another, and not correctors of our own faults. But now I beseech you, let us not merely accuse ourselves, but let us also acquire works of virtue, so that our life may be to the glory of God and we may find eternal glory, which may we be worthy to attain by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong glory and might, now and always and forever and ever, amen!
Chapter 18
The text: "The next day John was standing again, and two of his disciples.
He looked at Jesus as he walked and said: 'Behold, the Lamb of God.' And his two disciples heard him as he spoke, and they followed Jesus."
Interpretation: Human nature is negligent and quick toward perdition, not that it was created this way by God, but because of the evil of our wills.
Therefore it needs much teaching. For the earth, once it has received seed, immediately yields fruit, and it needs no second sowing.
But as for us, we would be blessed if, after receiving it many times, we were only then to yield fruit,
for at first the mind accepts teaching with difficulty, because of its great heat and because of the many thorns that choke it.
And then, when it has received the seed, from that point on it needs great diligence for the seed to grow, and again, when they have grown, so that they may remain firm,
for often, when the fruit has become full, something comes upon it and destroys it.
I have not spoken these words idly, but for this reason: so that when you hear of John that he says the same words,

you may not consider him a vain speaker, but may receive it with faith. For he wished that by that one saying alone all would hear, but since not many listened to him, because of their great negligence, he therefore rouses them a second time with his voice. For see how he says:
"He who comes after me was before me," and: "I am not worthy to untie the strap of his sandals," and: "He baptizes with the Holy Spirit and with fire,"

and: "I saw the Holy Spirit descending and remaining upon him," and he testified: "This is the Son of God." And no one listened to him, nor did anyone ask him: "About whom do you say this?" But he said again:

"Behold, the Lamb of God, who has taken away the sins of the world," and even so they did not come to understanding. Therefore he was compelled to say the same words again, so that by his word, as with a plow, he might plow up the hard ground of their minds, and he sowed the good seed in it. For this reason too he prolongs his discourse, for his one eager concern was only that he might make them understand Christ. For he knew that if only they recognized him, they would no longer need instruction about him from anyone else.

And so it happened, for when the disciples went and heard him for only one evening, they no longer returned to John, but attached themselves to him so fully that they took up John's work and appeared as preachers. For it says further on: "He found his brother Simon and said to him: 'We have found the Messiah, who is called Christ.'" See: when he was saying, "He who comes after me was before me," and, "I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandals," no one came to understanding. But when he spoke about his dispensation and brought his discourse down to a humble level, then the disciples followed him. For people do not come to love God so much when they hear something fearsome and of riches about him, as when they hear of goodness and a word of sweetness [?]. For when they heard, "He takes away the sins of the world," they immediately followed, as if they were saying:
"If the washing away of sins is taking place, why are we negligent, since here is the one who cleanses us without labor? Is delay not folly?"
Let sinners hear this word, those who put off their conversion until the day of death.
Gospel: "Again John stood, saw Jesus, and said: 'Behold, the Lamb of God.'"
Commentary: Christ says nothing, but John says everything, for just as a bridegroom says nothing, but others speak on his behalf and join the bride to him,
and once he has taken her, from then on there is no longer a mediator between them,

so too Christ came to receive the Church and himself kept silent, but his friend John brought the souls of men to be received by him; and when he had received them, from then on he arranged everything well for them and raised them up to those thrones of the Father.
But why did John not take his disciples aside by himself and say these words to them, but instead said before all the people: "Behold, the Lamb of God"?
Because there was nothing merely human about him, but everything was divine; for if he had spoken to them on his own and joined them to Christ, perhaps they would have turned back to him again.

But as it was, he preached among all, and they of their own accord chose to go to him for their own benefit and no longer for John's sake. For the prophets and apostles all preached Christ, some before the incarnation and some after the ascension, but John alone preached him before his face. For this reason he is called the friend of the bridegroom, for he made the beginning of good works.
Gospel: "And he looked at Jesus as he walked, and said: 'Behold, the Lamb of God.'"

Commentary: For not by voice only, but also with his eye he testified and rejoiced and was glad. And at this point he marvels at that great gift for which the Lord came, and he proclaims the manner of cleansing; and the Lamb signifies both of these. And he said, "He took away the sins of the world," yet he did not take them away only once, but he is always taking them away. It is not that he took them away only at the time when he was crucified, but from then until now he continually cleanses; not that he is continually being crucified, for once he offered a sacrifice for our sins, but he continually makes us holy through that one sacrifice. For just as he is the Word of God, and not a human word, and the Son of God, set apart from human sonship, and a prophet, but not like the others, and the good shepherd, not like other shepherds, and anointed, but not like the other anointed ones, so also he is the Lamb of God, but not like other lambs, rather the one who takes away the sins of the world. But why did John not go about throughout Judea and preach, but only stood on the riverbank and waited,

so that he might come and in this way John might show him to everyone? For this reason: because his concern was this, only to make him known and to persuade a few, at least, to listen to those words of eternal life.

But the greater and more surpassing testimony he left to him, so that he himself might accomplish it by deeds, as the Lord himself says: "I do not receive testimony from men, but the works which the Father has commanded me, they are what testify about me." And see how this way too was better, for as soon as he cast a small spark, immediately the furnace blazed up. For those who at first would not listen to those words said afterward: "Everything that John said about him was true."
And then again, if he had gone about preaching him, they would have supposed that he was doing this out of some human zeal, and they would not have held his testimony to be credible.
Gospel:
His two disciples heard him as he spoke, and they followed Jesus."
Commentary: John had other disciples as well, but they not only did not follow him, but were even jealous of him and said:
"Rabbi, the one who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you testified: behold, he is baptizing, and everyone is going to him,"
and again they murmured, saying: "Why do we fast while your disciples do not fast?"
But these two were better than all the others, and nothing of the sort happened to them; rather, as soon as they heard about him,
they immediately followed him. And they followed him not in order to slight their teacher, but rather because they believed his word.
And when they heard that he baptizes with the Holy Spirit, they followed him in order to learn what he has that is greater than John.

And see their eagerness joined with reverence, for they did not approach Jesus immediately and question him about lofty and great matters in front of everyone, but they were eager to speak with him in private,
for they knew that the words of their teacher were true.
Gospel: "Andrew, the brother of Simon, was one of the two who heard from John and followed him."
Commentary: Why did he give the name of [only one] and not tell us the name of the second, the one who followed? For some say that this was John himself, the evangelist, the writer of this Gospel.
But at that time there was no need at all to state his name in this place,
whereas it was necessary to state the name of Andrew, because further on he calls his brother.
And again, when you hear that Jesus said to Simon Peter: "Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men,"
and that this saying did not seem strange to him, it is so that you may know that he had already received his faith from the first from his brother.
Gospel: "Jesus turned and saw them following, and said to them: 'What do you seek?'"
Commentary: From this I understand that God does not anticipate our intentions with his gifts, but,
when we begin to will the good, then he pours out his many gifts upon us. "What do you seek?" he says.
What is this saying? Did he who knows the thoughts of people's hearts and sees hidden things ask a question?
But he did not ask in order to find out, for what need did he have to ask about this? He asked so that in this way he might give them greater boldness.

And he counted them worthy of speech and gladdened their hearts, for they were strangers to him and would doubtless have been ashamed to speak, since they held him in such regard because of that saying of their teacher. And therefore he asked, so that he might dispel their fear, shame and diffidence.

But they showed the longing they had for him not only by following, but also by their words. For before they had heard anything from him or learned anything, they called him teacher, placed themselves among the disciples, and showed him: "This is why we have followed you, to learn good from you." Therefore they did not delay, nor did they say: "Let us come tomorrow and listen," but they hastened to hear from him then and there, though it was the evening time, the tenth hour. See how they showed their eagerness.
O the wisdom of those blessed ones and the fervor of their faith!

And for this reason Christ did not give them a sign of the house, where it was, but said to them: "Come and see where I dwell," so that he might draw them all the more and show them that he had accepted them. And for this reason he did not say to them: "Come tomorrow and let us listen," but, as to his own friends and acquaintances, he said: "Come and see!" But how is it that he says in another place: "The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head,"

and here he says: "Come and see" where I dwell? But there he was indicating this: that he has no house or halls of his own, and not that he would not stay in a house. And so those disciples remained with him that night and learned teachings from him in a single night. Thus, as soon as dawn broke, both became teachers of others.

Homily 18: That every time is suitable for hearing divine words, and that we should flee from harmful conversations. Therefore let us strive to treat every other matter as secondary to hearing divine matters and words, and let us not consider any one time unsuitable for this. Rather, whether it is necessary to go to a stranger's house or to converse with unknown people, let us not be negligent in this on any account, for each of the affairs of this world has its own time, but for divine teaching every time is the proper time. For it is written: "In the law of the Lord he will meditate day and night." And Moses commanded the Jews to do this always, for as much as divine teaching enters into the soul, so much does it strengthen and enlighten it.

But we treat every hour as a time for vain and evil and soul-harming conversations: at dawn and at midday and at evening and by night we do this, and we set aside places for that idle talk. Yet if we hear divine teaching once or twice in a day, we are sated and grow weary of it.
What then is the cause of this? Only this: that our soul is grievously sick, and that its natural desire, which God gave it for desiring good things, we have turned toward evil things,
and for this reason it no longer longs for that spiritual food.
And this is a sign of great illness, when one has no desire for food.
And if in the body this is the mark of great illness, is it not all the more so in the soul?
But how can we strengthen what has become so enfeebled?
Only in this way: by constant exercise in the words of the prophets and the apostles and the Gospel and by all other teachings. And then we shall recognize
that it is far better to take these in than unclean foods, for that is what I call every harmful and idle conversation.
And tell me, what is better: that we talk about neighborhoods and cities and armies and battles, or about the affairs of heaven and

what is to become of us when we depart from this world? Or what is better: that we talk about our neighbor's affairs and speak evil of him, or that we talk about angels and virtues, which is of great benefit to us?
But some say: "When we speak once or twice about those divine matters, we exhaust everything, and we have nothing else left to say, and we grow weary of repeating the same words."
But what about those vain conversations, do you not consider this? You have spent all the days of your life in them, and have you still not exhausted the subject of those harmful and idle words?

But what shall I say of those still worse deeds that singers, buffoons and mockers present in their talk, by which people defile their own hearing, corrupt their souls, [?] the human mind with those wicked words, and gather every form of evil into their own minds? Evil images settle in their hearts, and the burning of fornication is kindled in their flesh when they bring a harlot into their midst, and she speaks those filthy words and makes those wicked gestures. She rolls her eyes wantonly, her mouth wounds the soul more than a sharpened sword, her body is like the devil's, and her cheeks, like the devil, do harm in many cunning ways. Have you not then been harmed even by my words? But do not be ashamed to say so, for our nature, inclined toward evil, seeks such things and is harmed even by hearing of them. But if, from my words alone, and merely by hearing them while standing in the holy church, the description of these words and the mention of those deeds appears harmful, what will become of those who shamelessly look on the very face of such wicked people? But perhaps one of you will say:

"If, as you say, even our nature seeks this, why do you blame us?" But it is not nature itself that has the love of evil things; rather, we have made it so. And further, even if it is a lighter charge against us, and not a great one, that we have a desire for evil, still the watching of those deeds is by our own will. And for this we deserve countless evils. For being burned by fire is also natural, so that if we come near it we are burned; yet that nature does not force us to fall into the fire. If we go in, the fault is ours and not nature's. Therefore I beg you: let us not pour ourselves into those evils, and let us not willingly fall into the fire, so that we may not be thrown unwillingly into that fire prepared for the devils. May we all be worthy to escape evils and to go to the bosom of Abraham, by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 19
This saying: "He first found his brother Simon and said to him, 'We have found the Messiah,' which is translated Christ, and he brought him to Jesus."
Interpretation: When God created man in the beginning, he did not leave him alone but gave him woman as a helper, for he knew
that great benefit would come from that union, even though that woman used the kindness wrongly.
But if anyone understands nature well, he will find great benefit from that union.
And one finds this benefit not only in the case of wife and husband; it is likewise also for those who are brothers.
This is why the prophet says: "What is so good, or what is so beautiful, as brothers dwelling together?"
This is also why cities and villages were built: so that we might be together not only bodily but also in way of life and in the bond of love. For since we are weak and each one cannot save himself,
God therefore arranged that we should help one another and fill up one another's deficiency.

I would like to prolong my discourse on this matter, to show how great a benefit unity is for us, but I hasten to speak of another matter, for the sake of which I have said all this. For when Andrew had stayed that night with Christ and had learned what he learned, he did not hide that treasure within himself, but he ran and gave to his brother as well of the good things he himself had received, and said to him: "I have found the Messiah," which is by translation Christ.

Do you see what teaching he learned in one night, so that he truly recognized Christ? Here he has now shown both the incomprehensible wisdom of the teacher, who so convinced him of the truth, and his own zeal as well, and that from the beginning they cared about this and awaited this,
for this is the speech of a soul that has long awaited his coming, and when it sees him,
it rejoices because its expectation has been fulfilled, and it brings the good news to others as well.
This is the conduct of good brothers! This is the goodness of a soul, when it strives for the benefit of another as well!
See from the beginning the good and obedient mind of Peter,
for he believed immediately and went to Jesus, and his brother brought him to the Lord,
so that he might teach him every good thing and give him to drink from that spring of immortality.
Gospel: "Jesus looked at him and said to him:
'You are Simon, son of Jonah. You shall be called Cephas, which is translated rock.'"
Commentary: Here he begins to display the works of his divinity and to reveal himself little by little through prophecy,
as he likewise did with Nathanael and again with the Samaritan woman, for no less than miracles do they astonish

people, these prophecies too, no less than miracles, for people often disbelieved the miracles and said: "He casts out demons by Beelzebul." But about prophecy nothing of the kind has been said anywhere.
If he displayed prophecy in the case of Peter and Nathanael, but not in the case of Andrew and Philip, it is because Andrew and his companion had firm assurance from John's testimony.
And Philip in turn believed when he saw how those standing there believed, but to Peter he prophesied and said:
"You are Simon, son of Jonah."

By what was known he made what was unknown credible to him, so that he might understand: would the one who knew his father's name not also know what is to come? Thus God is always glorified through prophecies.

For this work always belongs to God, and the demons have no power to imitate it. Although they strive greatly after miracles, and may perhaps perform them by illusion, they are utterly incapable of foreknowledge, and if they ever do attempt it, they do so by conjecture and deception, and they know nothing of the truth. But Peter answered the Lord nothing, for he did not yet know him well, for Christ too did not yet say to him: "I will call you rock. On this rock I will build the church," but: "You shall be called Cephas." For he was still speaking to him humbly and was not displaying his great authority.
But when he had taught him well the power of his divinity, then he spoke to him with authority: "You shall be called rock, and on this rock I will build the church."

And so he called Simon Peter, which means "rock," and the sons of Zebedee "sons of thunder," in order to show that he is the one who gave names in the old law: he called Abram Abraham, and Jacob Israel. To many he gave names from birth, such as Isaac and Samson and John, and to many others after the attestation of their parents, as he himself willed. At that time the names were of many kinds, but now all of us have one name, higher than all others, for we are called Christians and children of God and friends of the Lord and the body of Christ. This name is more sufficient than all of those to rouse us and to gain us the virtues.

Discourse 19: That we should use wealth well and not wickedly. Let us not, then, do deeds unworthy of this name of ours, we who are called Christ's, for Paul called us this, saying: "You are Christ's."

Let us understand the loftiness of this name. For if someone is called the man of a king or of a commander, he holds it a great honor to be called his. So then, we, upon whom is called the name not of an earthly king and ruler, nor of an angel or archangel or cherub, but of God himself, the King of all, shall we not lay down our life unto death, so that this name of ours may not be shown to be dishonored?
Do you not see how much honor those soldiers have who stand around the king?
But we have been made worthy to be close to Christ, not as to a king, but as the body is close to the head,
and should we not strive in every way to become like Christ? And if we wish to imitate Christ, hear what he says:
"Foxes have holes and the birds of the sky have dwellings, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head." And we too ought to live in this way,
but let me leave this aside because of your weakness and ask of you an easy thing: that you not be such great lovers of riches, and
just as I, because of your weakness, do not ask of you that perfect virtue, so you for your part should withdraw from that great wickedness.

And do not become slaves of your possessions, but become their masters. For riches are called "things for use" for this reason, that we should use them; for keeping belongs to a slave, but using belongs to a master. Riches were not given to us so that we might bury them in the ground, but so that we might distribute them to those who are in need.
And if God had wanted gold to be buried, he would not have given it to people but would have left it in the depths of the earth; but he gave it to us so that we might give to one another.

But if we hoard it, we are no longer its lord but its slave. And if you hoard it so that it may multiply, consider that merchants too scatter gold in order to gather in more: they board ships and travel to distant lands so that they may scatter their gold and gain more. And farmers scatter wheat in the ground so that they may bring in many times as much, and they labor over it for a long time. But you need no ship to travel to foreign lands, nor a yoke of oxen to plow the land, nor any concern about rain, or fear of hail, or the stirring of the sea, or fear of the rocks of the sea. Rather, this commerce and farming requires one thing: that you scatter your money, and that farmer will do all the rest, concerning whom Christ says: "My Father is the farmer."

How then is it not evil if, where this is given to us without labor, we are all negligent about it, while where there is great labor and care, and it is unknown whether it will come about or not, there we show all diligence?

Let us not, I beg you, let us not be so negligent about our own life. Instead, let us seek that in which the labor is not great and the profit is abundant, so that we may attain the eternal good things by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
Chapter 20
This saying:
"On the next day he wished to go out to Galilee, and he found Philip and said to him:
'Follow me.' Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter."
Commentary: The Lord says: "Everyone who seeks shall find."
And for this reason Philip too found discipleship to Christ. For whereas Andrew had heard from John, and Peter from Andrew, this man had heard from no one, except when he heard the word of the Lord,
and immediately he followed him and became his preacher, and he converted Nathanael, for he said to him:
"What Moses wrote in your Law and the prophets, we have found."

Do you see what kind of spirit he had, he who constantly trained himself in the words of the Law? And it is a marvel concerning Andrew and Peter and Philip, not only that they believed before seeing signs, but also this, that they came from such an untaught place, about which it says:
"Out of Galilee no prophet has arisen."
And yet such men appeared from there. But here too Christ displayed his power, for from so fruitless a land he brought forth such luminaries.
But how did Philip know that this is the Christ? I think that he learned it from Peter and Andrew.
And for this reason he followed quickly. And the evangelist also mentions his village, so that you may know that God chose the weak of the world.
Gospel: "Philip found Nathanael and said to him: 'What Moses wrote in the Law and the prophets, we have found: Jesus, son of Joseph, from Nazareth.'"
Commentary: Since Nathanael was learned in the Law and a seeker of the truth,
as Christ testifies, for this reason Philip brought forward the Law and the prophets as witnesses, so that he might persuade him in this way.
And if he called him the son of Joseph, do not be troubled,
for at that time he was still supposed to be the son of Joseph. And just as Andrew could not preach to Peter forcefully,
but he brought him to Christ. Philip did likewise: he did not say what Christ is like, or how the prophets had preached him,
but only hastened to bring him to Christ, for he knew that if he heard his teaching, he would no longer depart from him.
Gospel: "And Nathanael said: 'Can anything good come from Nazareth?' Philip said to him: 'Come and see.'
When Jesus saw Nathanael coming to him, he said of him: 'Behold, a true Israelite, in whom there is no guile.'"
Commentary: Because he said, "Can anything good come from Nazareth?", for this reason he praises him.
