And was it not rather blame that was called for? No indeed, for Nathanael did not speak this word out of wickedness and unbelief, but because he was learned in the Law and had read in the Scriptures that
"Christ is to be born in Bethlehem."
And he heard "from Nazareth," and for this reason he was astonished.
But see his goodness, for he did not say to Philip,

"You are deceiving me, and you yourself are in error," but he rose and followed, in order to learn the truth. And by not accepting that he came from Nazareth, he showed his steadfastness in the word of the prophets; and by going with Philip, he further revealed his own longing for the coming of Christ, for he reasoned: perhaps he was born in Bethlehem,
and Philip does not know it.

But see how his speech too is full of wisdom, for he did not say, "It is impossible that anything good should come from Nazareth," but in the form of a question and with gentleness he said to him, "Can anything good come from Nazareth?"

But see also the wisdom of Philip: when he saw that he did not believe, he did not leave him either, but persisted until he had brought him, and from the very beginning he showed the firmness that befitted the apostles.

But when Jesus saw Nathanael, he said: "Behold, truly an Israelite," for there is also the false Israelite. But he was not so, for his judgment was impartial [?] and true, not like that of the Jews, who before seeing him said, "Christ is born in Bethlehem," and when they saw him, they said out of their great envy,

"We do not know where he is from." But this man, both before seeing and after seeing, had one and the same mind, seeking what is good, and he understood that he had not been born in Nazareth, but was called a Nazarene because of his upbringing there.
Yet Christ did not say to him, "I am not a Nazarene," or

"I was born in Bethlehem," for many others too had been born in Bethlehem and were not Christ. Instead the Lord showed him in another way that he truly is the Christ, for when Nathanael said, "How do you know me?", Jesus answered:
Gospel: "Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you."
Commentary: See a man steadfast and calm: he did not become puffed up by that praise,
but began to question, in order to learn how he knew him.

And he questioned him as one would a man, but Jesus answered him as God: "Before Philip called, I saw you under the fig tree," for no one was with them when Philip and Nathanael were speaking, and the Lord told him the place, and the tree, and the substance of Philip's words,

so that in this way he might understand that he is true God. Having understood that he is undoubtedly the Christ, because of that prophecy and his knowledge of hidden things, he rejoiced and confessed and said:
"Rabbi, are you the Son of God? Are you the King of Israel?"
Do you see a soul rejoicing over the matter: "You are," he says, "the one whom I was always seeking"? Do you see his truthfulness and his love of God?
Instruction 20: That we should love God not by word only, but also by deed. In the same way, then, we too ought to rejoice, so that we may become worthy to know the Son of God,
but we ought to rejoice not in mind only, but also in deed, by doing his commandments. And if we anger him, how will it be evident that we rejoice over him?
Do you not see how, when some friend comes to us and we rejoice over him, we hasten in every way to fulfill his wish?

But if we do not fulfill his wish, even though we say ten thousand times that we rejoice at his coming, he does not believe that word. So too here: if we are to show that we truly rejoice at his coming, let us not anger him in anything; let us adorn the house into which he is entering, and let us set before him the supper that he desires. And what that supper is, he himself has said: "This is my food: that I do the will of the one who sent me." If we see him hungry, let us feed him, and if thirsty, let us give him drink. Even if our gift is small and worthless, he accepts it, whether cold water or two mites, for since he has no need of anything, he does not seek much either, but rather goodness of mind.

Only let us show that we love him and that we rejoice at his coming. Let us see how he is toward us: for he laid down his life for us, and after this he asks of us. And if we give him what was given by him, he accepts it as if we had given what was our own. I know that all Christians say, "Who would not love him?" And no one denies him in word and in mind. But love ought not to be in word only, for if we say in word, "We love," and do not act in deed, this is contemptible not only to God but also to men. Rather, let us show our love for him by deed, so that he too may acknowledge us on that day, when before his Father he acknowledges the worthy. For to him belongs the glory, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 21
This saying: "Nathanael answered and said to him, 'Rabbi, are you the Son of God? Are you the King of Israel?'
Jesus answered and said to him, 'Because I said to you that I saw you under the fig tree, you believe; you will see greater things than these.'"
Interpretation: We need great diligence, beloved, so that we may understand the depth of the holy Scriptures,
for they cannot be understood thus without toil; rather we need fervent prayer and great diligence, so that we may understand those words.

For behold, today too we have read no small question: how, when Nathanael said, "You are the Son of God," Christ answered, "Because I saw you under the fig tree, you believe this; you will see greater things than these."
And what is the question in this saying?
For when Peter, after seeing so many miracles, said: "You are the Son of God,"

the Lord blesses him, saying: "You have received this revelation from the Father." But Nathanael said this same thing before seeing miracles and before any teaching, and Christ said nothing of the kind to him,
but, as though he had said nothing, Christ in this way leads him up toward something higher. What is the reason for this?
Only this: that the words of this man and of Peter were the same, but they did not speak them with the same mind; rather, this one spoke with one mind and that one with another.
Peter confessed him as Son of God, as true God, whereas this man still regarded him as a man. That is why he also added:
"You are the King of Israel," whereas the Son of God is King not only of Israel, but of the whole world and of all creatures. Because Peter's faith was complete, Christ said to him:
"On this rock I will build the church." But because this man still fell far short of the measure of faith, he therefore added what follows and said:

Gospel: "Because I said to you, 'I saw you under the fig tree,' you believe; you will see greater things than this. And he said to him: 'Amen, amen, I say to you: from now on you will see the heavens opened and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man.'"

Commentary: Do you see that he raises him up from the earth and teaches him not to consider him a mere man? For how could he whom angels serve be a man? That is why he said: "You will see greater things than this," that is, the ministry of the angels. And what he says amounts to this: "This seems great to you, O Nathanael, and for this reason you have called me King of Israel;
but when you see the angels ascending and descending upon me, what will you do then?"
So that in this way he might persuade him,

so that he might confess him as King of the angels; for they continually came to him as servants: at the time of the crucifixion, and of the resurrection and the ascension, and when he was in the desert, and at the time of his birth, and many other times.
But to these words Nathanael answered nothing, and therefore Christ brought his speech only this far and left off,
so that he might come to understand the force of those words by himself, for: "He sowed the seed in good ground and left it, so that it might spring up."
Gospel:
"On the third day there was a wedding at Cana of Galilee.
And the mother of Jesus was there. And Jesus and his disciples were invited to that wedding."

Commentary: I have said on another occasion that he was known in Galilee, and that is why they invited him to that wedding; not that they had any lofty thought about him, but they invited him as one among many and as an acquaintance.
But he considered nothing beneath his dignity, he who put on the form of a servant and sits with tax collectors and sinners, for he always arranged what was best for us.
Gospel: "And when the wine ran short, his mother said to Jesus:
'There is wine here [?]'"

Interpretation: Before his baptism the Lord had performed no miracle, but from then on he began to work miracles. For in his childhood he had done nothing else wondrous, except, as Luke says, when he sat among the teachers at twelve years of age and taught and listened to teaching. Apart from this he had done nothing else at all, and for this reason he was unknown to everyone.

But if he had been performing miracles from the beginning, he would not have been unknown, just as, when he began to perform miracles, his name spread in a short time throughout all Syria. But it would have been unfitting in many ways to perform miracles from the beginning,

for many would also have become unbelievers, just as they did later. Would they not have become unbelievers all the more because of his youth? And the crucifixion would have been carried out early, which was not proper. But the Lord, in his wisdom, performed no miracle at all until his baptism, and for this reason he was unknown.

But his mother had knowledge of his greatness from that great and wondrous conception and from the preaching of John. And because it was the time of his manifestation, she said to him here in entreaty, "There is no wine," so that in this way the glory of her son might be revealed. For this reason the Lord said to her:
"What is there between you and me, woman? My hour has not yet come."

Yet it was not that he was despising his mother and therefore spoke to her in this way, far from it! Rather, it was to teach her well his own power, who he is, and how reverence and honor are due to him; and so that she might not regard him as other mothers regard their sons,
and because, where it was not proper, he would not listen to her, as when he was among the people and teaching, and they came and were looking for him, and he himself said,
"Who is my mother, or who are my brothers?" For the Lord always arranged what was best of all, and again, for this reason he refused to obey in this place,

for he did not wish to perform that miracle at his mother's word, so that it would not be doubted by many. Instead he waited for the masters of the house to entreat him, so that in this way the matter would be beyond doubt and praiseworthy. For all these reasons, then, he answered his mother in this way, to teach her too what was proper, and so that the miracles might be done as was fitting.

Homily 21: That it is necessary to acquire virtue, and that the holiness of parents avails us nothing. But you, understand all this; and again, when you hear that "A certain woman cried out: 'Blessed is the womb that bore you and the breasts that you sucked.' And the Lord said: 'But blessed are those who do the will of my Father,'" understand that he is saying this:
If she herself had not been truly great and holy and adorned with every virtue, my birth would have availed her nothing at all.
And if this is so with Mary the God-bearer, let none of us boast any longer, saying, "I have a holy son, or father, or brother, or some other relation."

For if we are not adorned with virtue, no one will avail us on that day; only virtues and hope in God will. For the Lord too had many relatives, those kin of his mother, yet we do not even know their names, whereas the apostles were not his relatives, but on account of their virtue they appeared so great.

So let us not pride ourselves on the holiness of our kin, but let us ourselves strive to become pleasing to God, for this is all the more cause for condemnation, if we have a holy father, or son, or brother, and we ourselves are wicked. I say all this because many negligent people, when someone teaches them about virtue, say: "Our father and grandfather and brother were holy men."

But I would say to such a person: "Wretched one, this is all the more cause for your condemnation, that you had such examples of virtue and did not imitate them, for the virtue of parents is always a condemnation to negligent children, as the prophet says in reproach of Israel: Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he kept purity."

And the Lord says: "Abraham your father rejoiced that he would see my day." But we who know all this, let us strive to become pleasing to God by our own virtue, so that we may not rely on the virtue of others and then come to realize it when it can no longer benefit us.
For it says:

"In hell who will confess you?" Rather, let us repent here and now, so that we may find the eternal good things, which may we be worthy to attain by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 22
This saying: "What is there between you and me, woman?
My hour has not yet come."
Interpretation: Teaching too involves much labor.
But you are masters of this labor, whether to make it heavy for us or to lighten it for us,
for if you turn aside from our words and do not carry them out in deed, you make the labor heavy upon us.
But if you carry out our words well, we regard this work not as labor but as joy, when we see the fruit of our words.
Now then, if it is our wish that this work not be a grief to us, show us the fruit of our words,
so that we may carry out what follows with joy as well.
For today too we have no small question to examine: that the mother of the Lord said to him, "They have no wine," and he answered, "What is there between you and me, woman?
My hour has not yet come." And afterward he did the very thing his mother had told him.
But what does this saying mean, which is spoken not only here but in other places too? For the Evangelist says:
"They could not seize him, for his hour had not yet come." And again he says:
"They wanted to lay hands on him and could not, for his hour had not yet come." And again he says: "Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son."
What then does this saying mean? For I have gathered many instances for this reason, so that I may give one explanation for them all,

for it is not that he, the Creator of times, was under the compulsion of times, nor did he say "My hour has not yet come" as though some hour were set before him and he could not act without it. Rather, he was indicating this:
that each thing ought to be done in its own time, for he did not do everything at once,

but each in its own time, so that nothing should be done in disorder. For it was not fitting that he should bring about birth and resurrection and judgment all at once. For he created the world, but not all of it at once: some things on the first day, some on the second day, and some on the sixth.
And again, the death of human beings and the resurrection for judgment had to take place, but God did not do both at once.

And again, he had given the old law, and then, in its own time, the new one as well. And so the Lord was not subject to times; rather, he himself established the order of times, as their Creator. For this reason he said here too: "My hour has not yet come." This saying means the following: the Lord was still unknown among that people, and only the disciples Andrew and Philip were with him, and those who were at the wedding did not know his glory.

And the Lord says to the Mother of God: "My hour has not come," that is to say: "I am not yet known among this people, and not everyone yet knows that the wine has run short. Be silent, then, so that they may entreat me first, so that I may not act at your word and the miracle become suspect." But why did he say:

"My hour has not yet come," and then do the very thing his mother had told him? First, in order to put to shame those who say, "He was subject to times." For if that were so, how could he have done the deed then, when he had said, "My hour has not yet come"? And again, so that he should not be entirely disobedient to his mother; and further, so as not to put a suspicion of weakness into anyone's mind. For his mother also told the servants to go to him and said, "Whatever he says to you, do it," since she knew that he had not refused out of weakness.
Gospel: "There were six stone water jars there, in keeping with the purification of the Jews, into which they would pour two or three measures each. And Jesus said to them:
'Fill those jars with water.' And they filled them to the brim."

Commentary: It was not idly that he said, "in keeping with the purification of the Jews," but so that no one could say that those jars were actually wine jars, that dregs had remained in them, and that when the water went in on those dregs it mixed and became wine. For this reason he said it, as if to say: there had never been wine in them, but they kept them there full of water for their purification. But why did he not perform the miracle before they were filled with water, which would have been more wondrous? For it is one thing to change one substance into another substance, and quite another to bring what does not exist at all into being. Yet although that deed would have been more wondrous, many would have regarded the deed as an illusion. Therefore he ordered the servants to do the filling, so that they themselves might be witnesses that it was water that had been poured in there; and again, in order to show that he is the same one who in the vine changes water into wine, and turns the substance that comes from rain into wine. For this reason he did this: because what takes place there over a long time, he did at that wedding in an instant.

Gospel: "And he said to them: Draw some out now and bring it to the steward of the feast." And they brought it, and when the steward of the feast tasted the water that had become wine, and did not know where it had come from, though the servants who had filled the jars with water knew, the steward of the feast called the bridegroom and said to him: "Every man serves the good wine first, and when they have become drunk, then the poorer wine as well; but you have kept the good wine until now."

Commentary: He commanded them to bring it to the steward of the feast, who was not drunk but alert, so that through him and through the bridegroom the matter might be understood and made plain. When they tasted the flavor of that wine, it was so good, for such were the miracles of Christ, far surpassing what is natural; and whenever he healed a weak limb, he made it more beautiful than the healthy one.
And here too the steward of the feast and the bridegroom were witnesses to the excellence of the wine, while the servants were witnesses that this water had been made into wine by Christ,
since they were the ones who had filled the vessels with water.
Homily 22, on gluttony. So at that time Jesus changed water into wine, and both then and now he does not cease to change slack and negligent minds,
for there are people who differ in no way from water, so cold and negligent are they.

So let us bring such minds to the Lord, so that he may change them from the likeness of water into the firmness of wine, so that they may be strong and a cause of joy both for themselves and for others.
And who are these cold ones, if not those
who do not despise the affairs of the world and vain pleasure,
but are lovers of glory and of pleasure, which pass away more quickly than flowing, unresting water?
For often the one who is rich today becomes poor tomorrow, and the one who is glorious today
is taken into prison tomorrow. And again, the glutton is likewise like water: he fills his belly mightily and at once it is emptied. For corruption,
as with water, makes it vanish,
and he immediately fills it again, and it is always flowing, like water,
for every affair of this world is by nature unstable, but pleasure and gluttony do not merely flow away themselves;
with their flowing they also sweep away the strength and purity of the soul and undo the health of the body. For a raging river does not eat away its banks
as much as many foods eat away health. And if you go to a physician's house and ask, you will hear that every cause of disease comes from this,
for a simple table is the mother of health. For this reason physicians have called not being sated health, and it is written in their books that not being sated with food is health.

Now if a shortage of food is the mother of health, then surely satiety is the mother of every disease. For gout and blindness and tremors and fits of madness and [?] and [?] head ailments, long [?], and many other things come not from want but from gluttony.

And they will also see the diseases of the soul that are born from it: greed, sloth, filthiness, and sleep, and every other evil. And again, there is no taste in their eating either, for fasting is the mother of the tastiness of food, while satiety dissolves and destroys the taste of foods. Therefore, since gluttony is so evil, let us flee from drunkenness and satiety and let us take our delight in the Lord, so that he may grant us the request of our heart and bestow on us the eternal good things, for his is the glory now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 23
This saying: "This Jesus did as the beginning of signs in Cana of Galilee."
Commentary: The devil strives greatly and always to destroy us. Therefore we need great diligence, so that he may find no place at all with us,
so that he may not little by little establish all his power among us; for it is an evil thing and a folly
if he strives so hard to destroy us and we do not labor for the life of our souls.
Now I have spoken these words because I am afraid that the wolf may snatch a sheep from the midst of the flock and carry it off through our sloth,
for the wound of the soul is invisible, and no one knows what is in a person except his own spirit.

And therefore my word is addressed to all, and let each one take it as he wishes. For I do not know who is sick or who is healthy; therefore I speak words of many kinds, sometimes about greed, and again about gluttony, and then about fornication, and again about almsgiving, so that in this way each one may take whatever medicine he wishes. For I am afraid that I may always be treating one particular passion while another passion, unnoticed, kills someone. Therefore I speak words of various kinds, so that you may cleanse yourselves of every passion and thus hear the divine words that we have also read today.
Gospel:
"This Jesus did as the beginning of signs in Cana of Galilee."
Commentary: Some say that this was not the beginning of his signs, but that it was the beginning of signs only in Cana of Galilee, as it says:
"This was the beginning in Cana of Galilee."
But I do not dispute about this; rather, I affirm this: that before his baptism he had performed no sign, but that after his baptism he began to perform signs.
Gospel: "And he revealed his glory."
Commentary: He revealed his glory as far as it was fitting for him; and if the Jews did not believe,
this is a mark of their wickedness; but his disciples believed,
for it was fitting to perform a sign where the disciples, or some others, would come to faith.
Gospel: "After this he went down to Capernaum, he and his mother and his brothers,
and his disciples with him, and he stayed there not many days. And the Passover of the Jews was near.
And he went up to Jerusalem and found in the temple the sellers of oxen and sheep and doves, and the money changers sitting, and he made a whip of cord and drove them all out of the temple."

Commentary: He went down with his mother to Capernaum and stayed there a short time for the sake of honoring her, and then he went up to Jerusalem and did there that wondrous deed, full of great authority,
For he drove out those selling oxen and sheep and all the money-changers, and said to them: "Do not make my Father's house a house of trade."
But another evangelist says: "He was driving them out and saying to them:

'Do not make my Father's house a den of robbers.'" Yet the evangelists do not contradict one another, God forbid! Rather, they show that he did this deed twice and not at one time: this one took place a short time after his baptism, and that one close to the time of his Passion.

But why did Christ do this, coming upon them with such wrath and driving them out with a whip, which he never did when they insulted and blasphemed him? It was because he was going to perform a miracle on the Sabbath and to accomplish many other such things, which they reckoned as transgression of the Law, and so that no one would have grounds to say that he was opposed to the Father and a destroyer of the Law.
For this reason he did this. For how could it be that he who showed such great zeal for the temple would be opposed to the King of that temple, who was served in it?

For the earlier times too, which he had spent in keeping with the Law, were enough to show that he was not an opponent and destroyer of the Law. But since those were to be forgotten by everyone, he therefore also did this before all the multitude that had gathered for the feast, so that all might see that he was one who sought the honor of God, and that he would choose to let anything at all come upon him for the honor of that house. And not by deed only, but by word also he showed his unity with God. For he did not say "the holy house," but "my Father's house."

See now, he even called him Father, and they were not angered, for they supposed that he was speaking merely in a plain way. But when he began to confirm that word, then envy came over them. And now they said to him: "What sign do you show us?" O senselessness! For they were seeking a sign for putting a stop to that evil business, and that great zeal for what is good did not serve them as a token of his majesty and virtue. But his disciples, who were full of goodness of spirit and sincerity, remembered the Scripture that says:
"Zeal for your house has consumed me." But those men did not remember that prophecy, and they said to him:
"What sign do you show us?" For they were grieved that he wished to do away with the occasion of their greed, so that by those words he might restrain them.
For this reason also the Lord did not give them a sign, just as earlier, when they asked for a sign.
And the Lord said to them: "An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign shall be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah."
And then he spoke that word to them openly, but here somewhat in a parable.
And he does this because of their utter senselessness, for he saw the wickedness of their minds. Otherwise, if it had not been so,
he who many times performed signs without their asking would not have refrained from showing a sign. But here, since he saw their wickedness, for this reason he, the seer of minds, said to them:
The Gospel:
"Destroy this temple, and on the third day I will raise it up."
Commentary: He says many such things which were not understood by the people of that time but were made plain to those who came afterward.

And why then does he do this? So that it might be shown that he knew from the beginning everything that was to come, as happened with this prophecy: after his resurrection the disciples remembered that word which Jesus had said to them. But at that time some were astonished at that saying, and some mocked,
and they said:
Gospel: "This temple was built in forty-six years, and will you build it in three days?"
Commentary: They spoke of forty-six years with reference to the last building, for the first was completed in twenty years.

But why did the Lord not explain that figure of speech and say, "I am speaking of my body and not of the temple," but instead kept silent? Because he knew that, on account of their unbelief, they would not accept that word,

for, in the first place, they did not believe in the resurrection, and furthermore, they did not believe this either, that he is God. The Lord indicated both of these by that one saying, when he said:
"Destroy this temple, and on the third day I will build it."

For when they demanded a sign, the Lord said this to them because nothing else could so clearly show that he is not a mere man as this: that he so prevailed over death, and so thoroughly undid its tyranny and its heavy warfare.
Therefore he says:

"When you lift up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he." When I rise and draw all the world to myself, then you will know that I have done all this as God and the only-begotten Son of God. But they were full of wickedness; for this reason some of the Lord's words they did not listen to at all, and others they listened to with a wicked mind.

But this must be inquired into: how did the disciples not know that he was to rise from the dead? The answer is that they had not yet been made worthy of the grace of the Holy Spirit. Therefore they repeatedly heard the words about the resurrection and could not understand those words, but kept wondering what those words might mean; for it is a very marvelous and strange thing to speak of raising oneself from the dead. For this reason he also rebuked Peter, for Peter did not yet know about the resurrection and said to him, "Mercy on you, Lord." And Christ did not reveal the force of that saying before the resurrection, so that they would not become unbelieving because of it; for the matter itself was very marvelous, and they did not yet know the Lord very well, who he is. Therefore he did not reveal it until his word had been fulfilled in deed, for no one becomes unbelieving toward a word fulfilled in deed, whereas many become unbelieving toward a mere word. So, once his word had been fulfilled in deed, he then gave them understanding of the things previously said, through the Holy Spirit, as he said: "He will teach you and remind you of everything that I say to you."

For how could those who abandoned him and fled on the night of his arrest have remembered the deeds and sayings of all those times, unless the Holy Spirit had reminded them, whom God gave them and whom they received through the beauty of their own virtue? For at first the coming of the Holy Spirit upon them took place so richly and gloriously by the grace of God, but the retaining of that grace came about through their virtue. For they showed a radiant way of life and great labors, and they despised this passing life and paid no regard to anything human, but rose above all of it and, like winged creatures, flew up to heaven; and for this reason they held the grace of the Holy Spirit unfailingly.

Homily 23, on mercy. Let us then imitate them ourselves, and let us not quench our lamps, but keep them shining through mercy, for the light of this fire is unquenchable. Let us gather oil in our vessels while we are still here,
for there, there is no marketplace, nor can anyone receive it from anyone else, except from the hands of the poor.

So let us gather it richly here, if we wish to enter with the bridegroom and not be left outside. For even if we accomplish ten thousand virtues, without mercy we cannot enter the kingdom. Rather, let us acquire it eagerly, so that we may become worthy of the eternal good things by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom glory befits the Father together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 24
This saying: "And when he was in Jerusalem, at the Passover, at the feast, many believed in him."
Commentary: Of the people of that time, some had turned to error and some listened to the truth,
and some of them would turn and then fall away again; these Christ likened to different kinds of ground: some to rocky ground, some to thorny ground, and some to good ground.
And the Evangelist indicates this and says: "When he was in Jerusalem, many believed in him, as they saw the signs that he was doing."
But Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them,
for the true disciples were those who turned and followed him not because of signs but through teaching.
Signs convert the coarser sort, and teachings the more discerning; and those who were converted through teaching were strengthened all the more by signs.
These are the ones Christ called blessed, saying: "Blessed are those who have not seen me and have believed in me."
But those who believed at this time were not very genuine. For this reason the Lord, who knew all things, did not entrust himself to them,
for he had no need of testimony from anyone, but he himself knew everything and saw their hearts.
For this reason he did not believe their words, and for this reason he did not entrust himself to them as to people who were firm, for trusting words is a human thing,
but seeing hearts belongs to God alone, who created hearts,
for the Prophet says: "You alone know hearts." So he had no need of witnesses in order to know the hearts of those he had created,
He who knew all things to come and all things unseen also knew how easily they would change toward evil, and for this reason he did not entrust himself to them.
Gospel: There was a certain man of the Pharisees, named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. He came to him by night.
Commentary: Elsewhere in the Gospel, too, this man is seen to have striven on Christ's behalf, for he said to them:

"Our law judges no one unless it first hears from him." And again, at the time of the Passion, he showed great zeal, for Nicodemus too came by night and brought myrrh and aloes, a hundred pounds. Even now he had faith in Christ, but not as he ought; for this reason he came to him by night, because by day he was afraid. But the man-loving Lord did not turn him away, nor did he drive him from his teaching, but taught him high and great teachings.
But hear what Nicodemus says:
Gospel: "Rabbi, I know that you have come from God as a teacher, for no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him."
Commentary: Nicodemus still had a merely human notion, and he spoke to him as to some prophet: "I know that you have been sent from God as a teacher."
But Christ did not rebuke him at all, saying, "Why do you have a merely human notion of me?" For the Lord himself says: "I did not come to judge the world, but to save the world."
And as I have often said, [?] "you have been sent from God as a teacher."
But it was so that he might save many and convince everyone that he does nothing contrary to the Father.
For this reason the Lord often speaks with humility, but in deed,
when he performs signs, he reveals there his own authority, as when he said to the leper: "I will it; be cleansed!" and:
"Young man, arise!"
and "Your sins are forgiven you!" and "Take up your bed and walk!"
and "I say to you, demon, come out!" and "Let it be done for you as you wish!" and "Today you will be with me in Paradise."
And from all of these we see his authority,
for no one had anything to say against his deeds,
but over his words many stumbled, those senseless people, and they would say: "He speaks arrogantly."
For this reason he does not speak an exalted word to Nicodemus openly, but teaches him his own power through a figure,
namely that he is able by himself to perform signs without any helper, for the Father begot him perfect and lacking in nothing. And see how he speaks to him, for since Nicodemus said:
"Rabbi, I know that you have come from God as a teacher, for no one can do these signs that you do

unless God is with him," and supposed that by these words he had greatly praised and magnified Christ, the Lord wished to show him that he had not yet even entered the door of understanding him, and that everyone who thinks such words about him is far from the kingdom. For this reason he said to him:
Gospel: "Amen I say to you: 'Unless someone is born a second time, he cannot see the kingdom of God.'"

Commentary: That is to say: if you have not received that spiritual birth and heavenly understanding, and have not received from heaven the teaching of the faith, you are outside the kingdom of heaven. Yet he did not say this to him so openly, but, in order to make the word painless, he therefore said:

"Unless someone" — that is to say, whether you or whoever else it may be — holds such a weak and human view of me and says, "If God were not with you, you could not do signs," and does not know that I myself am God and need help from no one, such a person will not be made worthy of the kingdom of heaven. Had the Jews heard this word, they would have laughed. But this man showed his love of learning. For this reason Christ, knowing his love of learning, spoke to him in a parable, in order to stir him to question and inquire into that word, for everything hidden leads the diligent to inquiry. And the word that he speaks is of this kind:
Unless you are born again by that heavenly birth and receive the Spirit of rebirth, you cannot understand anything about me worthily, for,

what you now say, that thought of yours, is not spiritual but natural, and whoever is not born in this way cannot see the kingdom of God. And by "kingdom" he also signified himself, as if to say: "Unless you are thus, you will not see me as is fitting." When Nicodemus heard this, he said to him:
Gospel: "How can a man who is old be born?

Commentary: How is it that you call him one who has come from God and yet do not believe his word? Instead you bring forward this form and manner of speech of unbelief, for this word, "How?", belongs to unbelievers. See how Nicodemus was troubled, for he understood that the word was directed at him, and he was amazed and trembled, for he had come as if to a man, and he was hearing everything that is beyond what is human, and he could not understand those words. For this reason he says, "It is impossible," so that he might lead Jesus to teach him more fully, and he says:
Gospel: "Can one possibly enter his mother's womb and be born a second time?"

Commentary: Do you see how, when someone understands spiritual words in a fleshly way and according to human affairs, they seem to him contemptible and false, when he examines them closely by the measure of his own affairs and does not accept them by faith without scrutiny? For Nicodemus heard of birth and did not understand that he was speaking of spiritual birth, but brought that great and lofty word down into fleshly lowliness, and for this reason that word seemed contemptible to him. For this reason Paul says, "The natural man does not accept anything spiritual." Yet even in this he preserved the honor due to Christ and did not reject that word, but said, "How is it possible?" and fell silent, for there were two obstacles: first, such a birth, and second, the kingdom, for the Jews did not even know of the kingdom, and for this reason the matter amazed him.

Homily 24: That we should not scrutinize the works of God but only believe, and on living virtuously. Let us not inquire into the works of God with human thoughts, but let us accept everything without doubting,
For the one who scrutinizes minutely gains nothing, but only brings judgment upon his own soul, and he does not find what he is searching for; for you have heard the word "birth."
Do not say, "How was he born?" Do not become unbelieving, but accept it with faith, for if Nicodemus,
who did not understand that spiritual birth, was held at fault, then what judgment will those receive who deny the awesome and beginningless birth of the Son?
For the mind of arrogant people is dark. But let us ask for understanding from heaven, so that in this way we may be enlightened;
and this will be given to us when we show forth good works,
for evil deeds also darken the mind, and a soul afflicted by passion is unable to understand anything good, but is always turbid and dark. So let us purify ourselves,

let us enlighten our minds, and let us not sow upon thorns, which are the cares and deceptions of this world. For just as thorns are hateful to the farmer and easily burned by fire, so are the affairs of this world; and just as serpents and vipers and all creeping things make their dwelling among thorns, so they do in the deception of the world. But let us bring that fire of the Holy Spirit, so that those thorns may be burned up and the beasts may be put to flight, and our land may become clean and able to receive the divine seeds. Let us plant that fruitful olive tree, that domestic plant, ever flourishing, giving light, working righteousness, which is mercy, which always enlightens the soul and the mind.

If we have it, we will be able to enter even the bridal chamber with boldness and to see the Bridegroom, by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
Chapter 25
The text: Jesus answered and said to him: "Amen, amen, I say to you: Unless someone is born of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God."
Commentary: Little children go to school continually and are eager to learn, and they even add nights to days; and all this is for human things,
but now I too ask of you a spiritual eagerness, so that you may listen eagerly to good teachings,
for this is why I always speak to you little by little and not all at once, so that you may remember my words well and easily.
But if anyone is entirely negligent and slack, listen, then, today as well to this reading: for when Nicodemus was astonished and said,

"A second birth for an old man is impossible," behold, the Lord explains to him how that birth comes about, which, although it was still hard to understand, was nevertheless easier than the former, for he said to him: "Unless someone is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God." You say that a second birth is impossible, but I say that not only is it impossible [?], but it is even necessary, for without it there is no life. For the earthly and fleshly birth is from the dust; for this reason it is far from what is spiritual. But that other birth is of the Spirit, and it brings one easily into the kingdom.

Hear, you unbaptized, and tremble at this pronouncement! This word is terrible, for it says that it is impossible for one who has not been born of water and the Spirit to enter the kingdom. But to Nicodemus that word still seemed strange, for it is an evil thing when a person understands spiritual matters in a fleshly way.
For, as I said before, the works of God must be believed without doubting and without prying inquiry.
If Nicodemus had done this, that word would not have seemed impossible to him,
but Christ wished to free him from that unbelief and to teach him that he was not speaking of fleshly birth.
Therefore he said to him, "Unless someone is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God," as if he were saying to him:
I am speaking of another birth, Nicodemus. Why do you bring it down alongside that earthly birth?
Why do you lower that lofty word? This birth is above these pains of the flesh, for although it is called birth,
it shares with the flesh in name only, and in reality it is foreign to it. For I wish to bring another birth into the world, so that people may be born in another way.
I have come to make a strange new creation, for at first I made man from earth and water;
and that creature became useless, but now I wish to create him from water and the Spirit. And if anyone should say, "And how can it be from water?"
I too will say to him: And how was he created from earth? How was that single clay divided into many forms?
Where do the bones and sinews and skin and liver and spleen and heart and blood and bile come from?
Where do so many powers and so many colors come from? For all this is not the work of earth.

How is it that the earth receives seed and makes it sprout, while the body receives it and corrupts and consumes it? How is it that the earth nourishes what is sown in it, while the body is nourished by what goes down into it and does not nourish these things?
And the earth receives water and changes it into wine, while the body often turns wine into water. So how is all this from the earth,
since it is contrary to the earth? Yet it is impossible for human beings to discover this,
and it must be accepted by faith. If so, must this not be done all the more with those spiritual mysteries?
And just as that lifeless earth, by the will of God, was so empowered and was changed into colors and powers of every kind,
so also through water, by the power of the Holy Spirit, that indescribable mystery comes to pass.
And do not become unbelieving, even though you do not see it, for you do not see a person's soul, yet you know that it is a soul. For at that time earth was the material,

but everything was the work of the Creator; and now too water is the material, but everything is the work of the Holy Spirit. At that time man became a living soul, and now the life-giving Spirit comes upon him, by whom the apostles also performed those great miracles. At that time man was created in the image of God, but now Christ has wholly united him to God. At that time he gave him authority over the beasts, but now he has raised our nature higher than the heaven of heavens and has granted us everything anew, and a new life. And at that time Adam was created from earth, and Eve from Adam's side, and Abel from the seed of Adam and also from one of them.

We cannot explain in words even things that are coarse and material, so how could we be able to express this mystery of baptism, which is higher than the human mind? For when this spiritual birth takes place, the angels too stand there, yet they cannot explain the mystery of that event; rather, they only stand and watch that great work and do nothing, but the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit do everything. Let us therefore believe the word of God, for it is far more trustworthy than what is seen, since bodily eyes are often deceived, but his word is never found in error. And it says: "This thing is a birth." And if anyone says, "And how is it a birth?", silence him with the word of God, which is a great certainty.
And if anyone asks us, "Why was water devised for this?",

we too shall say: "And why was earth brought in at the beginning for the creation of man?" And this is known to all, that it was possible for God to create man even without earth. So do not inquire into anything further, for the apostle Peter showed its great necessity when, on one occasion, the Holy Spirit came upon certain people before the water; yet the apostle did not disregard the washing of water, but said:
"What hindrance is there to baptizing those on whom the Holy Spirit has descended, just as on us?" But as for what the need for water is,
that too I will tell according to my ability, for its works are many, but of those many I will tell one.
It is this: that a divine figure is accomplished in it: burial, death, resurrection and life.
And all of this happens together, for we plunge our heads into that water as into a tomb, and there the old man is covered over and is entirely sunk, every part of him.
And again, when we lift up our head, the new man comes up with us,
for just as it is easy to plunge one's head into water and lift it out, so it is easy before God to bury and entirely sink that old man and to reveal the new.
And the head is plunged into the water three times, so that you may know that the power of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit accomplishes all of this, and that this matter is not in doubt.
Hear what Paul says:
"We were buried with him by baptism into death," and that "our old man was crucified."
And not only is baptism called crucifixion, but crucifixion is also called baptism, as he says: "The baptism with which I am baptized, you shall be baptized."
For just as we easily plunge our heads into water and lift them out, so too the Lord easily died and, when he willed, rose again, even though he was in the tomb for three days as a mystery.
Teaching 25: That the unbaptized person, even if he has myriads of virtues, goes to Gehenna. But now, we who have been made worthy of such mysteries, let us also acquire a life worthy of that gift,
and you who have not been made worthy of it, strive in every way that you may become worthy of it. And let us become one body and brothers to one another,
for as long as we are divided by this matter, there is no unity at all, even if we are brothers according to the flesh, for the unbaptized person is a stranger to the baptized.
The two have neither one father, nor one city, nor one food, nor one garment, nor anything else; rather, everything is different,
and everything belonging to the baptized is of heaven, but everything belonging to the unbaptized is of earth and of sin.
The king of the baptized is Christ, and that of the unbaptized is the devil and sin,
and they have no communion at all with one another. Let us hasten, then, so that we may all become dwellers in the heavenly city.

While we are in exile, let us go to that first fatherland of ours. But if any unbaptized person departs, even if he should have every virtue, he goes nowhere else but to the Gehenna of fire, and the venomous worm, and the outer darkness. But may that torment come upon no one; rather, let us hasten by good deeds and build gold and silver and precious stones upon that covering of the apostles, so that we may thus be found rich there, when we receive all our possessions there by the hand of the poor. For we owe Christ much, not money, but the debt of sins. Let us then lend money, so that our sins may be forgiven us, and let us not despise the hungry and naked here, so that there he may nourish us and clothe us with that garment of incorruption. If we give him drink here, we will not say, like that rich man: "Send Lazarus, so that he may moisten my tongue." If we receive him here, there he will prepare many dwellings for us.

If we go to him in prison, he too will release us from prison. If he is a stranger and we receive him, he too will receive us, who have become strangers, into the kingdom of heaven. If he is sick and we visit him, he too will soon free us from our infirmities. And therefore let us give small and worthless deeds in exchange for those great gifts. While we still have time, let us sow, so that when winter comes we may have a full storehouse, when the sea is no longer sailed, when that great day arrives; for then this great and wide sea is no longer sailed. Now is the time for sowing, and whoever does not sow will become pitiable. So let us not be negligent, but let us sow well and scatter money, so that we may gather fruit richly, by the grace and love for mankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
Chapter 26
This saying: "That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit."
Interpretation:
The only-begotten Son of God has made us worthy of great mysteries, of which we were not worthy,
for not only were we unworthy of gifts, but it was rather fitting that great torments should come upon us.
But he not only freed us from evils, but also made us worthy of such good things, and became a new creation for us, as Paul says:
"Whoever is in Christ is a new creation." Listen to him, how he says:
"Unless someone is born of water and the Spirit,
he cannot enter the kingdom of God." For we were not worthy even of the earth, yet he has given us even the heavens.
We could not keep ourselves from eating of one tree, and he has given us the kingdom of heaven.
Rightly did the apostle Paul say: "O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!"
For no longer is ours a birth subject to passion, but the mystery of water and the Holy Spirit,
for just as a mother's womb is the dwelling place and nurturer of the infant, so the water is a womb, the nurturer of the believer who is being baptized.
For just as it is said of the sun, "Like a bridegroom he comes forth from his bridal chamber," the same ought to be said of baptized believers when they come up out of the water,
for they have a brightness far greater than the sun.
However, one who is being born in the womb needs a length of time, but it is not so in the water; rather, everything comes about in an instant,
for where life is mortal and its beginning comes from corruption, there a length of time is necessary, for this is how it is:
a bodily thing is completed over a length of time, but a spiritual thing is not so.
But since Nicodemus was exceedingly shaken by such words, see how he reveals to him the greatness of the mystery, for he says:
"That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit."
He removes him completely from fleshly things, so that he may no longer seek to see these matters with the fleshly eye, for he says to him: "I speak not of the flesh, but of the Spirit."
O Nicodemus, does the Spirit then not give birth to flesh?

Do not think so! And if anyone should say: "Then how was it with the Lord's flesh? Was it not born of the Holy Spirit?" — understand that it was not born of the Spirit alone, but also of the flesh of the Virgin. For this reason the Apostle also says: "He was born of a woman, he came under the law," for that flesh was by the Holy Spirit, yet it was from the womb of the Virgin. But how this came about is impossible to explain. And this came about so that no one should think that the one born is alien to our nature.
Gospel: "That which is born of the Spirit is spirit."

Commentary: Do you see the honor of the Spirit? The work that the Father does, he also does, as he said above: "They were born of God." But here he says that the Spirit gives birth to them, for "that which is born of the Spirit is spirit." And this saying means the following: that which is born of the Spirit is spirit, for by birth here he does not mean coming into being, but birth of honor and grace. But since the Lord had spoken to him in this way and saw that he still did not understand, he therefore offered him a visible parable as an image and said to him:
Gospel: "Do not marvel that I said to you: In this way you must be born again. The wind blows wherever it wills."

Commentary: He saw him astonished and wished to show him some image, for he had drawn him away from bodily and material things when he said to him, "That which is born of the Spirit is spirit." And since he did not know what this saying was, he therefore led him back toward the bodily, yet he did not offer him an image from entirely coarse bodies, nor again from entirely bodiless things, for he could not fully understand; instead he found something midway between bodily and bodiless nature: the blowing of the wind.

For he says to him about the wind: "You hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes." And when he says, "It blows where it wills," he does not indicate some will on the part of the wind, but rather that unhindered blowing given to it by nature, which no one among men can hinder.
Gospel: So it is with everyone born of the Spirit.

Commentary: Here he has completed his argument. For if that which you come to know through hearing, and which strikes your face, and whose path you do not know, and whose substance you cannot comprehend either,
how will you search out the working of the Holy Spirit, you who do not know the nature of the wind, whose sound you hear?

And again, this saying, "It blows wherever it wills," serves as a figure of the Holy Spirit. For if this material and weak nature is like this, and it has been given to it to blow wherever it wishes, and no one can hinder it,
will not the Holy Spirit all the more spread forth its power wherever it wills, so that the laws of nature cannot hinder it,

nor the bounds of bodily birth, nor anything else? For that he speaks about the wind when he says, "You hear its sound," is evident from this: if he were speaking not about the wind but about the Holy Spirit, how would he have said to a Jewish man, who knew nothing of the Holy Spirit, "You hear its sound"?
And just as the wind is not seen, although its sound is heard, so too the grace of the Holy Spirit is not seen with bodily eyes,
nor is that spiritual birth; for the wind too is matter, although it is not coarse but fine.
And if you cannot see this material thing and yet do not marvel, how is it that you marvel at the Holy Spirit and do not believe?
But Nicodemus was still in the lowliness of the Jews and in weakness regarding all these figures; and therefore he said to the Lord:
Gospel: "How can this be?" Jesus said to him: "You are a teacher of Israel, and do you not know this?"

Commentary: Nowhere did he reproach him for wickedness, but rather for lack of understanding. But what did this birth have in common with the things of the Jews, that he should have learned of it from them? Yet it had much in common with them,
for there was the first-created man, and again she who was made from his side,
and the births from barren women, and all those deeds that were accomplished on the waters, on that water from which Elisha brought up the iron,
and again the Red Sea, which the Jews crossed, and the pool which the angel stirred, and the matter of Naaman the Syrian, who was cleansed in the Jordan.
And all these foreshadowed the figure of baptism, and the prophets, moreover, said much about this, as it says:
"To the people that is to be born, whom the Lord has made," and, "Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle's," and, "Receive the light, receive the light, Jerusalem!"
and, "Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven." And again, the birth of Isaac from a barren woman, and that of many others, was a figure of this same birth,
and also of the birth from the Virgin.

And he reminds him of all this and says to him: "You are a teacher of Israel, and do you not know this?" "Amen, amen, I say to you, what we know we speak, and what we have seen we testify to, and no one accepts our testimony."

He wished to satisfy him completely, and for this reason he said: "What we know we speak, and what we have seen we testify." For among us the eyes are trusted above all else, and when we are speaking to someone to convince him, we say this: "We have seen it with our own eyes." In the same way Christ speaks to him in human fashion, because of his weakness. And to show that his word is true, he says to him: "What we have seen we testify," so as to convince him that it truly is so and not otherwise.

By "seeing" in this place he means true knowledge, for he saw everything to come before it came to be. For this reason, having said, "What is born of the Spirit is spirit," he added, "What we have seen we testify," for that thing had not yet been done, but he saw everything before it came to be. As for the words "what we know," he says them either of himself and the Father, or of himself alone.

The saying "No one receives" is not that of an angry man; rather, he was stating how the matter had turned out. For he himself, by both word and deed, showed all meekness and gentleness, in order to teach us meekness as well, so that when we say something to certain people and they oppose us, we should not become angry. For no wrathful person accomplishes anything good; rather, he destroys everything good.

Teaching 26, on wrath. For this reason we must with all diligence keep far from wrath and from tumult, which is the fuel of wrath. For anger is an evil passion and a manifold darkening of the soul. Therefore we must guard against it on every side, for it is an evil thing if we are able to tame wild beasts yet neglect our own mind that has turned beastly. For rage is a fire that burns up the soul, harms the body, and makes it ugly.

If the wrathful man, at the moment of his anger, were able to recognize what he himself is like, no other teaching would be needed, for nothing is worse than a wrathful man. Wrath is an evil drunkenness, worse even than drunkenness and more dreadful than demon possession. So let us put away from ourselves anger and clamor, according to the word of Paul the apostle, and at the moment of anger let us remember our sins. And when you are angry with your slave and beat him, and he stands silent and meek, let that be sign enough for you. For although he is a slave, he is nevertheless a human being, and he has an immortal soul and has the same gifts from God as you do. And if he who is equal to us in spiritual honor endures our words so meekly for the sake of this bodily authority, which is nothing, what answer shall we give to God, when out of fear of him we do not bridle our minds in the way that slaves do out of fear of us? Let us therefore consider all this, remember our sins, and flee from this evil passion, so that we may find rest for our souls by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 27
This saying: "If I tell you earthly things and you do not believe, how then, if I tell you heavenly things, will you believe?"
"And no one has ascended into heaven except he who came down from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven."
Commentary: As I have said many times, now too I say the same thing:
that Jesus wished to utter those lofty words about his own divinity, but because of the weakness of his hearers he often does not do so,
and he often speaks words full of lowliness, for these were of much more benefit to those weak in mind than those lofty words,
which they were not able to understand. But it was enough for the lofty words to be spoken once or twice, so that from them we might understand his loftiness and glory according to our capacity,
whereas if he had not spoken lowly words again and again, many would not have been won over.
But so that, on the other hand, no other harm might come from the lowliness of the words and bring his hearers utterly low, for this reason he states the cause of his lowly speech.

For when he had spoken about baptism, whatever he said, and about the spiritual birth that takes place on earth, he wished to speak also about his own ineffable and incomprehensible birth, yet he did not speak of it,
and he also stated the reason why he does not speak of it, which is the coarseness and weakness of those hearers.
And for this reason he says: "If I tell you earthly things and you do not believe, how then, if I tell you heavenly things, will you believe?"
And so it is clear that wherever he speaks some human word, he does so because of the weakness of his hearers. As for "earthly" here, some say it refers to the saying spoken about the wind,

meaning: if I have offered you an image drawn from the earth and you still did not believe, how will you believe loftier words? But if you call baptism "earthly" in this place, either because it takes place on earth,
or because he gives it the name "earthly" in comparison with his own awesome birth,
this explanation too is good, for although this birth of baptism is heavenly, yet if someone speaks of it alongside that lofty birth of the Son from the Father, beside that it is earthly.
And he did not say to him, "You do not understand," but, "You did not believe."
For when a person does not accept those matters which he is able to understand with the mind, lack of understanding may rightly be charged in their case,
but when he does not accept those matters which are impossible to grasp with the mind and which must be accepted by faith alone, he has the disease of unbelief.
And when the Lord had rebuked him in this way, he then showed him that he knows not only this, but also what is greater than all of it.
For this reason he said to him: "No one has ascended into heaven except he who came down from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven," since he had said to him:
"We know that you have come from God as a teacher."

For this reason the Lord says: Do not suppose that I am like the other prophets, who were from the earth, for I have come from heaven, and none of the prophets has ascended into heaven. But I came from heaven and yet have not been absent from the heavens, for I am in the heavens. Do you see how great and lofty this saying is? Yet in comparison with his glory it is small, for he is not only in the heavens but everywhere.

But for now, for this weakness of Nicodemus, even these words were sufficient. In this place he gives the name "Son of Man" to the flesh, but from this lesser nature he has named his whole self, including the nature of his divinity. For he does this often: sometimes by the name of his divinity alone he signifies both the divinity and the humanity.
And again, sometimes by the name of his humanity alone he likewise signifies both natures, that of the divinity and that of the humanity.
Gospel: And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up.

Interpretation: First he spoke of his great benefaction, which he gave to people through baptism, and now he has gone on to speak of its cause, in no way inferior to that benefaction, namely the benefaction of the cross. So too Paul, when he was speaking to the Corinthians, mentioned these two together, saying: "Was Paul crucified for you, or were you baptized in the name of Paul?" For above all else these two deeds show his inexpressible love for humankind,
for he died for his enemies, since at that time we were all his enemies,

and not only this, but through baptism he grants us complete forgiveness of sins. But why did he not say plainly, "I am to be crucified," but instead led his words to that ancient type? First, so that they might know that the old is close to the new and shares with it and is not foreign to it; next, so that you might know that he did not go to crucifixion under compulsion; and again, so that you might understand that this event did him no harm, and that all others were being saved by him, so that no one might say: "How can faith in one who was crucified and killed save anyone?" For this reason he led us to that ancient event, so that we might reflect: if the Jews looked at a serpent of bronze and were saved, how much more will anyone be saved who believes in God crucified for us?
And not that [?] weakness; for since he mentioned death and crucifixion, so that the one who heard might not say
that death has mastery over him and that he suffers some harm,
for this reason he said:
"All who believe in him shall have eternal life."

And this is evident: how could death have mastered him who grants life to others? And if those who believe in the crucified one are saved, how could the crucified one suffer any harm, he who is the source of life? Do you see how in every place [?] how could the crucified one suffer any harm, he who is the source of life, which the human mind does not readily accept, but faith, which is above that weakness of the mind, readily accepts? But from where did it come that God so loved this world? From nowhere else but from his own goodness alone.

Teaching 27, on mercy to the poor. Let us then be ashamed before that love of his; let us be abashed before his great love of mankind. For he did not spare his only-begotten Son for us, yet we grudge our possessions for his sake, and indeed for the sake of our own selves. Are we not then worthy of great punishment? For if some man takes hardship and labor upon himself for us, we too rejoice to take hardship upon ourselves for him, and we do not grudge bestowing all that we have on him.
But toward Christ we do not do even this, he who laid down his life for us and poured out his precious blood, for us who were his enemies,
and he redeemed us from eternal punishment, and now we do not give him even a paltry thing. Who will deliver me from the eternal fire?

Do we not punish our own selves? Do we not willingly hand ourselves over to eternal Gehenna? For we do not receive him who laid down his life for us; and we ought to give not only our possessions but even our very lives. And even then it would be nothing worthy of his benefaction. But we do not understand any of this; rather, we are senseless and wicked,
and we adorn slaves and horses with gold, but to our King we often do not give even bread,

and if he is naked, we do not clothe him, but rather drive him away in anger. And he does all this so that we might give him occasion to spread his abundant mercy over us; and he comes naked so that you might provide the occasion for clothing yourself in the garment of incorruption. Yet some of your garments are eaten by moths, some lie idle to no purpose, and with others you adorn yourself so that the people of the neighborhood may see you, while you have no wish to adorn your soul.
Why are you so eager to adorn yourself? What good is there in that? For harlots too adorn themselves in this way, and even more so;

but true adornment is virtue, which makes the soul beautiful. This I say continually and will not cease from saying, for I do not pity the poor so much as I pity your souls. Consider whom the rich man's mercilessness harmed more, Lazarus or himself?

In the same way you will be harmed by mercilessness far more than the poor are. And you would speak those same words of the rich man in that fire and would find no mercy. But may no one ever hear that voice; rather, may we all attain to the bosom of Abraham by the grace and love of mankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and for ever and ever. Amen.
Chapter 28
The text: For God did not send his Son into the world in this way so that he might condemn the world, but so that the world might be saved through him.
Commentary: Many negligent and sin-loving people use these words as a pretext for their own laxity and say:
There is no hell and no torment, but God forgives us all our sins. To such people Scripture says: "Do not say: His mercies are many,
and he will be lenient toward my sins," for mercy and wrath are with him, and as great as his mercy is, so great also is his reproof,
for recompense is given to us according to our sins, as the prophet says: "You have repaid each person according to their deeds."
And this is the great love of God for humankind: God has divided our affairs into two lives:
the one in this present world, and the second in the age to come. And he appointed this one life as the time of contests, and that other as the time of crowns and rewards.
And in this too he has shown us great love for humankind,
for we have committed many sins and from youth to old age have not ceased defiling the soul, yet he has given us forgiveness of them all through holy baptism and has granted us holiness. And again,

whoever receives the mystery of holy baptism from infancy and then afterward defiles his soul is worthy of countless torments, yet for him too God has opened the door of repentance and has given many means of cleansing his sins.

Consider all this, what forms of goodness these are: first, that he gives us complete forgiveness of sins through baptism, and again, if we sin, he remits those evil deeds of ours through repentance and grants us time to repent. And because of all this Christ said to Nicodemus: "God did not send his Son to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him." For there are two comings of Christ: first this one, and then the second, which is yet to be; but the two are not for the same purpose. For he came the first time not to call us to account, but to forgive our sins; but he will come the second time not to forgive us, but to call us to account. Therefore he says of the first: "I did not come to judge the world, but to save it," and of the second he says: "When the Son of Man comes in the glory of his Father, and sets the sheep at his right hand and the goats at his left."

And if he had not forgiven us in his abundant goodness, his first coming would have been a judgment of humankind, for even before his coming there was the law by nature, and also the law and scripture and the words of the prophets and miraculous deeds and words about eternal torments and many other such things;

and it would have been just for him to demand an account for all of that, but in his love for humankind he forgave us everything that came before. Otherwise we would all have perished, for all have sinned and fallen short of the glory of God, but we were justified freely by his grace. Do you see the incomprehensibility of his goodness? But if someone should say: "If he did not come to judge the world, how does he say, 'Whoever does not believe is already judged'? If it is not the time of judgment, how has he been judged?"
Rather, understand that he is saying either that the very fact of unbelief and of remaining unbaptized is itself a torment, for to be outside the light is evil enough in itself,
or else by this saying he points to the coming judgment of the age to come,
for just as a murderer, even if he is not condemned by the word of a judge, is nevertheless condemned by the very nature of his deed, so too is the unbeliever,

for the Lord also said to Adam: "On the day you eat of that tree, you shall die." Yet after eating he lived for a long time. How then did God say to him: "On the day you eat, on that same day you shall die"?

But even though death did not actually come about at once, nevertheless by that command of God and by the nature of the matter, and since the sentence of death had gone forth against him, it was as though he had died, even though he lingered for some length of time.
For so that no one, on hearing "I did not come to judge the world," should suppose that there is surely no judgment,
for this reason he spoke this word, so that we might know that there will be a judgment.
And this is the great goodness of God, that he not only gave his Son, but also delayed the time of judgment, so that sinners might have a time for repentance.
Gospel: Whoever believes in the Son will not be judged.
Commentary: "Whoever believes," he says, not whoever inquires with a divided heart. And if anyone should say: "And if someone believes rightly but has evil deeds, what will happen?"

Then understand that the apostle Paul does not even name such people true believers, for he says: "They confess with words, but deny with deeds." But I will say this as well, that the Lord says: "Whoever believes will not be judged."
That is to say, he will not be judged on this count, but for those evil deeds he will receive a greater judgment; yet he will not be judged for unbelief, if he is a believer.
Do you see how he began from fearful things and again ended his discourse upon fearful things? For at the beginning of the discourse he said: "Unless someone is born of water and the Spirit,
he cannot enter the kingdom of God," and here at the end he says: "Whoever does not believe has already been judged."
But do not suppose that this respite will benefit in any way one who does not repent, for the unbeliever is in no way better off than those who are in hell.
Gospel: And this is the judgment, that the light came into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light.
Commentary: Now this saying means the following: that people are judged for this reason, because they forsake the light and love the darkness and do not wish to come to the light.
For "if I had come to judge and not to forgive sins," they would have had an argument, that it was for this reason that we became unbelievers.
But since "I came to lead out of the darkness and to bring to the light," who then would have mercy on one who does not wish to come from darkness to light?
As he says in another place: "They hated me without cause," and: "If I had not come, they would have no sin." For one who has no light and for this reason sits in darkness is worthy of mercy,
but one who remains in darkness after the coming of the light is no longer worthy of mercy.
And he also stated the reason why people love the darkness.
Gospel: For their deeds were evil.
Everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, so that his deeds may not be exposed.

Commentary: For if he had set up a tribunal and were judging, they would have had an argument for not coming to him, because they were afraid. But since he came to forgive, why did they not come to him and receive forgiveness, as many tax collectors and sinners did?
But those who had indeed chosen to remain in darkness and in sin
were afraid of virtue, and for this reason they chose to remain in sin until death. But some pagans say,
those who do not wish to come to the light and to separate themselves from sin, saying: "Are there not many pagans who practice virtue, and Christians who are sinners?"
But I say this: that there are indeed many sinful Christians, but pagans who practice virtue are found nowhere, God forbid!
And do not tell me of those who may perhaps be found who by nature are not lovers of fornication or not lovers of silver,

but find me even one who resists the battle of the passions. And if you do find one anywhere, you will find that his conduct is for the sake of glory from men; and he who acts for the sake of men, when he then finds a hidden moment, God forbid that he should bridle his desire! But so that we may not bring in contention, let us say that a pagan is a doer of virtue: is he not all the more to be pitied, who here labors and suffers hardship and there goes to Gehenna, because he did not come to the light? For the light came of itself; it was not that they sought it or strove for it. It came of itself, and they did not receive it. For who would there be who had abandoned sin and yet would not come to the light? But whoever remains in the darkness of unbelief, let it be known that he remains there for love of his sins.

And do not say this: "There is a certain pagan who does not fornicate or does not steal," but know that he does all that for the sake of glory from men, and in secret he does not shrink from sin. Or else it is for the sake of glory from men that he does not come to the light, because he is ashamed before his neighbor or before his own people. And this is wickedness, for every slave of arrogance is worse even than a fornicator and does worse evils.
Teaching 28: On vainglory. But let us flee from vainglory, brothers, for it is worse than all the passions.
From it are born greed and the love of possessions; from it arise hatreds and battles and tumults,
for he who seeks ever greater glory is always in battles and evils and never finds an end to his desire.
And all this comes from vainglory. For where does the multitude of ornaments and slaves and mansions that many people have come from? It is not that all of it is needful to them,
but it is so that they may make many witnesses of their arrogance and pride.
But if we overcome it in some way, we shall make many other passions vanish along with it.

And there will no longer be anything to prevent us from living on earth as if in the heavens.
