But by life he here means that lofty, divine life, and not this ordinary life that all people have. For from this it is clear that he does not speak of human life but of the divine and holy life, because by this human life all people live,
even unbelievers and those who have not eaten of his flesh.

Do you see how he was not speaking of this life, but of that eternal life? For his saying means the following: "Whoever eats my flesh, when he departs from this world, will not perish, nor will he be tormented." And again, when he said, "I will raise him up on the last day," he did not speak of the general resurrection of all, for all will rise, but of that chosen and good resurrection, which will have its reward in abundance.
Gospel: Your fathers ate manna and died, but whoever eats this bread will live forever.

Commentary: See now, he repeats this saying many times, in order to establish it firmly in their minds and to persuade them concerning the resurrection and eternal life. For this reason he also mentions the resurrection and has promised eternal life, to show them that this life is not now but will come after the resurrection. And if anyone should say, "How is this known?", let him listen to all the Scriptures, for in every place he sent them to the Scriptures and commanded them to learn the truth from them. And when he said, "This bread gives life to the world," by this saying he wished to move them to jealousy, so that they would be jealous of others' entry into life and would not remain outside. And he repeatedly reminds them of the manna, in order to show how great a difference there is between this gift given by him and the manna, and to bring them to faith.

For if he was able for forty years, without labor and sowing, to nourish them in this way, would he not now much more do such a thing, if he wished, he who has come with greater mercy toward humankind? For if all that was a type and was done thus without difficulty, would the thing not now much more be done, where the power of the truth is great: of never perishing and of existing in that true life? And he mentions life in every place, for life is desired by human beings and nothing is so sweet as not dying. For in the Old Covenant too this was the good: length of days and life for a long time, but now it is not only length, but unending life. And further, on top of all this, he also wishes to show that he wishes to do away with the sentence brought down on us as a curse because of our disobedience; and now he dissolves that decree which leads to death, and in its place brings in eternal life, the opposite of that former thing.
Gospel:
"He said this in the synagogue, and was teaching at Capernaum."

Commentary: All this he said, it says, at Capernaum, where the greatest number of mighty works had been done, and for this reason they ought to have believed his words. And he taught in synagogues and in the temple, first, so that the multitude of the people might listen to him and be converted, and also so that he might show everyone that he is not opposed to the Father.
Gospel: "Many of his disciples who heard this also said: 'This word is hard.'"

Commentary: "Hard" means, it says, difficult and laborious. And how could they say this? Since he was saying nothing of the kind, for he was not teaching about bodily virtues but about faith, why then is this word hard? Is it because he makes the promise of life and resurrection, or because he said, "I came down from heaven"?

Or that "It is impossible for one who does not eat his flesh to have life"? And are these things hard? And who would say, "These things are hard"? Why then did they say, "It is hard"? Only because it is difficult to accept, beyond their weakness and full of fear. And they supposed that he was speaking to them beyond his own worth and above himself, and they said, "Who can listen to it?" For they were justifying themselves, those who wished to go away from him. But when Jesus knew in his spirit that they were murmuring (for this too was a work of his divinity, that he revealed the hidden things of the heart), he said to them, "Does this cause you to stumble?" He did this also in the case of Nathanael: "Because I told you that I saw you under the fig tree, do you believe? You will see greater things than this." And here too he now likewise says to them:
Gospel: "Does this cause you to stumble? What if you should see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?"

Commentary: In the same way he also said to Nicodemus: "No one has ascended to heaven except the one who came from heaven, the Son of Man, who was in heaven." What is this? Is he perhaps adding hidden things on top of hidden things? But no, may it not be! Rather, by the loftiness and abundance of his teachings he wished to convert them. For whoever says this simply, "I came down from heaven," and adds nothing else, causes all the more stumbling. But those words of his, when he said, "My flesh is the true life of the world," and, "As the living Father sent me, I also live because of the Father," and, "I came down from heaven" — all this served to dissolve unbelief. For when someone says something only once, it may perhaps even become doubtful whether it is true; but whoever demonstrates the truth of his word in this way, many times over, with the testimony of many witnesses and with such great deeds, makes every doubt vanish.

So this is how the Lord acted, and he did and said everything in order to deliver them from that thought by which they supposed him to be the son of Joseph. It is clear, then, that he did not speak those words to increase the stumbling, but rather to dissolve the stumbling completely,
for whoever supposed him to be the son of Joseph would not accept those words,
but whoever believed that he had come down from heaven and was ascending there again would readily believe all his words.
And after these words, behold, see how he speaks to them yet another word that dissolves the stumbling:
Gospel: "It is the spirit that gives life, but the flesh is of no benefit."
Commentary: Now this saying of his means the following: that the words spoken about me must be heard spiritually,

for whoever hears them in a carnal way will gain nothing and find no benefit. And this was the carnal thing: that they doubted how he had come down from heaven, that they supposed he was the son of Joseph, and that they said, "How can he give us his flesh to eat?"

All this was carnal, whereas those matters must be understood spiritually and mystically. And if someone should say, "How could they have known and understood what the eating of his flesh is?" — nevertheless they ought to have
asked him and awaited the time for understanding, and not stumbled so immediately and said, "This thing is impossible to do."
Gospel: "The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life."
Commentary: And what does this mean, "they are spirit"? It means that they are spiritual and that nothing carnal is attached to them, nor the concerns of this weak nature,
but they are set apart from every earthly matter and from the laws and customs of the earth, and they have another power, far removed from and exalted above all this.
So just as here he said "spirit" in place of "spiritual," so too when he said "flesh," he did not say it about flesh itself,
but about hearing in a carnal way. He was also showing them that they always desire what is carnal, whereas they ought to have desired what is spiritual,
for if anyone understands these words in a carnal way, he will gain nothing. What then is the flesh? Is it not flesh?
Yes, truly, as he says: "The flesh is of no profit." He does not say this about his own flesh (far from it!) but about those who understand in a fleshly way.

But what is it to understand in a fleshly way? Only this: that a person looks at these words in such a merely simple way and does not regard them at all as a great and lofty mystery, for this is what is fleshly; but it is necessary
not to understand in this way with the outward eye; rather, all those mysteries must be seen and perceived with the inward eye, for this is what is spiritual.
Gospel: "Whoever does not eat my flesh and does not drink my blood does not have life in himself."

Commentary: How then is the flesh of no profit, when without it life does not come about? Do you see that this saying, "The flesh is of no profit," was not said about his own flesh but about hearing in a fleshly way?
Gospel: "But there are some of you who do not believe."

Commentary: Again he confers his customary dignity on his words, for he speaks of hidden things to come, and shows that he does not need glory from them and that he says all this not for that reason, but because he has pity on them. And when he said "some," by this word he set his disciples apart from them, for earlier he had said to them, "You have seen me and do not believe," but here he says:

Gospel: "'There are some of you who do not believe,' for Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who do not believe, and who it was that would betray him. And for this reason he said: 'No one can come to me unless it has been given to him by my Father.'"

Commentary: In this place the evangelist shows the voluntary character of his dispensation and his freedom from resentment. And this phrase too, "he knew from the beginning," is not here without purpose, but so that you may understand his knowledge from the beginning, long beforehand, and that he knew everything before these words, and did not come to know the betrayer after the stumbling and the murmuring, but before all this, which was a work of his divinity. Then he says:

"Unless it had been given to him from heaven by my Father," in order to persuade them to confess God as his Father and not Joseph, and to show that faith in him is no small or ordinary matter. It is as if he were saying: I am not shaken, nor do I find it strange of those who do not believe, for I have known all this from the beginning, how it is going to be; before it happens I know everything, and to whom the Father has given. But when you hear "has given," do not understand it in this way, that he has given to some just so, for no reason, and does not give to others; rather, understand and believe that whoever makes himself worthy of the gift, to him it is given.
Gospel: "Because of this many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him."

Commentary: Again, the evangelist did not say "they went away" but "they turned back." This means that the progress they had gained toward the virtues they turned back again to evil, and they destroyed the faith they had, and they separated themselves from him. But the Twelve did not do this. See, then, what he says to them:
Gospel: "Do you also wish to go away?"

Commentary: He says this to show again that he does not need service from them, and that it was not for this reason that he received them. For if he had received them for this reason, how would he say this same thing to them too? For why did he not praise them?

Why did he not express admiration for them? First, in order to fulfill what befits a teacher, and to show that this is rather the way in which they ought to be held fast. And if he had praised them, perhaps they would have supposed, "He says this to gain our favor," and something merely human would have happened to them. But this, his showing that he did not need their being with him, held them fast all the more. And see how wisely he spoke to them. He did not say to them, "Go away," for that is a form of expulsion, but he asked, "Do you also wish to go away?" This removed all constraint and compulsion, so as to show that he does not want them to remain with him out of shame and deference toward him, but only if they rejoice and are thankful. Nor did he openly accuse them, but he showed how it is proper to be with him. But with us everything happens in the opposite way, and rightly so.

For this reason the departure of those who are with us seems to us a loss. But he said nothing to curry favor with them, nor anything by way of driving them away, but he asked; not that he despised them, but he did not wish to keep them by compulsion and constraint, for to be with him in this way, by compulsion, is the same as not being with him. Hear, then, what Peter said:
Gospel: Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life, and we have believed and have come to know that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God.

Commentary: Do you see that it was not those words that were the stumbling block, but the blindness and lack of understanding of those hearers? And indeed, if he had not spoken them, they would have gone on expecting bodily food from him all the time. For see how these Twelve too were with those other crowds and heard his word. And at the last he spoke even harsher words to them, and in spite of all this they said, "To whom shall we go?"

This statement shows the great love they had for him. They were showing that Christ is more precious to them than everything, more than fathers and mothers and all created things, and that if they go away from him, they no longer have anywhere they could go. And then, so that it might not be supposed that he said "To whom shall we go?" for the reason that there was no one to receive them, he therefore added and said, "You have the words of eternal life." For those others listened to his words carnally and with human thoughts, but these listened spiritually, adorned with faith. It was about this that the Lord said, "These words are spirit and life," that is to say,
do not understand my words according to human affairs, for spiritual teachings are not of that kind,
They are not enslaved to fleshly laws, as the Apostle says: "Do not say, 'Who will ascend into heaven?'"
That is, to bring Christ down; or "'Who will descend into the abyss?'" That is, to bring Christ up from the dead.
Gospel: "You have the words of eternal life."

Commentary: See now, these men had accepted the resurrection and all that eternal rest. But look at that brother-loving and good Peter, how he answered on behalf of the whole company, and does not say, "I have believed," but "We have believed."
Notice how he speaks in keeping with the words of the Teacher and not as the Jews do, for they were saying, "This is the son of Joseph." But he said:
"You are the Christ, the Son of the living God," and:

"You have the words of eternal life," for he had listened well to those words of the Teacher which he spoke: "I will raise him up on the last day, and he shall have eternal life." For he showed that he remembered all his words, when he himself repeated them.
But as for Christ, see what he did: he did not praise Peter, nor did he marvel at him, but answered and said to him:
Gospel: "Did I not choose you twelve? And one of you is a devil."
Commentary: But since Peter said, "We have believed," the Lord then set Judas apart from that company.
For in that other place he said nothing about the disciples, but only when Jesus asked, "What do you say about me?" he said to him:
"You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." But here, since he said:
"We have believed," for this reason he rightly did not leave Judas within their company.

He said this so that, by speaking of it from the very beginning, he might turn back the wickedness of his betrayer. For he knew that those words would profit him nothing; yet he was doing his own part, so that he might in every respect leave undone nothing that it was fitting for him to do. And see that wisdom!
He neither fully exposed him nor concealed him: the first, so that he might not come to greater boldness and shamelessness;
and the second, so that the betrayer might not think that this plan of his was hidden and unknown to him. For this reason, further on, he brings greater reproofs upon him,
for at first he counted him together with others and said, "There are some of you who do not believe." And that he said this about the betrayer, hear what the Evangelist says:
Jesus knew from the beginning who they were who did not believe, and who it was that would betray him. Since, then, he persisted in the same way even so,
hear what he says more harshly: "One of you is a devil," and he brings this fear upon them all, so that that wretched man might understand.
It is good here to inquire why the apostles say nothing here, whereas at that last saying of his they were afraid and each one said to him, "Is it I?"
and "Peter beckoned to John to ask about the betrayer, who he was."
What, then, is the reason for this? For since it had not yet been said to Peter, "Get behind me, devil,"

For this reason he was not even afraid, since indeed the Lord had rebuked him, when he had spoken with great zeal and it had not pleased the Lord, but he called him Satan. After this, when he heard, "One of you will betray me," he rightly trembled.
And now, then, he does not say, "One of you will betray me," but: "One of you is a devil."

He said this in order also to show that nothing human is found in his teaching. For since all the others had left him and only they remained with him, and through Peter they all confessed him as Christ, so that they might not think of him, "He is speaking to us in a human way for this reason," he therefore removes his word from everything human. And the meaning of what he says is this: "There is nothing that will restrain me from reproving the wicked. Do not think that because you have remained with me I would therefore say something to you in a human way, or that because you have followed me I would therefore not reprove the evil. For even what is higher than these things cannot restrain me from this; for whoever remains shows the love of the teacher, but whoever has been chosen by him and afterward falls away gives the foolish cause to think of a lack of understanding; yet not even this will restrain me from reproving."

And even now the pagans bring forward this very thing as an accusation against Christ, out of their lack of understanding and their wickedness, for they do not know that God makes no one good by force, nor does his choosing compel with regard to times to come, but he only calls to the good and teaches it,

for, so that you may know that his calling is not by force, hear what is written: Many of those who were called perished. For this reason also it is clear that both life and perdition depend on our own will.

Teaching 47, on the love of money. Since, then, we hear all this, let us too strive to be watchful and vigilant always. For he who dwelt in that holy company and had received such great gifts from the Lord, who had performed so many miracles, for he was one of those others whom Jesus sent out to raise the dead and cleanse lepers, since, then, such a man was seized by that evil disease of the love of money and sold his teacher, and those benefactions and gifts of the Lord profited him nothing, neither his being with him, nor that washing of the feet, nor that sharing of his table, nor that carrying of the purse, but rather all of this became condemnation for him, therefore I implore you that we too may be afraid,

Let us not become like Judas in love of silver. For even though we do not sell Christ, yet when we see a poor man dying of hunger, or afflicted by cold and drawing near to death, and we despise him, we will be condemned with the same judgment. And again, when we unworthily approach to partake of the holy mysteries, we will perish in the same way as the murderers of Christ. And again, when we rob and oppress those lower than ourselves, we bring great judgment upon our own heads, and justly so. How long will we hold on to the love of these passing things, in which there is no profit at all? For the wealth of unprofitable things is not good. How long will we be nailed to vanity? How long will we not look toward the things of heaven, not wake up, and not become sated with these earthly things, these worthless things that flow away faster than rivers of water? Will we not learn their worthlessness even from our own experience of these things? Let us call to mind those who grew rich before us: did not all their glory become a dream? Did it not become a shadow and a withered flower? Did not all of it become a fable and a tale? They say, "So-and-so grew rich"; and now where is his wealth?

It has perished and decayed. But the sins that were committed through that wealth remain, and for his sins there is torment. What is more, even if neither torment nor the kingdom lay before us, we ought to feel shame because of nature itself, that those of our own kin are poor. Yet now many of us raise dogs and hawks and leopards and other wild beasts of every kind, and despise poor people who are afflicted by hunger. What is foreign is more honored by us than our own nature, and what is one's own is more honored by us than that with which we have no kinship at all. Or is it good and honorable to live in well-built halls, to gaze at ceilings coated with gold, and to possess countless slaves? May it not be so!

Rather, it is evil and unprofitable, for there are other halls and ceilings better and more honorable than these. It is good to delight the eyes by gazing on such halls, for there is no one to prevent it. Do you wish, then, to see a beautiful ceiling?

I will show you. When evening comes, look up at the sky adorned with stars. Or will you say, "That ceiling is not mine"? But understand that it is yours far more than this one is, for it was made for you and it belongs in common to you and your brothers, whereas this one is not yours but belongs to those who will inherit it after your death. That one will be of great profit to you, when by its beauty it gives you understanding of the Creator; but this one will do you great harm, when it becomes your accuser on the day of judgment, when you are clothed in gold while the poor man, who is Christ, has not even a little clothing.

No, brothers, let us not be so senseless. Let us not pursue the things that flee from us; let us pursue those that await us. Let us not throw away our life, but let us take hold of the hope of the age to come. Let the old among us reflect that, behold, death has drawn near; let the young in turn reflect that the time of death is unknown, and that day comes like a thief in the night. Therefore let us all take care and teach one another to despise these passing things and to care for those that do not pass away, so that we may become worthy to find those eternal good things, by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and unto the ages of ages. Amen.
Chapter 48
This text: "After this Jesus went about in Galilee, and he did not wish to go to Judea. The feast of the Jews, which is the feast of Tabernacles, was near."
Commentary: Nothing is worse than envy.
Through it death entered the world. For when the devil saw man in honor, he could not bear that good of his.
Therefore he strove in every way to kill him, and the fruit of this root is always of this kind.
In this way Abel was killed, and David was very nearly put to death through envy at the hand of Saul. Through it the Jews too became the killers of Christ, and for this reason the evangelist says:
Gospel: "After this Jesus went about in Galilee, and he was not able to go to Judea, for the Jews were seeking to kill him."
Commentary: What are you saying, O blessed John? Was he not able, he who had the power to do everything he wished?
For did he not say, "Whom do you seek?" and immediately throw them down backward? He who many times was among them and they could not see him, was he not able to do this?
And how, at the last also, did he pass through their midst in the temple, when the assembly was gathered and those killers were there,
and speak harsh words to them, so that even they were amazed, saying: "Is this not the one they were seeking to kill?
And behold, he speaks boldly to them and they say nothing to him." What then are these riddles? Yet they are not riddles, far from it!
But I say this: he displayed both the works of divinity and those of humanity, and when he says:
"He did not have the power," he speaks as of a man and of one doing human deeds. But when he says:
"He stood among them and they could not seize him," then he shows us the works of his divinity and his power. For he also ate as a man, and he was God, and he truly possessed both:
both divinity and humanity. For the fact that he stood among them and they could not seize him shows his invincible power, and again, the fact that he was afraid reveals the economy of his humanity,
so that neither Paul of Samosata could utter his blasphemy, nor again Marcion, for he stops the mouths of both.
Gospel: "After this there was the feast of the Jews, which is the feast of Tabernacles."
Commentary: Now this phrase "after this" signifies nothing other than that he left a long time in between;

And this is evident from the following: when he sat on the mountain, it was Passover, but here the evangelist mentions Tabernacles. And he has taught us nothing more of what was done during those five months, except only the miracle of the five loaves and the discourse he addressed to those who ate. He said nothing else about the events of those five months, for five months pass from Passover to Tabernacles.

Yet he never ceased performing miracles, neither by day nor in the evening, and many times by night as well, as when he came to the apostles on the sea at night, as all the evangelists say. Why then does the evangelist pass over those many miracles? For this reason: he could not recount all of his wonders, but he was eager to tell of those events that gave rise to some accusation or dispute on the part of the Jews; for among the wonders he performed, many were alike. We have often heard that he healed the sick and raised the dead and did wonders; but where they have something unusual to tell, or some suffering and affliction that befell him, that is what they relate: "How can this also be, that even his brothers did not believe in him?" For there is no small reproach in this matter too, and that truth-loving practice of theirs is worthy of wonder, how they do not at all shrink from telling things that appear shameful. And so now he passed over many signs and teachings and wonders and said this:

Gospel: His brothers said to him: "Depart from here and let us go to Judea, so that your disciples too may see the works that you do. For no one does anything in secret and wishes it to be made public. If you do this, reveal yourself to the world." For not even his brothers believed in him.

Commentary: And what word of unbelief did they speak, those who were entreating him to perform signs? Yet their very words are a mark of great unbelief, and so is that untimely boldness, for they supposed that because of their kinship it was proper to speak to him boldly. The opening seems to be that of friends, but these words are full of great bitterness, for they charge him with both timidity and love of glory. For this saying, "No one does anything in secret," is the language of those accusing him of timidity and of those who held his deeds in suspicion; and again this, "He wishes to be made public," is an imputation of love of glory.

But you, consider the power of Christ: for of those who spoke these words, one became the first bishop of Jerusalem, blessed James, of whom the apostle Paul says, "I saw no other of the apostles except James, the brother of the Lord"; and also Jude, and he too became very great and wonderful. Yet at that time they were still very ignorant, even though they too were at Cana when he turned the water into wine, and still they had not understood at all.

Where then did such great unbelief come from in them? From their own will and from envy, for envy often arises toward one's own kin. But some say that here he calls the great crowd disciples, and not the Twelve.
See then what Christ did, how gently he answered, for he did not say to them, "Who are you, that you say this to me and teach me?" Instead he answered.
Gospel: "My time has not yet come."
Commentary: But by this saying, I think, he also signifies something else, for perhaps they were even planning to hand him over to the Jews, and for this reason he said:
"My time has not yet come," that is, the time of crucifixion and death. "And why do you hasten to kill me before the time?"
Gospel: "But your time is always ready."

Commentary: That is: "Even if you are always with the Jews, they will never kill you, since you are zealous just as they are, but they are planning my death at once. Therefore for you there is always time to be with them, if you wish, for nothing will come upon you from them.
But my time is when the time of my crucifixion arrives and my death is appointed."

And that he was saying this he also made clear by the words that follow, when he said to them, "The world cannot hate you," for how would they hate you, he says, you who plan such things and are eager for such things?
Gospel: "But it hates me, because I reprove it, for its works are evil."
Commentary: But let us learn from all this not to be angry, and not to treat the counsel of others as unworthy, even if those who give the counsel are lowly and contemptible,
for if the Lord meekly bore those who counseled him in unbelief, who were advising what was improper and not with good will, what mercy shall we find, we who are earth and ashes,
and who grow angry at those who counsel us if they are even a little inferior to us?
See then how meekly he turns aside that accusation, for when they said,
"Show yourself to the world," he himself said, "The world hates me," so as to refute that word of theirs, as if to say:
I am so far from seeking human glory that I never cease reproving them, I who know that from this envy is born, and hatred, and death is prepared. And if you say,
"When did I reprove?", tell me, when did I cease from reproving? Did I not say, "Do not think that I will accuse you to the Father. There is one who accuses you: Moses," and:
"I know you, that you do not have the love of God," and, "How can you believe,
you who receive glory from men and do not seek the glory of the only God?"
And by these words he also signifies something else: that their hatred toward him arose from this, that he reproved them so boldly, and not from his breaking the Sabbath.

But why does he send them to the feast and say to them, "Go up to this feast, but I am not going up now"? For this reason: to show that they are of no help to him, but since they do not wish to be with him, he leaves them to do the things of the Jews. And why did he go up, since he had said, "I will not go up"? He did not say, "I will not go up," but, "Now, he says, I will not go up."
Gospel: "For my time has not yet been fulfilled."

Interpretation: For he was to be crucified at the Passover still to come; how, then, did he not go up to that one too? For if he was not going up because the time had not yet arrived, it was not at all necessary for him to go up then. But he did not refrain from going up for this reason, in order to suffer, but in order to instruct them. But why did he go up secretly?

For he had the power to go up openly and to bridle their lawlessness, as he did many times, but he did not wish to do this continually. For if he had gone up openly and had blinded them again, he would have displayed the sign of his divinity all the more and revealed it. Since, then, they supposed that [?] "for if, because the time had not yet arrived," [?] for this reason he himself showed both the dispensation of his humanity and his fearlessness: that, although he knew the time of the passion, he would go up there then most of all. And when he says to them, "Go up to this feast yourselves," this means: "Do not think that I am forcing you by compulsion to be with me, and against your will." And the saying, "My time has not yet been fulfilled," indicated that it was still necessary to perform other signs and to deliver teachings, so that more of the people might believe and the disciples might be strengthened all the more, when they saw the boldness of their teacher and what he endured.

Teaching 48, on anger. Let us too, then, learn goodness and meekness from all this, for he says: "Learn from me, for I am meek and lowly in heart." Let us learn in this way and bridle all wickedness. If anyone exalts himself over us, let us humble ourselves, and let us not be avengers and thereby kill our souls. For anger is a beast, an evil and fierce beast. Let us, then, say to ourselves in the time of wrath the words of Scripture: "You are earth and ashes"; and again: "The moment of his anger is his fall"; and: "A wrathful man is unseemly." For nothing is more evil than an enraged face, nor uglier. And if nothing is uglier than the face, what could be uglier than an enraged soul? For just as when someone stirs dung, its stench rises all the more, so too is the soul when it is agitated by anger and a great storm is within it. Or do you say, "I cannot bear it when another insults me"? But why can you not bear it? For if he [?] tells you the truth in those insulting words, you ought rather, even before him, to accuse yourself.

But if he is lying, do not be angry; rather, laugh and sigh for him, for "whoever says to his brother, 'Fool,' is liable to Gehenna." When he insults you, consider the torment he is to enter because of his anger and insult, and not only restrain your anger but also shed tears for him. For no one gets angry at a sick or wounded person, but rather pities him, and the angry soul is in just such a state. Even if you want to do him harm, keep silent, and know that in this way you have wounded him severely; but if you go on to add insult to insult, you only kindle the fire further. Or do you say, "If I keep silent, everyone present will accuse me of weakness"? But consider that they will speak of you not as weak but as greatly wise, and they will be amazed.

But if you are insulted and become angry and insult in return, then you yourself prove that you are senseless and that those words are true. For if they were not true, why would you become angry? If someone says to a rich man, "You are poor," why does he not become angry, but rather laughs? Because he knows that he is not poor. So if we too are insulted, let us laugh at the insult, and we shall prove that nothing of what those words say is found in us. And further, even if this is not so, how long shall we fear the words of men? How long shall we despise the King of all and remain nailed to the earth?
"For since there is envy and strife and division among us, are we not carnal?" Let us therefore become spiritual and bridle that evil beast,
for there is no difference between anger and madness; rather, this is a raging demon, and it makes a person worse than one who is demon-possessed, for the possessed person is pitiable,

but the angry person deserves countless torments. For he willingly throws himself into that pit of perdition, and before the Gehenna of the age to come he is already punished here, since night and day he brings tumult and evil turmoil upon the eyes of the soul. Now therefore let us drive this evil passion away from us and show gentleness in every way, so that in this world we may deliver ourselves from evil and in that age escape those bitter torments, and may find rest of soul here and in the age to come find the kingdom of heaven. May we all be made worthy to attain it by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 49
The text: "Having said this to them, he remained in Galilee, and his brothers went up to the feast. Then he himself also went up, not openly but as if in secret."
Interpretation: The things that the Lord did in human fashion, according to the divine dispensation, he did not only to confirm his incarnation, but also to teach us virtue, for,
if he had done everything as God, how could we know what ought to be done when we fall into such circumstances?

Now my point is this: behold, we have heard from this evangelist that he went in among those enraged Jews at the very time they were seeking to kill him, and by the power of his divinity he bridled them.
Now if he had always acted in this way, we would not be able to do this. But he acted so in order that, when such a situation arises, we might know what we ought to do,

whether simply to give ourselves up to death, or to manage things with a little contrivance, so that the word of the divine preaching may go forward. For what should we have done, we who are not able to go in among our adversaries without their seeing us?
For this reason we learn this too from him, for it says:
Gospel: Having said this, Jesus stayed in Galilee. But when his brothers had gone up, then he himself also went up, not openly, but as it were in secret.

Commentary: Now what it says, "his brothers went up," is an indication that he did not wish to go up with them, and for this reason he stayed there; and when he did go up, he did not make himself known, although they were eager that he should make himself known. But why,
when he always spoke with boldness, did he hide himself here? But consider how this statement stands, for the evangelist does not say:
"secretly," but "as it were in secret," for it was thus reckoned that he was in secret, and he did this in order to teach us to do good deeds with understanding.
And besides this, his going there in the midst of their tumult did not happen only once, but also afterward, when the feast had passed.
Gospel: "But the Jews were looking for him and saying, 'Where is he?'"
Commentary: Fine indeed are the deeds they did during their feasts! For they were always preparing to kill, and during the feasts they were eager to seize him.
For in the same way they said in another place as well: "What do you think? Has he not come to this feast?"
Gospel: "And they were saying, 'Where is he?'"
Commentary: Out of their great hatred and enmity they could not bear even to call him by name.
Oh, the great modesty they showed during the feast, the great piety, to speak in reproach, in that during the feast they were eager to hunt him down!
Gospel: "And there was murmuring about him among the people."
Commentary: But I think that they were also enraged on account of the place where he had performed a miracle, and they were afraid
that he might perform another as well; and so they were talking about him and, involuntarily and against their will, were making him known.
Gospel: "And some were saying, 'He is good'; and others were saying, 'No, but he deceives the people.'"

Commentary: Now this statement, "He is good," belongs to the great multitude, and the other belongs to the rulers and priests, for this statement, "No, but he deceives the people," indicates this. But what was he doing that he was deceiving? Tell me, then, was he deceiving, and did he not truly perform the miracles? But the event itself showed this, whether he performed them by illusion or in truth.
Gospel: "Yet no one spoke openly about him for fear of the Jews."
Commentary: Do you see how those leaders were corrupted, while the people were sound in mind, yet did not have the courage they ought to have had?
Gospel: "And when the feast was already half over, Jesus went up to the temple and was teaching."

Commentary: By that delay he made them more eager to hear his words. For those who had been looking for him during the first days, when they saw that he had suddenly come, surely surrounded him, both those who spoke well of him and those who called him a deceiver: the former so that they might hear his teaching again and profit from it and marvel, and the latter so that they might find a pretext and seize him. So they spoke of his deceiving the people because of the words of his teaching, for they did not understand the power of his words. But those who said:

"He is good," said so because of his miracles. But he himself let the matter rest until their anger had softened, and only then did he come, so that they might be able to hear his words, when wrath would no longer stop their ears. The evangelist has not revealed to us what he taught or what he said, but says only this, that "his teaching was marvelous," and that "it moved them to wonder." And so great was the power of his teaching that those who had been saying, "He deceives the people," turned around and marveled: "How does this man know letters without having studied?" Do you see how even here their amazement is full of wickedness? For the evangelist does not say that his teaching seemed marvelous to them, or that they accepted his teachings, but that they marveled, he says, at where this man knew all this from. They ought therefore to have understood that what was in him was not merely human. But since they did not understand this and only marveled, see what he says to them:

Gospel: "This teaching of mine is not mine, but belongs to him who sent me." And again he answers that suspicion of theirs, in order to make them understand the Father and to stop their mouths. Gospel: "If anyone does his will, he will know about this teaching, what it is, whether it is from God or whether I speak on my own."

Commentary: But what does this saying that he speaks mean? It means this: "Wipe away that lack of understanding, and the wrath and envy and hatred that you hold against me without cause, and then nothing will any longer prevent you from recognizing that this teaching of mine is truly the words of God. For now those evil thoughts of yours darken you and do not allow you to understand my words; but if you wipe away all that evil of yours, then nothing will hinder you any longer."
But he did not say this so openly about their evils, lest their hearts be wounded all the more. Yet although he did not say it openly, he indicated all this through the saying that he spoke:
Gospel: "Whoever does his will shall know about this teaching, what it is, whether it is from God or whether I speak on my own."

Commentary: That is to say: or whether I say something foreign and contrary. For when he says "on my own," this expression always signifies this: "I say nothing outside his will, but all that the Father wills, I also will."
Gospel: "If anyone does his will, he will know this teaching."
Interpretation: What, then, does this mean: "If anyone does his will"? It is to say this:

If anyone is eager to practice the virtues and to please God, he will understand the force of these words. If anyone wishes to understand the words of the Scriptures, he will know whether they bear witness to my words or not. But how is it that this teaching is both his and not his?
For he did not say, "This teaching is not mine," but first he said, "The teaching is mine," and only then did he add and say, "It is not mine."

For he says, "This my teaching is not mine." How then is it possible that one and the same teaching should be both his and not his? It is like this: it is his because he did not speak in this way after learning from anyone, but without having been taught; and it is not his in this sense, that the teaching was the Father's. But how then does he say in another place:
"All that is the Father's is mine, and all that is mine is his"? For if this, since it is the Father's, is not yours, O Lord, then surely that saying is not true, for:
"Since it is the Father's," for that very reason it ought to be yours. But this saying, "It is not mine," strongly signifies the close belonging between him and the Father, as if he were saying:

"It has no separation," as though it were another's: even though the person is another, I so speak and act that it cannot be supposed that it is not truly the Father's, but rather that it is just the same as the Father's own word or deed.
And again he brings in yet another argument, between wisdom and also a human manner, in order to convince them.
And what is this argument? He says that whoever wishes to establish some teaching of his own does this for no other reason than to gain glory for himself.
But since I do not seek my own glory, why would I strive in vain to establish my teaching, if it were not truly from the Father?
For when someone speaks anything of himself, that means something of his own and separate. For this reason he says, "in order to establish his own glory." But if:
"I seek the glory of him who sent me," why would I teach you from that alien teaching?
Do you see how there was a certain reason for which he said that, and why he said to him, "I do nothing of myself": so that they might believe that he did not long for human glory?
For this reason, whenever he speaks with humility, he says, "I seek the glory of my Father," in order to convince them that he does not love glory from them.

Now the reasons for this humble way of speaking are many: first, so that he might not be thought unbegotten; and so that they might not suppose him to be opposed to the Father; and in order to confirm his humanity; and because of the weakness of those hearers;
and in order to teach people humility and not to speak grandly about themselves. But of his speaking loftily and with authority there is only one reason: the sovereignty of his nature.

And for this reason it was not fitting always to address such speech to those people without understanding. For if, when he said, "Before Abraham I am," they stumbled because of it, what would they have done if he had always spoken such lofty words to them?
Gospel: "Moses gave you the law, and none of you keeps the law. Why do you seek to kill me?"

Commentary: What agreement do these words have, or what connection do they have with what was said earlier? For they were laying two charges against him: first, that he breaks the Sabbath, and second, that he calls God his own Father and makes himself equal with God.
But this was not merely their suspicion and opinion; it was true, and he himself also spoke this way and constantly affirmed that he is equal to God. For the word that he spoke, namely:

"As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wishes"; and again: "That all may honor [?], that as they honor the Father"; and: "The works that he does, I also do": all of this is indicative of equality. And concerning the law, then, he says: "Do not think that I have come to abolish the law and the prophets." In this way he knew how to wipe out the wicked notions of their minds as well; but their thought about equality he not only does not wipe out, but even confirms. For this reason also, when in another place they said, "You make yourself God," he did not dispel that suspicion, but confirmed it and said: "That you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins," he said to the paralytic: "Rise, take up your bed and go to your house." So he confirmed that one charge of theirs, for he showed that he is not opposed to the Father, but does everything in equality with him. But here he stands against that second charge, which they were making about the breaking of the Sabbath, and he says to them:
Gospel: "Did not Moses give you the law? And none of you keeps the law."

Commentary: But why did he say "none"? Because all of them were seeking to kill him. And the force of his word is this: Even though I broke the law of the Sabbath, yet I saved a man, and it was for the sake of his life that I broke the Sabbath. And if that deed of mine was a transgression of the law (which it was not), still, even if it was, it was for the sake of a man's life, and it was not fitting for me to be judged by you, who greatly transgress the commandments of the law; for that transgression of yours is the complete abolition of the law. And then, after these words, he teaches them at length. Although many teachings had been addressed to them before as well, he spoke to them then loftily and in keeping with his own dignity, but now more humbly.

Why, then, does he do this? Because he did not wish to embitter them continually, and at this time their anger had grown and their envy was great. Therefore he wishes to subdue them by these two means: first, that he exposed the evil design of their heart, that they were seeking to kill him; and second, that he speaks to them so meekly and sweetly: "A man who tells you the truth." And he also showed them that, since they are murderers, they ought not to judge others, for they are not worthy to. But you, observe the humility of Christ's speech and the arrogance and wickedness of their speech, for they said to him:
Gospel: "You have a demon with you. Who is seeking to kill you?"

Commentary: This speech comes from anger and wrath and from a soul grown shameless, one that is not at all ashamed by reproof and supposes that he has become afraid. And further, just as robbers, when they plot some evil against someone, want that man to be off his guard and bring this about by their denial, so these men also act. But he left off reproving them even in this, so that they might not become more shameless, and he took up again the same argument he had been making about the loosing of the Sabbath, and he stopped their mouths from the Law. And see how wisely he did everything, as if he were saying to them: "It is no wonder if you disobey me, since you disobey even the Law, which you think you obey and of which you say, 'Moses gave it to us.'

So it is nothing surprising if you do not believe my words either, for you were saying, 'God spoke to Moses, but as for this man, we do not know where he is from.'" For this reason he shows that they were despising and reviling Moses as well: "For he gave you the Law," he says, "and you did not listen."
Gospel: "I did one deed, and you all marvel."
Commentary: Do you accuse me for this very thing, for which acceptance and thanks were due? For he does not mention what was done by the Father, but presents it in his own person:
Gospel: "I did one deed," he says.

Commentary: He wishes to show that not doing it would have been the loosing of the Law, and that there are many other things more binding than the Law. For Moses too undertook to admit a commandment over the Law, and one more binding than the Law, since circumcision is more binding even than the Sabbath, for it is not from the Law but from the fathers. "But I have done something better and higher even than circumcision,"
and here he did not mention the commandment of the Law, as he did when he spoke of the priests who profane the Sabbath, and here he stops their mouths with a stronger reason.
As for "you marvel," this means: "You are in turmoil and agitated." For if the law of the Sabbath had to be kept firmly, circumcision would not have been more binding than it.
Gospel: "If a man receives circumcision on the Sabbath"
Commentary: Do you see that the Law is all the more firmly established when it is loosed?
Do you see that even the loosing of the Sabbath is the keeping of the Law,
for if the Sabbath were not loosed,

the loosing of the Law would come about? And from this it appears that "I too have in some way established it." And he did not say, "You are angry with me because I did something greater than circumcision," but he only stated the deed and left the judgment of it to them, so that they might judge whether complete healing is not better than circumcision.

For if a man receives a sign that is in no way profitable for righteousness, and for this the Law is loosed, are you angry over this, if I loosed the Sabbath so that he might be freed from such a disease?
Gospel: "Do not judge by appearances"
Commentary: What then does "by appearances" mean? It means: do not, for this reason,
that Moses is greatly honored by you, base your decision on him,
but look at the nature of the deeds and make your judgment accordingly, for this is judging with righteousness. For why did no one complain about Moses?

Why did no one disobey the command to break the Sabbath, given by a commandment that came in from outside the Law? Rather, he accepted that a commandment not laid down by the Law but from outside it should be made greater than the commandment of his own Law, which is marvelous. But you, who are not lawgivers, champion the Law beyond measure by means of an unlawful commandment. And when he said "a whole man," he shows that circumcision is a partial kind of health. What then is the health that circumcision gives? The soul of the man, he says; I restored him, who was not injured in one member only but corrupted in every part. Therefore, "Do not judge with partiality."

Teaching 49. On justice. This was said not only to the people of that time but also to us, so that we may not pervert justice in any matter but may strive for justice in every way. And whether someone is poor or rich, let us look not at persons but at deeds, for "You shall not show pity to the poor man in judgment." And what does this saying mean? It means: do not lean toward the side of injustice, even if the unjust person is poor. Now if it is not right to turn aside from justice out of mercy for a poor man, is it not much less right to do so for the sake of a rich man? I say this not only to judges but to all people, so that we may never pervert justice but may always keep it well, for the Lord loves justice. "But he who loves falsehood hates his own soul." So then, let us not hate our souls; let us not love falsehood, for what is the profit of falsehood?

For even if there is some profit for the body, it is small and amounts to nothing, and in the end we shall perish miserably; indeed, even here we gain nothing from it. For when we make merry with an evil mind, is this thing not a punishment and a torment? So let us love justice, and let us nowhere despise this law. For what shall we gain from this life if we do not acquire virtue in it as provision for the age to come? Or what will friends and relatives avail us there, or anyone's favor shown on behalf of falsehood? And why do I say this? Even if Noah or Job or Daniel were our father, this will not profit us at all when our deeds are evil. Only one thing is needful for us: virtue of soul. This is able to save us and deliver us from those eternal torments, and may it make us worthy of the kingdom of heaven by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, amen. Part II
Chapter 50
Text: Some of the people of Jerusalem were saying, "Is this not the man whom they were seeking to kill?
Look, he is speaking openly, and they say nothing to him. Can it be that the rulers have truly learned that this is the Christ? But we know where this man comes from."
Interpretation: Nothing in the holy Scriptures is said simply in this way, for they were spoken by the Holy Spirit.
Therefore we must examine everything in minute detail, for often great power is found in a single word, as is the case with this passage now before us.
Gospel: "Some of the people of Jerusalem were saying: 'Is this not the one whom they were seeking to kill? And look, here he is, speaking openly, and they say nothing to him.'"

Commentary: Why is it said here, "some of the people of Jerusalem"? Because the evangelist shows us that those who had witnessed his greater and great signs were the most pitiable of all: they who had seen the great sign of his divinity gave heed in everything to the judgment of those corrupt rulers. Or was it not a great wonder that those who went about seeking to kill him, when he came among them, had their hands bound? For who did all this? Who quenched that furnace of their anger? Yet, on top of all this wonder and his other countless signs, behold their senselessness: "Is this not," they say, "the one whom they were seeking to kill?" See how they accuse themselves and say, "the one whom they are seeking to kill, and they say nothing to him," he who was openly among them and boldly rebuking them, by which their rage was made all the greater.

But do they do nothing? Can it be that they have truly come to know that this is the Christ? And you, what do you say about him, O Jews? What do you think of him? They say: "We say this: that he is not the Christ." For this reason they also said: "We know where this man is from."
O this wickedness! O this evil speech! They do not even follow the decision of the rulers, but bring in another evil, one worthy of their own folly.
Gospel: "We know, they say, where he is from; but when the Christ comes, no one will know where he is from."
Commentary: And how is it that, when Herod questioned your priests, they said, "He is born in Bethlehem," and again certain others said:
"We know that God spoke to Moses, but as for this man, we do not know where he is from"? We know, they say, where he is from, and again: we do not know, they say, where he is from.
Behold the words of drunken men! And again they say: "Surely the Christ does not come from Galilee? Does he not come from Bethlehem?" Behold this speech of men driven mad:
We know and we do not know, they say; and the Christ comes from Bethlehem; and when the Christ comes, no one will know, they say, where he is from.
What could be plainer than this madness? For their eagerness was directed to one thing alone: not to believe. Hear, then, what the Lord answered:
Gospel: "You both know me and know where I am from, and I have not come of myself. And he who sent me is true, whom you do not know; but I know him, for I am from him, and he sent me."
Commentary: And again in another place he says: "If you knew me, you would know my Father also." But how is this, since he says to them:

"You know me and where I am from," and again he says to them: "You know neither me nor my Father"? Can it be that his words contradict one another? Far from it! Rather, they even strongly bear witness to one another. But when he says:
"You do not know me," he is speaking here of another kind of knowledge, as it is written: "The sons of Eli, lawless sons, who did not know the Lord"; and again he says:
"Jerusalem did not know me," as again the apostle Paul says: "They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him." And can knowing and not knowing belong to one and the same matter?

But by this he means: "You know me" and "You know that I am the Son of God." For in "where I am from" he is not speaking here of a place, and this is evident from the following statement, in which he says:
"I have not come of myself, but he who sent me is true, whom you do not know." Here he is speaking of ignorance shown by deeds, in accordance with the saying of Paul:
"They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him." And the sin did not come from ignorance, but from wickedness and an evil mind.
And they knew this, yet did not want knowledge. But see what consistency these words have! For how, when he was reproving them, he spoke their very own words.
For when they said, "We know where this man is from," he himself also said:

"You know me too." And why did he say this to them? Were they perhaps saying, "We do not know"? No, but it was for this reason. For what were they saying? "We know where he is from." And they were saying it for no other reason than this: that he is from the earth and is the son of the carpenter.
But he was lifting them up to heaven and saying, "You know where I am from," that is to say:

"I am from heaven, not from where you say, but from where the one who sent me is." For the saying "I have not come of myself" indicates this: that they too knew that he had been sent by the Father, even though they did not declare it openly.

Therefore he reproves them on two counts. First he brought into the open what they were saying on their own, in order to shame them, and then he revealed everything devised in their minds, as if he were saying to them:
"I am not in this way one of the common sort, of those who have come in vain, but the one who sent me is true." What does this saying mean: "The one who sent me is true"?

It means this: since he is true, he has surely sent the one he sent for the sake of truth; since the sender is true, the one sent is also true. And he also does this in yet another way, for he catches them by their very own words. For they were saying, "When the Christ comes, no one will know where he is from." By this too he shows that he is the Christ. For they were speaking the words "no one will know" with reference to some determination of place, and from this too he shows that he is the Christ, for he came from the Father, and everywhere he testifies that knowledge of the Father belongs to himself alone, as he says: "Not that anyone has seen the Father, except the one who is from the Father."
And he enraged them by these words. For saying "You do not know him," and again, when they were saying "We do not know," the reproof that they do know, is enough to enrage them.
Gospel: "They sought to seize him, and no one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come."

Commentary: Do you see how they were invisibly bound, and a bridle was put on their anger? But why did he not say, "He invisibly restrained them," but said instead, "His hour had not yet come"? For this reason: the evangelist wished here to speak of him in a humbler and human way, so that his humanity too might be firmly established. For since in every place he spoke of the lofty matters of the divinity, he has therefore also sown these human words in between. And when he says, "I am from him," it is not as a prophet who sees him and speaks in this way, but as one who always sees him and is with him.

For he says, "I know him, for I am from him." Do you see how, above and below, he prepares this statement, "I have not come of myself," and "He who sent me is true"? For all this was so that he might not be thought a stranger to God. And see how great is the benefit of those humble words, for it says:
Gospel: "After this many believed and said: When the Christ comes, will he do more signs than these which this man has done?"

Commentary: How many signs? For there are three signs: that of the wine, that of the paralytic, and that of the son of the royal official, and the evangelist has told of nothing more. From this we know that the evangelists passed over many of his signs and did not write them down, but tell us those on account of which the rulers spoke evil of him and sought to seize him and kill him.

But it was not the multitude of the people who were doing this, for they were not lovers of power, nor did they envy him; rather, the priests were the doers of all this, for those of the great crowd said, "When the Christ comes, will he do greater signs?" Yet even this faith was not sound, but was that of a coarse and ignorant people, for the words of those who said, "When the Christ comes," were not those of people fully convinced that he is the Christ. Either it is as I have said, or else it is this: since the rulers were asserting, "This is not the Christ," the people said, "Well then, let us say: This is not the Christ. Will that someone, who they say is another, be better than this one?" As I always say, those who are coarse in mind and without understanding are not converted so much by teaching and persuasion of words as by a sign.
Gospel: "The Pharisees heard the murmuring of the people about him, and the chief priests and the Pharisees sent servants,
to seize him."

Commentary: Do you see that the breaking of the Sabbath was only a pretext, and that what really troubled them was this: that here they had nothing they could state as a pretext concerning his words or his deeds? And since they could find no other pretext on account of the people, they wanted to seize him, yet they did not dare to do it themselves, for they were wary of such an uproar, but sent their servants. O the tyranny and madness! O the great folly! For they themselves had fought against him many times and could not prevail, and they ordered their servants to do the deed, so that they might give rest to their anger. And he himself had spoken at the pool too, and to them, and they did nothing of the kind, but only sought to, without laying a hand to the deed. But here they could bear it no longer, when they saw that the people were going over to him. But Christ answered:
Gospel: "For a little while I am with you"

Commentary: And he who had the power to bend them and frighten them speaks words full of humility, as if he were saying: "Why do you hasten to kill me and get rid of me? Wait for me yet a little while, and then, even if you wish to keep me with you, I will not stay." And then, so that they might not understand this as death, since that comes upon everyone (for they imagined this too), and so that no one might imagine this, he said:
Gospel: "And where I am, you cannot come"
Commentary: For if he were going to remain in death, they too could go there, since we all go there.
So these words at once bent the ignorant, frightened the proud, and made the lovers of learning eager to listen, when they heard:
"Yet a little while," and that they would no longer be able "to hear the teachings." And he did not say: "For a little while I am with you," that is to say:

"Whether you persecute me or fight against me, for this little time I am here," but rather: "For a little while I am with you," that is to say: "Whether you persecute me or fight against me, for this little time I am with you, and I will not cease to carry out my dispensations for you and to teach for the life of souls,
and then I go to him who sent me." This was enough to frighten and grieve them, and he indicates that it would be needful for them, for he says:
Gospel: "You will seek me": not only will you not forget me, but you will even seek me.
Commentary: And where, then, did the Jews seek him? As Luke says,
women lamented for him, and many others too. And later, when their city was being taken captive, would they not have remembered Christ and those wonders of his, and sought his coming?

And he said all this because he wished them to come to what is good, for these words, "It is yet a little while," and the seeking of him after his departure and the failure to find him, all this was enough to convince and convert them.
For if he had not been going to make himself longed for, they would not have believed; and again, if it had been possible to find him, they likewise would not have been afraid.
And again, if he had been going to remain with them for a long time, perhaps even so they would have become negligent. But in every way he frightens and unsettles them; and again this saying, namely:
"I go to him who sent me" makes it evident that no harm comes upon him from that enmity of theirs, and that his crucifixion is voluntary.

So he told them two predictions: first, that after a little time he is to depart, and second, that they will not be able to come to him. For this foreknowledge of his own end was not of human nature. For see what David says:
"Make known to me, O Lord, my end and the number of my days, that I may know what I still lack."
And no one knows this matter. But,
I think that this saying was addressed to those servants, and by it he made them bend, when he showed them that he knows the time of his departure, as though he were saying to them:
"Wait for me only a little while longer, and I will depart."
Gospel: "The Jews said to one another: 'Where does this man intend to go?'"

Commentary: And why do they inquire about this? For those who desired with all their might to be rid of him, and who were seeking every means so as not to see him, ought not to have inquired about this, but rather to have said: "Yes, we rejoice; and when is this going to happen?" But they were wounded by those words, and they inquire among themselves in their folly:
Gospel: "Where is he going? Does he perhaps intend to go to those dispersed among the Gentiles?"

Commentary: Who are "the dispersed Gentiles"? This is what the Jews called the Gentiles, because they were dispersed in every place. But now this reproach has come upon them as well, for formerly that whole nation of theirs was together, and a Jew was not found anywhere else but only in Palestine. But what is this saying: "Where I am, you cannot come"? For if he were going to the Gentiles, why would he have said: "You cannot come"? But when they said, "He intends to go to those dispersed Gentiles," they did not say, "to lead them astray," but "to teach them." Thus, when they heard these words, their anger calmed and they believed; for had they not believed, they would not have inquired what this saying is.
Homily 50. On righteousness. But he said all this to them, and yet I fear lest this be said to us as well, because of this life of ours,

full of sin: that we cannot come where he is, because of these evils of ours. For concerning the disciples he says: "I desire that where I am, these also may be with me." But concerning us I fear lest the opposite be said, that is: "Where I am, you cannot come." For when we do what is contrary to his commandments, how could we go there? For in this world too, a soldier who angers the king is not permitted to see the king, but is in prison and in torments. For when we plunder and are greedy, when we harm others and are merciless, how could we come there? And consider those virgins, how they were not permitted to enter where he was, but turned back when their lamps had gone out; that is to say, grace had abandoned them.

For that flame of the grace of the Holy Spirit which was given to us grows if we wish, and if we wish, it is entirely extinguished. And when it has been extinguished, there will then be nothing else upon us but fog and mist. For this reason also it has been said: "Do not quench the Spirit." And it is quenched when it has no oil, and when a wind of violent blowing arises, and again when it is in constriction and distress, for this is how fire is extinguished. And this fire is constricted by the cares of the world and extinguished by evil desire, but nothing extinguishes it so much as mercilessness, rage and robbery. For whoever, besides not having oil, also pours cold water on it, how could he light that lamp?

And that water is the water of greed, which chills the soul grievously. Let it not be that when we too depart from here we have nothing else with us but ash and dust and much smoke, which would accuse us of having had lamps and having extinguished them. For where there is smoke, it is evident that a fire was there and went out. But far be it from us to hear with our ears that bitter voice: "I do not know you." And from what does the hearing of this voice come about, "I do not know you"? Only from this: that when we see a poor man, we are as if we had not seen him. And when we have no mercy on the hungry poor man, who is Christ, how will Christ have mercy on us when we need mercy? For whoever despises the afflicted and does not give of his own, how could he ask to receive what is not his? Therefore I beseech you, let us strive in every way that oil may not fail us, but that we may adorn our lamps and enter with that immortal Bridegroom into that incorruptible bridal chamber, of which may we all be made worthy by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 51

This saying: On the last day, the great day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried out and said: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink, and whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said: 'Rivers of living water shall flow from his belly.'"
Interpretation: Those who approach this divine preaching and hear the faith must show the desire that a thirsty person has for water, and when they do so,
then they will be able to establish those divine words firmly in their hearts.
For when the thirsty receive water, they drink it with great desire until they quench the burning heat of thirst that is in them.
In the same way, those who hear the divine words, if they receive them with great thirst, will not grow weary of drinking such a drink.
For such a matter calls for hunger and thirst, as the Lord says: "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness," and again, behold, in this place he cries out and says:
Gospel: "Whoever thirsts, let him come to me and drink."

Commentary: Now the meaning of this saying is this: "I bring no one by compulsion and against his will, but whoever has zeal and burns with desire, let him come, and I call him." But why did the evangelist say:
"On that last, great day"?
Because it was a great feast, and the days between Passover and this feast, and those other days, they spent in enjoyment, and at that time all of them would gather? But why does he say "last"?
So that you may know how he taught that whole multitude with boldness. For at the first feast he did not go, and he gave his brothers the reason
why he did not go; and at the second he again did not go; and at the third he no longer said any such thing, so that his word would not be undone by their enjoyment and become useless.

But on that last day, when each of them wished to depart for his home, he then gives them the provision for the journey of life and speaks with a loud cry: first, to show the boldness he had for the sake of the truth, and his fearlessness; second, because of the multitude of people gathered; and so that they might understand that he is speaking of spiritual drink. For this reason he said:
Gospel: "Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly."
Commentary: In this place he calls the heart the "belly," just as Scripture says in another place: "Your law is in the midst of my belly."

But where did Scripture say that "rivers of living water shall flow from his belly"? Scripture has nowhere spoken this saying. But understand how this saying stands, for this is how it ought to be written and read: when he says, "Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said," at this place the sentence must be divided and a pause made, so that the words "rivers shall flow from his belly" no longer belong to the same statement. For since many were saying:
"This is the Christ," and, "When the Christ comes, will he do more signs?"
for this reason he wished to show that rightness of mind is required, so that people should have faith in me not because of signs alone, but also from the Scriptures.
For many saw even his signs and did not believe, and they said: "Does not the Scripture say that the Christ comes from the seed of David?"

For this reason he spoke of the Scriptures, to show that he does not flee from their testimony, and he sends them to the Scriptures, for earlier too he said: "Search the Scriptures!" And again he says:
"It is written in the prophets," and again: "They shall all be taught by God," and again: "Moses accuses you." And so here he says:
"Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, from such a one, from his belly, shall flow rivers of living water."

For he was indicating the richness and ungrudging abundance of his grace, as he says in another place: "A spring of water flowing to eternal life," that is, that he would have much grace; and in another place he says "eternal life," meaning that which is at work. For when the grace of the Holy Spirit is established in a person's mind, it wells up more than any spring, and it does not fail, nor become empty, nor cease. And in order to indicate both the unfailing nature of his grace and its incomprehensibility, he therefore named it a spring of water and a river, not one river but many and countless. And again, there, by the flowing he showed its richness and breadth. And if you wish, consider the wisdom of Stephen, or the tongue of Peter, or the irresistibility of Paul's wisdom, or that of this very speaker, John, who wrote this Gospel.

See, if you wish, the breadth and depth of his wisdom: how nothing was able to withstand the rivers that came forth from them, how nothing could endure their battle, neither the anger of the peoples, nor the uprising of tyrants, nor the efforts of demons, nor daily deaths; but, like rivers going with great force, so they swept everything along toward the Kingdom and went on.
Gospel: "But this he said about the Spirit, which was to be given to those who believed in him, for the Holy Spirit had not yet been given."

Interpretation: And how did the prophets preach beforehand, if the Holy Spirit had not yet been given? For the apostles did not cast out by the Holy Spirit the demons that they cast out at that time, but by the authority given by him, as he himself said: "If I cast out by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast out demons?" And he said this to indicate that before the crucifixion they did not cast out by the Spirit but by the authority that came from him. And when he was about to send them out to preach, then he said to them: "Receive the Holy Spirit," and again: "The Holy Spirit came upon them; then they performed signs."

But earlier, when he was sending them out, it is not written: "He gave them the Holy Spirit," but: "He gave them authority," and he said to them: "Cleanse lepers, cast out demons, raise the dead; freely you have received, freely give." But concerning the prophets it is acknowledged by all that the Holy Spirit was given. What then does this saying mean? Hear, then: the Holy Spirit was indeed given to the prophets, but the grace of the Holy Spirit had been withdrawn from the earth from the day when he said: "Behold, your house is left desolate." And even before that saying it had begun to fail, for there was no longer a prophet among them, nor did that grace come upon them, since the Holy Spirit had been withdrawn and was about to come richly and powerfully.

Now the beginning of its coming came about from the crucifixion, as did the giving of those very great graces, for that gift was more wonderful, as he says: "Do you not know of what spirit you are?" And again it is written: "You have not received the spirit of slavery, but the spirit of adoption." For those of old had the Holy Spirit, but they could not give it to others, whereas the apostles filled many myriads. And since such grace was going to be received, and such grace had not yet been given, for this reason he says: "The Holy Spirit had not yet been given," for the Lord was speaking about this grace. For this reason the evangelist said: "The Holy Spirit was not yet," that is, that exalted grace of this kind had not yet been given.
Gospel: For Jesus was not yet glorified.

Commentary: He calls the crucifixion glorification. "Jesus was not yet glorified" means that he had not yet been crucified, for the glory of Christ is the cross. For we were enemies and sinners, deprived of the grace of God and people who grieved God, whereas that grace was a sign of reconciliation. And the gift is not given to enemies or to those who are hated, but to friends and to those who are pleasing. Therefore it was necessary that the sacrifice offered for us should first be offered, and that he should dissolve the enmity by his flesh, so that we might become friends of God, and that after this the great gift should be given to us. For if this was done in the case of the promise to Abraham, would it not all the more be done in the case of this grace?
