Their question is mistaken, for how could he have sinned before birth? Or if his parents sinned, how could he have been punished?

So what led them to ask about this matter? This: that earlier, when he healed that paralyzed man, he said to him: "Behold, you have been healed; from now on sin no more." And they understood that he had been paralyzed because of sins, and for this reason they said here: "Behold, that man was paralyzed because of sins."

What then will you say about this? Could it be that this man too has sinned? But this is impossible, for he is blind from birth. Or is it because of the sin of his parents? But this too is unfitting, for a child is not called to judgment on account of its parents. For just as we, when we see a little child in suffering, say in wonder, "What can this one's guilt possibly be?", so too the disciples asked this question in amazement. And the Lord answered them: "Neither this man sinned nor his parents, that he should be born blind." But this saying that he spoke does not show that they were without sin, for he did not say simply, "They did not sin," but:

"They did not sin so that he should be born blind," but "so that the Son of God may be glorified." For both he and his parents did sin, but his blindness does not come from this. He said this, however, not to show that this is so in this case while certain others became blind because of the sin of their parents, for it is impossible that one person should sin and another be punished for his sin. Otherwise, if we say this, we should also say that he sinned before he was born. For just as he said that this man was born blind neither because of his own sins nor because of his parents', so it is in every case. And for this reason Ezekiel removes that suspicion and says: "As I live, says the Lord, this proverb shall no longer be, which is spoken: 'The fathers ate sour grapes and the children's teeth were set on edge.'" And Moses says: "A father shall not die for a son."

But if anyone should say, as it is said, "who repays the sin of the parents upon the children to the third and fourth generation," we say about this that the commandment does not apply to all, but was spoken about certain people, those who came out of Egypt. And the saying means this: since those who came out of Egypt, after so many signs that had been done in the time of their parents, became worse than those who had never seen a sign at all, therefore he says: "What came upon them, the same shall come upon these also, for they have done the same deeds." And whoever reads it will truly know that it was said about them. But why was he born blind?
For this reason, he says: that the glory of God might be shown in him.

Behold, here another difficulty appears, for someone might say: "What is this? Was it not possible for the glory of God to be shown without this man's torment?" But it was not said that it was impossible, for it was possible for the glory of God to be shown even without him; rather, it was said so that it might be shown in him as well.

But if anyone should say that this suffering came upon him unjustly so that God might be glorified, then let the one who says such a thing tell me: what harm would have come upon him even if his eyes had never been opened at all?
For I say that a greater good came to him through blindness, for his inner eyes were opened. For what did the Jews gain from their eyes?

Did not a greater judgment come upon them, because eyes had been given to them and they became blind? But what evil came to this man from blindness, since because of it the eyes of his soul were opened?
For just as the evil things of this world are not evil, so also the good things are not good; rather, only sin is evil, whereas blindness is not evil.
And he who brought him from non-existence into existence had the power to leave him thus.
But some say: "This statement that he makes, 'that God may be glorified,' does not express the cause but the outcome," as when he says:
"For the judgment of this world I have come, that those who did not see may see, and those who saw may become blind"; and again Paul says:
"What can be known of God has become manifest to them, so that they may be without excuse," yet he did not show it to them for this purpose, that they might be without excuse;
and again in another place he says: "The law came in so that deficiency might multiply," yet it did not come in for this purpose, but so that sin might be checked.

Do you see how it turns out that this refers to the outcome? For just as some skilled master builder might build half of a house and leave half, so that, if anyone should say of the part already built that it is not his building, he might show by completing the unfinished part
that he had made that part too, so Christ renews this body of ours, as if it were a ruined house,
for he healed the withered hand and strengthened the loosened knees, made the lame walk, healed lepers, raised the dead, gave light to blinded eyes, and created what did not exist,
all of which were matters of natural infirmity. And he gave life to all of it, so that in this way he might show his power. But as for his saying:
"that the glory of God may be revealed," he says this about himself and not about the Father, for the Father's glory was evident; for since they had heard that
"God created man, dust, from the earth," for this reason he himself also did likewise, for if he had said:
"I am the one who took dust from the earth and made man," this statement would have been hard for them to accept; but since he showed his power by a deed, his work was no longer beyond belief.

And for this reason he took dust from the earth, which he formed with spittle, and in this way he reveals that hidden glory of his; for it is no small glory when they understand that this is the Creator of creatures. For from this one deed he demonstrates everything, since the proof of the greater made the lesser credible as well; for man is more honorable than the whole world. And again, among our members the most honorable of all is the eye; for this reason he made the eyes not in an ordinary way but in this manner, for although that member is small, it is of greater use to the body than all the others. And for this reason the apostle said: "If the ear should say, 'I am not an eye, I am no longer of the body,' is it for this reason not of the body?"

For all our members are heralds of the wisdom of God. But more than all of them is the eye, for it leads the whole body. It produces beauty, it adorns the face, it is the lamp of all the members; for as the sun is the light of the world, so also is the eye of the body. If you darken the sun, you have destroyed the whole world; and if you darken the eyes, the feet too become useless, and the hands too, and the soul is no longer able by itself to know things, since it no longer sees anything of created things and does not come to true understanding. For by the sight of created things we know the God of all, for his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are seen, being known through created things. Therefore it is evident that the eye is the lamp not only of the body but of the soul as well.

For this reason also the eyes are established as if in a royal place, seated on high above the other senses. And these the Lord now creates and bestows on that eyeless man. And further, so that it may not occur to you that he needs matter in order to act, and so that you may know that he did not need that clay in the beginning either — for he who created those higher natures from nothing, could he not have made these without matter? — and so that you may know that it was not because he needed matter to do this that he took clay, but to show that he is the one who first created man from earth: for this reason, when he had anointed him with the clay, he said to him, "Go and wash!" so that you may know that "I do not need clay for the making of eyes, but it is so that my glory may be manifested." And so that you may know that he was speaking of himself when he said, "so that my glory may be manifested," he therefore added and said:
Gospel:
"I must do the work of him who sent me"

Commentary: That is to say, "I must submit myself and do the works that are able to show that I have power to do the works that the Father does, and not only works like them, but those very same works." For this is a figure of a greater inseparability. Who then is able to set his eyes upon him who does those works of the Father? For he did not only create the eye, nor only open it, but he also bestowed sight, which is also a figure of the breathing-in of the soul; for if that is not at work, the eye, even though it be perfect, can never see. Now then it is evident that he both gave that power of the soul and bodily created that member, and the arteries [?] and veins and blood and everything else of which our body is composed.
Gospel: "I must work while it is still day"

Commentary: What are these words? Or what is their force? Listen then, for this is what he is saying: "while this day still lasts," that is, while it is still good for people if they believe in me, and it is of profit to them, as long as they are in this world and the time for doing good works is given.
Gospel: "Night is coming"

Commentary: That is to say, the end is coming, and the time of that age, when no one is able to act any longer, for then neither faith nor repentance will help. For he calls faith a work, as when they asked him: "What shall we do, that we may perform the work of God?"

He said to them: "This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent." But how is it that no one can do this work then? Because there is no faith then either, but all will be obedient involuntarily. For he himself was doing everything for their good, so that they might believe here, because there it no longer profits them. And for this reason he himself went to the blind man, and not the blind man to him, for it is evident that the man was worthy of healing, and that if he had been able to see, he would have believed even then, or if he had heard about him from someone. And this is evident from his later courage and faith, for he did not doubt at all, nor did he say, "What is this thing, that he made clay and smeared it on my eyes and said to me:
'Go and wash in Siloam'? Is he not able, if he has the power, to heal and then to send me to Siloam? For I have washed there many times, and it has done me no good.
If he had any power, he would have healed me himself now," as Naaman said about Elisha when Elisha commanded him to go and wash in the Jordan, and he was unbelieving.
But the blind man did not act in this way. He did not become unbelieving, he did not contradict, he did not doubt, asking who ever had his eyes opened with clay. He said nothing of the kind.
Do you see this firm faith?
Gospel: "The night is coming."
Commentary: By this he shows that even after the crucifixion he would have care for the lawless and would bring many to faith, for:
"It is still day," he says; but after this he separates them completely. This is what he was signifying when he said:
Gospel: "As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world."
Commentary: Just as he also said to others: "Believe while the light is with you." But if anyone should say:
"How is it that Paul names this life night and that life day, while Christ names this life day and that one night?" Yet Paul does not oppose Christ, far from it!
Rather, he too speaks just as the Lord does; although the words are not the same, the meaning is the same. For he says: "The night is passing away, and the day has drawn near."

And he designates this life as night on account of those who are in unbelief and evil, or in comparison with that life, which is day. But Christ calls that age night for this reason, that no deed is done then, neither sin nor virtue; and he called this life day because,
if anyone wishes, he is able to do good. And Paul called this life night because those who conduct themselves in it with wickedness and unbelief are in darkness.
Homily 56. On mercy. So he was teaching the believers, saying: "The night is passing away and the day has drawn near," since they were going to receive that glory and eternal light.
And he gives the name night to the old man and to the old life, for he says: "Let us put off the works of darkness."
Do you see that he calls the doing of evil deeds night? Therefore let us walk openly and becomingly, as in the day, so that that eternal light may be given to us.
For if this light is so good, consider what that one must be like; for how much better and greater is the radiance of the sun than the light of a small lamp?

And for this reason it is said that even the sun will be darkened by that glorious light. But if in this world we go to great expense and labor for bright and beautiful houses, is it not right that we should wholly mortify and destroy our flesh, so that in that eternal age we may gain the world of the glorious one? And that light is too bright for the eye to bear. For here we must have hardship and quarrels and lawsuits and rivalries with others, but there is nothing of the kind there: no envy, no collapse, no lawsuit over boundaries. And the dwellings of this world we must surely leave, but that one stands forever; and all this will pass away, but that one does not grow old. This one a poor man cannot acquire, but that one can be acquired with two mites, as that widow did. That is why I grieve that such great good things lie before us and we are so negligent.
We are eager to build splendid houses here, but there we do not wish to acquire even a small dwelling. For where do you love to be:
in this world, in the royal city, or in a desert place? Do you not prefer to live in those royal dwellings? But I am leading you to a city whose craftsman and builder is the Lord.

There, I beg you, build with a small outlay and a little labor a house which the hands of the Lord build, and that is true property, whereas everything of this world is worthless and vain and a work of folly. Tell me: if someone brought you to the land of Persia to see that country and to return at once, and then told you to build houses and great mansions there, would you not charge him with foolishness, for calling you to such vain expense? How then do you do this here in the world, you who are to depart from here after a short time? Or do you say, "I will leave it to my children"? But they too must leave everything a little after you, and perhaps they will leave it even before you, and all this labor is worthless. But there, there is nothing of the kind; rather, the property is unshakable, and whoever has acquired it, the guardian of that property is Christ. This property needs no cares and anxieties, for when God is the one doing the work, what need is there any longer of care and hardship? For he takes all your wealth that you give to the poor and builds you a house there.

And not only is this marvelous, but this even more: that he builds it such as is pleasing to you, for he is a good craftsman and has great pity on you. And if you are poor and are building that house, no envy from others will come upon you, for none of the envious see it; rather the angels see it, who rejoice greatly in your good. And your neighbors are not wicked men, but those holy and good ones: Peter and Paul and John and those like them, the prophets, the martyrs, the angels and the archangels. Therefore, brothers, let us spend all that is ours on the poor, so that we may find such dwellings, which may we all be worthy to attain by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 57

This passage: "And when he had said this, he spat on the ground and made clay from the spittle, and he smeared the clay on the eyes of the blind man and said to him: 'Go, wash in the pool of Siloam.'" Whoever desires profit from the Scriptures
must not pass by even one small word.
And for this reason it has been commanded that we search the books, for many words are found
which appear easy and yet have great power hidden within them. For see what sort of word this one is too, which we have now read:
Gospel: And when he had said this, he spat on the ground
Commentary: What he said, in saying "when he had said this," means this:
that the glory of God may be revealed, and that "I must do the work of him who sent me."
For this is why the evangelist has reminded us of those things said earlier: to show that he confirmed his word by deeds.
But why did he make the clay not with water but with spittle? Because he was going to send him to Siloam, and so that no one might attribute the deed to that spring,

but so that it might be known that it was that which came out of his mouth that opened the blind man's eyes. For this reason he made the clay with spittle. And again, so that no one might think the deed belonged to the earth, for this reason he commanded him to wash.
But why did he not do the deed immediately, but sent him to Siloam?
For this reason: so that he might learn the faith of that blind man, and so that the mouth of the ingratitude and senselessness of the Jews might be stopped.
For while he was going to Siloam, would not many have seen him smeared with clay?
And all saw him, both those who knew him and those who did not.

For since it is not easy to verify the opening of a blind man's eyes, for this reason, by that long road, he makes many people witnesses and beholders of that miracle, so that no one could any longer say, "Perhaps it is not so." And again, besides all this, he also signified that he is no stranger to the Law,
since he sent him to Siloam. For there was no suspicion that Siloam might perhaps receive the glory of that sign,

for blind men had many times washed there and nothing of the kind had occurred; rather, there too it was the power of Christ. For this reason the evangelist also added the interpretation of the name, that it is translated "Sent," as the Apostle says,
that: "They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them," and that rock was Christ.
So then, just as Christ was the spiritual rock, so also Siloam is spiritual, and
I think that the sudden coming of its water signifies a hidden mystery,
which is the unexpectedness of his appearing. But see the mind of the blind man, obedient in everything, for he did not say at all:
"If it is this clay and spittle that will open my eyes, what need do I have of Siloam?
But if Siloam is needed, what need is there of this spittle and clay? Why did he anoint me, or why did he command me to wash?"
But he said nothing of the kind; rather, he was prepared for one thing only: to carry out his command in everything. But if someone should say,

"How is it that when he had removed the clay, he then received his sight, since that clay was what completed his eyes?", we will say nothing else to him but this: "We do not know how it came about." And what wonder is it if we do not know, since neither did the evangelist know the matter, nor the healed man himself? He knew the fact, but how it came about he did not know. And for this reason, when they questioned him, he told them: "He anointed me with clay, and I washed, and now I see." But how it came about, this he was unable to say.

Gospel: But the neighbors and those who had seen him before, for he was a beggar, said: "Is this not the one who sits and begs?" And others said: "This is he." But some said: "No, but he is like him."

Commentary: For the wonder of the deed brought them even to unbelief at such great works, which were done not for the sake of unbelief, and they said: "Is this not the one who sits and begs?" Oh, the love of God for humankind! How with all eagerness he healed such beggars and lowly people, so that in this too he might put the Jews to shame, in that he counted worthy of the same care not only rulers and nobles but also the poor and the lowly, for he had come for the salvation of all. And when they were in doubt, he said: "I am he." Was he not ashamed of his former blindness? Nor was he afraid of their anger, nor did he [?] the proclamation of his benefaction.
Gospel: They asked him: "Who opened your eyes?" He said to them: "The man who is called Jesus."
Commentary: What are you saying? Does a man do such a deed? But he did not yet know anything of his greatness, and only said: "He made clay and anointed my eyes."
See how truthful he was, for he did not say from what he made it, since what he does not know he does not say; for he had not seen that he spat on the ground, but knew only the healing.
Gospel: "And he said to me: Go to Siloam and wash!"

Commentary: And from what did he recognize his voice? From his words, which he was speaking to the disciples. And he related all of this, yet he could not tell the manner of his healing. But if faith is due in these visible things, how is faith not all the more due in invisible things?
Gospel: "They said to him: 'Where is he?'"

Commentary: For they were embittered against him with wrath. But see how Christ is never with those who have been healed, for he did not seek glory from the people. And see also how the blind man says everything truthfully. They wanted to find Christ and bring him too to the chief priests, but since they did not find him, they brought the blind man to the Pharisees, so that they might question him more harshly. For this reason the evangelist points out that "it was the sabbath": to reveal their evil passion and also the reason why they were inquiring, namely so that they might denounce the miracle as improper, on the supposition that it was a transgression of the law. And this is evident from the fact that when they saw him, they asked nothing else except: "How did he open your eyes?"

See how they do not say, "How did you receive your sight?" but, "How did he open your eyes?" so that they might provide grounds for an accusation against him as one who works on the sabbath. But he, as he had spoken earlier, no longer spoke the name, but only told them briefly:
Gospel: "He put clay on my eyes, and I washed, and now I see."
Commentary: It is evident that the Jews had earlier made many accusations about Christ, saying: "Behold, Jesus does such things, that he anoints with clay on the sabbath."
But see how the blind man was neither troubled nor terrified. For when he spoke earlier, it was not so wonderful,
but when they brought him into such fear, he said nothing contrary to his earlier words either. For the Jews brought him before the Pharisees
so that he might deny it, but he proclaimed it all the more,
and this happens to them with every miracle, and we shall show this more fully below. But see the conduct of the Pharisees, for some were speaking more harshly:
Gospel: "This man is not from God, for he does not keep the sabbath." Others said: "How can a sinful man perform such a miracle?"
Commentary: Do you see that they were being swayed by the miracles, and do you hear what they say, those who earlier sent men to arrest him? Now they say this, although not all of them,
for they were rulers and came to unbelief out of love of glory. Yet many of the rulers believed in him and did not confess it.
And again, the multitude of the people was held in contempt and could not be bold; they could not speak boldly because of fear, and the rulers because of love of glory.
And for this reason he said to them: "You cannot believe, you who receive glory from men." And those
who were seeking unjustly to kill him said, "We are of God," but of the healer of the blind they said, "He is not from God, for he does not keep the sabbath."
But in response to this statement they said: "A sinful man cannot perform such a miracle,"
for they maliciously passed over the miracle in silence and brought into the matter the supposed transgression of the law,
for they did not say, "He heals on the sabbath," but, "He does not keep the sabbath."
And again, these others spoke weakly, for they ought to have shown that the sabbath is not broken,

But they speak only of the signs, because they still supposed him to be a man. Otherwise, had this not been so, they could also have answered in this way: that he was Lord of the Sabbath and that he made it.

But they held no such [?] thought, and none of them dared to say openly anything that they knew about him, but only doubtfully, some out of fear, because they lacked boldness, and some out of love of power.
Gospel: For there was a dispute among them.
Commentary: This dispute began first among the people and afterward spread among the rulers as well, and some were saying:

"He is good," and others were saying, "No, rather he is leading the people astray." Do you see how senseless those rulers were? For they showed no courage, but at once joined themselves to the Pharisees again. Otherwise, if they had separated from them completely, they would soon have come to know the truth, for a good separation does occur. For this reason also the Lord said, "I did not come to spread peace on the earth, but a sword," for there is a true unity and there is a good division. For those who were building the tower united for evil, and those same people, though unwillingly, were divided again for good. And again, those who were with Korah united for evil, and therefore they in turn were divided for good. And Judas joined himself to the Jews for evil. So there is a good division and there is an evil union, and for this reason he says, "If your eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out, or if your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off."
And if it is good to cut away a limb that is joined to us for harm, is it not much more good to separate from friends who are joined to us for harm?
Therefore unity is not good in every case, just as division is not good in every case.

Homily 57, that one must flee from the wicked. Now I say all this so that we may flee from the wicked and join ourselves to the good. For if we cut off what is rotten and incurable, lest the rest of the body also suffer the same affliction, is it not much more necessary to do this with those seized by the sickness of wickedness, whom we see to be incurable? For if we are able both to set them right and not to be harmed ourselves, this is good, and we ought to do it. But if they are incurable and unbending and are harming us, then it is good to cut them off from us, and often this action benefits them all the more. For this reason also the Apostle said, "Root out the wicked one from among you," and again, "so that the one who did this deed may be rooted out from among you." For union with the wicked is an evil thing, since no disease can affect those near it as harmfully as being in the company of wicked people, for "evil counsels corrupt good morals."

So let no one have a wicked friend. And if we have wicked sons as well, let us cast them out, and let us not hold back on account of nature, or of the law of nature and of sonship. Is it not much more necessary to flee from friends, if they are wicked?

For even if no harm at all comes upon us from them, still we cannot escape evil suspicion, for those outside do not even inquire into one's life, but judge us by our companions. This I command to all, for it is necessary to plan what is good and to do it before God and before men. Let us therefore strive in every way not to cause our neighbor to stumble, for even if our life is good and yet causes others to stumble, it has lost everything. But how does a good life cause others to stumble? In this way: when association with wicked people brings evil suspicion upon it. For when we are confident in ourselves and keep company with the wicked, even if we ourselves are not harmed, yet we harm others. I say this to all, so that we may understand how great an evil is born of this practice, for even if I am not harmed, or some other person of knowledge, yet a weak and ignorant brother is found, and he is harmed.

And on account of this one's weakness too we must [?not] cause stumbling, even if a Christian is not harmed, but a pagan sees it and is harmed; for the Apostle says: "Let us be without offense both to Jews and to Gentiles." And so we must order ourselves in such a way that not even any of the unbelievers may have a word of harm against us. And just as those who do good cause God to be glorified by their life, so those who do not have a proper life cause the name of God to be blasphemed. But may it not be that any of us should be such a person! Rather, let us strive so to make our deeds shine that our heavenly Father may be glorified and that we may receive glory from him, which may we all be worthy to attain by the grace and love for mankind of our Lord Jesus Christ,
through whom and with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever,
Amen.
Chapter 58
This saying: They said to him who had formerly been blind: "What do you say about him, since he opened your eyes?"
And he said to them: "He is a prophet." The Scriptures must not be read carelessly, but with great diligence,

so that we may not go astray. For behold, here too it seems to me a cause for wonder how, when they had said, "This man is not from God, for he does not keep the Sabbath," they again asked him, "What do you say about him, since he opened your eyes?"
And they do not say, "What do you say about him, since he broke the Sabbath?" What then shall we say here?
For they put forward the word of his justification instead of an accusation. But this I say: those who asked this are not the ones who were saying,
"This man is not from God," but they are the ones who said, "A sinful man cannot do such signs,"

for they wanted to put the others to greater shame, and so that no one might say that they were helping him, for this reason they brought into the midst the one who had experienced his power, and asked him. But see the wisdom of that poor man:
for better and more knowingly than all he answered first and said, "He is a prophet," and he was not frightened by the judgment of those perverse Jews, who contradicted the word and said:
"How can this man be from God, who does not keep the Sabbath?"
Gospel: The Jews did not believe concerning him that he had been blind and had received his sight.
Commentary: That they called his parents. And see in how many ways they set about doing away with that miracle;
but the nature of truth is such that the more anyone wishes to conceal it, the more it shines forth,
for these Jews too wished to conceal it, and yet they acted as though they were willingly hastening to make it known,
for first they asked him, "How did he open your eyes?" so that they might accuse him of some evil, as in another place. Since they had nothing to say, they said:

"He casts out demons by Beelzebul." And here too, since they had nothing to say, they said, "He breaks the Sabbath," and again, "He is a sinner." O you blinded ones! When you were inflamed with anger, did he not ask all of you together:
"Which of you convicts me of sin?"

And when none of you could say anything, he rebuked you, for if you had had anything to say, you would not have kept silent. And you who, when you heard that "he is before Abraham," wanted to stone him; and [?] said: "He is not from God."

And you gave yourselves the name of God's own, you murderers, and to him who performed so many signs you said, "He is not from God." If you had had even some shadow of error, you would not have kept silent. But when they could not establish this accusation about the Sabbath and had grown weak on every side, they then turned to another wickedness and devised something worse and more foolish, namely:

"They did not believe, it says, that he had been blind and had received his sight." But when they said, "He does not keep the Sabbath," it is evident that they did believe, and all those who believed and those who knew him spoke about him. But, as I said, falsehood always harms itself and cannot conceal the truth, but rather makes it shine the more, as happened now. For so that no one could say, "Perhaps it was not he?", for this reason it became evident through that summoning of his parents, done in order to conceal it,

for the parents acknowledged that he, the blind man, was their son. For since they could not frighten him, but he proclaimed boldly, they then wished to damage that miracle by means of the parents. And see the wickedness of their questioning, for they stood them in their midst so as to frighten them, and began to question them with anger:
Gospel: "Is this your son, of whom you say that he was born blind?"

Commentary: And they did not say, "who was once blind," but "of whom you say that he was born blind." So they questioned with malice and wickedness. O defiled and utterly foul ones! What father would wish to say such a thing falsely about his own son? For as to what you said: "If he is blind, how does he now see?" O this foolishness! You have said this falsely, they mean, for by these two things they wished to bring them to denial: first, "for you say that he was born blind," and second, "and how does he now see?" So three questions were put: first, whether he is their son; second, whether he was born blind; and third, about his gaining sight. And they acknowledged the two and kept silent about the third.

And this too happened for the sake of greater truth, so that no one else but the healed man himself, as the most trustworthy, might acknowledge the matter, for how would those parents have said anything falsely,
The truth of which they kept silent about for fear of the Jews, and they said:
Gospel: "We know that this is our son, and that he was born blind; but how he sees, we do not know, or who opened his eyes, we do not know. Ask him; he is of age."

Commentary: They showed him to be trustworthy and in this way kept silent, for he is neither blind nor foolish, but able to testify concerning himself. And they said this for fear of the Jews. And see again how the evangelist revealed their mind,
since they had then sent for the man who was healed. For this reason they summoned him a second time, and they did not say so openly and shamelessly:
"Deny that Christ healed you," but they wanted to accomplish this deed under the appearance of something good, for they said to him:

"Give glory to God." For if they had said to his parents, "Deny, saying, 'He is not your son,'" or, "He was not born blind," that word would have been shameful; and if they had said to him so openly, "Deny that Christ opened your eyes," this too would have been open shamelessness. For this reason they contrived the matter in this other way and said:
"Give glory to God and confess that this man has done nothing."
Gospel: "We know that this man is a sinner."
Commentary: How is it, then, that you did not convict him when he said, "Which of you convicts me of sin?"

Or: "How do you know that he is a sinner?" For he understood that this is the giving of glory to God, and he said nothing. When Christ met him, he praised him and did not blame him, nor did he say to him, "Why did you not give glory to God?"
but he said this to him: "Do you believe in the Son of God?"
For he understood that this is the giving of glory to God, since the one who honors the Son is the one who honors the Father. For this reason the blind man was justly not blamed.
But as long as the Jews were expecting his parents to deny it, they said nothing to him.
Then, since they gained nothing from this matter, they went back to him, saying, "He is a sinner."
Gospel: He answered and said to them: "Whether he is a sinner, I do not know. One thing I know: that I was blind and now I see."
Commentary: Was the blind man afraid, then? Far from it! How then does the one who said, "He is a prophet," now say, "Whether he is a sinner, I do not know"?
It was not that he had this thought, nor was he persuaded of this, but he wanted to show his glory by the testimony of the deed and not by his own word,
for if, after many words, he said, "If he were not true, a sinner could not do this deed,"
and they grew angry and said, "You were born entirely in sin, and you teach us?"
if he had said it at the very first, what would they have done?
Gospel: "Whether he is a sinner, I do not know."

Commentary: It is as if he were saying: "I say nothing yet about this, but this I know for certain, that 'a sinner cannot do this deed.'" And so he made his testimony beyond doubt and free of suspicion, so that he would not appear to be his praiser, but was testifying according to the fact. Since, then, they could not do away with him by means of the fact, they turn back again to the earlier matter and search into the manner of the healing. As dogs, when they search for a cornered animal, run about on every side, so these too begin to ask with their former words: "What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?" But see what he did. Since he had overcome them and knew it, he would no longer speak to them with reserve. While the matter needed to be made clear, he made it clear with reserved words; but since he had now prevailed with a brilliant victory, from then on he began confidently to go on the attack against them, and he said to them:
Gospel: "I have told you, and you do not believe. Why do you still wish to hear?"

Commentary: Do you see the boldness of the beggar toward those men, the scribes and Pharisees? So strong is truth and so weak is falsehood. For the former, even if it finds worthless people, makes them brilliant, whereas the latter, even if it is with the mighty, shows them to be weak. And this saying means something like this: "Do you not listen to what has been said? I will speak no more, nor will I answer you anything." But what they said to him as an insult, he received as an honor, for they said to him:
Gospel: "Are you his disciple? But we are disciples of Moses."
Commentary: Far from it! For if you were Moses' disciples, you would also be Christ's. But you are neither Moses' nor Christ's.
This is why Christ said to them earlier: "If you had believed Moses, you would also have believed me."

Gospel: "We know that God spoke to Moses, but as for this man, we do not know where he is from." How do you know, or who told you? "Our parents," you say? And is he not more trustworthy than parents, he who proves by so many signs that he has come from God and speaks of heavenly things? And they did not say, "We have heard," but "We know." What they have heard they call knowledge, as if they had seen it, and what they have seen they hold as lower than what they have heard. For the one they had not seen but had heard of, whereas the other they had not merely heard of but had seen. Gospel: The man answered: "This is a marvel, that you do not know where he is from, and yet he opened my eyes."

Commentary: For if a man who is undistinguished before you, and not honored by you, does such deeds, how much more evident is it on every side that it is God, and that he has no need of any human help.
Gospel: "But this we know, that God does not hear a sinner."
Commentary: Since he said earlier: "How can a sinful man do such signs?"
For this reason he takes up their own word and reminds them of it, so that they may be held firmly to it: that if he were a sinner, he could not do signs.

Do you see how earlier too, when he said, "Whether he is a sinner, I do not know," he did not say it in doubt, but knew firmly that "he is not a sinner"? For this reason, when he found this moment, he said:
Gospel: "This I know,
"For God will not hear a sinner, but if anyone is a worshipper of God and does his will..."
Commentary: Here he has shown that he is truly a doer of the works of God.
For since they were calling themselves worshippers of God, he added for them and said:

"and does his will"; for it is not enough merely that a person should know God. Moreover, you who question me idly and in vain, and who seek to hear not for the sake of the truth, but so that you may do away with what has been said...
Gospel: "Or do you also want to become his disciples?"

Commentary: See, now he has placed himself in the company of his disciples, for "Do you also?" shows that he had made himself a disciple of his, and he rebuked them and wounded them. And it touches them all the more, for this is the act of a soul grown bold and winged, and disregarding of the father. It greatly showed his honor and indicated that they were reviling in vain so wonderful and true a Christ, and that he would suffer no harm from their contempt. He exalts what has been said:
Gospel: "Never since the beginning of the ages has it been heard that anyone opened the eyes of one born blind." That is to say,

it is evident, he says, that he does not hear sinners; yet this man has even performed a miracle, and such a miracle as no one among men has performed. And therefore it is evident that he has surpassed all in virtue, and that his work is above that of all men. But hear what they said. Gospel:
"You were born entirely in sin, and do you teach us?" And they drove him out.
Commentary: For as long as they expected that he would deny it, they kept summoning him and even held him trustworthy.
But if he was untrustworthy, why did they question him even twice?
But since he spoke the truth fearlessly, at the very moment when they should have marvelled all the more at what had been done, they condemned him all the more.

But what is this saying: "You were born entirely in sin"? For here they also maliciously reproach him for his blindness, and they were making out that he had been born blind because of sins, which was impossible.
And that is why Christ said: "I came into this world for judgment, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind."
Gospel: "You were born entirely in sin, and are you teaching us?"

Commentary: And what did the man say? He did not lay down a rule of his own, but stated a thing known to all: "We know that God does not hear sinners." And they drove him out. See this preacher of the truth, how poverty did not become a hindrance to wisdom.

Do you see how much they said to him, and yet he bore witness to the truth by deed and word? Teaching 58: that it is necessary to learn from the holy scriptures and to keep away from evil spectacles. All this is written so that we may imitate it.
For if a poor and blind man, who had not even seen him, showed such boldness and stood up against all of them,
frenzied men and demons as they were, and chose to be cast out rather than to trample on the truth,

How much more is it fitting for us, who have spent so long a time in the faith and have seen so many miracles, to whom a greater good has been given than to him, whose inner eyes have been opened, who have seen those great mysteries and been called to such honor, that we should show all boldness on his behalf toward those of ours who turn against him.
And this we will be able to do,

if we had boldness, and if we listened to the Scriptures well and not carelessly. For if anyone would come here to church and listen diligently, one year would be enough to give him great experience. But now some are in so wretched a state that, after so much hearing, they do not even know the names of the books. Nor are they ashamed, nor do they tremble at entering the holy church carelessly. But if they go to charioteers, or pipers, or those who practice other devilish pursuits, they are there every day and listen diligently.

But when God speaks to us through the prophets and apostles, we grow sleepy and bored, we scratch ourselves and yawn. We are afraid of going there in the heat, we consider the winter rain a great obstacle, and we sit at home. But when the time for the games and the horse races comes, we go there, where there is no roof, and we endure cold and heat and rain and mud and the length of the road. But here, where there is a roof and wonderful teaching, we become negligent about the profit of our souls. For this reason we are skilled in those vain things, but untaught and inexperienced in what is good and useful. And if someone calls you an entertainer, you consider it an insult. Yet if you are called to watch an entertainer, you do not flee, and you pursue the very thing whose name you hate. But here, where both the name and the thing are honorable, Christianity, you do not even know what the thing is. What is worse than this folly?
And there are some who, if someone asks them, "Who is Amos?" or "Who is Obadiah?" or "What is the number of the prophets?" or "Who are the apostles?"
cannot even open their mouths. But about horses, and about poets, philosophers and orators, they speak words sharper than these. And then, on top of all this, they say:
"And what harm is there in this?" or "What loss is it?" And I groan over this, that they do not even know the thing to be harmful, nor do they understand its evil.
O man, God has given you the time of your life so that you might serve him, and you waste it in vanity and in nothing good.

And still you say, "What evil is there in this thing?" If you waste a little silver for nothing, you count it a loss; yet you waste all your days uselessly and in devilish pursuits, and does this not seem a loss to you?

You ought to spend your days in psalmody and prayer, but you throw them away in tumult and the abuse of foul words, in useless merriment and in the business of the games. You use up your days to your own harm, and on top of all this you say:
"What evil is there in this thing?" And do you not know that anything at all should be disregarded sooner than time?
For if you lose gold, you may soon find it again, but time that you lose you will never find again.
For our times are being cut short, and if we do not use well these days that have been given to us, what shall we say on that day, when we arrive there?
For if you had ordered your son to learn some craft, and he sat at home and did not go to school,
Would the teacher not be right to answer this, saying to you: "If he did not come to learn, how am I to present him to you as a skilled craftsman?" So too it will be in our case, if God says to us:
"I gave you time to learn this craft, which is the fear of God. Why then did you waste that time in vain? Or why did you not go to the teacher continually to learn?"

For the fear of God is not a craft of fleshly things, as the prophet says: "Come, children, listen to me, and I will teach you the fear of the Lord." And: "Blessed is the man whom you teach, O Lord, and from your law keep [it] for him." But when you have wasted this time in evil, what word will you find to answer the Lord? Yet some say: "And why has he not appointed long periods for our life?"
But, O this great ingratitude! For the very thing for which we owe great thanks, that he has shortened the labors and made the rest long and immortal, do you groan over this?

However, I do not know how we came upon these words and drew out our discourse. Therefore it is right to stop again, for this too comes from our faintheartedness, that here, when the discourse grows long, we become weary, but there we do not leave from midday until evening. But I beg you, grant me this favor and nail yourselves to good works, so that I may thus rejoice over you and be glad, so that I may boast of you and you may inherit a reward from God, if through my teaching you come from evil to good and become acceptable to God. And you will not only inherit the reward in that age, but will also rejoice here, for such is virtue that, along with the crowns of that age, it brings us great joy here as well. Let us then believe these words, so that both here and in that age we may inherit joy, by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 59
This passage: "Jesus heard that they had cast him out, and he found him and said to him: 'Do you believe in the Son of God?'
He answered and said: 'Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?'"
Interpretation: Those who suffer and are insulted for the sake of truth and for Christ are the ones who are honored,
for just as whoever leaves everything for his sake has found everything, and just as whoever hates his own soul for his sake has loved it, so too whoever is insulted for his sake
is honored all the more, as happened in the case of that man who had been blind. For the Jews cast him out of the temple, and the King of the temple found him.
He was separated from the evil assembly and met the fountain of life; he was insulted by those who despise Christ and honored by the King of the angels,
for such are the rewards of truth. So too we, if we leave behind possessions here, find boldness there;
if we are afflicted here, we find rest there; if we are insulted here for God's sake, we shall be honored both here and there, in the kingdom of heaven, forever.
But when they had cast him out of the temple, Jesus found him, and the evangelist shows that he went deliberately to see him. And see what good he did him,
for he bestowed on him the chief of all good things: that is, he made himself known to him, whom he had not known before, and he numbered him among his own disciples.
But see how the evangelist relates everything, when he said: "Do you believe in the Son of God?"
He said to him: "Who is he, Lord?" For he did not yet know, although he had been healed, because he had previously been blind, and when he had been healed he was seized by those wicked men.

For this reason, as a commander receives a brave soldier, so he received him and said to him: "Do you believe in the Son of God?" What does this mean, that after so many answers and such boldness on his part he asks him, "Do you believe?" It is not that he was ignorant, but he wished to make himself known to him and to show him that he had accepted his faith. For this reason he said to him: "Do you believe in the Son of God?" He asks him as one made grateful, and first he brought him to a longing for himself, for he did not say at once:
"Believe," but first he asked. And he answered: "Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?" Behold, this is the word of a soul full of longing.
Gospel: "Jesus answered and said: 'You have both seen him, and he who is speaking with you is he.' And he said: 'I believe, Lord,' and he worshiped him."
Commentary: He did not say to him, "I am the one who healed you," but he passed over all of this in silence and said: "Do you believe in the Son of God?"
And he showed his great longing and at once worshiped him, which few of those who were healed did, such as those lepers and many others.
And when he had worshiped him, for this reason Christ said:
Gospel: "For judgment I have come into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind."
Commentary: With this word he both strengthened him in faith and alarmed the Pharisees, for they were there with him. And as for "For judgment I came into this world,"
that means: so that those who condemned him might become liable to greater torment.
And they are condemned. But here he speaks of two kinds of seeing and two kinds of blindness: spiritual and bodily.
Gospel: "Some of the Pharisees who were with him heard this and said to him: 'Are we blind too?'"
Commentary: And in another place it says: "We have never been slaves to anyone, and we were not born of fornication." So here too they understand only the bodily sense,
but he himself showed that it would be better if you were blind, and said:
Gospel: "If you were blind, you would have no sin."

Commentary: Since they regarded the matter as worthy of shame, he turned it back upon them: "It would be better if you too were blind," so that he might cut off from them their human way of thinking and humble their arrogance.
Gospel: "But now you say, 'We see.'"
Commentary: Just as he said there, "He of whom you say, 'He is our God,'" so he does here also,
and what they held to be greatly praiseworthy, he showed to be the bringer of greater torment. For the sight that God gave for good, they used for evil.

And then he speaks about their blindness, for it is so that they may not be able to say, "It is not because of our blindness that we have not followed you, but because you are not true," that he makes all this discourse of his. For this reason the evangelist did not say in vain:
"Some of the Pharisees who were with him heard,"
but in order to remind us that they were the ones who earlier were casting stones,

And Christ began first to show what a deceiver is and one who is not true, so that in this way he might put them to shame, when he showed them that he was the good shepherd and that they did not follow him. Therefore he says:
Gospel: "Amen, amen, I say to you, whoever does not enter the fold of the sheep by the door, but enters from another side, he is a thief and a robber."

Commentary: See the deeds of the robber: first, that he does not enter openly; second, that he does not enter by the door, that is, not according to the Scriptures. And here he alludes to those who were before him and those who will be after him: Antichrist [?] and the false christs, and Judas and Theudas.

And he rightly called the Scriptures a door, for they open to us the knowledge of God; they make us sheep and do not let the wolves come near. For like a strong door, so they have barred the entry of heretics. Through them we recognize shepherds and those who are not shepherds, and what the fold is, and the sheep, and their care. For whoever does not make use of the Scriptures, but devises another way by himself, he is a thief. For this reason he said to the Jews, "Search the Scriptures and Moses," and many times he brought forward the prophets as witnesses.

And by these words that he said, "enters from another side," he also alluded to the scribes, for they taught by the commandments of men and transgressed the Law. And see again those signs of the shepherd, how he says:

Gospel: "He who enters by the door is the shepherd of the sheep. To him the doorkeeper also opens, and the sheep hear his voice, and he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out, and he goes before them." Nothing prevents us from understanding Moses here as the doorkeeper, for the words of God were entrusted to him here. "And the sheep hear his voice": for since they were calling him a deceiver, he himself wished to show them that, on account of their unbelief, it is not right to call him a deceiver.

For they themselves did not listen to him, nor did they follow him as sheep, but became apostates from him. For since this is the work of the shepherd, to enter by the door, and he entered by the door, whoever was disobedient to him and did not follow him was certainly not a sheep. For those who were sheep followed him, and those who did not follow harmed not his shepherding, but made themselves strangers to the sheep by their own wickedness. And if further below you hear again that he gives himself the name of door, do not be surprised, for he gives himself the name both of door and of shepherd and of his own [?] sheep.

And he proclaims his own dispensation in various ways: for when he leads us to the Father, he calls himself the door and the way of life; but when he cares for us, then he calls himself the shepherd; and when he was slain for us, then a sheep; and when he signifies our nourishment, then the bread of life. But here he speaks of the shepherd, whose [voice] the sheep hear. Gospel: "And he calls his own sheep by name, and he leads them out and goes before them."

Interpretation: How, then? For this is not the way of a shepherd, since a shepherd follows behind the sheep and not in front. But this shows that he will direct everyone toward the truth. And for this reason he does the opposite of other shepherds, as when he was sending out the sheep among wolves, which shepherding is exceedingly marvelous. And in this place he also alludes to the blind man, for he called him among the Jews,
and he heard his voice and followed him.
Gospel: "And they do not follow a stranger, for they do not know the voice of the stranger."
Interpretation: He speaks here of Theudas and Judas and those like them, and those who were to come after him.
And he showed that he was separate from them. And first he made the distinction from that one by means of the Scriptures, for he did everything according to Scripture, but they did not;

and he made a second distinction from the separation of the sheep, for not only while he was still here, but even after his death they believed in him, whereas those others they abandoned immediately; and,
again, a third, for they came as tyrants, but he fled from all human glory; and further, because he always strove for the life of the sheep,
but they strove for their destruction; and they gave up those entrusted to them and fled, but he himself laid down his life for them.
And everything came upon them against their will, but he took it upon himself willingly.
Gospel: "Jesus spoke this parable to them, but they did not understand what he was saying to them."
Interpretation: And why did he not speak to them plainly? For this reason: so that they might listen with greater eagerness.
And since he has finished this, he now adds further and says:
Gospel: "I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will go in and go out and find pasture."
Interpretation: Thus they will be at rest. And he calls authority and dominion pasture; that is to say, he will remain within and no one will be able to drive him out, as happened with the apostles,
for they went in and went out fearlessly, as lords of the whole world.
Gospel: "All who came before me were thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not listen to them."
Interpretation: This too he said about Theudas and Judas, who stirred the people to revolt.
Gospel: "The thief does not come except to steal and kill and destroy."
Interpretation: As in the case of Theudas and Judas, through whom all the people who followed them perished.
Gospel: "I came that they may have life and have it more abundantly."
Interpretation: And what is the more abundant life? The kingdom of heaven. But he does not call it by name; rather, he returns again to that name of life, which was familiar to them.
Gospel: "I am the good shepherd."

Commentary: Now he speaks of the Passion and shows that it comes about for the life of the world and that he does not go to it unwillingly, and he again speaks of the figure of the shepherd and of the hired man:
Gospel: "For the good shepherd lays down his life, but the hired man, whose own the sheep are not, when he sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep and flees."
Commentary: Behold how he shows his lordship to be equal with the Father's, since he is the shepherd and the sheep are his, whereas the hired man flees because of the wolf.
Gospel: "And the wolf snatches the sheep."

Commentary: This is what those earlier ones did: Theudas and Judas and those like them. But he himself, when they seized him, said to them, "Let these men go," so that the word he had spoken might be fulfilled: "Not one of them was lost." Nor did he allow the invisible wolf, that is, the devil, to snatch the sheep; for the devil is not only a wolf but also a lion, and he seeks someone to devour, and he is also a serpent and a dragon.

Homily 59: On keeping the commandments of Christ and on the love of material goods. Therefore I beseech you, let us hear the voice of that true and good shepherd and obey him, and let us not listen to the voice of a stranger. And what is his voice? "Blessed are the poor in spirit!

Blessed are the pure in heart! Blessed are the merciful!" If we do this, we are with the shepherd and the wolf will not be able to attack us, and if it comes near us, it will immediately be crushed. For our shepherd is one who loves us so much that he lays down his life for us, and he is mighty, the King of all.

But since he is both mighty and loving toward us, what then is there to hinder us from being saved? Nothing except our own negligence, for he says: "You cannot serve God and mammon." So now let us serve God, and let the tyranny of mammon not come upon us, which is worse than every other tyranny: the love of riches, which is full of envy and assault [?], of filth, greed and drunkenness. For it makes free men slaves, not slaves of men but of passions, for this is a diabolical slavery, by which many souls have been darkened; and those who are darkened cannot recognize their perdition, and indeed do not wish to recognize it, but rejoice in that evil, and if anyone wishes to set them free, they become enraged.

O man, it was not for this that you were created, to serve gold and silver forever; it was not for this that God made you in his own image, but so that you might please him, find the eternal good things and delight with the angels. Why then do you cast yourself into that utmost baseness in exchange for such honor? For your brother, who was born of the same font as you, is wasting away from hunger while you burst with satiety; he is naked while you add garments upon garments as food for worms.

And would it not be better if you clothed the poor, so that the garments would be safe from decay and theft and eternal life would be granted to you? Or is the body of Christ not more honorable than a bedstead and a chest?
For it not only keeps garments from decay but even makes them more splendid, and you need neither doors nor bolts to guard them for fear of thieves,
For it is safe from all theft and is stored up in the heavens. I will not cease to speak always of this love,
and you do not listen to me, but may this not be true of all of you.

But listen to me, rich and poor, for the poor too are able, if they wish, to show mercy with bread and cool water, by visiting the sick, with a word of consolation, and by lodging a stranger in their house. For we do not seek an abundance of money from the poor, but seek this from the rich; but as for the poor, let each of them do good works according to his own ability, and God will accept it.

How many wish they had been alive at the time when Christ lived on earth, so that they might have received him into their house! But behold, it is possible even now to do this deed, if anyone wishes: that you may call him into your house and receive a blessing from him, and hear on that day: "Come, you blessed of my Father, and inherit the kingdom prepared for you before the creation of the world, for I was hungry and you gave me food," and what follows. Now, if we wish to hear this voice, let us clothe the naked, receive the stranger, feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, and go to the sick and to the one who is in prison,

and let us find on that day boldness and forgiveness of sins, and let us attain the eternal good things by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and unto the ages of ages, amen.
Chapter 60
This saying: "I am the good shepherd; I know those who are mine and mine know me, as the Father knows me,
and I also know the Father, and I lay down my life for my sheep." Great, beloved, is the leadership of the church, and it requires much wisdom and courage,

as Christ said: that one should lay down his life for the sheep and never leave them desolate, but should always fight against the wolf. For by this the true shepherd is distinguished from the one appointed for wages,
for the latter seeks only his own gain and neglects the sheep, while the former cares rather for what concerns the sheep. And having said what the work of the shepherd is,
he mentioned two who do harm: one who slaughters and steals, and a second who abandons and flees.
And by the first of these sayings he alluded to Theudas and Judas,
and by the latter to those Jewish high priests who did not care for the sheep entrusted to them, for they neither sought the lost, nor brought back the one who had strayed, nor healed the broken,
for they fed themselves and not the sheep.

But the Lord showed how far he was from this, for he laid down his life for the sheep; for he did not give up those who believed in him, but he himself died for them. Therefore he always said: "I am the good shepherd." But why do they not say here, as they said before:
"You testify about yourself, and your testimony is not trustworthy"?
Because he had many times shut their mouths by signs and by speaking boldly. But since he had said:
"My sheep will hear my voice," so that no one might say, "What have you said about the unbelievers?", he therefore added and said:
"I know my own, and my own know me," as it is written:
"He did not cast away the people whom he foreknew." For this reason he says:
"I speak of those whom I foreknew, who are going to be good."
Gospel: "I know my own, and my own know me."
Commentary: But they do not know me in the way that I know, for as I know the Father, so the Father also knows me; but others cannot equal my knowledge.
Gospel: "As the Father knows me, I also know the Father."
Commentary: I know him as well as he knows me.
For this reason he also said: "No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, with that true knowledge."
Gospel: "And I lay down my life for the sheep."
Commentary: He says this many times in order to show the love he had for the believers, for when he said:
"I am the light and the life," it was counted as boasting by those foolish and blind people; but when he said, "I die for them," he shut their mouths, and they no longer had a word to say.
For this reason they can no longer say, "You testify about yourself, and your testimony is not true,"

for he was showing great goodness in taking death upon himself for the sake of his own killers. For this reason too, fittingly and at the proper time, he introduces the word concerning the gentiles and says:
Gospel:
"I have other sheep also, which are not of this fold; they too must be brought to me."
Commentary: See, here again this word "must" does not indicate compulsion but announces what will certainly come to pass, as if he were saying: "Why do you marvel

if these are going to follow me and hear my voice? For when you see others following me and hearing my voice, then you will marvel all the more." And as for his saying, "who are not of this fold," do not be astonished at this word, for the division exists only through the Law, as the Apostle says: "Neither circumcision avails anything, nor uncircumcision."
Gospel: "They too must be brought to me."

Commentary: He shows that both were scattered and without a shepherd until the good shepherd had come, and then he foretells the unity to come, that they will be one flock, as the Apostle says: "so that [?] he might gain both of them in himself together as one new man."
Gospel: "For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life, so that I may take it up again."

Commentary: And what could be humbler than this saying, that our Lord was loved on our account, because he was dying for us? But what does this saying mean? Did the Father perhaps not love him before this time, and is it only now that he begins to love him? For we are the cause of his being loved. Do you see how he employs this humble language? But why did he say this here? Because they called him a stranger and named him a deceiver, one who had come to harm them. Therefore he says to them: "Even if for no other reason, you owe me your love for this reason: that I love you so much that I am even dying for you. And since I love you, the Father also loves you so much that he loves me for dying for you." Again, he also shows this: that he does not come to that deed unwillingly. For if he were coming unwillingly, how would that deed be a cause of love?

And again, he says it to show that the deed is also very pleasing to the Father. But if he says this as a man, do not be surprised, for we have often stated the reason for this, why he speaks in human fashion. And to state again a matter that we have often stated is tiresome.

Gospel: "I lay down my life, that I may take it up again. No one shall take it from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it up again." But since they had often plotted to kill him, he therefore says: "If I do not will it, your labor is in vain." And from the first he confirms the second, the resurrection by means of the death, for this is wondrous and glorious, for both became a new wonder. But let us understand this saying well, for it says: Gospel: "I have power to lay down my life."

Commentary: We do not have power to lay down our lives, unless we kill ourselves. But he speaks thus: "I have such power that if I do not will it, no one is able to kill me." This is not the case with human beings. Rather, if we are delivered into the hands of our enemies, we have no power to lay down our life. Or do they not kill us against our will?

But it was not so with him; rather, he had power to lay it down and not to lay it down. And when he had said, "No one shall take it from me," he added, "I have power to lay down my life," that is: I alone am lord over death and over not dying. But he did not say this from the beginning, for that saying would not have been believable. Only when he also had his deeds as witness, for they had often fought against him and could accomplish nothing, did he then say it, for he had escaped from their hands countless times. And then he said, "No one can take it from me," for he was going to death voluntarily. And since this is so, it is clear that when he wills, he lays it down, and when he wills, he is also able to take it up. For since death was in his power, the resurrection too was in his own power, and he who had power to lay down his life likewise had power to take it up.
Do you see how from the first he also made the second known, and confirmed the resurrection by means of the death?
Gospel: "This commandment I have received from my Father."

Commentary: What commandment? What is dying for the world? Did he perhaps wait at first to hear it from the Father, and only then will this deed, not having known it before, and did he need instruction?
And who that has understanding would imagine this? For just as, when he said above, "For this reason the Father loves me," he indicated a voluntary act and did away with any suspicion of opposition,
so also here he says, "I have received the commandment from my Father." He indicates nothing other than this:

"This deed that I am doing is greatly pleasing to him," so that when they killed him, they would not think that the Father had abandoned him, and could not reproach him as they were going to reproach him, saying, "He saved others, and he cannot save himself," and again:
"If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross."
And so that, when you hear, "I have received the commandment," you would not say, "That virtue and the accomplishment of that deed were foreign to him," for this reason he said beforehand:

"The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep," and he showed that the sheep were his, and that the whole deed was accomplished by him, and that he had no need of a commandment; for if he had needed a commandment, why would he say:
"I lay it down of myself"? For one who lays it down of himself has no need of a commandment. And he also states the reason for doing this,
that is, that he is a shepherd, and a good shepherd.
And a good shepherd has no need of anyone else to teach him to shepherd well. And if this is so with human beings, is it not so much more with God? For this reason the Apostle also said:
"He emptied himself." And this saying, "I have received the commandment," indicates nothing other than unity with the Father,
and the reason for speaking so humbly and in such a human way is the weakness of those who were listening.
Gospel: There was again a division among the Jews because of this, and some said, "He is possessed by a demon and is raving. Why do you listen to him?" Others said:
"These words are not those of one possessed by a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?"
Commentary: Since his words were beyond human power, they called him possessed by a demon; and see, they have said this to him three times, for first they said, "You have a demon.
Who is seeking to kill you?" And again they said, "Did we not say rightly that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?"
And again here they say this: "He is possessed by a demon and is raving." And indeed they said it to him not three times but many times, for that saying,
"Did we not say rightly that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?"
indicates that they had said that thing to him many times. But some said, "These words are not those of one possessed by a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?"

Since some had set about those wicked opponents and had already stopped their mouths by words, they brought the deeds into the open, as if to say: "His words are good; if you do not believe the words, look at the deeds."

But Christ answered nothing to all this. For earlier he had answered, "I do not have a demon," but now he says nothing more to them, because, since he had shown everything by deeds, he therefore kept silent in word. For they were not even worthy of his word, who called him demon-possessed on account of the very deeds for which he ought to have been confessed as God, and who, moreover, were at odds with one another. But Christ endured everything with silence and meekness, so that he might teach us to endure everything with meekness.

Teaching 10, on mourning for one's own sins and on almsgiving. Let us then imitate him, who not only endured, but did countless good things to those who insulted him and sought to kill him. And why do I say, "did good"? For he even laid down his life for them, and when they crucified him, he entreated the Father on their behalf. Let us too, then, imitate him, for this is the discipleship of Christ: that a person be meek and humble. But how shall we acquire meekness if we do not remember our sins and mourn and weep? For where there is mourning, anger cannot dwell; where there is the contrition of mourning, hot temper is not found. For when the mind is afflicted by mourning, it is utterly unable to become angry, but, bowed down, it mourns and weeps. For this world too is a time of weeping and mourning, since we are defiled by many sins, both in deed and in word, and there await us the Gehenna of fire and expulsion from the Kingdom, which is worse than everything.

And since this is so, how do you dare to indulge in laughter and revelry, you who hear of the wrath of the King and stand there carelessly and do not tremble? Do you not hear how he says that on that day the King will say to those on the left: "Depart from me, you accursed, into the fire prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry and you did not give me food," and what follows? Hear the parable of the virgins, how they were cast out of the bridal chamber, since "they did not have the oil of mercy." Hear the prophet, how he says: "Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy." For we ought likewise to show mercy to our neighbor, just as we ask it from God. And this is good mercy: when we give out of our want and not out of our surplus. And if we do not give even out of our surplus, I do not know what mercy we will find on that day, or how we will escape torment. For since those virgins, after such great labors, found no consolation, what shall we do, we wretched ones?
For thus Christ will reproach us: "I was hungry and you did not give me food," and: "As much as you did not do for one of the least, neither did you do it for me."
For every person, whether great or small, so long as he is a believer, if we do not show mercy to him, we will hear this word.
For what difficult thing does he seek from us? For he does not say, "I was sick and you did not raise me up," but: "You did not visit me." Nor does he say:
"I was in prison and you did not bring me out," but: "You did not come to me."
The lighter these commandments are, then, the heavier are the torments on their account, if we do not fulfill them.
For what is easier than going to prison, or what is better, where you may see some in bonds, some in torment, some hungry, some sick and pitiable? Even if you were a stone,
you would become tender-hearted when you see those human conditions, and you would also call to mind the eternal judgment,
and in this way you would drive from yourself anger and lust and love of this passing world, and you would understand
that if there are such terrors and torments and judgments at the hands of men, what then will it be before God?

For this reason the wise man also said: "It is good to enter the house of mourning rather than the house of laughter." And when you are like this, in that age to come you will hear those words of blessedness. Therefore, brothers, let us not be negligent toward what is good, but let us come and comfort the afflicted who are in prisons. But if you say: "It is not godly men who are in prison, but murderers and robbers and thieves," yet it has not been commanded us to have mercy on the good and to torment the wicked, for the Lord says: "Be merciful, as your Father in heaven, for he makes his sun shine on sinners and on the righteous."
So you too, do not be a merciless judge, but understand that we too are liable for many sins, which are able to bring us to hell,
for we have called even brothers "fool," and we have looked at women with lust, which is adultery, and many times we have received communion unworthily,
defiled by iniquities and sins, which is worse than everything. Let us therefore not consider the sins of others, but let us remember the sins of our own selves.
For Christ kept company not only with the righteous but also with sinners, such as the Canaanite woman and the Samaritan woman and that harlot and many others,
and we, defiled by many sins, despise those who were made from the very same earth from which we too were made. What are you saying:
"In prison there are wicked men"? And in the city, are all good? For the wicked are not few here either, and all of us are liable for sins.
Why then do we leave aside our own sins and look at those of others, and, where it is the time for love of humanity, do I search out wickedness?
Rather, let us look at ourselves, at how we too once were, and in this way let us become kind,
for we too were once disobedient, foolish and led astray, slaves of various lusts,
wicked, haters of brothers and children of wrath. But when God saw how we were as if in prison and bound with such a chain, he was not ashamed, but came to the prison.
And he delivered us from there and brought us to the kingdom and made us higher than the heavens, so that we too, according to our ability, might imitate him.
For when he said to the disciples: "If I, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet,
for I have given you an example, so that as I have done, so you also should do," he spoke not only about the washing of feet but about everything.
So likewise we, whether someone is wicked or good,

Let us not grow weary of doing good, and often one may even find a man who is great before God. For Abraham too welcomed everyone, and later he welcomed angels.
