For how many enmities with others did the builders of these mansions incur! How many robberies, how many losses!
And what profit came of all that? Eternal torment and not a single consolation to be found, and here too everyone now speaks evil of them.

Or when we see the portraits of many men, of rulers, painted on their panels, do we not mourn all the more? Truly the prophet spoke well when he said: "Every man toils in vain," for truly zeal for such things is vanity. But it is not so with those dwellings and abodes of heaven, for here one man toils and another takes his rest in what was built, but there each is lord over his own labor and will receive his reward many times over. Let us seek that reward; let us build houses there, so that we may find rest through Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and power, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, Amen.
Chapter 66
This saying: "All the people of the Jews learned that he was there, and they came not only for the sake of Jesus,
but also to see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead." Just as wealth becomes harmful to careless men,
so too does authority, for the one leads to greed and the other to arrogance. And see here too how the multitude of the people was better,
while the rulers were utterly lost, for the unlearned people often believed in him, as the evangelists say: "Many of the people believed in him."
But the rulers were unbelieving, and they themselves said: "Has any of the rulers believed in him? Is it not this unlearned crowd that has believed in him,
who do not know the law and are accursed?" And so they cursed the believers, while calling themselves, those killers of God, wise.
And here too, then, when they saw the sign that Christ had done, many believed; but for the rulers that other evil was not enough, and they wished to kill Lazarus as well.
O wicked men, you said about Christ: "He breaks the Sabbath and makes himself God,
and the Romans will come because of him and carry us off captive." What will you say about Lazarus? What evil has he done? See how murderous their mind was,
for although the Lord had performed many signs, they had not been so enraged over any one of them,
for this one was more exalted than all the others, and the walking and speaking of a man four days dead was a wonder.

Yet in the case of the blind man and the paralytic they gave the Sabbath as a pretext and turned the people away, but here they had no pretext, and therefore they fought against the man who had risen from the dead,
for here they could no longer say even this: "He is opposed to the Father," since the prayer had shut their mouths. And since they could find no other pretext,
they then wished to kill him. And they would have done the same to the blind man too,

if they had not had the Sabbath there as a pretext. Moreover, that man was poor and of no account, and they cast him out, but this one was a man of distinction, and for this reason many had come to comfort his sisters, for the Lord raised him in the presence of all, and everyone went to see him. And this is why they were enraged like wild beasts: because during the days of the feast everyone was running to Bethany. And they wished to kill him and counted the deed as nothing,
so murderous were they. And for this reason the prophet says:

"Your hands are full of blood." But how is it that the Lord, who no longer went about boldly and had been in the desert, now again goes there boldly? Because by his departure he had calmed their anger, and now he came again when their wrath had been quieted. And again, that multitude of people who went before him and followed behind him was enough to disturb and distress them, for no other miracle could so sway the people as that of Lazarus. And another evangelist says that "they spread their garments on the roads" and "the whole city was shaken." With such honor he entered. And he did this in order to fulfill one prophecy and to prefigure another, so that his entry became the end of one prophecy and the beginning of another. For it became the fulfillment of that prophecy which says: "Rejoice, daughter of Zion, for behold, your king comes to you, gentle."

But his sitting on a donkey was a sign of something to come, namely, that the unclean race of the Gentiles was going to submit to his commandments. But how is it that the other evangelists say that "he sent disciples to bring the donkey and the colt," whereas this one says nothing of the kind and says only, "He found a donkey and sat on it"? It is because the others told how it happened and how he sent them, and this one did not wish to tell again everything they had said. Instead he says: "He found it and sat on it, and the people spread palm and olive branches and garments before him," in order to show that they regarded him as higher and greater, and not merely as a prophet. And for this reason they said: "Hosanna, blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord."

Do you see that this was what distressed them, that everyone believed he was not an opponent of God? And the people believed for this reason, because he said, "I have come from the Father." But what is the meaning of the saying, "Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion"? Since many of the kings who had sat in her were wicked and gave the city over to its enemies, it therefore says, "Be of good courage," for this one is not like them, but gentle and kind.
Gospel: His disciples did not understand this, that it was written about him.

Commentary: Do you see how ignorant they were of many things, because he did not reveal them? And when he said, "Destroy this temple, and on the third day I will raise it up," they did not understand.
And again another evangelist says that "this saying was hidden from them," and they did not know that he must rise from the dead. But this was rightly hidden,
for it was beyond their capacity, as another evangelist says: "When each one heard,
they were grieved and distressed." But this saying spoken about the donkey, why was it not revealed?
For this too was great and beyond their capacity. But see this love of wisdom of the evangelists, how they are not at all ashamed to reveal their former ignorance, for they knew that it was written,

But they did not know this, that it had been written about him. For if they had known everything from the beginning, how he would be handed over and crucified, they would have been made to stumble, because from the beginning they were expecting his kingdom here, and they were unable to understand that saying about the kingdom.
Gospel: But the crowd was testifying that he had raised Lazarus from the dead.
Commentary: That is to say, they would not have turned to him so suddenly if they had not believed because of that miracle.
Gospel: But the Pharisees said to them: "Do you see that you gain nothing? Look, the whole world has gone to follow him."
Commentary: These words, I think, were spoken by those whose mind was good but who could not bring themselves to be bold, and now they said to those who were seeking to kill him,
"Do you see that you are troubling yourselves uselessly and in vain?" And here they call the people "the world."
Gospel: There were also some of the Gentiles who had come up to worship at the feast, and they wished to see Jesus, and they approached Philip,
and Philip told Andrew, who had come before him, and so they told Jesus.

Commentary: Now the Lord had never before told them to teach the Gentiles, but said to them: "Do not go on the road of the Gentiles," so that he might cut off every excuse from the Jews. But since they were fleeing from him and the Gentiles were fleeing to him, and it was the time of his passion, and the sending of the apostles to the Gentiles was to take place after the crucifixion, while these were hastening to him before the crucifixion, for this reason he said to them:
Gospel: "Now the hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified."

Commentary: For earlier he did not allow them to go, and said: "Do not go on the road of the Gentiles," and again he said: "I was not sent except for the lost sheep of the house of Israel," and: "It is not good to take the bread from the children and give it to the dogs."

And so, until they crucified and killed him, he did not abandon them. But when they themselves hated and killed him, from then on it was no longer needful to remain with them, for they themselves separated themselves and said: "We have no king but Caesar."
Then, therefore, he abandoned them, because they had abandoned him. For this reason he says: "How many times I wished to gather your children, and you were not willing." But what is this saying:
Gospel: "If a grain of wheat does not fall on the ground and die"

Commentary: He said this about the crucifixion, so that they would not say that it was when even the Gentiles had approached him that he was killed. And for this reason he says: "My death itself will bring them all the more and will make my preaching grow." And then he also offered this matter as an image, for: "This happens even with wheat, and by its death it bears greater fruit. Then will this not happen all the more with me?"

Homily 66, on the right faith. But Paul too mentioned this saying when he spoke about the resurrection. Now then, what forgiveness will those find who disbelieve in the resurrection, since its image is shown every day through seeds and plants?

And as for the work that God does, it is not proper to inquire into it, how he brought us from nothing into being, for some are in sin and some in righteousness. Many who are in sin spend many years, while those pleasing to God have often spent only a short time. Now then, when will each receive his recompense, if there is no resurrection? But some evil-speaking people say:

"Yes, there is a resurrection, but the flesh does not rise," for they do not hear the word of Paul, who says: "This corruptible must put on incorruption." For this word is not said about the soul, since the soul does not decay, whereas resurrection is spoken of that which has fallen. So it is the flesh that falls. Or why do you not want the resurrection of the flesh? Can it be that God is not able? But that is the utmost blindness. Or is it not fitting? But why is it not fitting that what shared in labors and afflictions and death should share in the crown as well?
For if it were not fitting, it would not have been created in the first place, nor would the Lord himself have put on flesh; but he put on flesh and raised it up.

And hear what he says: "See, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have." Or why did he raise Lazarus, if resurrection without the flesh were better? But do not be led astray by the heretics, beloved, for there is a resurrection and a judgment, and those who do not believe this are the ones who do not want to give an account according to their deeds. But let the resurrection be as Christ rose; for he is the beginning and the firstborn of those who have fallen asleep, he who committed no sin and rose from the dead in the flesh. And let us turn away all those evil teachings,
for this teaching of no resurrection is not that of the apostles, but is that of Marcion and Valentinus.
Let us flee from it, for a good life without right faith is of no benefit, just as faith too is of no benefit, just as faith is of no benefit without good works.

Let us therefore beware of evil words, we who know this invincible power of God; let us flee from their words. I say this to you, for if you were sharpening your minds every day from the Scriptures and arming yourselves against them,
I would not keep you back from battle with them,
for the truth is strong; but I fear that you may enter into battle with them unarmed and be defeated,
for nothing is weaker than those who are bereft of the help of the Holy Spirit,

and if they speak words of philosophy, do not be afraid, for they know nothing good and every wickedness, and what a single lowly widow taught by us knows, Pythagoras did not know. Rather, their philosophy lies in clothing and hair and beard, while within they are entirely full of uncleanness and worms and stench,

for the first of them said that water was God, and the second fire, and another air, and they did not attain an understanding of the incorporeal and immaterial God, even though they did at last learn about him in Egypt from the ancient writings.

But let us end our discourse here, for if we were to speak of each of their words and deeds one by one, it would cause great laughter, what they say about God and the soul and matter. But I will leave all of that aside and say this to you: listen to the Scriptures and learn from them, and avoid the much-talking of the heretics, as blessed Paul commands Timothy, who was full of wisdom and also had the power to work miracles. Let us therefore listen to him, and put vain words far from us, and acquire good works: brotherly love and mercy, so that we may attain those eternal good things by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong glory and might, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 67
This saying: "Whoever loves his soul shall lose it, and whoever hates himself in this world shall keep it for eternal life."
Commentary: This present world is sweet and full of every desire, yet not for everyone, but for those who are nailed to it.
But if someone looks up to heaven and sees the beauties that are there, such a person will soon disregard himself,
for the beauty of bodies too seems beautiful so long as another, more beautiful, has not appeared, but when a more excellent one appears, then the former becomes contemptible.

Here, then, if we too wish to contemplate those beauties and those good things of the Kingdom, let us quickly free ourselves from the bonds of the world, for all love of the things of the world is a bond.
And for this reason Christ says:
Gospel: Whoever loves his soul shall lose it, and whoever hates his soul in this world shall keep it for eternal life.
If anyone serves me, let him follow me, and where I am, there my servant shall be also."
Commentary: How then is this, that whoever loves his soul shall lose it?

That is, whoever carries out its evil desires and indulges it beyond measure. For this reason it is written: "Do not follow the desires of your soul," for this is what destroys it and holds it back from the way of the virtues, just as again: "Whoever hates his soul, he shall save it." And what is this saying, "whoever hates"? That is, whoever does not obey its will. And he did not say, "whoever does not obey," but "whoever hates it," for just as we do not wish even to hear the voice of those we hate, nor are we eager to see their faces, so too, when the soul seeks what is contrary to the will of God, one must turn away from it. For since he was then about to speak to them about his death, and knew beforehand that when they heard those words about his death they would be greatly distressed, for this reason he magnified the matter in advance, as if he were saying this:

"Why do I say that if you do not nobly bear my death, and indeed even if you yourselves do not die, there will be no profit for you?" And see how he comforts them by his word. For this saying was very heavy and hard to hear: "Death is due to you, that you may be handed over into the hands of enemies and be killed." And not only then, but now too, when the hopes of the age to come have been revealed, the cup of death is hard. And there are people who, when they see beautiful palaces and the affairs of this world, shed tears when they remember that death lies before them. So great is the desire and love of this vain world and its manifold deception. But Christ wished to loosen such bonds of the world. Therefore he says:
Gospel: "Whoever hates his soul in this world will keep it for eternal life."
Commentary:
And he said this to them in order to dispel their fear. And hear what he says:
Gospel: "If anyone serves me, let him follow me."
Commentary: He said this about death; that is, a servant must without hesitation follow his lord.
And he said this at the time when, because of his great prayer, they were confident that they would suffer no more, since he had then told them of afflictions and deaths.
Now he goes on to speak of the reward as well, that is: "Where I am, there my servant will be also," in order to show them
that resurrection follows that death,
for where is Christ? In the heavens.
So let us too go there, even before the resurrection, in spirit and in mind.
Gospel: "If anyone serves me, my Father will honor him."
Commentary: Why did he not say, "I [will honor] him"? Because they did not yet have the kind of thought that was needed, for
how could those who did not even know this, that his resurrection must take place, have understood anything lofty?
For this reason he also told the sons of Zebedee, "It is not mine to give, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father."
And he himself is the one who carries out the judgment; but here he also intimates that unity, for [he means]: "As servants of the beloved Son, so will the Father receive you."
Gospel: "Now my soul is troubled, and what shall I say? 'Father, save me from this hour.'"

Commentary: Again someone may say, "And how was he urging them toward death? For this saying now is not that of one urging toward death." But understand that it is all the more that of one urging toward death, so that they might not say that he is beyond human pains and for that reason easily urges us toward death, we who are men and by nature afraid of death, while he has no experience of this matter. Therefore he shows that he too is distressed by death, but since it is the better course, he does not avoid it.
But all this belongs to human nature and not to the divinity. Therefore he says:
Gospel: "Now my soul is troubled."
Commentary: But if this were not so, what coherence would this saying have with what follows it: "Father, save me from this hour"?
And he is so shaken that he even seeks deliverance, if it were possible. All these are weaknesses of human nature, on account of which he says:

"I have nothing that I should say and ask for deliverance from this hour, for it was for this that I came to this hour," as if he were saying: "Even if we are afraid and distressed by death, we ought not to flee from it. For I too am now distressed, yet I do not speak so as to escape from it, for what is coming must be accepted."
Gospel: "Father, glorify your name."

Commentary: That is to say, "I am now distressed, but rather I speak the opposite word: 'Glorify your name,'" that is, the hour of the crucifixion has now arrived. And in this way he shows his human nature,

since nature does not want death, but wants to remain in this life. And in this way he shows that he was not outside human conditions. For just as hunger or sleep are not a fault, so too the desire for this life and the unwillingness to die are not a fault, but a natural thing. Christ had flesh wholly pure of sin, yet he was not apart from natural things; rather, he had every natural thing that was sinless. And if he had not had them, how would he have been in the flesh? And he has also taught us another thing by these words: that if some matter should ever come upon us and fear should arise in us, we should not flee from the matter that lies before us.
Gospel: "Father, glorify your name."
Commentary: That is to say, "I am now distressed, but rather I speak the opposite word: 'Glorify your name.'"

He shows that he is dying for the sake of the truth, since he calls that deed the glory of God. And so indeed it came to pass after the crucifixion, when the whole world turned and came to know the name of God.
Gospel: A voice came from heaven, saying: "I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again."

Commentary: "Again" means after the crucifixion. Now hear what Christ said: "This voice did not come for my sake, but for yours." Yet they supposed it was thunder, or the voice of an angel. And why did they suppose this? Was that voice not clear and loud? It was because the voice quickly became imperceptible to them, for they were carnal in mind, and coarse and slack. Some of them perceived only a sound, and others perceived also that it was some kind of speech, but what it was they did not know. And Christ said to them:
Gospel: "This voice was not for my sake, but for yours."

Commentary: Why did he say this word? Because he was opposing the statement they had made: "He is not from God." For how could one who was glorified by God not be from God, the one for whose sake God's name is glorified? For this reason he himself said: "This voice did not come for my sake, but for yours," that is: "It did not come so that I might learn something I do not know, for I know everything that belongs to the Father." For they were saying that an angel was speaking to him, or "It was thunder," and they took no care to find out. Therefore he said, "It came for your sake," so that in this way he might persuade them to ask what it was. But they, being frightened, did not ask what it was, though they had no idea at all what it was. And so it did not seem necessary to them to understand the saying: "This voice did not come for my sake, but for yours." Do you see that all the lowly words were spoken for their sake, since otherwise the Son had no need of help?
Gospel: "Now is the judgment of this world; now the ruler of this world will be cast out."

Commentary: If anyone should say, "And what connection does this saying have with that one?", understand that it has a great connection. For since the voice had said, "I will glorify," saying, "I have glorified, and I will glorify again," he therefore also shows the manner of the glory, what it is like, namely, that the ruler will fall down and be cast out. But what is the judgment of this world? It is as if he were saying: "There was a court and a vengeance, for he killed the first man, who had been made liable for sin, since it was through sin that death entered; but he has not found this in me. Why then did he hand me over to death? Or why did he put it into the heart of Judas to betray me?" And let no one say here that this was God's dispensation.

And what could anyone have done? For this was the work of his wisdom, as he willed and as he knew; but he did not ordain for anyone that a particular person should do that deed, for it came from the wicked mind of those who did the deed, and from the devil. Otherwise God would have willed the destruction neither of Judas nor of the Jews, had they not done it themselves, of their own will and through the devil. It is for this reason that he says it is the judgment of the world. And now, as in a court, what shall we say to the devil? This:

"Behold: you brought death upon all, since they were liable for sin; but why did you hasten unjustly to the death of Christ? Now therefore, since you brought death upon that sinless one, through him the whole world has been redeemed and judgment has been made for its redemption, and you have been cast out from your rule. It is as when some wicked tyrant slays everyone he finds, and then kills the king's son, and by that son's death the blood of the others slain by him is also avenged. So too it has come about through the Son of God: for all the evils the devil did against us, and for all the audacious acts he committed against Christ, judgment will be called down." And for this reason the Lord said:
Gospel: "Now the ruler of this world will be cast out.
And when I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all people to myself."

Commentary: That is, also from among the Gentiles. And so that no one should say, "How will he be cast out, if he overcomes even you?", for this reason he says, "He does not overcome me, for how could he have overcome the one who was going to draw all people to himself?"
And he did not speak of the resurrection, but of what was greater than the resurrection: "I will draw all people to myself."
Gospel: "I will draw all people to myself."
Commentary: How then does he say above, "The Father draws"? But it is like this: whomever the Son draws, the Father draws. And he says "I will draw,"
as of people held captive by a tyrant and unable to come by themselves.

And in another place he calls [?] this matter "plundering," saying, "No one can plunder the vessels of a strong man unless he first binds the strong man." He says all this to show his domination, and what he called "plundering" there, he called "drawing" here.

Teaching 17, on mercy. But we who know all this, let us rise and glorify the Lord, not by faith alone but also by works. Otherwise it is no longer glory but blasphemy, if we despise his commandments. For God is not so blasphemed through the sin of the pagans as when a Christian is evil and wicked.

Therefore I beseech you to strive in every way to glorify God, for it says, "Woe to that servant through whom the name of God is blasphemed." For what mercy could we ever find, we who have been commanded to give to others and yet seize from others? Blessed is the one through whom the name of God is glorified. So let us not be here as though we were in darkness, but let us flee from every sin. For if God punishes those who do not feed the hungry, and condemns the one who does not clothe the naked, what will become of those who strip the clothed? We will not cease to speak such words, and perhaps those who do not listen to us today will listen tomorrow, and those who are disobedient tomorrow will listen on another day.

But if some persist in disobedience, we shall be blameless, for we have done our part. Yet may none of you become disobedient, so that neither we may be put to shame nor you be condemned, but that all may stand with boldness before the throne of God, and we may boast of you, so that we may have your virtue as a consolation for our evils, through Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong glory and might, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 18
The text: The people answered, "We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever, and how do you say that the Son of Man must be lifted up?
Who is this Son of Man?"

Error is easily recognized and is weak, even if it covers itself in countless forms. And just as those who daub and plaster a leaning wall that is close to falling do not strengthen it with that plaster, so those who lie are easily exposed, as happened here with the Jews. For when Christ said to them,
"When I am lifted up, I will draw all people to myself," they answered and said to him:
"We have heard from the law that the Christ remains forever, so how do you say that 'the Son of Man must be lifted up'?
Who is this Son of Man?" But if they knew this from Scripture, that the Christ abides forever and ever, how did they not also know the other thing, of which he was speaking?
For in all the Scriptures there is mercy [?] concerning the passion and the resurrection.
Isaiah said, "As a sheep he was led to the slaughter," and what follows;
and David said something similar to this in the second psalm and in many other places, and he spoke together of both the passion and the resurrection; and the patriarch said:
"He lay down and slept like a lion," and then he added and said, "And who will raise him up?" And he shows together the death, concerning the passion and the resurrection.
But these people thought that they would show that he is not the Christ, and in this way they confessed that the Christ truly abides forever.

And see their wickedness, for they did not say, "We have heard that the Christ will not suffer but will remain forever." Yet the passion was not becoming destructive of immortality. And from this it is evident that they understood much and were acting deceitfully on purpose. For they heard from him that the Son of Man must be lifted up, and they did not believe, but said, "Who is this Son of Man?"

And this too they said with wickedness, as though showing that they do not know that it is he. But Christ wished to shut their mouths and to show them that the passion is no hindrance to remaining forever, and therefore he said to them:
Gospel: "For a little while the light is with you."
Commentary: He shows that his death is a departure, for the light of the sun does not perish, but for a little while it is hidden from us and then appears again.
Gospel: "Walk while you have the light."

Commentary: Of what time does he say this? Of the whole of this life in the world, or of that time which was before the crucifixion? I think that he speaks of both, for because of his incomprehensible love for humankind many believed even after the crucifixion. And he says these words in order to make them eager for faith,
as he did above, when he said thus: "For a little while I am with you," and here too he says:
Gospel: "Those who walk in darkness do not know where they are going."

Commentary: This was truly fulfilled in the Jews, for in all the things that they do, they do not know what they are doing, but they walk as if in darkness. They think that they are walking on the right road, but they are walking on an evil and crooked one. They keep the Sabbath and the old law, and they do not know what they are doing. And therefore he said to them, "Walk while you have the light, that you may be sons of light," that is, "my sons," as the evangelist said earlier:

"Not by the will of the flesh, but they were born of God," that is, also of the Father. Here he himself speaks of their being born, so that you may know that the power of the Father and of the Son is one.
Gospel: Jesus said this to them and went away and hid from them.
Commentary: Why did he hide now, since they neither took up stones nor spoke an evil word to him,
except that he was a seer of hearts and saw that their anger was inflamed, and he went away in order to soothe their envy.
And see how the evangelist indicated this, for he immediately says: "So many signs Jesus did before them, and they did not believe in him." Which "so many"?
As many as the evangelist has not written down, for, as he himself says, the greater part of his signs they have not written down. But when Christ had withdrawn and come back again,
he said to them: "Whoever believes in me does not believe in me, but in the one who sent me." For he always acts in this way:
he begins with lowly words, leads his discourse to the Father, and raises his discourse to a loftier level; and,
when he sees their obstinacy, he goes away from them, and afterward comes back to them again and again begins to speak with lowly words, as when he said: "As I hear, I judge."
And then he raised his discourse, saying: "As the Father raises the dead, so also the Son raises them."
And then he hid himself and came back to them in Galilee, and he spoke his teaching and said: "He has come down from heaven," and he hid himself and appeared again at the Feast of Tabernacles.
And thus he always carried out his teaching in many ways, by hiding himself and appearing,
by lowliness and loftiness, just as he did here also.
But he did so many signs and they did not believe in him, so that the word of Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled, which he spoke:

"Lord, who has believed what we have heard, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?" And for this reason they could not believe, for Isaiah said again: "He has blinded their eyes and dulled their hearts, so that they may not see with their eyes, nor understand with their hearts."
Isaiah said this when he saw his glory.

And he spoke about him. "Behold, here again is this saying, showing that these things are not a matter of cause but of outcome." For it is not that they did not believe because Isaiah said, "They will not believe"; rather, since they were not going to believe, Isaiah therefore said so.
But why is it that the evangelist does not speak in this way? Instead he says, as it were: "The unbelief came from the prophecy, and not the prophecy from the unbelief," for he says:

"For this reason they could not believe, for Isaiah said." For in this place he wishes to show the infallibility of Scripture, that whatever it said all came to pass, so that no one might say: "Why did Christ come," since he knew that they would not listen to him? For this reason he also brings in the prophets, who knew this. But he came so that they might have no excuse for their sin, for whatever the prophet said, he said such things as were undoubtedly going to happen, for if it were not going to happen, he would not have said it. And if this saying is "They could not," it stands in place of saying "They did not want to." And do not be surprised, for in another place he says: "Whoever is able to bear it, let him bear it."

And so in many places he calls will "power", as when he says: "The world cannot hate you." Nor is this usage found only in Scripture, but often among people too, as when someone says: "I cannot love so-and-so", calling a strong will "power"; or that so-and-so "cannot be good", and they mean will by "power". And again the prophet says: "If the Indian should change his skin and the leopard his spots, then this people too, who have learned evil, would be able to do good." He does not say that doing virtue is impossible, but: "They do not want to", and for this reason they cannot. So here too the evangelist is saying this: that it was impossible for the prophet to lie, but not that they could not believe because of their word. For it was possible for them to believe, and he would have remained truthful, for then he would not have foretold this. For such is the custom of Scripture.
Gospel: Isaiah said this when he saw his glory

Commentary: Whose glory? The Father's. But John says this about the Son and Paul about the Spirit. Yet they do not confuse them in their persons, far be it! Rather, they speak in this way because their honor is one. For everything of the Father is the Son's, and what is the Son's is the Holy Spirit's, and those words are the Holy Spirit's. For all that the angels say are the words of God; but what God says are not the words of angels. In the same way these words are the Spirit's.
Gospel: and he spoke about him

Commentary: What did he say? "I saw the Lord sitting on high thrones" and what follows. Here by "glory" he means that vision, and the smoke, and those hidden mysteries, and the sight of the seraphim, and that lightning coming forth from the throne, on which the powers were unable to look.
Gospel: and he spoke about him

Commentary: What did he say? When he heard a voice saying: "Whom shall I send to this people?" he said: "Behold, here I am, send me." And he said: "Hearing they shall hear and shall not understand", for he blinded their eyes and hardened their heart. Look, here again is another question, but it is easy if you understand it well. For just as the sun harms weak eyes all the more, not because its nature is such, but because they are weak, so it happens to those who contend to know the words of God by their own understanding. For about Pharaoh too it is said in this way: "I will harden his heart", and this too is a custom of Scripture.

And again it is written: "He gave them over to an untested mind", that is, he let them go, he permitted them. For Scripture does not say "He gave them over" in the sense that they should do evil involuntarily, but because their mind was evil, and on account of the wickedness of their hearts he let them go and left them. And when a person has been abandoned by God, the devil, out of envy, makes him do whatever he wishes. For this reason he frightens the hearer and says: "He hardened and gave over." For of his own will he not only does not give us over, but does not even abandon us. And listen to what he says:
"Is it not your sins that separate you from me?" And again he says:
"Behold, those who remove themselves far from you shall perish"; and the prophet Hosea says: "You have forgotten the law of the Lord your God; I also will forget you"; and the Lord himself says:
"How many times have I wished to gather your children, and you were not willing"; and Isaiah again says: "I came, and there was no man; I called, and there was no one who listened."
All this they say so that we may understand that it is we who make the beginning of God's abandoning us, and that we become the cause of our own perdition,
for God not only does not wish to abandon and punish us, but even when he punishes us, he does this too not willingly but unwillingly, for he says:
"I do not desire the death of the sinner"; and when Jerusalem was about to perish, Christ wept over it, as we do over those we love.

Instruction 68, on love. Therefore, we who know all this, let us strive not to be abandoned by God, but let us labor for our souls and strive to love our neighbor. And let us not cut ourselves off from our own members, which is the deed of madmen, but rather let us strive to heal our members if they are sick. For with these bodily members, if we see one of them that has grown weak, we do not cease with all diligence to heal it, and even if we are unable, still we do not cease.

Likewise, then, let us strive to act toward these members of ours, and let us bear one another's burdens, so that in this way we may fulfill the law of Christ and attain the eternal good things, by the grace and love for mankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong glory and might, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
Chapter 69
This saying: "Yet many of the rulers believed in him, but because of the Pharisees they could not confess it,
so that they would not be cast out of the assembly, for they loved the glory of men more than the glory of God."
It is good to flee from all passions harmful to the soul, but above all one ought to flee with all diligence from those passions
which give birth from themselves to many other sins and passions, such as love of money,
for that disease is evil and harmful even in itself, but it is worse for this reason, that it is the root of all passions;
and likewise is vainglory. And behold, these men fell away from faith in Christ because of their passion for this passing glory.
Gospel: "Yet many of the rulers believed in him, but because of the Pharisees they could not confess it, so that they would not be cast out of the assembly,
for they loved the glory of men more than the glory of God."
Commentary: So they were not really rulers, but slaves of an evil slavery. But afterward this fear too was dissolved,
for rulers and priests also came to believe through the apostles,
and the grace of the Holy Spirit, when it came, strengthened them all. But Christ then said:
Gospel: "Whoever believes in me, believes not in me but in him who sent me."
Commentary: As if he were saying: "Why are you afraid to believe in me, when faith in me is so great and reaches to God?"
Do you see how in every place he shows his inseparability from the Father?
But he never said this: "Whoever believes the Father believes me," for they were weak and would have said in their folly, "Look, we believe God, and we do not believe you." Instead he says:

"Whoever believes me believes the Father," to show that their faith toward the Father is of no use to those who did not believe him. And so that they would not think he was speaking of a mere man, he therefore said:
Gospel: "Whoever has seen me has seen the one who sent me."

Commentary: Here he does not speak of bodily sight, for God is not seen with bodily eyes; rather, he speaks of the sight of the mind. By this saying he also shows that unity, as in: "Whoever believes in me."

What does this saying mean? It is as if someone were to say that whoever draws the water of a river draws not the river's water but water from the spring. And yet even this image is still too weak for the matter at hand.
Gospel: "I, the light, have come into the world."

Commentary: Since in the Old Testament the Father is called this in every place, in the New he too is therefore named in the same way, under this image. For this reason Paul also calls him the radiance, and in this way shows the great unity of the Son with the Father. And he is the light who has freed us from error and dispelled spiritual darkness.
Gospel: "Whoever hears my words and keeps them, I will not judge him, for I did not come to condemn the world, but to save the world."
Commentary: So that they would not think that he passed over those who despised him out of weakness, he therefore says:
"I did not come to condemn the world." And then, so that they would not become slack and negligent because of this saying, he added:
Gospel: "Whoever despises me and does not keep my words has his own judge."
Commentary: If the Father judges no one, and you did not come to judge the world, who judges him? "But the word that I speak, that will judge him." For since they were saying:

"He is not from God," therefore, so that at that time they could no longer say these things, my words will take away from them every argument and will condemn them. [?] These are the words which he spoke: "I have not come of myself," and:

"The Father who sent me gave me a commandment," and others of this kind: "what I should say" and "what I should speak." All these will shut their mouths on that day and take away from them every excuse. For he spoke all these words of a humble form for their sake, so that they might turn back; and since they did not turn back, he will therefore condemn them by those words. But what does this saying mean,
namely: "The Father who sent me, he gave me a commandment, what I should say or what I should speak"? How can this be?
Surely it was not at the time he was being sent that he learned what he was to say, not knowing it before?
And what then would be worse than this, if someone were to understand this saying in that way and not understand the reason for the humble words?
For Paul says that he himself and the disciples know what the good, pleasing and perfect will of God is,
and did the Son not know until he received a commandment?

And how could this be possible? Do you see how, for this reason, he lowers his speech exceedingly? In order to convert them and to stop the mouths of those who came after them, for this reason he shows such great lowliness,
so that by it he may persuade them to understand that these words do not belong to his nature, but are spoken because of the weakness of the hearers.
Gospel: "And I know that his commandments are eternal life; and what I speak, as he told me, so I speak."
Commentary: Do you see the lowliness of these words? But what does this mean, seeing that he says:
"The Father raises the dead and gives them life? So also the Son gives life to whomever he wishes."
So then, he gives life to whomever he wishes, and is he not able to speak of himself?
But this is the meaning of this saying: that the matter does not have such a nature, nor is it possible, that the Father should say one thing and I another; rather:
"What he says, that same thing I also say; and I know that his commandments are eternal life." He says this to those who called him a deceiver and said:

"He has come to harm us." But when he says, "I judge no one," this means, "I am not the cause of their destruction." And for this reason, at that last time, when he wished to withdraw from them and no longer go to teach them, he says this word to them:
"I have said nothing of myself, but everything that I have said is the Father's."

And for this reason he brought his speech down to such lowliness, for it is evident that until the last moment of his departure from them he did not cease speaking these words to them. And his last word was this:
"As the Father commanded me, so I speak."
If I were opposed to him, I would also have said what is opposed to him, so as to glorify myself; but as it is, I have so referred all glory to him that I have said nothing such as:
"This is mine," but I have always confessed everything to be the Father's. Why then do you not believe me, when I say:
"I have received a commandment from the Father"? And by these words I dispel those evil suspicions of yours, I who speak every word of the Father, and all that I do,
he does, for he is with me, and the Father has not left me alone.
Do you see how in every place he shows his unity with the Father and no division at all? For when he says:

"I have not come of myself," he does not abolish his own authority, but abolishes any estrangement and opposition. For if men are lords over themselves, how much more is the only-begotten Son? As the Apostle says: "He emptied himself and put on the form of a servant and gave himself for us." But as I always say, vainglory is evil, evil! For this is what it did to those who did not believe, and to others who believed wrongly.

Teaching 69, on vainglory. Let us therefore always flee from this beast, for it is cunning and many-colored, and it spreads its venom in every place, even in outward appearance, and in luxury, and in bodily beauty. Because of it we always seek more than is needful; because of it beauty of clothing is sought; from it greed has increased among us.

But beware of this evil, O brother. If you wish to have glory, practice virtue, practice mercy; then both angels and men will praise you, and God himself will receive you. For as long as you adorn the body, your labor is vain and you are in sin; but if you spend on the poor, your praise will be great in every respect. Why do you adorn the body, yet have neglected the soul, which is full of impurity? For it was necessary to show greater zeal for adorning the soul. But as for us, beloved, even if we do not do more, let us at least labor for the soul as much as for the body. For if someone were to ask you: "Which do you prefer: to be by nature beautiful, stately, fair, and strong, and to be dressed in a shabby garment?

Or to be dressed in a fine garment, and to be by nature wretched, colorless, and feeble?" Would you not choose natural goodness rather than that of clothing? And if this is so for the body, will it not be so all the more for the soul? Or do you think that, if the soul is defiled and foul, it would gain anything from gold and silver? Turn this adornment inward and clothe the soul with it, for scarlet and purple robes are of no benefit to the body: they give it neither health nor beauty, for they cannot make what is black white, nor make what is ugly beautiful. But if you clothe the soul with it, it immediately makes the soul white, even if it is black, and makes it beautiful, if it is ugly. For the Lord says: "If your sins are like crimson, I will make them white as snow." Therefore, brother, give alms, and everything will be good, so that, thus crowned, you may dwell in those eternal mansions, and we may attain those good things. May we all be worthy to find them by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong glory and might, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
Chapter 70
This saying: "And before the feast of the Passover, which is the Passion, Jesus knew that his hour had come, that he should depart from this world and go to the Father,

for he loved his own who were in this world, and he loved them completely." "Become imitators of me," says Paul, "as I am of Christ." For this is why he put on flesh and took on our nature: so that by means of it he might teach us virtue. For Scripture says:
"In the likeness of this flesh of sins, and for the sake of sin, he condemned sin in the flesh." And he himself says: "Learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart."
And he taught all this not by word alone, but also by deed: for the Jews called him a Samaritan and a deceiver and threw stones at him,
and at times the Pharisees would send servants to kill him, and at times they would seek a means of seizing him, and they themselves reviled him many times,
And all this without cause, they who were unable to find even one fault, but rather in return for those many good deeds.
And in the face of all this he still did not cease doing good to them by word and by deed as well. And when a certain servant struck him a blow on the ear, he answered him:
"If I speak evil, testify about the evil; if I speak well, why do you strike me?"
Now these words he spoke to enemies and murderers. But let us see

what he now does with the disciples, and still more, what he does with his betrayer. For this was the one who more than all ought to have been hated, because he was a disciple, and had become a sharer of that table and bread, and had been made worthy to see such great wonders, and yet he did what was more wicked than anyone, for he delivered him into the hands of enemies.
And see how he honors such a man and washes his feet,
so that perhaps he might restrain him from wickedness in this way. And he had the power,
if he had wished, to wither him as he did to the fig tree, and to melt him as he melted the rocks, and to rend him,

as he did to the veil. Yet he did not wish to restrain him from the evil against his will, but so that he might turn back of his own accord. For this reason he washed his feet, and even at this that wretched and pitiable man was not ashamed.
Gospel: And before the feast of Passover, which is the Passion, Jesus knew that his hour had come.
Commentary: It is not that he knew it only then and had not known it from the beginning, but it was then that he did what he did.
Now he knew his departure from the beginning. In lofty language the evangelist gives his death the name "departure," and he says:
"When he was about to leave them, then he showed them greater love." For this expression that he uses, "he loved" and "he loved them completely,"
signifies that he left no deed of love that he did not do for them.

But why did he not do such a deed as this earlier? It was because he kept great deeds for the last, so that he might the more kindle their love and attachment toward him, and show that he loved them, and give them consolation beforehand for the afflictions that were coming upon them.

Now he calls them his own on the ground of intimate belonging, for he calls others his own too, but on the ground of creation, as when he says: "His own did not receive him." For that belonging is that of being created, meaning: "His own creatures did not receive him." But here he says: "He loved his own who were in the world." This belonging is that of love. And what is it that he says: "who were in the world"? It is because there were also those of his own who had passed away, such as Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and those like them, but they were not in the world; here, however, he speaks of those who were in the world, namely the apostles. Do you see that he is the God of the Old and the New? And what is this expression, "he loved them completely"?

That is to say, he remained to the end in his love for them, and he says this as a sign of that great love, for in another place he says that the sign of love is the complete laying down of one's life; but that had not yet been done. And why did he do this? Because it was greatly to be wondered at that, at the very time when he had appeared in splendor among all, he should then do so humble an act. And further, by this deed he left them no small consolation as he was departing from them; for since they were about to enter into great sorrow, he therefore gave them beforehand a consolation equal to that sorrow.
Gospel: And as the supper was taking place, and the devil had entered into the heart of Judas son of Simon Iscariot, that he should betray him,

Interpretation: The evangelist has introduced this statement here in amazement, as if to say: "Such a wicked man, who had resolved to hand him over, him he washed." And he also shows the man's great wickedness, in that neither the sharing of the bread bent him, nor the fact that the good teacher bore with him in this way up to the very last, until the time of his departure.
Gospel: Jesus knew that the Father had given everything into his hands, and that he had come out from God and was going to God.

Interpretation: Or is this the force of this saying? He says this: "Such a one, and so great, who had come out from God and was going to God, who holds all things by a nod, did this deed and did not consider it beneath him to do it." Or else he says this: "He who had come out from God and was going to God, and who holds all things, would lose nothing by such a deed, even though he performed this act of humility." And as for the words "The Father gave everything," in this place, as I think, he calls the salvation of the believers a giving. For when he says, "All things have been given to me by my Father," he calls this giving the salvation of the believers, just as he says, "They were yours, and you gave them to me."

And further he says, "No one can come to me unless the Father brings him." But when you hear of giving, do not understand anything human, for he is showing his unity and honor with the Father; for just as the Father gives to him, so too he gives to the Father. And blessed Paul indicates this when he says, "When he hands over the kingdom to God the Father." But in this place he spoke in human terms, in order to show his great care for them and his incomprehensible love toward them; for he cared for them as truly his own and taught them humility, the mother of all the virtues, of which he said that it is the fulfillment of virtue. But why then this saying, "He came out from God and is going to God"? It means that he was doing deeds worthy of one who had come out from him and was going to him. In this way he trampled down all haughtiness.
Gospel: He rose from the supper and laid aside his garment.

Commentary: See how he shows humility not by the washing alone but in another way too: for he got up not before sitting down, but after all had sat down; and then he not only washed their feet, but took off his garment and washed them in this way.

And not this alone, but he who clothed the heavens with cloud girded himself with a towel. And even this was not enough for him, but he himself poured in the water and filled the basin with his own hand, and he did not order another to fill it, but did everything himself, that he might teach us
that whenever we do some such thing, it must not be done carelessly, but with all diligence. And he washed the feet,
as I think, of his betrayer first, for it says:
"He began to wash and came to Simon Peter, and Peter said to him:
'Lord, will you wash my feet with those hands, with which you opened the eyes of the blind and cleansed lepers and raised the dead?'" And he said nothing more to him, but only this:
"You, Lord?" For this word by itself is enough to show that great glory. But how is it that no one else said anything or stopped him, but only Peter?

What then is the reason for this? I think it is this: that he first washed the feet of his betrayer and then came to Peter, and the others learned from Peter's rebuke that it is not right to resist. But in this place the evangelist does not accuse the betrayer, but tells the matter as it happened.
Gospel: And he came to Simon Peter, and Peter said to him:
"Lord, will you wash my feet?" Jesus answered: "What I am doing you do not know now, but you will know after this."

Commentary: That is, how much benefit there is from this deed, and what great gain from this wonder, which is able to lead to humility. But Peter still tried to stop him and said to him: "You shall never wash my feet."
What are you doing, O Peter? Do you not remember those earlier words, when you said:

"Far be that from you, Lord?" And he himself answered you: "Get behind me, devil." And even so are you not afraid? But Peter says: "Yes, for this is more terrible and greater." Since, then, he did this out of great love, for this reason the Lord frightens him by that very thing and says to him:
Gospel: "If I do not wash you, you will have no part with me."
Commentary: But that fervent and eager Peter answered:
Gospel: Not only the feet, but the hands also and the head.

Commentary: When he was stopping him he was vehement, and in yielding he appeared more vehement still, for both came from love. But what is it that he said to him, "You will know after this"? When was he making it known? Well, after this: when you cast out demons in my name, when you see me ascending to heaven, when you learn from the Father that I am sitting at his right hand, then you will know what this deed is.
But when Peter said, "Not only the feet, but the hands also and the head," Jesus answered:
Gospel: "One who has been washed needs nothing but the feet only, for he is wholly clean; and you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you."

Interpretation: Since, then, they were clean, it is evident that he washes their feet for this reason, that we might learn humility. But how were they clean? For they had not yet received the Holy Spirit, but sin still reigned, and the bond of the curse still remained, for the blood of Jesus had not yet been offered. How then did he say to them, "You are clean"?

But so that you should not understand it to mean that they had been completely cleansed of sins, he added and said: "You are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you." That is to say: "Through this word you have received cleansing, you have accepted the light, and you have been set free from the error of the Jews," as the prophet says: "Wash yourselves, make yourselves clean, remove wickedness from your souls."

And since they too had removed all evil from their souls and were with him with a sincere mind, he therefore says: "One who has been washed, according to the word of the prophet, is clean." For there the prophet was not speaking of the washing with water that the Jews practiced, but of the cleansing of the mind.

Moral teaching on righteousness. Let us too, then, become clean; let us learn to do good. But what is good? To judge for the orphan and to vindicate the widow. For this word about orphans and widows is great in the Scriptures, yet we do not hold it to be great. For see how great its grace is, for he says: "If your sins are like scarlet, I will make them white as snow, and if they are like dyed cloth, I will make them white as wool."
Therefore, then, let us hasten to lend a helping hand to orphans and widows,
for the tears of a widow have no small power, but are able to open the heavens.

Therefore, then, let us not do them harm, but let us have mercy on them and lend them a helping hand, and let us too find abundant mercy both in this world and in the age to come. For through this deed we shall find forgiveness of many sins and shall stand boldly before the throne of Christ, which may we all be worthy to attain by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong glory and might, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 71
The word: And he took his garment and reclined again and said to them: "Do you know what I have done to you?" It is an evil thing,
beloved, it is an evil thing to come into the depth of evils, for from then on one becomes incorrigible.
Therefore we must struggle diligently so that wickedness may not master us, for it is easier not to fall into evil than for one who has fallen to climb out.
For look at Judas: once he had cast himself into that evil wickedness, how much help he received, and yet he was not saved from it. For he said concerning him:
"One of you is a devil." And again he said: "I am not speaking of all of you"; and again he said: "Not all of you believe." And he did not take in a single one of these.
But now, when he had washed their feet, he took his garment and reclined again, and then he said to them: "Do you know what I have done to you?"
No longer to Peter alone, but to all of them he says: "You call me 'Lord and Teacher,' and you say well, for I am."
Gospel: "You call me"
Commentary: He brings in their own word and then adds, "I am," for he took up their word,
so that what he said might not be burdensome; and by his own word he makes the confirmation of their word inoffensive and beyond doubt,
for he says, "I am." Do you see how, when he speaks to the disciples, he reveals himself? For as he says:
"Call no one teacher on earth"; and again he says: "Call no one father on earth, for one is your teacher and father."
But this "one" is said not only of the Father, but also of himself; for if he were not speaking also of himself, how could he have said, "that you may become children of light"?
Or if he calls only the Father teacher, how does he now say, "I am"?
Gospel: "If I, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet,
for I have given you an example, so that as I have done to you, so you also should do."

Commentary: What is this saying, "so do"? That is: with such zeal. For if the Lord did so to servants, shall we, who are servants, not do so to our fellow servants? For this reason he showed us the higher example, so that we might look to him and do the lesser. Where now are those who despise their fellows? The Lord washed the feet of his own betrayer, that wicked man and thief, and at the very time of the betrayal, when he was incurable, and he was even a sharer of his heart. And do you act arrogantly toward your fellow and raise your eyebrows?

Now therefore let us wash one another's feet, and those of our servants too; for what great thing is it if we wash the feet of servants? For here slavery and lordship are distinctions of names only, but there it is the truth of the facts, for by nature he was Lord and we are servants, and yet he did not consider washing feet beneath him.

What then shall we answer, we who have such examples of humility and do not imitate them at all, but rather do the opposite and exalt ourselves as if we were lords by nature, and do not discharge what we owe? For the Lord has made us debtors, since he made the beginning of this deed, and debtors for the lesser part, for he was Lord, while we are servants, as he himself said:
"If I, the Lord and Teacher, have washed you, should you not all the more do so to one another?" So that they might no longer say, as they did before, "Who is greatest of all?"

and might not stumble against one another, for this reason he humbles their mind, teaching that even if one is very great, you must not despise your brother. And he did not say the higher thing: "If I, the Lord and Teacher, have washed the feet of the betrayer," but he spoke of all, and left that for them to understand. For this reason he said, "Whoever does and teaches shall be called great," for this is teaching: the showing forth of the deed. And what could be higher than this? Or what arrogance would this deed not humble?

For he who sits upon the cherubim washed the feet of his betrayer, while you, man, who are earth and ashes, dust and powder, boast and exalt yourself. Of how many torments are you worthy? For if you love loftiness of mind, come, and I will show it to you. How is it that you do not know that whoever boasts over the vain affairs of this world has a very low and worthless soul? For neither does humility come about without loftiness, nor loftiness without humility. For just as little children love the worthless things of play but cannot understand great matters, so it is with the affairs of the world. But let whoever is wise despise all this and seek what is of heaven. As for the fool, let him turn to weaving the spider's web, which is what the affairs of this world are, and at the hour of death he will have nothing in his hands.
Gospel: "Amen, amen, I say to you: A servant is not greater than his lord, nor is an apostle greater than the one who sent him.

If you know this, you are blessed if you do it. I do not speak of all of you. I know whom I have chosen, but it is so that the scripture may be fulfilled, which says: 'He who ate bread with me has lifted up his heel with me.'"
Commentary: What he said above he says again now, namely:
"If a servant is not greater than his lord, nor an apostle greater than the one who sent him, and I am Lord and Teacher and I have done this, is it not all the more fitting for you also to do this?"
Then he further shows that they know everything he is telling them, by saying, "If you know this," which is to say:
"I speak to you not as to the ignorant but as to those who know, and if you do it, you are blessed,
for I tell you this so that you may also carry it out in deed,
for the Jews also know, but they are not blessed, since they do not do it. But I do not speak of all of you."
Oh, what forbearance toward wrong! For he still did not expose the betrayer, but continues to conceal him, in order to give him time for repentance,
and he both exposes him and does not expose him by the words he spoke: "He who ate bread with me."

But I think that the other saying as well, "A servant is not greater than his lord," he said for this same reason: so that if ever affliction and insult should come upon them from servants or from their inferiors, they would not stumble,
but would call to mind the deed of Judas, who saw such great good things from him and repaid his benefactor with evil.
Therefore he added: "He who ate bread with me has lifted up his heel against me." And he left out everything else and mentioned only this, which was most able [?]. For this reason he added,
saying: "He who ate bread was nourished by me, and he who was also a sharer of my heart did this." And he said this so that he might do good to evildoers. And when he said,
"I do not speak of all of you," he then set that one man alone apart, so that all the others would not be afraid, and then he said:

"He who ate bread with me," in order to show concerning that wretched man that he did it not without understanding, but deliberately and through evil training. And he did not say "he betrays me," but:
"He has lifted up his heel against me," in order to reveal his wickedness and treachery.
Discourse 71, on not doing evil to enemies, and on Joseph. All this is written so that we may not bear grudges against those who do evil to us, but may rather grieve for them,
for it is rather those who do evil who are harmed, and they are worthy of much weeping,

more than those to whom they do evil. For the greedy man and the slanderer do great harm to themselves, but they greatly benefit us, if only we wish it. For if someone seizes what is yours and you give thanks to God, you have gained much profit through your thanksgiving, while he has earned great judgment and guilt.

For even if you are weak and unable to do evil to the one who does evil to you, you are still able to be angry with him, to curse him and to bear a grudge; and if you do not do this, but rather pray for him and bless him, you will receive a reward. And by this it will become known that even if you had the power to harm him bodily as well, you would not harm him. For if you pray for him and bless him, you become like God, as the Lord says: "Pray for those who do evil to you, that you may become like your Father in heaven."

Do you see how much good we gain from those who do evil to us, if we wish it? For nothing so gladdens God concerning us as not repaying evil for evil; for we have been commanded not only not to do evil, but rather also to pray for and bless those who do evil to us. For see how much good Christ did to his betrayer: he washed his feet, he rebuked him in secret, he made him a sharer of his table, he gave him a kiss. And that man was not converted, yet the Lord persisted in the same and did not cease doing good.

But let me teach you from the old law, through the servants of God, so that you may thus know that we have no excuse at all when we bear grudges. And if you wish, let us speak of Moses, or let us take our discourse back even earlier than him; for the more ancient the examples are, the more we are outdone, because virtue was hard to achieve then, since they had neither scripture nor earlier examples, but nature labored alone and unaided. For this reason Scripture praises Noah and says: "Noah, a righteous and holy man in his generation," that is to say, at a time when those who hindered virtue were many. And who before Moses showed himself long-suffering?

Blessed Joseph, who shone forth in holiness and even more in long-suffering: for the innocent one was sold, he who served his brothers and did good to them. They denounced him, and yet he went again to the wilderness and brought them food, and when he did not find them, he searched for them and did not lose heart, but behaved as a brother toward those merciless men. But in return for all this they sold him, and because of them he came to dwell in prison, and still he said nothing evil about them. And afterward, when he received authority, he fed them and delivered them from many evils. For if we suffer evil from a neighbor, it cannot destroy our virtue. But they did not act this way; instead they accused him falsely, and reproached him for his vision, and threw him into a pit, and they ate the food he had brought, while they watched their brother naked in the pit and had no pity on him. What could be worse than this deed?
Or than which murderers were they not more wicked?
And then they took him up and gave him to vile barbarian men,
but when he became king, not only did he forgive that evil, but he also freed them from that sin as far as was in his power, and he called the affair God's providence and not their wickedness.
And what he did to them he did not do out of remembrance of wrongs, but for the sake of his brother.

And then he embraced them, and the one they had killed wept over them, and he brought them all down to Egypt and did them countless good things. So what word of defense will we have, we who, after the Law and the coming of Christ, do not imitate even those who lived before the Law? Who will deliver us from torments, for nothing is worse than remembering wrongs?

And this is shown by that debtor of ten thousand talents, who was forgiven and then had the debt demanded of him again. For he was forgiven because of God's love for humankind, and it was demanded of him because of his own wickedness. But let us forgive our neighbors every fault and do good to them, so that we may attain God's love for humankind and that eternal good things may be given to us, by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong glory and might, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 72

This saying: "Amen, amen I say to you: If anyone receives the one I send, he receives me, and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me." Great is the reward for serving and giving rest to the servants of God, for he says: "Whoever receives you has received me, and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me."

And what could be equal to receiving Christ and his Father? But why, when he had said, "If you know, blessed are you if you do this," did he immediately add this: "Whoever receives you receives me"? He did this for the following reason:
for since they were going to go out into the world and endure many afflictions, he therefore consoles them in two ways. First, in that he says to them:
"If you keep me in mind and remember all that I endured, you will endure everything easily."
And again, second, in that he promised such a reward to those who receive them. And he indicated both of these by saying:
"Blessed are you if you do this." And secondly he said, "Whoever receives you receives me," so that in this way they might have consolation on both counts.
And when he had commanded both of these things, as to preachers of the whole world, he then reflected

how the betrayer had been deprived of both of these, and has neither the crown of patience, nor would he be received by anyone. For this reason he was troubled, and the evangelist shows that he was troubled on this account, for he says:
Gospel:
Having said this, Jesus was troubled in spirit, and he testified and said:
"One of you will betray me."

Commentary: Again he brought that fear upon all of them, for he did not speak by name. And they, although they knew of nothing evil in themselves, nevertheless held Christ's word to be more trustworthy than their own thoughts. Therefore they looked at one another. But what is this, that all of them looked at one another?

And Peter, the most fervent of all, beckoned to John. For since the Lord had rebuked him, and again when he would not allow himself to be washed he had been held back from his own will, and he always appears to rush forward out of fervor and to be restrained, therefore he was afraid and neither spoke nor kept silent, but wished to learn through John's mediation. But perhaps someone may inquire why it was that, when all were afraid and distressed and Peter, the head of the disciples, was trembling, John at that moment, as if in delight, was reclining in the bosom of Jesus; and not only this, but he also leaned on his breast and embraced him. And again this too is to be inquired into: how is it that he says about himself, "whom Jesus loved"? And none of the other evangelists said this about him. For the Lord loved all of them, but this one he loved more than all.

But if no one else has said this about him, and he says it himself, do not be surprised, for Paul too does this at the proper time, when it is fitting, as when he says, "I know a man fourteen years ago." And the other evangelists have also set forth no small praise of him. Or do you think it small that they say, "He said to him, 'Follow me,' and immediately he left his father and everything and followed him"? And with Peter he alone, together with James, went up to Tabor, and again in another place he brought only him into the house. And when he went to pray, he took them out with him. Or did this one set forth small praise of Peter, when he says, "Christ said to him, 'Peter, do you love me?'" And in every place he shows Peter's great fervor, and how intimate he was with John, when he said, "Lord, what do you say about this one?"

He was speaking out of great love. But if it had not been fitting and had not come to this point, this one would not have said this either. For when he said, "Peter beckoned to John," if he had said nothing else, he would have given us much to inquire about, so that we would search for the reason.

For this reason it says: "He was reclining on Jesus' bosom." Or do we take what this phrase says as a small matter, when you hear that Jesus gave such boldness to his disciples? But if you seek the reason for this, he was beloved, for it says for what reason he does this: in order to show himself a stranger to that evil deed of betrayal. For this reason he leans on him and speaks with confidence. But why did he lean on his breast? First, because he did not yet know him as was fitting, and as they afterward came to know who he is, or what he is like; and second, because the Lord was consoling his sorrow, for their faces were changed and their souls troubled. And for this reason Jesus draws him all the closer to himself and consoles him by word and by deed,
And see his truthfulness and sincerity: he does not state his name, but says, "whom he loved," just as the blessed Paul says:
"I know a man, fourteen years ago." But when that blessed one asked, only then did the Lord reveal him, and even then not by giving his name, but he spoke thus to him:
Gospel: "It is he to whom I shall dip the bread and give it."
Commentary: And the manner of this act is a shaming one, yet he was not abashed even by that table, for he partook of that bread, he who received that bread from the hands of the Lord himself.

And who would not have been softened by this? But he was not softened. For this reason the devil entered into him with authority only then, when he saw his shamelessness and boldness, for as long as he belonged to that company,
he did not dare to enter him, but approached him from outside and fought against him.
But once he had become known and had been set apart, then he entered into him completely, for it was not even fitting that one so unbending should be with him.
For this reason he separated him, and when he had separated him, then the devil took hold of him, and at once Judas left them and went out from them by night.
Gospel: Jesus said to him: "Friend, what you intend to do, do quickly!" None of those reclining at table understood this.
Commentary: Oh, what senselessness, how he neither bent nor was ashamed,
but became more wicked and went out. But this saying: "Do quickly!"
does not mean that he was urging and advising him, but he was reproaching him and showing that he wished him to turn back; but since he saw his unbending obstinacy, he let him go.
Gospel: And none of those reclining at table understood this.
Commentary: For the Lord said: "He to whom I shall dip the bread and give it, it is he." So how did they not understand?
Only because John spoke to the Lord secretly, and likewise the Lord told him secretly, so that the betrayer should not be exposed, to whom the Lord was saying openly:
"What you are doing, do quickly," and they did not understand. But Jesus said this in order to confirm his word which he spoke to the Jews:
"I have authority to lay down my life and I have authority to take it up again," for as long as he did not will it, no one could take his life from him;
but since he himself willed it, the matter became easy. For this reason he said: "What you intend to do, do quickly!"
And no one understood that saying, for otherwise the disciples would have cut him down and Peter would have killed him; but no one understood. But did John too, then, not understand?

Nor did John understand it, for they were far removed from such schemes, and John did not know that the betrayal would take place at that moment; rather, they supposed that he had told him to make preparations for the feast.
Gospel: So he took the bread and went out, and it was night.

Commentary: Why does he also mention the time? So that you may recognize his eagerness for wickedness, for not even the hour of night could hold him back. And they supposed that he had spoken about caring for the poor, for he took great care for the poor, so that he might teach us also to practice mercy. This is what the disciples supposed, for not even this shamed that wicked Judas, since he did not expose him in this way until the very last moment. And it is right for us to act likewise, so that we do not expose the sins of others, even if they are incurable; for after this the Lord too, when Judas came to betray him, allowed him to kiss him and took such a thing upon himself. And now he begins to speak to the disciples and to call glory that lawless crucifixion and that death of reproach, to teach us that every deed, however reproachful and hateful it may be to all, becomes great glory when it is done for God and in a godly way.
And for this reason he says:
Gospel: And when Judas had gone out, Jesus said: "Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God also has been glorified with him."

Commentary: By these words he lifts up and reassures the slackened minds of the disciples, so that they should not only not grieve but even rejoice. For this reason too he rebuked Peter from the first, because to enter into death and through death to conquer death is great glory.
