And this is what he meant when he said: "When I am lifted up, then you will know that I am he." And again he says: "Destroy this temple, and on the third day I will raise it up." And again he said: "No sign will be given to you except the sign of Jonah." For how is it not great glory when after death he is able to do more than even before death? For the disciples performed greater signs, so that the resurrection might be made credible.
Gospel: And "God also will glorify him with himself."
Commentary: That is to say, not through another, but through himself.
Gospel: "And he will glorify him immediately."

Commentary: Immediately with the crucifixion; for it was not after a long time, nor would he wait for the time of the resurrection, nor reveal it brilliantly only then, but immediately, at his very crucifixion, his majesty was revealed. For the sun turned back, darkened, and the rocks split, and the curtain was torn, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose; and the tomb was sealed and guards were set over it, and the body of the dead man arose; and the fortieth day passed, and the grace of the Holy Spirit came down, and all proclaimed him, the Lord Jesus.

For this reason he says: "God also will glorify him with himself, and he will glorify him immediately," for he will glorify him not through angels, nor through archangels, nor through any other powers, but through himself. And how did he glorify him through himself? Because he did everything for the glory of his Son, even though the Son did everything. Do you see that the Son attributes his own works to the Father?
Gospel: "My children, yet a little while I am with you, and you will seek me, and, as I said to the Jews:
'Where I am going, you cannot come,' so now I say to you."
Commentary: He begins these distressing words after the supper, for when Judas went out, it was not evening but night.
And since the Jews were about to come shortly to lead him away, it was therefore necessary
that he should tell them everything that was needful, and that they should remember all of it, and even more that the Holy Spirit should remind them, for at that time it had slipped the minds
of those who had been seized by the sleep of sorrow, as another evangelist says, and again here too he says:
"Because I have said this to you, sorrow has filled your hearts." And how could they at that time have learned all those words well?
But afterward the Holy Spirit reminded them of everything, and no small benefit came from these words for understanding the glory of Christ.
But why does he distress their souls and say to them: "A little while I am with you"?
For he was speaking to the Jews; but why does he now say to these: "I said it to the Jews, and I say it to you also"? Yet he is not joining them with those — far from it!
Rather, he spoke this phrase, "As I said to the Jews," in order to remind them of that saying, so that they might know that he did not learn of it only at the time when the event had arrived,
but knew it beforehand, and they themselves were witnesses, having heard his word.
For this reason he added and said, "My children," so that when they heard, "As I said to the Jews," they would not say that he was speaking to them as he had to those,
for he was speaking not to distress them but to comfort them, so that those hard things would not come upon them unexpectedly and throw them into confusion.
Gospel: "Where I am going, you cannot come."
Commentary: He shows that his death is a passing over to something better and a going to a place where corruptible bodies cannot enter,
and he says all this to him strengthen their longing for him and make it more fervent, for we know
that when we see one of our loved ones departing, we become full of longing, and all the more when we learn that he is going to such a place where we cannot go. But this saying, "Where I am going,
you cannot come," he said to the Jews in order to frighten them, but to the disciples in order to strengthen their longing, as if to say:
"Such is that place that not only they, but not even you, the beloved, can come there."
And by these words he also makes known the honor of his own nature.
Gospel: "And I say to you also now."
Commentary: What is this "now"? It means this: "I spoke to them in one way and I speak to you in another, and not as to them."

But where did the disciples seek him, and where did the Jews? The disciples sought him when they were fleeing out of fear of the Jews, while the Jews sought him when those countless evils, beyond all words, came upon them, as the diligent Josephus says,
when their city was taken captive and divine wrath came upon them from every side,
And so the Lord spoke to them because of their unbelief, but to these for this reason: so that that sorrow might not come upon them unexpectedly.
Gospel: "A new commandment I give you."
Commentary: For since they were about to fall into turmoil and distress because of these words, as men who would be left orphans,
he therefore consoles them by clothing them with that great good, which is love, as if to say:
"You are sorrowful because of my departure, but if you love one another, you will be stronger." For this reason he added and said:
Gospel: "By this all will know that you are my disciples."

Commentary: With this word he consoled them, when he told them, "You will be my disciples forever," and that "this assembly will not be dissolved," since he also gave them a sign. And he said this when the betrayer had gone away from them. How then does he decree as a new commandment that which is written in the old as well? For this reason: that he himself renewed it in this way, for he added and said, "As I have loved you." For it is not that you had some good, and in return for that good I gave you my love; rather, you had done no good, and I showed such great love. And for you too it is right to do good to your neighbors in this way, so that you love them without any obligation." And he left off speaking of the miracles he was going to perform, and he says that his discipleship is made manifest through love, because this is what reveals holy men, for it is the cause of all virtue, and through it, he says, we are all saved, for:

"This, he says, is my discipleship, and by this all people will praise you, when they see you, because you imitate my love." And if someone should say, "Was not Christ's discipleship made manifest rather through miracles?" — no, for many will say to me on that day, "Lord, Lord, did we not cast out demons in your name?" And I will say to them, "I do not know you." And again, when they were rejoicing that the demons obeyed them, he said to them, "Do not rejoice that the demons obey you, but that your names are written in heaven." But if anyone should say, "Was not the world converted through miracles?" let him understand that it was converted through miracles for this reason: because love existed from the first. Had it not existed, the miracles would not have endured either; rather, this is what made them good, for the heart and soul of all were one. Had they been divided from one another, everything would have perished.

Teaching 72, on love. For he was not commanding this to them alone, but to all who were going to believe in him through their word. For even now nothing else makes the pagans stumble with regard to us except this, that there is no love. But the apostles loved one another mightily, as you have seen with Peter and John, how they were, and again how Paul was toward them, who possessed every virtue. For this thing springs up from a virtuous and holy soul, but where there is wickedness this plant withers; for when lawlessness multiplies, the love of many withers. And miracles do not convert the pagans as good deeds and a virtuous life do, and nothing makes life so radiant as love does. For when the preaching had not yet spread abroad, miracles were rightly to be sought.

But now it is rather good deeds that we must acquire, for nothing so shames the pagans as virtue, nor does anything make them stumble so much as wickedness. For when someone sees a teacher of love living in hatred and greed and robbery, will he not regard that teaching as a lie? And we become the cause of their remaining in error, for they recognize the error of their own faith and love this faith of ours, but they are corrupted by our deeds. And if you say, "Why do they not imitate the first ones?" — rather, they seek benefit from us, at whom they look, and they say, "Show us your faith by deeds," and when they see us living in evils, they remain in their own way. For this reason, then, judgment is summoned upon us not only for the evils that we do, but also for this, that the name of God is blasphemed because of us. How long, then, shall we be enslaved to these many passions?
Let us now withdraw from them! Let us not be like those senseless people of whom the prophet says: "Let us eat and drink, and tomorrow we shall perish."

For this reason too he reproached them: "Will you dwell alone upon the earth?" For this reason I fear that we may remain in evil and meet with eternal judgment. Rather, let us take up virtue, so that we may attain those eternal good things by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong glory and might, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 73
This saying: "Simon Peter said to him, 'Lord, where are you going?'
Jesus said to him, 'Where I am going, you cannot follow now, but you will follow afterwards.'" Great is love, and hotter than fire,
and it reaches up to the height of heaven, and nothing among the affairs of the world becomes a hindrance to it,
for when Peter, with that fervent heart, heard, "Where I am going, you cannot come," he immediately said to him:
Gospel: "Lord, where are you going?"
Commentary: He said this out of the ardent desire he had to follow him, but he did not dare say openly, "I will follow you," and only asks.
But the Lord answered not his words but his mind, saying: "Where I am going, you cannot follow."

Now, do you see that he wanted to go with him, and that this is why he was asking? But he heard: "Afterward you will follow me!" Even so he could not calm his desire, but was so eager that he even said to him:
Gospel: "Why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you."
Commentary: Since he had passed beyond the fear of the betrayal and had shown himself to be one of the faithful, he then began to question, while the others were silent. What are you saying, Peter?
For he himself said, "You cannot," and you say, "I can"? Now then, learn by experience that you cannot, and that your love is nothing if God's help is not there.
And from this it is evident that the Lord permitted that fall of presumption to happen because of his great love and mercy, for he wished

that Peter should come to know his own weakness from the Lord's words. But since he persisted in his vehemence, the Lord then let him go, so that he might learn his own weakness when he did not have the Lord's help,
for when the Lord said, "I shall be delivered into the hands of enemies," he said to him: "Forgiveness be to you,
Lord," and the Lord rebuked him, and he did not learn. Instead, when Christ again wished to wash his feet, he tried to prevent him. And now, when he heard:
"You cannot follow me," he said, "Even if all deny you, I will never deny you." And so that he should not come to boasting and learn to answer back,
for this reason he corrected him, so that he would no longer oppose him,
as Luke says: "Jesus said: I have besought the Father for you, that your faith may not fail you." That is, "that you may not perish!"
And by all this he teaches humility and exposes human nature:

that it is nothing of itself. For he corrected him so that he should not become one who answers back when he received the governance of the world, but so that he would remember the things that had befallen him and know his own weakness. And this did not befall him just once, but within one short time he denied three times, so that you may know that he did not love as much as he was loved. And after that fall he said to him: "Do you love me more than these?", so that you may know that his love had not withered, but that this happened by God's permission. For he accepts Peter's love but does not want opposition. For if you love, you ought to listen to the words of the one you love; for he told you and those with you that you cannot. Why then do you dispute?
Do you not know what the word of God is?
Gospel: "I will lay down my life for you."

Commentary: For since he had heard that no one has greater love than this, immediately, as one seeking perfection, he set about reaching that measure. But Christ shows that it belongs to him alone to promise the deed with such authority, and therefore he said to him:
Gospel: "The cock will not crow before you deny me three times."

Commentary: That is, right now, for there was not much time until cockcrow, since he was speaking to them at that untimely hour of the night, for the first and also the second watch of the night had passed.
Gospel: "Let not your hearts be troubled."

Commentary: Trembling came over the others, since they had heard that he foretold to Peter himself the threefold denial before the cock's crowing. And this distress was constricting their hearts. Therefore he began to comfort them, saying: "Let not your hearts be troubled." In this way he showed them the power of his divinity, in that whatever came into their minds, he told them openly.
Gospel: "Believe in God and believe in me!"

Commentary: That is to say: believe, for through me you will pass beyond all those difficult matters and trials, for faith in me and in my Father is able to save you from all evils, and nothing will have power over you. And then he says:
Gospel: "In my Father's house there are many dwelling places."

Commentary: Just as he comforted Peter, saying: "Afterward you will follow me," so too he sets hope before these, so that they might not say that he gave the promise to him alone. Therefore he said to them: "In my Father's house there are many dwelling places; if it were not so, I would have told you that I go to prepare a place for you." That is to say: "The same place that will receive Peter will receive you too," for there is a great abundance of dwellings there, and there is no need of preparation. For since he had said: "You cannot come to that place," so that they might not imagine: "We shall surely perish altogether," therefore he says to them:
Gospel: "So that where I am, you also may be."
Commentary: "And I have so much eagerness for this matter that, if it had not been prepared from the beginning, I would have gone,

and prepared a place for you, and would have come and taken you away," so that in this way they might be confident and full of hope. And so that they might not suppose that he was saying this to them as consolation and that it was not really so, therefore he added and said to them:
Gospel: "Where I am going you know, and the way too you know."
Commentary: For he was showing them that those words were not spoken in vain. And he said this to them since he saw their souls, that they were seeking to learn this,
for Peter did not speak those words for the sake of knowing,
but in order that he might follow; and since the matter seemed possible to him, it afterward became apparent that it is impossible.
Therefore he desired to know it, and therefore the Lord said to them: "The way too you know." For just as, when he said:
"You will deny me," and no one else said anything, yet he knew their thoughts and said to them: "Let not your hearts be troubled," so also here, when he said:
"You know," he was indicating the desire of their heart, and he himself gave them the occasion for asking. And this word: "Where are you going?"
Peter said out of desire and love, but Thomas out of fear, for Thomas said to him: "Lord, we do not know where you are going, and we cannot know your way." That is to say:
"We do not know the place, so how could we know the way that leads there, to where we do not know?"

And see with how much reverence he spoke, for he did not say: "Tell us the place," but: "We do not know where you are going." For all had been hearing this from the beginning, and the Jews too were astonished as to where he was going.

And if they wished to know, would not his disciples have wished it all the more, who had never been far from him? And they were afraid to ask, and yet they did ask, out of their great longing and distress. But Jesus said to them:
Gospel: "I am the way, I am the truth, I am the life, and no one comes to the Father except through me."

Commentary: Why, when Peter asked, did he not say to him immediately, "I am going to the Father," but instead, "You cannot follow me now"? Rather, he thus took up such a great multitude of words, whereas to the Jews he rightly did not explain it.
But why did he not tell this man the matter, since he told even the Jews, "I came forth from God and I am going to God"?
And again he said to them, "Where I am going, you cannot come," and in this way he cast them into distress. But he did not tell the disciples and Peter for this reason,

for he knew their great zeal, and Peter could not force him to let him go with him; and he himself accomplished what he intended by the concealment of this saying. And since they no longer dared to follow him by force, only then did he reveal it to them, for when he said, "Where I am going, no one can come without me."
Gospel: "I am the way."
Commentary: That is to say, "Through me you will come to the Father."
Gospel: "The truth and the life."

Commentary: He said this so that all of this would undoubtedly be so, for nothing from me will be false, but rather life, and not even death will be able to prevent you from coming there. For since "I am the way," you will no longer need a guide, and since "I am the truth," these words will not prove false. Now they understood the word about the way and acknowledged it, but those other words they did not understand; yet they did not dare to ask about what they did not understand. Nevertheless, in all this they received great consolation from the way, since he said to them, "I am the way," that is to say, "Since I am the lord of bringing people to the Father, you will undoubtedly come,
for apart from me there is no other way by which anyone might come to the Father."

For when he said, "No one can come to me unless the Father brings him to me," and again said, "When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all people to myself, and no one comes to the Father except through me," in this way, in every place, he makes himself equal with the Father. But how is this? For when he said to them, "Where I am going you know, and the way too you know," he immediately said to them again, "If you had known me, you would have known my Father also; from now on you know him and you have seen him." It is not that he contradicts his own words, far from it! Rather, it was like this: the disciples knew him, yet not as was fitting, for they knew him as God, but they did not know him as Father, except at the last, when the Holy Spirit came and gave them all understanding.

Such, then, is the word of the Lord: "If you had known my essence and nature, you would have known the Father's also; and from now on you know him and have seen him." The one saying, "you will know him," concerned the time to come, and the second, "you have seen him," concerned that present time, that is to say:

"through me." And by seeing he means the understanding of the mind, for it is possible to see those who are visible and not to recognize who they are, but it is impossible both to know and not to know those who are known. For this reason he says: "You have seen him," as he appeared to the angels; and it was not his nature and essence that appeared, but it is said: "He appeared according to their capacity." And in this way he shows that:

"Whoever has seen him has seen the Father." Yet they saw him not in his essence and nature as he is, but clothed in human flesh. And elsewhere it is customary to call understanding "seeing," as when it says: "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God." And by "pure" it means not only those pure of fornication, but those who are far from all sins, for every sin defiles the soul.

Homily 73. On almsgiving, and not on plundering. Let us also, then, strive with all our strength to wipe away the filth of sins from our soul. For baptism cleanses first, and afterward other works, since God in his love for humankind has given us, after baptism, many means of cleansing, of which the first is almsgiving, for by almsgiving and faith sins are cleansed. But by almsgiving I do not mean that which is done from seizure and from the plunder of possessions, for that is not almsgiving,
but wickedness. For what benefit is there in stripping one person and clothing another? For even if we were to give to the poor all that was seized, it would be of no benefit.

And Zacchaeus shows this, who gave back fourfold all that he had seized. But we seize much and give little, and by this we expect to win God's favor, though it is by this that he is the more angered. For tell me: if you found a donkey dead on the road and dragged it off and brought it into the sanctuary, would not everyone laugh at you? Now then, I prove to you that almsgiving done from what has been plundered is more loathsome than this, for every sin is an evil stench.
And hear the prophet, how he says: "My wounds stink and are rotten."
But you ask the Lord in words to forget your sins, yet by your deeds you do not let him forget them; instead you remind him of them every day,
for you lay the gains of wickedness on the altar and give them to the saints. Or do you say:
"I am not giving what was stolen, but something else, which was my own"?
And does one not understand that even if a small amount gained unlawfully falls into a great quantity of wealth, it defiles all of it, just as a little dung ruins a pure spring and makes it stink?
We wash our hands when we go to church, but not our hearts, and we do not know that it is not the hands that say anything,

But the soul makes supplications to God, for we strive to do things so worthless and small, and we despise the great ones. For if praying with unwashed hands is improper, is it not far worse to pray with a defiled soul? For this reason the Jews too, having turned to evil deeds, were eager to wash their hands with water. Therefore Scripture says to them: "Wash your soul from wickedness; how long will foul thoughts remain with you?"

Let us wash, then, not with mire but with the water of mercy, and not with acts of greed. First turn away from seizing and robbing, and then show mercy. Turn from evil and do good; restrain your hands from seizing, and so direct them to mercy. If with the same hand with which we strip others we also clothe others, this is abominable before the Lord. For it would have been better for Cain too if he had not made an offering. And if he who offered what was inferior provoked anger, will not he who offers what belongs to another provoke great anger? For he will say to you: "I did not teach you robbery, and do you honor me with what was robbed? Do you perhaps suppose, lawless one, that I too am like you? Now I will reprove you and set your sins before your face." But may not even one of us hear this voice; rather, may we perform pure mercy and inherit the eternal good things, by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and might, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
Homily 74
On the passage: "Philip said to him: 'Lord, show us your Father, and it is enough for us.'

Jesus said to him: "Have I been with you for so long, and do you still not know me, Philip? He who has seen me has seen my Father." The prophet said to the Jews: "The face of a prostitute has come upon you, and you have become shameless toward all."
But, as I think, it is fitting to say this not only to that city, but also to those who shamelessly stand opposed to the truth. For when Philip said to him:
"Lord, show us your Father," he himself answered: "Have I been with you for so long, and do you not know me, Philip? He who has seen me has seen my Father."
And after all this there are still some who dare to separate the Son from the Father.
And what closeness is greater than this? For some, because of this saying, fell into the heresy of Sabellius,
but let us leave both these and those, as exceedingly lawless, and let us look at the truth of these words, for he says:
"Have I been with you for so long, and do you not know me, Philip?"

What then does this mean: "Are you the Father whom I seek?" "No," he says. For this reason he did not say "I know him," but "Do you not know me?" This saying signifies nothing other than this: that the Son is nothing different, but what the Father is, the same is the Son, apart from fatherhood. For the one is Father by his personal property and the other Son, but in everything else they are one. From where, then, did Philip come to this saying?
And Jesus said: "If you had known me, you would have known my Father also."

Now both Philip and Thomas asked about the Father, and he told them nothing plainly. For this reason Philip also wished to ask: "Show us your Father, and we need nothing else." And Christ had said: "If you had known me, you would have known my Father also," but he said again:

"Show us your Father," as though he already knew him perfectly. But Christ had set him upon the way and was assuring him that the Father is known through him. Yet he wished to see him with fleshly eyes, perhaps because he had heard of the prophets that they saw God. But by no means did they see the nature of God; rather, they saw visions, produced in a distinct manner. For this reason it says: "No one has ever seen God," and again the Lord says: "You have neither heard his voice nor seen his face." And again it is written:

"No one shall see my face and live." But Christ said to him by way of reproof: "Have I been with you for so long, and you do not know me?" And yet he was seeking to see the Father. But this is what I said: that while he remains only in sonship, he shows the Father wholly in himself. So he distinguished each one individually and said: "Whoever has seen me has seen my Father," so that no one could say that he himself is both Father and Son.
For if this were so, he would not have said: "Whoever has seen me has seen my Father." But since Philip was saying:
"Show us your Father and it is enough," as though he had seen him, he therefore shows him that he does not know even him.

For if he had known him, he would also have known the Father. For this reason he said: "Whoever has seen me has seen my Father." And this saying means something like this: "It is possible to see neither me nor him,"
for Philip was seeking to see with his own eyes, and he supposed that he had seen Christ as one ought, and he was seeking to see the Father as well.
And for this reason the Lord showed him that he had not seen even him. But if anyone should say that by seeing he meant understanding him with the mind, I do not oppose this either, for he said:
"Whoever has understood me has also understood the Father." However, he was not saying this, but was speaking about essence, in order to show the oneness of essence.
For this reason he said: "Whoever sees my essence has seen the Father's." But let us see what Philip was seeking to see: was it the wisdom of the Father, or his goodness?

No, but what God is, his very essence. And for this reason Christ answers: "Whoever has seen me has seen my Father." And for this reason he also rebuked him again and said: "Have I been with you for so long, and you still do not know me, Philip?"

You have heard so many teachings and have seen the signs that I performed with authority, and all the other works that were proper to divinity and that the Father alone does: sins loosed and hidden things revealed, death put to flight, new eyes made from clay. And "do you not yet know me, Philip?"

For since he was also clothed in flesh, he therefore said to him: "Do you still not know me? If you have seen the Father, seek no longer to see anything else, for in him you have seen me. If you have seen me, inquire no further, for in me you have come to know him."
Gospel: "Do you not believe that I am with the Father?"
Interpretation: This means: "I appear in the same essence."
Gospel: "The words that I speak to you, I do not speak of myself,"
Interpretation: Do you see this surpassing closeness and the form of oneness of essence?
Gospel: "but my Father, who is with me, he does the work."
Commentary: How is it that he began by speaking about words and said, "The words that I speak to you," and then came to works, saying, "The Father does those works"?

For the consistent thing would have been if he had said, "The Father who is with me speaks the words." But here he stated two matters, concerning teaching and concerning miracles; or else he spoke this way because his words were works. But how does the Father do them?
For the Lord also says in another place, "If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me." So how does he here call the Father the doer?

But by this saying too he signifies the same thing, that there is no division between the Father and the Son. And this saying that he speaks amounts to this: "The Father would not act in any other way than as I do, nor do I act in any other way than as the Father does." And in another place he says, "My Father works until now, and I also work," for there he was signifying the unchangeableness of the works, but here their unity. And if he appears lowly through these words, do not be surprised, for he first said, "Do you not believe?" and only then began these words, so that you may know that he speaks this way in order to bring them to faith, for he is the examiner of hearts and knew everything hidden.
Gospel: "Do you believe that I am with the Father, and the Father is with me?"

Commentary: When you heard "Father" and "Son," you ought to have sought nothing else to reveal their unity. If this is not enough to show you the one essence, understand it from the works, that "He who has seen me has seen my Father." And then he shows that he is able to do even greater works. And he did not say, "I do greater than these," but, what would be far more wonderful than that, "I have the power to give this grace to others as well, so that they may do greater than these."
Gospel: "Amen, amen I say to you: whoever believes in me, the works that I do he too will do, and he will do greater than these.

And I am going to the Father," that is: "From now on the doing of miracles is yours, for I am going away." And since he had made known what he wished, for this reason he immediately said: Gospel: "Whatever you ask in my name, I will do it, that the Father may be glorified in the Son."

Commentary: Do you see how again he himself does this? "I will do [?]," he says. And he did not say, "I will ask the Father," but, "that the Father may be glorified," he says. And earlier he was saying that "God will glorify him in himself," but here he himself glorifies the Father, for when the great power of the Son is revealed, then the Father too is glorified. And what is this, "Whatever you ask in my name"? It is what the apostles would say: "In the name of Jesus Christ, rise and walk!"
For all the miracles that they did, he was doing, for the hand of the Lord was with them.
Gospel: "Whatever you ask in my name, I will do."

Commentary: Do you see this authority, that he does it through others? How then do the wicked speak in vain, saying that he himself needed help? And the saying, "I go to the Father," means this: "I shall not perish, but I remain in my own honor and am in the heavens." All this he said for their consolation, for since they did not yet know the word of the resurrection and were distressed, he therefore promises: "I am ever living, and whatever you ask, I will give you." And he shows that he will remain forever, and not only remain, but also display even greater power. And in this way he made them glad.

Homily 74: That virtue is a spiritual sacrifice and that love of money comes from vainglory. But let us also follow him and take up our cross, for it is written: "Put to death your members that are on the earth." Let us then quench desire, put anger to death, slay envy. And this is a living sacrifice, which does not turn to dust, nor scatter as smoke, nor need fire and wood and a knife, but has the Holy Spirit as its fire and knife. Take up this knife and cut away the excess of the heart, and open the blocked hearing, for disease and evil desires block the ears from hearing the word of God. For when love of money comes, it does not allow the words of mercy to enter, and hatred blocks the entrances of love. And every passion is like this. But let us root out evil desires, for we have only to will it and all is quenched; and it is we who give the passions dominion over us.
And do not look at the tyranny of the love of money, but understand that this tyranny comes from you. And this desire is not natural, for,
since all natural things came into being from the beginning, whereas gold and silver did not appear at all until a long time later.
From where, then, did this desire grow? Only from vainglory and slackness. And of desires, some are necessary, some are natural, and some are neither of these; that is, as many as there are
without which a person dies, those are necessary, and they are natural as well: the desire for eating and drinking and sleep;
but the passion of the heat of the flesh is natural, yet not necessary, for many have overcome it and have not died.
But the desire of the love of money is neither natural nor necessary; rather, if we wish, we will not admit it!

For the Lord also said concerning virginity: "Those who are able," but concerning the love of possessions he said: "Whoever does not leave all his possessions and follow me is not worthy of me." For what is easy he commands us, but what not all are able to do he has left to the will. Why then do we make ourselves without excuse before God? For one who is overcome by a fiercer [?] passion is not so deserving of judgment as one who has become so feeble [?] before a weak passion.

For what shall we say when he says to us: "You saw me hungry and did not give me food"? Are we perhaps poorer than that widow, that we should plead poverty as our excuse? For God does not seek abundance of wealth but goodness of mind, and even this comes from his love for humankind. Therefore let us strive, according to our strength, to do good, so that we may attain those eternal good things by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong glory and might, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 75
This saying: "If you love me, keep my commandments, and I will ask my Father, and he will give you another Comforter,
who will remain with you forever, the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, for it neither sees him nor knows him."
We ought to acquire deeds, and not always words, for speaking in words and constantly preaching is easy,
but carrying out the word in deed is not easy. Why, then, did I say this?
Because there are many now who say, "We fear the Lord and love him," and yet in deed do the opposite, whereas God seeks love in deed.
This is why he said to the disciples: "If you love me, keep my commandments." For since he had said to them:

"Whatever you ask in my name, I will do for you," it was so that they would not suppose he does this just so, without any condition. Therefore he said to them: "If you love me, then every request of yours will be done for you."
And since, on hearing "I am going to the Father," they became sorrowful, he therefore says to them:
"This is not love of me, that you are now sorrowful, but rather if you keep my words. For I have given you a commandment,
that you love one another and that you do to one another as I have done. If you keep these commandments, then you truly love me."
Gospel: "I will ask the Father, and he will send you another Comforter."

Commentary: Behold, here is another saying of lowliness. Since they did not yet have a lofty understanding of him, and kept seeking to be with him always, and those words of his and his bodily presence, and would accept no consolation, he therefore said to them: "I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Comforter," that is to say: "Such as I am, he will give you another Comforter."
Let those darkened by the heresy of Sabellius be ashamed, and the blasphemers of the Holy Spirit as well,

for the marvel of this saying is this: that those heresies, standing apart and far removed from one another, he slew with a single wound. For in saying "another" he showed the distinction of person, while in saying "Comforter" he showed the unity of nature. But why did he say, "I will ask the Father"?

Because if he had said, "I will send to you," they would not have believed him as they do now, and his only concern was that they should be convinced. And afterwards he does indeed send him himself, when he says to them: "Receive the Holy Spirit." But here he said:

"I will ask the Father," so that he might make his word credible. For John says: "Of his fullness we have all received." Yet would he have had it from another, so as to receive it? And again John said: "He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire." Or what more would he have had than the apostles, if he had asked the Father to give it to others, since the apostles many times did this without asking? Or if he is sent from the Father by request, how did he come of his own accord? Or how is he sent by another, he who is everywhere and distributes to each one as he wills? And he said with authority: "Let us set apart Paul and Barnabas." They were serving God, but he brought them to his own work, not because his work is one thing and the Father's work another, but so that he might show his own authority. What then is this saying: "I will ask the Father"?

He indicates the time of the coming. For when he had cleansed them by that sacrifice, the shedding of his own blood, then the Holy Spirit came. But why did he not come while he was with them? Because the offering had not yet been offered. But once sin had been undone and they were going out to meet trials, then the coming of the one who strengthens was needed. Why then did the Holy Spirit not come immediately after the resurrection? So that they might be inflamed with great longing for him, and he might then come with greater grace. For as long as Christ was with them, they were not in sorrow; but once he had gone and they had become afraid, they then received him with greater longing. And this saying, "that he may remain with you forever," means this: he will not depart even after the end.

But since they heard "Comforter," so that they would not expect another incarnation and imagine they would see him with the eye, he therefore said to them: "whom the world cannot see, for it does not see him; yet he will not be with you in the way that I am, but he will dwell in your souls." For this is the meaning of the saying: "he will remain with you." And he calls him the Spirit of truth, so that by this he might signify those old types.
Gospel: "And he will be with you"

Commentary: What is this saying, "with you"? Only this, which he himself said: "Behold, I am with you." And he also indicates this as well: that what has happened to me will not happen to him, nor will he depart from you.
Gospel: "whom the world cannot receive, for it cannot see him"
Commentary: In this place he calls understanding "seeing"; for this reason he added and said:
"it does not know him,"

for Scripture many times calls true knowledge "seeing," and in this place he calls the wicked "the world." And for this reason he comforts them in deed with that gift so lofty, greater than the others.

See in how many ways he has exalted the word spoken about him. For he said: "another Comforter of theirs, like me"; and he said: "I will not leave you"; and he said: "he comes to you alone." So then he said:

"will be with you," and even so he did not dispel their sorrow, for they were seeking him himself and the familiar custom of being with him; and therefore he wished to comfort them with this word also, and said:
Gospel: "I will not leave you orphans, for I will come to you."
Commentary: Do not be afraid, he says, for it was not for this reason that I spoke of sending another Comforter, as though I would be lost to you entirely; it was not for this reason that I said:
"He will be with you," as though I would no longer see you, for I too will come to you; I will not leave you orphans.
For since at the beginning of the discourse he said, "My children," therefore here he says:
"I will not leave you orphans." And at the beginning of the discourse he said, "You will come where I am," and, "In my Father's house there are many dwelling places."

But here, since that time was far off, he gives the Spirit. Yet again, since they did not understand by that word and did not receive fitting comfort, he therefore said to them, "I will not leave you orphans," for they were seeking this above all. But so that they would not again suppose a coming of the same kind as before, see how he indicated what that coming of his would be like, for he said:
Gospel: "A little while longer and the world will no longer see me, but you will see me."
Commentary: As if he were saying, "I am coming to you,"
but not in the same way as before, but to you alone, for the Spirit too is of this kind, given to you alone.
Gospel: "For I live, and you too shall live."

Commentary: For the crucifixion does not separate you from me; I will only be hidden from you for a short time. And by life he means not only this life of the present world, but the eternal one as well.
Gospel: "On that day you will know that I am with my Father, and you with me, and I among you."

Commentary: His being with the Father is on account of their one essence, while his being with them is on account of their love and of help from God. Being with the Father and being with them do not have one meaning, even though it is said with one word,
for Scripture often says different things with one word and with different meanings. For we too are called gods and children of God, yet this is not understood in the same way of us and of God.

And again, the Son is called image, and so are we, but it is not the same, for there is a great difference. And again it is said, "You are Christ's and Christ is God's." Yet Christ is not God's in the way that we are Christ's; rather, his being with the Father is on account of his consubstantiality, whereas "I will be with you" means, "I will give you great help always."
Gospel: "Whoever has my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me."

Commentary: For merely having them is not enough; keeping them is also required. And why does he say these words to them so many times, as when he said, "If you love me, keep my commandments," and "He who has my commandments and keeps them," and "If anyone hears these words and keeps them, he it is who loves me"? By all this he indicates their grief and distress. For he had spoken many words about death, such as "He who hates his soul in this world will keep it for eternal life," and again, "He who does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me," and he was going to say many other things. For this reason he says, by way of reproach:

You think that you are so grieved because of your great love, but is grief rather a mark of love? And to show that he wished to prove this point, see how he said: "If you loved me, you would rejoice, because I am going to my Father.

But as it is, all this has come upon you from fear and from death. Such fear is not the keeping of my commandments, for you ought to be crucified, if you truly loved me, since my word teaches you not to fear those who kill the body,
for such people the Father also loves, and I will reveal myself to them."
Gospel: Judas, not Iscariot, said to him: "Lord, what is it, that you reveal yourself to us"
Commentary: Do you see their souls filled with fear? For he was terrified and troubled, and he thought that it would be as when we see the dead in a dream.
He thought that he would be seen in this way. But so that they would not imagine this, hear what he says:

"I and the Father will come and make our dwelling with him," as if he were saying, "As the Father reveals himself, so do I." And not only by this, but also by the words he spoke, "We will make our dwelling with him," he removed that suspicion of a seeing like a dream. But you, notice that troubled disciple, and how he did not dare to speak his thought openly. For he did not say, "Woe to us, for you are dying, and you are going to show yourself to us like one of the departed." He did not speak in this way, but said: "What is it, that you reveal yourself to us and not to the world?"

So they answered him on this point: "Because you love me and you keep my commandments." So that afterward, when they saw something, they would not think it an illusion, he tells them the reason in advance: "It is for this reason, because you keep my commandments." He says, "The Spirit too will appear in this way." For he told them all this so that they would not think it an illusion when they saw something, they who, despite all this, would still have thought it an illusion if he had not eaten with them.
Gospel: "He who does not love me will not keep my words, and the words that you hear are not mine, but those of him who sent me."

Commentary: "Neither do they love me, nor my Father, those who will not hear these words." For if the form of love is the keeping of the commandments, and these commandments are the Father's, then whoever does not listen to them loves not only not the Son, but not the Father either. But how are those words both yours, Lord, and not yours, for you say:
"My words are not mine"? That is to say: "I say nothing outside his will, but everything of ours is one."
Gospel: "These things I have told you, because I was with you; but the Comforter, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you everything that I have told you."

Commentary: For since many of his words were hidden and some they could not understand, and so that they would not be grieved or say, "Which commandments?", for this reason he released them from that anxiety and said to them: "The Comforter will remind you of everything and teach you."
For although these words are hidden now, yet he is the one who will reveal them well.
So that they would not be grieved, he therefore tells them that as long as he is with them, the Comforter does not come, and they can understand nothing lofty and great.
And he says all this to them in order to teach them to bear his departure courageously, as the cause of great good things.
And he repeatedly gives him the name Comforter because of the griefs that were then upon them.
Since, then, despite all this they were still distressed and trembling, and were thinking about the hardships and his departure, therefore see how he calms them again and says to them:
Gospel: "Peace I leave you."

Commentary: As if he were saying to them: "Why do you fear the disturbances of this world, as long as you have peace with me? For this peace is not of the same kind as that of the world, for that peace often comes about for evil, since it is senseless, and it will profit those who have it nothing; but I leave you peace so that you may have it with one another, and thus you will be strong." And since he said, "Peace I leave you," which was a form of departure, then, so that they would not become grieved, he added further:
Gospel: "My peace I give you."
Commentary: What are these two peaces of which he said, "Peace I leave you" and "My peace I give you"?

It is this: the first saying, "Peace I leave you," he spoke concerning peace with one another, as if to say, "I command you to have peace with one another," which was also done for other saints. But "My peace I give you" means: the peace which I made between soul and flesh and between angels and men, I who made peace in the heavens and on earth, and undid the middle wall of partition, the enmity, by my flesh. That peace, then,
by which I did all this, I now give to you as an inheritance. For this reason he also says to them: "Let your hearts not tremble, nor be afraid."
Do you see that part of their grief was because of love and part because of fear? "You have heard that I said to you: I am going away and I will come to you:
"If you loved me, you would rejoice that I am going to the Father, for my Father is greater than I"?
And to what joy was this persuading them, or to what consolation?

What then is this saying? For they did not know the teaching of the resurrection, nor did they have the thought about him that they ought to have. For how could they have it, when they did not even know this, that there is a resurrection, but supposed the Father to be superior? So he says to them: "Even if you fear on my account, as though I could not help myself, and you are not confident that after the crucifixion I will see you, yet since you have heard that I am going to the Father, you ought to rejoice, for I am going to one who is greater, and he is able to undo all evils."

But why did he say, "You heard that I said to you"? That is to say: "I am so confident that these things will come about that I am not afraid to speak of them beforehand, and I told you beforehand so that, when it happens, you may believe that I am telling you the truth. If I were not confident, I would not have said it." Do you see this word of humility? For when he said to them, "Do you think that I cannot entreat my Father, and he would now set before me here twelve legions of angels?", he said this word with reference to their suspicion, for no one, even if he were mad, would say that he was unable to help himself but needed angels.

For since they thought of him as of a man, he therefore mentioned angels, for he only asked them, "Whom do you seek?" and immediately threw them to the ground. What he is saying is of this kind: "As long as I am here, you may suppose that we are in danger, but if I go away, be confident, for no one will any longer be able to overcome." And he said all this in accordance with the weakness of the disciples: "For I am confident," he says, "and I am not afraid, for this is why I told you beforehand. But since you do not understand this saying, I therefore bring in consolation from the Father, whom you hold great, through him." But when he had consoled them, he again says something to distress them:
Gospel: "I will no longer say much with you, for the ruler of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me."

Commentary: By the ruler of the world he means the devil and wicked men, for he is not the lord of men, or of heaven, or of earth — God forbid! — but because of those who willingly give themselves over to him, he is for this reason called the ruler of darkness, for by darkness he means evil deeds. "But he will find nothing in me," he says, "rather, I suffer willingly."
Gospel: "So that the world may know that I love my Father."

Interpretation: "For it is not that I am liable to death, but for love of the Father I endure it." He said this so that he might again strengthen their souls, and so that they might know that he goes to death not unwillingly but voluntarily, and that he has held the devil in contempt. And it was not enough for him only to say, "A little while I am with you," but again and again he turns over those distressing words, and along with them the comforting ones as well, until he should convince them. For this reason he says at one time, "I go away and I come," and "Where I am, there you also shall be," and "You cannot follow me now," and "The Father is greater than I," and "I have told you before it comes to pass," and that "I do not do this under compulsion, but for love of the Father," so that they might understand that the matter is not harmful, since the one who greatly loves him and is loved by him wills it so.

For this reason he often spoke those distressing and comforting words together, in order to test their minds. For this saying, that "He will be with you," and that "It is better for you that I go away," was a matter of comfort. For this reason he said many things: that "He will be with you," and that "The world cannot receive him," and "He will remind you of everything," and "the Spirit of truth," and "the Holy Spirit," and "the Comforter," so that they might not be sorrowful, as though they would have no one to support and help them. And he says, "It is better," so that they might understand that he would make them spiritual.
Homily 75: On the power which the apostles were to receive from the Holy Spirit, and on virtue and wickedness, and on angels and men. And so indeed it came to pass,
for those who had been afraid and trembling, once they received the Holy Spirit, immediately went fearlessly into battle against sword and fire and beasts and seas and every affliction,
and those unlearned and ignorant men received such wisdom and boldness
that they astonished everyone; for they were made of clay, and the Spirit turned them into iron, and nothing overcame them.
For such grace, if it finds slackness, drives it away; if it finds evil desire, destroys it; if it finds fearfulness, chases it away, and it no longer leaves a person in the human condition,
but, as with one who belongs to heaven, it leads his mind wholly there.
And for this reason none of them any longer had anything as his own, but all were in prayer with joy of heart.
For the fruit of the Spirit is this: love, joy, peace, faith, gentleness.

Let us therefore acquire that invincible help of the Spirit by keeping the commandments, and we shall not be inferior even to the angels. For they too have such glory by their own mind, and it is not that they have no need of reverent care,

Otherwise that one of them would not have fallen at all; but because he did not guard his mind, he became worse than wicked men and took on the likeness of beasts. And again, all the saints who lived on earth in the flesh did the good that they did, for they were on earth as pilgrims and strangers, and their citizenship was in the heavens. Therefore do not say, "The flesh hinders me [?], and I cannot bear the sweat and labors of virtue." Do not accuse the Creator with these words. Look at all the saints who were in the flesh and what they did: the flesh did not prevent Paul from doing what he did, nor did it prevent Peter from receiving the keys of the kingdom. Enoch was translated in the flesh, and Elijah likewise was caught up in the flesh; Abraham and his son Isaac and Jacob, the son of Isaac, shone forth in the flesh; and Joseph in the flesh fought against that fornication-loving woman. And why do I say "the flesh" only?

For even if someone clothes the flesh in chains, it does no harm to the gaining of virtue. And why do I speak of chains? Neither prison nor strong bonds can destroy virtue. For the bond of the soul is not of iron, but is evil desire, unseemly fear, and all the other passions. These bind the soul even if the body is free. But some say, "These passions too are born of the flesh." Yet this statement is vanity and an empty excuse. For if sin belonged to the flesh, these passions would come upon everyone; for just as eating and drinking and sleep are common to all, so these too would be common to all. Since many have escaped them, it is evident that they do not come from the flesh, but from the negligence of the soul. Let us therefore cut off negligence and not lay the blame on the flesh,

but let us make the flesh subject to the soul, so that in this way we may attain the eternal good things, by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and might, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
Chapter 76
On this saying: "Rise, and go from here. I am the true vine and you are the branches. My Father is the vinedresser." Lack of learning loosens the soul and makes it fearful,
just as learning in divine matters makes it courageous and lofty. For when the mind is not zealous, then the soul becomes fearful, not by nature but by choice.
For when I see a man who was once courageous and is now fearful, I no longer say that the matter is one of nature.
For all natural things are unchangeable. And again, when I see those who are fearful now and a little later have become bold, I understand the same thing and attribute it all to the will.

For the disciples too were very fearful at first, before they had learned all that they needed to learn and before they had received the grace of the Holy Spirit; but afterward they became more courageous than lions.
And Peter, who could not bear the rebuke of a single maidservant, overcame kings and rulers, and even when crucified and tortured he did not fall silent,

Rather, everything would have seemed to them like a dream. But before the crucifixion, was it not so? For this reason Christ said to them: "Arise, let us go from here." Why did he say this? Did he perhaps not know at what hour the Jews would come, and was he afraid that they might come unexpectedly and spoil that good teaching? Far from it! Flee from this thought, for this was far from him. Why then did he say: "Arise, let us go"? For after that teaching he entered the garden, which was known to Judas; and if they had come there, could he not have held back their eyes, he who by a mere question struck them down like dead men? Rather, he spoke that word for the sake of the disciples. Since they were sitting in a fearful place, and it was night, and he himself was saying, "A little while longer, and I will not be with you," fear of this was upon them, and they could not listen well to those words.
For this reason he led them to a safer place, so that they would not keep looking around and expecting an attack,
but would listen calmly, for he was about to relate great mysteries to them. For this reason he said to them:
Gospel: "Arise, let us go from here. I am the true vine, and you are the branches."
Commentary: What does he signify by this parable?
That whoever does not listen to these things that have been said has no life, and that the miracles to come would be done by his power.
Gospel: "My Father is the husbandman."
Commentary: What is this? Does the Son need cultivating? Far from it!
For this parable does not signify that. And see with what precision he begins the parable: he does not say that the roots receive the husbandman's labor, but the branches;

for nothing is said here about the root, but this is said so that they may know that without his power they are able to do nothing, and that their faith must be joined to him as the shoot is to the vine.
Gospel: "Every branch that does not bear fruit with me, the Father will cut off."
Commentary: In this place he speaks of deeds, in order to show that without good deeds it is impossible to be with him.
Gospel: "And every one that bears fruit, he will cleanse."
Commentary: That is, he labors greatly over it and lends it a hand.
Yet nothing is said about the root, which needs all the digging and care,

but he speaks only about the branches, to show that he himself is sufficient for himself, whereas they need much help, even if they are very virtuous. For this reason he says that he cleanses the one that bears fruit,
for whatever is fruitless cannot remain in the vine because of its unfruitfulness, but whatever bears fruit, he makes more fruitful.
This saying was also spoken about the tribulations then coming upon them: "For he will cleanse," it says, that is, "he will prune," so that it may become more fruitful. And by this he shows
that trials make them stronger; and further, so that they would not say, "About whom does he say these words?"
Then he said to them: "Already, behold, you are clean by the word that I have spoken to you." Do you see how he shows himself to be the one who labors over those branches?
[He says,] "I have made you clean," and above he said, "The Father does this," but here he speaks of himself as the one who does it, for there is no division at all between the Father and the Son.
Gospel: "Abide in me."

Commentary: That is to say: "I have made you clean, and now you too must show your zeal." And then, to show that it is not because he needs their service that he tells them this, he therefore went on to say: "Just as the branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it remains on the vine, so neither can you unless you abide in me."
For here he strengthens their souls, which had gone slack from fear, and nails them fast to himself and gives them good hope,
for the root stands firm, but being cut off or remaining depends on the will of the branches. And so he has shown that the good comes from both sides, and now he asks it of us first, and says:
"Whoever abides in me and I in him." Do you see how the Son, just like the Father, cared for the disciples?
For the Father cleanses, but the Son makes them firm in himself, and he makes being established on the root the source of bearing fruit, for
whoever is on the root but is not cleansed does bear fruit, though not as he should.

But whoever does not remain on the root bears no fruit at all. Yet it has been shown that the cleansing also belonged to the Son, and the remaining on the root to the Father, who begot that root. Do you see how everything of theirs is one and shared, both the cleansing and the remaining on the root? Great is that hardship, when one cannot bear fruit, yet he was not content with this alone, but gave them still greater fear, namely this as well: "He is thrown out and withers," when he no longer has the help of the Worker and becomes bare of grace and desolate. And what is the end? "And he is set alight in the fire." But whoever remains in him will not be so. So he shows us what it is to abide in him, and says: "If you abide in me" and "if my words abide in you." Do you see how the acquiring of good deeds is required above all? For when he told them, "Whatever you ask, I will do for you," he immediately added, "If you love me, keep my commandments."

And here too he says: "If you abide in me and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you." He said this to show that those who plot evil against him will be burned up, while these will bear fruit; and he laid the fear of them upon their adversaries and showed that they were invincible, and said:
Gospel: "By this let my Father be glorified, that you bear much fruit."
Commentary: With this saying he makes his word credible, for if fruitfulness is the glorifying of the Father, he will surely not neglect his own glory.
Gospel: "And you will be my disciples."
Commentary: Do you see how whoever bears fruit is his disciple? But what is this saying of his, "In this he will glorify"? It means that he rejoices "when you abide in me and bear fruit."
Gospel: "As the Father has loved me, I also have loved you."

Commentary: In this place he again speaks a word in human fashion, which among people is a form of great love. For he who took death upon himself, and who deemed us, who were slaves and enemies and fighters against him, worthy of such great honor and brought us up to heaven, what could be the measure of his love? So then he says to them: "Since I love you, no longer be afraid. And since the Father wills that you become fruitful, if you take care." But again, so that they would not become wholly negligent, he therefore said to them:
Gospel: "Abide in my love."

Commentary: For you are masters of this matter. And you will do this "if you keep my commandments, just as I have kept the commandments of my Father." Again this word is spoken in human fashion, for how could the lawgiver be under the law with everyone else? Do you see what I am always saying? Here too it is the same, for he speaks such words because of the weakness of his hearers; he was speaking according to their suspicion, and he shows in every way

that they would be without fear and their enemies would perish, and that all that they have, they have from the Son, and that no one would overcome them. But see how he speaks to them: for he did not say, "Abide in the love of the Father," but "in my love," and so that they could not say, "When you have made us fighters against everyone, you now leave us and go away," he shows that he does not leave them, but that, if they wish, he is as united with them as the root with the branches. And again, so that they would not rely on this word and fall into negligence, he therefore says that this good will not be shaken, if they are not negligent; and further, so that he would not draw the matter to himself alone and become a cause of stumbling, he therefore said to them:

"By this my Father is glorified," for in every place he shows them his own love and the Father's love which he had toward them, for it was not those matters of the Jews, but those things that he would give to them; and so that they would not say, "We have fallen away from our ancestral ways, we have been made naked and desolate of everything." Therefore he says: "Look at me, how the Father loves me, and yet, behold, I am entering into these sufferings that lie before me. And so you too should know that I am not leaving you now because I do not love you. For if I am killed and do not take this as a sign of the Father's not loving me, neither should you grieve.
For if you abide in my love, not one of the evils will be able to harm you, because of my love."
Homily 76, on the love of Christ and on greed. Since, then, love is great and invincible, and not an empty word but a lofty deed, let us therefore hasten to fulfill it in deed.

Then we were enemies and he reconciled us, but now, since we have been made friends, let us abide in friendship. He began, and shall we not follow him? It is not for his own profit that he loves us, for he needs nothing from anyone, but for the sake of our salvation; and shall we not love him, out of love for our own selves?
We were enemies and he loved us; and shall we not love the one who loves us, we who now do the opposite?
For every day God is blasphemed because of us, through our robberies and our acts of greed.
And perhaps one of you will say to me: "Look, every day you speak to us about greed." But would that not I alone were speaking to you,
but that wives and friends too, and children and servants, and neighbors, and even walls and stones, if it were possible,

were crying out about this matter, so that you might cease from it at least a little. For this disease has seized the whole world and has darkened the souls of all. And great is the tyranny of mammon. Oh, what a marvel!
We were redeemed by Christ and we serve gold; we preach one kingship and are slaves to another, and whatever it commands us,
we do it all with eagerness and obey, and we disregard friendship and nature and the law of God and everything else.
For this reason no one looks up to heaven and no one remembers that eternal judgment,
but the time will come when there will be no profit even from these words, for "In hell who will confess you?"
Gold is desirable and delightful, but not so much as the kingdom of heaven, for the rich man is hated by many in this world,

whereas the one who practices virtue is honored and loved by all. And if someone should say, "The poor man is despised by everyone, even if he is virtuous," understand that he is despised not by men but by brute beasts, while by a wise man he is all the more to be praised. If an earthly king were praising us, we would no longer seek praise from anyone else; yet if the King of the angels praises you, O man, do you seek praise from flies and gnats? For those men who love these passing things are even worse than these. How long shall we wallow in this mire? How long shall we make ourselves objects of praise for men full of gluttony and vanity?

For they have knowledge only of vain men, and in regard to virtue they are without understanding. But you, O man, who wish to practice virtue, do you display yourself to men ignorant of virtue? For this reason you will never succeed.

For this reason I beg you: let us disregard those many and vain things, and let us seek praise from God and not seek worthless riches. And let us not regard poverty as an evil, for it becomes for us a teacher of all wisdom and patience. For Lazarus too lived in poverty and received a crown from God, and Jacob longed to be filled with bread alone, and Joseph lived in the utmost poverty, and was not only a slave but also a prisoner, and is it not for this, then, that you marvel at his story?

And I do not praise him so much when he was distributing the wheat as when he was in prison, nor when he was wearing a crown, but when [he wore] a chain, nor when he was sitting on cloths, but when he was being sold. Now then, let us take all this to heart and weave for ourselves the crown of the virtues. Let us not seek wealth and luxury and honor and bodily power, but poverty and hardship and the endurance of virtue. For the end of those things is full of turmoil and great tumult, but the end of the virtues is heaven and the good things of heaven, which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him. May we all be worthy to attain these by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong glory and might, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 77
On this saying: "I have said this to you so that my joy may remain with you, and your joy may be full.
This is my commandment, that you love one another,
as I have loved you." Every good thing has its reward only when it reaches its end. But if it breaks off merely midway through the work, it becomes the shipwreck of that work.
And just as a ship filled with great wealth, if it does not reach the harbor but sinks in the sea while still far off,

has gained nothing from all its great labor and from traveling its course, but rather the greater the labor it has undertaken, the greater the disaster that has come upon it, so too with souls that fall away from their labors before the end: their struggle has become vain.
That is why Paul also said: "Honor and glory to those who, by endurance in good works, run the race." This is what Christ is now doing for the disciples.

For he had received them, and they were rejoicing with him; and then the time of the passion came, and they were hearing those words of sorrow, and their joy was about to be broken off. For this reason, after he had told them many things and comforted them, he then said to them:
Gospel: "I have said this to you so that my joy may remain with you, and your joy may be full."

Commentary: That is to say: "Do not depart from me, and do not break off your course. For you were rejoicing with me and were very glad, but sorrow has come; yet now I will dispel it, so that this joy may be with you to the end." And he shows them that this time deserves not sorrow but joy. For he says: "I saw you stumbling and I did not disregard it, nor did I say, 'Why do you not stand firm with courage?' Instead, I spoke words of comfort to you. In the same way, I wish to keep you in love. You heard about the kingship and the kingdom, and you rejoiced; so that your joy may be full, I have told you all this for that reason."
Gospel: "This is my commandment, that you love one another, as I have loved you."
Commentary: Do you see the love of God, how it is united with our love?

For this reason he sometimes speaks of two commandments and sometimes of one, for it is impossible that someone should have the one and the second not follow it. For sometimes he says: "On this hang the law and the prophets."
And sometimes he says: "As you wish that people should do to you, do also to them, for this is the law and the prophets," and:
"The confession [?] of the law is love," which he also intimates here, for if abiding in joy comes from love,
and love comes about from keeping the commandments. And the commandment is this: that we love one another.
For abiding with God comes about from love for one another.
But he did not speak thus of love simply; he also showed its manner, for he says: "As I have loved you." Again he shows that his departure from them is not a matter of hatred but of love.

And all the more was it fitting to be amazed at this, that "I lay down my life for you," he says. Yet he nowhere said this in the way he does in this place, except that earlier he was speaking about the good shepherd,
but here he teaches them love and shows them its greatness, and he also makes them understand about himself, who he is.
But why does he magnify love in every place? Because it is the sign of the disciples. It is the accomplisher of virtue.
And Paul shows this, as a faithful disciple of Christ:
Gospel: "You are my friends if you do what I command you. I no longer call you 'servant,' for a servant does not know what his lord does.
But I have called you 'friend,' for everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you."
Commentary: How then did he say to them: "I have much to say to you, but you cannot bear it now"? For he gives us to understand nothing else now by this word which he said:
"Everything that I have heard from the Father I have told you," except that he shows this: "I say nothing foreign, but everything is the Father's."
And since this is the manner of love, that one should relate even secrets, for this reason he says: "I have told you even mysteries."
But when he says "everything," he means those things which it was proper for them to hear. And then he shows yet another manner of love and says:
Gospel: "You did not choose me, but I chose you."

Commentary: That is: "I sought your love." And not even this was enough, but he said: "I have appointed you," that is: "I have planted you, so that you too may go," he says, that is, that you may spread out, "and bear fruit, and your fruit may remain."
And if the fruit remains, how much more would you yourselves remain? For not only have I loved you, he says,
but I have also shown you great benefactions, for I spread out your branches and fruit over all the earth. Do you see in how many ways he shows his love?
First, by relating those hidden mysteries; second, because he was the first to seek their love; third, because he bestowed great good things on them; fourth,

because he took suffering upon himself for them. And by these deeds he showed that he would remain with them forever, for by his help they would bring forth fruit, and for this reason he says to them:
"Whatever you ask of my Father in my name will be given to you."
But how is this, that they ask the Father and it is the name of the Son that brings about the giving? It is so that you may recognize the unity and the equality of the Son with the Father.
Gospel: "I say this to you, so that you may love one another."
Commentary: This means: "I do not say this to you by way of reproach, that I lay down my life for you," and that "I have chosen you," but "I say all of this to you so that you may love one another."

But since persecution and reproach from many are hard to hear of, and can humble and distress even a lofty mind, Christ for this reason first told them many words of consolation, and only then came to speak of this matter. For he had calmed their souls beforehand, and he also showed in many ways that these things are for their betterment, like those other matters. For just as he showed that they ought to feel joy and not grief at his going to the Father, because he was not abandoning them but was doing this out of his great love for them, so here too he shows that they ought to feel joy and not grief. And see how he did this: he did not say to them, "I know that this matter is distressing, but endure it for my sake," for this would not have been enough to console them. Instead he showed that if the world hates them, this is a mark of their virtue, for:
"If you were of the world," he says, "the world would love its own," but "since you are not of the world, for this reason the world hates you." And then he adds further and says:

Gospel: "A servant is not greater than his master; if they persecuted me, they will persecute you also." By this he showed that they would all the more be made like him. And as long as Christ was in the flesh, all the warfare was directed against him; but once Christ had departed from here, all their warfare was turned [against the disciples]. And this is their consolation, that they were being made like their Lord. And further he gave them a third consolation too, and indicated that the Father also was being dishonored along with them, and for this reason he said to them: "All this they will do to you for my name's sake, because they do not know the one who sent me."
And then he gave them yet another consolation, for he showed that those who dishonor them will be handed over to grievous torment. And for this reason he said:
"If I had not come and spoken to them, they would have no sin; but now they have no excuse for their sins. Whoever hates me hates my Father also."
And by this saying he indicates that their judgment will be no small one, for since they made excuses and said, "We persecute him for the sake of the Father," for this reason the Lord spoke thus:
"They have no excuse for their sin, for by word I taught what is good, and by deed I acted according to the law of Moses."
And of this they themselves are witnesses, who said, "Never has anything like this been seen in Israel," and:

"Since the beginning of the ages it has not been heard that anyone opened the eyes of one born blind." And so that they might not say, "Why do they persecute both you and us?", for this reason he told them beforehand: "You are not of the world, just as I am not of the world. If you were of the world, the world would love its own." And again, so that they might not say: "If they persecuted you, they will persecute us too; and if they did not keep your word, then for that reason they will not keep ours either; if you performed signs among them,
which no one else performed, and they did not believe,
if they hate both you and your Father, why are you delivering us into their hands? And how will they believe us?"
And so that they would not say all this, for this reason he spoke to them a word of consolation: Gospel:
"When the Comforter comes, whom I will send to you from my Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from my Father, he will testify concerning me.
And you also are witnesses, because you have been with me from the beginning."
Commentary: "He will be trustworthy," he says, "for he is the Spirit of truth"; for this reason he called him "the Spirit of truth,"
for he knows everything, since he proceeds from the Father, just as he said about himself:
"I know where I come from and where I am going." And "whom I will send to you": behold, it is not the Father alone who sends the Spirit, but the Son as well. And "you also are witnesses,
