for you have been with me and have seen me. It is not that you have heard about me from others."
For this reason the apostles said afterward: "We who ate and drank with him."
Gospel: "I have told you this so that you may not stumble."
Commentary: That is, so that when you see that many do not listen to you but torment you, you may not stumble, but may remember these words, that I told you:
Gospel: "The hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he has offered a sacrifice to God."
Commentary: "They will regard killing you," he says, "as something good and virtuous." And then he also gave them consolation and said:
"They will do this to you because they do not know my Father, nor me.
This is enough to comfort you: that all this will come upon you for my sake and for my Father's sake, as I told you before:
'Blessed will you be when they persecute you and revile you and falsely say every evil thing against you for my sake.
Rejoice and be glad, for your reward will be great in heaven.'"
Gospel: "I have told you this so that, when that hour comes, you may remember that I told you this."

Commentary: That is: "When all this happens, then you will know that every word of mine was true. And I told you for this reason: so that it might not come upon you unexpectedly and throw you into confusion, and so that you might not say, 'We did not know beforehand all that was to come.'

Remember, then, that I told you, and that you are suffering all this for my sake and for my Father's sake, and that they did the same to me as well, and that everything they do is unjust and lawless."

Homily 77: that one must endure with long-suffering the afflictions that come upon us for Christ's sake; and on almsgiving. And now let us too, beloved, in the time of trial remember all this, and let us look to the leader and perfecter of our faith, Jesus, and remember that everything is for the sake of his name. And if we remember this, everything will seem easy to us. For if a man suffers hardship for his friends and rejoices, how should he who suffers for God not rejoice? For if he counts that shameful act of crucifixion, endured for us, as glory, ought we not all the more to do the same? But if we ought in this way to endure tortures and disregard them for Christ's sake, what shall we do, who do not even disregard money and greed? Therefore, when some affliction comes upon us, ought we not to consider, not the affliction itself, but the reward and the crown that will come because of it?

Just as a merchant thinks not of the length of the roads but of the profit, so we too ought to think of the kingdom of heaven and of boldness before God. So likewise, when the sweetness of sin comes upon you, remember the eternal torment, and that taste will pass away. And again, if virtue seems hard to you, clothe its face with the rest of the eternal reward, and it will seem easy to you. For the perfect no longer act for the sake of a reward; even without it virtue seems beautiful to them, and they practice it because God so wills. But whoever is weak, let him think of the crowns as well. Let us act in the same way concerning almsgiving, and let us not despise our brothers, for it is said:
"With the measure with which you measure out, it will be measured out to you." How long, O men, shall we imitate the beasts in mercilessness and be ignorant even of our own nature?
Let us consider that day when we shall stand before Christ, when we shall be seeking mercy, and Christ will bring into the midst those
whom we disregarded and to whom we showed no mercy, and he will say to us:
"What you did not do for one of my brothers, you did not do for me." For then it will no longer be the poor who speak,
but God will speak to us in their place,
just as it was no longer Lazarus who spoke to the rich man, but Abraham in his place. So it will be with those poor
whom we despise, for then it is we who will be pitiable and poor.

And what answer shall we give to him who has raised us up to heaven, while we do not even give him bread; to him who gives us his precious body and blood, while we do not even hold out a single cup to him? Do we not see that God has given us everything in common, and that if some are poor in money,
this too is for the sake of the rich, so that through their almsgiving their sins may be stripped away?

But you, who are so merciless over this thing of no account, it is evident that if you had some greater power, you would commit countless murders and would begrudge others even light and life. How long will you be rich and he poor?
Until evening, which is death,
and after that no longer; for so worthless is this life, and death is at the doors. What profit will you have from those many treasures and possessions?

Why are the heralds of your mercy not many? For those treasures of money only multiply enemies for you, but whatever you give to the poor will reach God and will become for you a release from sins, and glory from God and honor from people will be gained for you.
Why then do you harm yourself in this way?

For by almsgiving you benefit yourself more than you benefit them. You benefit them in the body, but for yourself you gain eternal boldness and glory, which may we all be worthy to attain by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong glory and might, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
Chapter 78
This saying: "I did not tell you this from the beginning, because I was with you. But now I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, 'Where are you going?'
But because I have told you this, sorrow has filled your hearts."

Great is the tyranny of sorrow, and great courage is required of us to stand against this passion, so that we may take from it whatever is useful and leave the rest, for it does have something useful in it.

When we grieve over sins, then it is good, but when we are caught up in human troubles, then sorrow is useless. And therefore, since the disciples of Christ had not yet reached the measure of perfection and this passion of sorrow was battling them, see how the Lord consoles them. For those who earlier had asked him many questions, as when Peter said to him, "Lord, where are you going?" and Thomas said to him, "We do not know where you are going," and Philip said to him, "Show us your Father": when they heard, "They will put you out of the synagogue," and, "Whoever kills you will think that he has offered a sacrifice to God," they were so terrified at these words that they could not say a word to him. And for this reason the Lord said to them in reproach:
"I did not tell you this from the beginning, because I was with you. But now I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, 'Where are you going?'
But because I have told you this, sorrow has filled your hearts." For I knew it from the beginning, he says,
"and it was not out of ignorance that I did not tell you, but because I was with you."
But how is it that he did not tell them from the beginning? Did he not say to the Twelve, "They will bring you before kings and rulers and will torment you"?

How then does he say, "I did not tell you from the beginning"? Torments and evils had indeed been told to them earlier as well, but he had not told them this, that killing them would be so highly esteemed, as if it were the offering of a sacrifice to God,
for this distressed them more, when they heard that they were to be slaughtered as evildoers and merciless men. Or else it is also this:
that at that time he was speaking only about the Gentiles? But now he told them, "The Jews too will do this to you," and, "The event is near."
But why did he tell them now, and not at that time when the Holy Spirit came? So that you may learn that they were abundantly full of virtue.
For the Holy Spirit had not yet come to them, and even so they did not flee from him. From such words as these, understand what sort of men they would have been,
when they received the Holy Spirit. For if they had heard this and had taken all of it upon themselves after the coming of the Spirit, we would have said that it was grace that was doing everything.
But as it is, all of this is the fruit of their own mind and is a clear sign of their love for Christ.
Gospel: "That I am telling you the truth."
Commentary: See how he comforts them, for he says:
"I do not say this to please you; rather, even if you are grieved ten thousand times over, I am telling you what is better for you. For this is your wish,
that I should be with you, but the better thing is not so, for if I do not go away, the Comforter will not come."

See here how great the authority of the Spirit is, for he says: "If I go away, I will send him to you, and he will come and will convict the world." That is to say: "Even the works done by me are enough to shut the mouths of the wicked and to take away their excuse,
but when he too comes and does likewise, with greater teachings and great miracles,

then they will become liable to a greater judgment, when they see that all of this is being done in my name. For now they say: 'He is the son of the carpenter, whose father and mother we know.' But when they see wickedness driven out in my name, natures healed, and demons put to flight, what will they say then? For the Father has testified concerning me, and the Spirit too will testify; even though he also testified before, now too he will testify and will convict the world concerning sin." That is, he will take away their every excuse and show that they have sinned unforgivably, and he will confirm that "I have never sinned; and concerning righteousness, because I am going to my Father and you will see me no longer,"

that is, that he will reveal our spotless life, of which going to the Father is the sign. For since the Jews were saying that he is not from God and is a sinner, he therefore says that the Spirit will take away this excuse too, and will convict them on this account too, when that Holy Spirit comes and reveals my righteousness and that "I have gone to the Father and will be with him forever." For this is what the saying he spoke indicates: "You will see me no longer." See, then, how by these two means that evil suspicion of theirs is dispelled, for neither is the working of miracles the act of a sinner, nor is being with God forever. And therefore they will no longer be able to say, "He is a sinner," or, "He is not from God."
Gospel: "And concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world has been judged."

Commentary: Here again he brings forward the argument of his own righteousness, for if the saints from the beginning could not accomplish this deed, and I have done it and have judged the ruler of this world, how can they say, "He is a sinner," and, "He is not from God"? For they say of me, "He is a deceiver and has a demon with him." But on this point too they will stand convicted, for if I were such, how could I have judged the ruler of this world?
Gospel: "I still have much to say to you, but you cannot bear it now; but when that Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all truth."

Commentary: And what is it that is greater than you? Is it the Spirit, that now we cannot bear these things, but when he comes, then we will bear them? Far from it! For he says: "He will not speak anything of himself, but whatever he hears, that he will speak, and he will tell you what is to come, for all that the Father has is mine." For since he told them: "He will teach you all things and remind you and comfort you," and:

"It is necessary that I depart and that he come," and: "Now you cannot bear it, but then you will bear it, and he will guide you into all truth," so that they should not from this [?] reckon the Holy Spirit greater than him and fall into lawlessness, for this reason he told them: "He will receive from me," that is: "What I say, he too will say the same." And as for "He will not speak anything of himself," that means: "He will say nothing opposed to me or foreign to my words." Just as he said about himself: "We do not speak of ourselves," that is: "I say nothing foreign to the Father," so he also speaks about the Spirit. And as for "He will receive from me," that means "from my understanding, for my understanding and that of the Holy Spirit are one, and he will tell you what is to come." For they were eager for this, since they kept asking about future events; for this reason he says: "He will tell you all that is to come."
Gospel: "He will glorify me."
Commentary: That is: "He will accomplish all the miracles in my name."
For since greater miracles were going to be performed after the coming of the Holy Spirit, for this reason he again shows their equality and says: "He will glorify me."
And as for his saying: "He will guide you into all truth," what truth does he mean?
Rather, it is this: since the Lord, because of the flesh that he had put on, and because of the weakness of the disciples, and so that they should not say:

"He is praising himself," and because of the Jews as well, could not continually speak of lofty matters and matters of his glory, for this reason he says: "He will tell you all truth." But so that they might not say:
"Do you not know all truth?" for this reason he added and told them: "He will not say anything of himself,
for no one knows God except the Spirit of God himself,"
but he will say nothing foreign to what I have said, for he will receive from me, meaning that he will speak in accordance with my own words,
for "all that the Father has is mine."
And he will speak with the Father's word, and in this way it is evident that he speaks my own words. But why did the Holy Spirit not come before Christ's departure? Rather,
since the curse had not been undone and sin had not been blotted out,

he would not come, for it was necessary first for the enmity to be undone and for us to be reconciled to God, and only then for that gift to come. And why does he say: "I will send him to you"? How is he sent, who is everywhere?
Rather, this means: I will prepare you in such a way that he may come and be pleased to dwell among you.

And again he said this so that he might show the distinction of persons, for he himself also had the power to do all of it. But he did this also so that they might understand the honor of the Holy Spirit as well, just as the Father had the power to bring things that are not into being, yet the Son brought them. So it is here also, for in baptism too the name of the Father alone, or of the Son, or of the Holy Spirit, is able to do everything, yet we invoke all three names, so that we may understand the sharing of honor of all three, and may understand it at the time of the sharing of those good things. Otherwise, so that you may know that the Son alone also has the power to forgive sins, and the Holy Spirit too, hear concerning the Son how he says to the Jews: "The Son of Man has authority to forgive sins," and again: "that you may become sons of light," and: "I will give them eternal life." And concerning the Holy Spirit, hear what he says: "It is the Spirit that gives life," and: "The Spirit is life and righteousness."

And the apostle says: "But you were washed, but you were sanctified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God." Since, then, they had heard much about the Father and had seen many works of the Son, but about the Holy Spirit they knew nothing of this kind, for this reason he came and performed signs and gave them perfect understanding, so that in this way they might come to know him too. But again, so that they might not reckon him superior to the Son, for this reason he said to them: "Whatever he hears, he will speak," and: "He will glorify me." Not that he needed hearing and teaching, for what could he have heard, he who had said everything through the prophets? Whether about the abolition of the law, or about his divinity and the dispensation, everything had been spoken by him.
Gospel: "And he will tell you what is to come."

Commentary: Here he shows his honor even more, for this above all else is the proper work of God: the telling of things to come. But if he were to learn even that from another, what more would he have than the prophets? Rather, here he signifies the true understanding concerning God, even if he were to say something else. And the saying, "What he receives from me he will tell you," signifies this: either from the great grace that came upon my flesh, or from the understanding that I have. Not as though he needed it, or were learning from another, but it is one and the same, both mine and his.
But why did he speak in this way and not otherwise? Because they did not have a fitting understanding of the Holy Spirit, and therefore he labors toward one thing only,

that he might be made trustworthy to them and that they might not stumble. For since he had told them, "One is your teacher, Christ," so that they might not suppose that if they obeyed that one they would become disobedient to this one, for this reason he says to them:
"His teaching and mine are one, and what I was about to teach you,
of that he too will speak to you. And do not suppose that his teaching is something different, for it is mine, and he will confirm my glory,

For there is one will of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." So likewise the Lord wishes us also to be, as he said: "That they may be one, as I and you, Father, are one." And there is nothing equal to unity and love.
Homily 71, on unity and love. In this way one is not one, but many. For if two or ten are of one mind,
that one is no longer one, but each of them is multiplied tenfold, and you will find that one among the ten and those ten in the one.
And if he has an enemy, whoever speaks against the one, it is as if he were speaking against the ten, for he is struck down not by one mouth but by ten.
And if that one grows weak, he is not weakened, for the other nine parts are alive and vigorous and cover his weakness.
Each of them has twenty eyes and twenty hands and feet likewise, for he does not see with his own eyes only,
but also with those of the others; nor is he carried on his own feet only, but also on those of the others; nor does he work with his own hands only, but also with those of the others.
They have ten souls, for he does not care for himself alone, but the others also care for him.
And if they are a hundred, it will be the same among them, and their strength increases.
Do you see the work of love? How it makes that one person invincible and manifold, how one person is able to be in many places,
so that the one is in both Persia and Rome? And what nature cannot do, love can do,
for one part of him is here and one part there, or rather he is wholly
here and wholly there. And if the power of love enters among a hundred and among two thousand, consider how far the power of love will surpass all bounds. Do you see the increase of love?
For this is the marvel, that it makes the one a thousandfold. Why then do we not acquire this power, so that we may thus be more beautiful?
This is higher than all wealth, better than all righteousness and every good; this is better even than light; this is a bringer of joy. How long shall we confine love to one or two?
But consider the opposite: suppose there were someone who did not have even one friend, which is a matter of the utmost folly. What sort of life would his be?

For even if he is ten thousand times rich and lives in delight and luxury, he has not one of the good things, but is naked and desolate of everything. But the one who has many friends, even if he is poor, is richer than the rich; and whatever he himself cannot say or do, he can accomplish through those friends. This brings great joy and rest and freedom from fear, for it is impossible for any evil to befall one whose guardian is love.

And the king's guards are not such good guards as this one, since they do their work under compulsion and out of fear, while this one acts willingly and with all eagerness; and the king is afraid even of those very guards, whereas here there is nothing of the kind. Let us therefore acquire this good thing and carry on this good trade through the poor, so that it may be a comforter of poverty; and for the rich, that they may be free of fear; for the ruler, that he may rule well; and for the servant, that the ruler may look on him kindly. This is the cause of gentleness, this is the work of goodness, for even wild beasts are those that do not love one another, or rather they are evil and savage. For this reason we live in cities and there are neighborhoods, so that we may gather with one another and that there may be no lovelessness arising from solitude. But if someone should say, "And what do you say about the monks who live in the mountains?", understand that among them the work of love and unity is great; they flee from the tumults of the world, but they are of one soul toward many and well united,

and indeed they have withdrawn far from the affairs of the world for this very reason, that they may further this. For since strife and envy over worldly affairs give birth to hatred, for this reason they have withdrawn from all of this and practice love well. For it is not the case that love toward others does not arise in solitude, since it is not outward activity that produces love but the mind, whether one is alone or among the people. And for this reason many praise those who live alone; yet if they did not love them, how would they praise them? And they in turn pray for the whole world, which is a great form of love. For this reason also at the time of the liturgy we kiss one another, so that the many may become one, and we offer prayer for the catechumens. This is the cause of all good things; if we hold it dear, we may both order our life well in this world and attain the kingdom of heaven, which may we all be worthy to attain by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 79
This saying: "A little while, and you will not see me, and again a little while, and you will see me, for I am going to my Father."
The disciples said to one another: "What is this that he says to us: 'A little while, and you will no longer see me'?"
Nothing so unnerves a soul gripped by sorrow and anguish as words that add to its sorrow [?],

when they are spoken again and again. Why then, when Christ had said, "I am going away and will no longer speak to you," does he repeatedly tell them this again: "A little while, and you will no longer see me," and again: "A little while, and you will see me," and: "I am going to my Father"? For after he had comforted them by those words spoken about the Holy Spirit, he now distresses their minds again. But he does this for this reason: he is testing their mind and training it, and accustoming them to hear distressing words well, so that they may bravely endure his separation from them. For those who had first been greatly pained by this in word were going to endure it in deed as well.
But if anyone understands it well, this too was a consolation, that he said, "I am going to the Father," for by this he indicates that his death was a departure and not some suffering.
And he set before them another consolation as well, for he did not say only this, "A little while, and you will no longer see me," but he also added this:

"A little while, and you will see me," for he made them understand that he would come to them again, and that his separation from them would last a short time, but his being with them would be everlasting.
But they did not understand this. And so it is astonishing that they heard this many times and yet were as if they had not heard it.
But why did they not understand? As I suppose, it was because of the grief they had, for it made them forget those words, or else because of the words' hidden meaning.

For this reason they also supposed that he had said two contradictory things, which were not contradictory, for they say, "If we are to see you, where are you going?" "If you are going away, how will we see you?"
For this reason they also say, "We do not know what he is saying," for they knew this, that he was about to depart, but they were ignorant of this, that after a little while he would come to them.
For this reason he also reproaches them, because they did not understand that saying. For he wished to establish firmly among them the saying spoken about his death. Therefore he said to them:
Gospel: "Amen, amen, I say to you that you will weep and lament, and the world will rejoice."

Commentary: These words are about his death and crucifixion, which became the bringer [?] of their grief. And in "the world will rejoice," by "world" he here means that people who seek after vanity, who rejoiced over it. But since they did not want his death, they therefore earlier believed that he would not die, and then, when they heard that he would die, they began to dispute and to doubt, for they did not know what this meant:
"You will weep and be grieved, but your grief will be turned into joy."

But he himself showed that after the grief there would be joy, that this grief produces joy, and that this grief lasts a short time, while the joy will last forever. Therefore he drew a parable from the affairs of the world and said to them:
Gospel: "A woman, when she gives birth, is in grief, because her hour has come."
Commentary: He uses a parable that the prophets too, because of the surpassing severity of its pains, adopted as an image of great griefs. And this saying is to this effect:
"Pains will come upon you like those of childbirth, but that grief of childbirth becomes the cause of joy; so too it will be for you."

And by these words he also makes credible the saying about the resurrection, and shows that departing from here is like someone coming forth from a mother's womb into this light, as if he were saying:
"Do not be astonished, for through such grief he leads you to something better," for a mother too,

when she becomes the mother of a child, becomes so in this way, through grief. And he also indicates another mystery here, for by these words he shows that he himself loosed the pains of death and brought about the birth of the new man; and he did not say:

"Only let that affliction pass" — but that she should even remember it at all, no, he says: such joy comes. So also will it be with the saints. And the woman does not rejoice over this, that a person has come into the world,
but because she has had a child.

For if she rejoiced over that, nothing would prevent those who had not given birth from rejoicing when another woman also gave birth. Why then did he speak thus: "She rejoices, because a person is born into the world"?
Because the likeness in his parable applied only to this: to show that the sorrow is passing and the joy is everlasting, and
that it is a passing over into life, and that great profit comes from those pains. And he did not say, "A child is born," but "a person,"
for here he is intimating his own resurrection, and not speaking about his death,
with which he was in labor and was about to give birth, but about the kingdom. Therefore he did not say, "She has had a child," but, "A person is born into the world."
Gospel: "And you also now have affliction, but I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you,
and on that day you will ask me nothing."

Commentary: Again by these words he establishes nothing other than that he is from God, for then, he says, you will all know it. And what does this mean: "You will ask me nothing"? It means this: "You will have no mediator; rather, it is enough that you only speak my name, and you will receive everything." And he shows the power of his name, since when they do not see him and only invoke his name, they will accomplish everything. And remember when they prayed, saying: "Grant your servants to do signs and to speak boldly by your name," and the place where they stood was shaken.
Gospel: "Amen, amen, I say to you, if you ask anything of my Father in my name, it will be given to you. Until now you have asked nothing in my name; ask and you will receive."

Commentary: And by these words he again shows that it is better for him to go away, since then their requests would be fulfilled all the more, as if he were saying: "Do not suppose, since I will no longer be with you,
that I would abandon you altogether, for my name will give you greater boldness." Since those words were hidden, therefore he said to them:
Gospel: "I have told you this in parables; but the hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in parables."

Commentary: "Behold, the time will come, he says, when you will understand everything plainly," for he is speaking of the time of the resurrection as well, saying: "Then I will tell you plainly about my Father." For he spent forty days, when he stayed with them after the resurrection, and spoke to them about the kingdom of God. "And now you are in fear, he says, and cannot hear these words well, but then, when you see me risen and present with you, you will be able to hear everything boldly."
Gospel: "On that day you will ask in the name of my Father, and I do not say to you that I will entreat and ask my Father, for my Father himself loves you."
Commentary: "For my love, which you will have as your help in every matter, is enough, for because of this the Father too has loved you.
Gospel: "For you too have loved me and believe: I came forth from God and came into the world. And again I leave the world and go to the Father."

Commentary: Since that saying about the resurrection comforted them not a little, and also this one, "I came forth from God and am going back there," he therefore turns these words over again and again: first, to confirm to them that they believe rightly, and second, so that they may understand that no evil will come upon them.

And when he told them, "A little while, and you will not see me," and, "A little while, and you will see the Son," they were then, reasonably enough, unable to understand, but now no longer. What is that saying, "You will not ask me"? That is: "You will no longer say to me, 'Show me your Father,' or, 'Where are you going?'" For you will come to know all understanding, and your Father will be to you just as he is to me. And with that saying he comforted them all the more, for they heard, "You will be friends of the Father." For this reason they said to him:
Gospel: "Now we know that you know all things"
Commentary: Do you see that he answered everything according to their thoughts, as they themselves also confessed?
Gospel: "and you have no need that anyone should ask you"

Commentary: That is: "Before you hear it, you know what we stumble over or what we are built up by, and you have given us rest, since you said, 'The Father loves you, because you have loved me.'" After such things and so many of them, only now did they say, "We know that you know all things." Do you see how they were not in perfection, but still weak? And as though they were granting him a favor, they said to him, "Now we know." But the Lord said to them:

Gospel: "Now indeed you believe. Behold, the hour is coming, and has arrived, when you will be scattered, each to his own place, and will leave me alone; yet I am not alone, for my Father is with me."

Commentary: Since they said, "Now we know," he therefore tells them: "You need much further teaching, for as yet you know nothing, but you fall far short of [?perfection]. For now you will hand me over to my enemies alone, and you will be scattered out of great fear, and such fear will seize you that you will not even be able to flee together, but will be scattered. Yet no evil will come upon me from this." Do you see how this saying is again one of humility? And he reproves them for this, that they always need words of humility. For since they were saying, "Behold, you speak to us openly and tell no parable at all, and therefore we believe," he shows that they do not yet believe as they ought, nor does he accept their words.

But he said this for a reason, and was referring them to another time. "My Father is with me" he said for their own sake, for again and again he intended this to be known. And further he showed that he had not yet given them full understanding through these words, but only meant to calm their minds, lest they should think some human thoughts, such as, "We will find no help from him." Therefore he said to them:
Gospel: "I have told you this so that you may have peace with me. But do not be afraid, for I have overcome the world."

Interpretation: That is: "So that you may not scrape these words out of your minds; for even though you are in the world, you will have tribulation, not only now, when I am being handed over, but after this as well. But be brave in your minds, for no evil will come upon you. When the teacher conquers the enemies, the disciples have no need of fear,
for I have said already that I have struck down the ruler of the world, and you will come to know it again when all obey you."
Homily 79, on patience. So victory is possible for us too, if we wish it, through hope in the leader of our faith, and if we walk the road that he traveled.
And in this way not even death will overpower us. It is not that we will not die, but let no one say, "If we die, we are not victors over death."
For a soldier too is valiant when they fight him and he conquers, and not when enemies are not fighting him.
And we would be mortal only if we were to remain in it completely.
So we too are not mortal because we enter into it; rather, since we do not remain in it, we are therefore immortal.
But if someone speaks of the corruption of bodies,
they are not corrupted so as to be corrupt forever, but so that they may become better.
So let us conquer the world, let us hasten to immortality, let us follow the King, let us too raise up a victory, let us despise desires,
let us move our souls to heaven; in this way the whole world will be conquered by us.
If we despise it, it is conquered; we are strangers and passing through.
So let us not be grieved over anything in the affairs of the world. For even if you were rich and renowned and went to a foreign land,

where no one knows you, and were insulted there, it would not pain you as it would in your own city if someone insulted you. Indeed, in that foreign land you endure even hunger and thirst and every hardship.

So now in the same way consider that you are a stranger and passing through, and let nothing trouble you in this foreign land, whatever may come upon you, for you have a city whose builder and maker is God, and this sojourn lasts only a short time.
You would endure unflinchingly insult, beating and every hardship, for we are in a foreign land.
The evil would be if we were despised in that land and before its citizens; that is great disgrace and great distress. But where a person has no acquaintance, there he bears everything easily.

Therefore let us count the hardship of this world as nothing. For many people, for the sake of sin, are in much hardship and toil and endure it all for the sake of the demons; and shall we not endure for the sake of God?
And indeed virtue is full of every kind of tranquility,
for the fruit of the Spirit is love,
joy, peace, long-suffering and things like these. We never need any unprofitable expense, nor reproaches along with the expense; but even if we spend one cup of cold water for God's sake,
its reward will not fail us, but will be given to us abundantly, and God will be grateful to us.
But since all this is so,
What word shall we answer to the Lord if we abandon this and pursue what is opposed to it, and of our own will cast ourselves into the fire of Gehenna? For this reason I entreat you:
Be on your guard and heal your souls of this spiritual sickness, and let no one cut off hope, for even the prodigal son did great evil,
but once he returned to his father's house, he was given his former honor.
So let us too imitate him and turn back to that same good Father, and be set free from that captivity,

so that we may attain the kingdom of heaven by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong glory and might, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 80
The passage: These things Jesus said, and he lifted up his eyes to heaven and said: "Father, my hour has come; glorify your Son, so that the Son also may glorify you."
The Lord says: "For whoever does and teaches shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven," and rightly so,
for to philosophize in words is easy, but to show what is good by deeds is a great thing.
For this reason also Christ, when he was teaching about not holding on to wrongs, made himself the model of that deed.

And again now, after the teaching, he turned to prayer, in order to teach us that in a time of trial we should leave everything behind and flee to God. For since he had said, "In the world you will have tribulation,"
and they were distressed, he now makes them glad again through prayer, for they still looked on him as a man, and he did this for their sake,
just as he prayed over Lazarus and stated the reason: "I said this for the sake of this people, so that they may believe that you sent me."
But if anyone should say, "Before the Jews he rightly did this, but why does he do it before the disciples?", here too he did well, for those who after so many deeds say,
"Now we know that you know all things," needed to be strengthened more than anyone.
And see this also: the evangelist does not even call this act a prayer,
but says, "He lifted up his eyes to heaven," and he calls it speaking to the Father.
And if elsewhere it speaks of bending the knees and of lifting up the eyes in this way, do not be troubled,

for from all this we learn how fervently prayer ought to be performed: that we should look to heaven not only with the bodily eye but also with the soul, and that we should bend the knees with contrition of mind.
For Christ came not only to reveal himself but also to teach great virtue, and,
so that he might teach not only by word but also by deed, let us then hear what he says here:
Gospel: "Father, my hour has come; glorify your Son, so that the Son also may glorify you."

Commentary: Again he shows us that he does not come to the passion unwillingly. For how could he have come unwillingly, he who prayed for this to be done and called that event glory, and not only his own glory, he who was being crucified, but also the Father's?
For so indeed it came about, and not only the Son but the Father also was glorified, for before the crucifixion not even the Jews knew him, as it is written:
"Israel did not know me," but after the crucifixion the whole world knew. And next he states the manner of that glory, how he would glorify him:
Gospel: "As you gave him authority over all flesh, so that to all whom you gave him he may give eternal life."

Commentary: Doing good is always the glory of God. But what does this saying mean, "As you gave him authority over all flesh"? He shows that the preaching is not confined to the Jews alone, but spreads over the whole world, and he foreshadows the salvation of the Gentiles. For since he had said, "Do not go on the way of the Gentiles," and was going to say after this, "Go and make disciples of all the Gentiles," he shows that the Father also wills it so. For this greatly offended the Jews, and the disciples did not readily permit themselves to join in prayer with them, until they received that teaching of the Holy Spirit. And when Peter came to Jerusalem, he could only with difficulty escape their accusations, by the account of the sheet.

But what does this saying mean, "You gave him authority over all flesh"? Let us say to the heretics: "When did he receive authority over them: before their creation, or after their creation?" For he himself says it was after the incarnation and resurrection, and it is then that he says: "All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth.

Go and make disciples of all the Gentiles." What, then, does this saying mean? Did he perhaps not have authority over his own creatures? He who created them did not have authority, and how could that be? For he made all things from the ages, and in those earlier times he punished some for sin and honored others for virtue. Or did he have authority then, and was it afterward taken from him and given back again? And what devil would say this? But if he had the same authority both then and now, for as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills, and since all this is so, what does that saying mean which he spoke when he was sending them to the Gentiles? It was for this reason: so that they would not think that saying vain because of the word he had spoken earlier: "I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the children of Israel."

And for this reason he shows them that the Father also wills it so. And if he spoke in this way, in the manner of humility, do not be surprised, for he did everything for their sake, so as to build them up the more, for they were being built up upon him. And again, he assured the generations after them, by that very excess of humility, that he was speaking because of the weakness of his hearers. But what does this mean, "all flesh"? For not all believed. Yet this is not his fault, but the fault of those who did not listen to their words. Those who listened were saved, but those who did not listen destroyed themselves of their own will.
Gospel: "So that to all whom you gave him he may give eternal life."

Commentary: Do not be surprised at this, for he speaks here in a human way. He does this for the reasons stated before, for he always took care not to say any great word about himself, because of the weakness of his hearers, since they did not have lofty knowledge of him. But when John speaks on his own account, he no longer does this, but raises his discourse to what is higher and says: "All things were made through him, and without him not one thing was made of all that was made," and: "He was life, and he came to his own." And he did not say, "He received authority," but rather says: "He gave others authority to be children of God." And Paul likewise says: "equal to God." But he himself makes request in a human way and says:
Gospel: "that to all whom you have given him he may give eternal life; that they may know you, the only true God, and him whom you have sent, Jesus Christ."
Commentary: He said "the only true God" on account of those other gods of the pagans, who are not gods but demons, for he was about to [?] to the pagans.
But what do you say, wicked heretic, that the Son is not true God?

O darkened one! He spoke this word about the idols, in opposition to them, saying "the only true God," and not that the Son is not true God. For the Son is truth itself, and how could he not be true God? For it is far higher to say, "He is truth itself," than, "He is a true man."
So too the Son: since he is himself true, how could he not be true God?
Or how does he make us gods, if he himself is not true God?
But we have spoken about this matter elsewhere, with close examination. Therefore let us speak about the next passage:
Gospel: "I have glorified you on earth."
Commentary: He rightly said "on earth," for in the heavens he was glorified, he who by nature had the glory of divinity and was worshiped by the angels.
So he is not speaking of that glory which he has by nature, for that glory, even if there is no one to glorify him,
remains in its fullness. Rather, he is speaking of this glory which comes about through the service of human beings.
And therefore that saying too, "Glorify me," is of the same kind. So that you may know that he is speaking of this kind of glory, hear also what follows.
Gospel: "I have finished your work, which you gave me to do."

Commentary: The work had as yet only a beginning, or rather not even a beginning, for he had not even been crucified at that time. So how does he say, "I have finished"? But either he is saying this: "I have finished my part," or he was speaking of what was to come as though it had been done,
or rather let us say this: that since that root of good things had been planted, it was as if everything had been done.
For the fruits too followed upon this root, and all that was to come after it he joined to it.
Therefore he again says in humility, "which you gave me to do," for if he were one to listen and learn, this would be far beneath his glory,
for this is evident in many ways, that he came to this work by his own will, as Paul says:
"Thus he loved us, for he gave himself for us," and that "he humbled himself and took the form of a slave," and again he himself says: "As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you."
Gospel: "Glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world existed."
Commentary: Among men you did not have glory, on account of that garment of humanity; but do you ask for glory from God? What then is this saying?

But understand that this saying concerns his dispensation, for the nature of the flesh had not yet been glorified, nor did it have incorruption, nor did it yet share in the royal throne. For this reason he did not say, "Glorify me on earth."

Homily 80, on wealth and poverty. Such glory, then, let us also find according to our measure, if we strive. For this reason the apostle says: "If we suffer with him, we shall also be glorified with him." But we are worthy of countless tears, we before whom such great glory lies, and through our negligence we are deprived of all this. For even if there were no Gehenna, we are to be pitied, we who have the power, if we wish, to reign with the Son of God, and yet deprive ourselves of all this. For even if it were necessary to be cut apart limb by limb, and to die countless deaths, and to give up countless souls and as many bodies, for the sake of that glory it would be nothing.

But as it is, we do not even despise for its sake riches, from which after a little while we shall be parted even against our will; we do not disregard riches, which plunge us into countless evils, which remain here and are not ours. And since what lies before us is not only the loss of this glory but also Gehenna, the sleepless worm, the unquenchable fire and the gnashing of teeth, how shall we endure all that? How is it that we do not lift up our eyes, but are every day in tumults and reproaches and vain words, and nourish earth? For this flesh that we fatten is earth, while we have neglected the soul. We do not seek true necessities, but take care for useless things: we build splendid tombs, and acquire very costly houses and a multitude of slaves, and we set stewards over everything, overseers and chief overseers, while our soul stands desolate and we take no care of it at all. What then will be the end of all this?

Do we not fill one belly? Do we not clothe one body? What is all this great commotion? Why do we lay waste the one soul that has been allotted to us, and defile it, and cast it down into that evil bodily slavery? For whoever seeks much is a slave of many, even if he thinks he is lord of all. He is the slave of his own slaves and can do nothing without them; and so, since they serve him in everything, he is their slave.

I know that someone will laugh at these words, but such people are all the more pitiable for this, that they do not know that this is slavery and not lordship. Would you wish that another should feed you and give you drink, while you yourself were unable to do it? Would that not seem a pitiable thing to you? Or if you were unable to walk, and others had to carry you? So then is every affair of this world. For the angels are blessed for this reason, that they have no need of such cares; and we too, the less we have, the nearer we come to the life of the angels, and the more we are hemmed in by many cares, the more we sink into this vain life and world. For look at those who have dropsy: when are they better off? When, from their great burning, they cannot be sated with water, or when they are sound and do not need so much? Ask old men which life they consider better: when they were young and were able even to serve others, or now, when they need many servants?

Do you see that abundance is vain in every way in bodily matters? Or if being without a house were restful, would you not prefer it to the toil of building houses? Do we not call Adam blessed for this, that he needed nothing while he was in paradise, neither house, nor clothing, nor anything else? But why do we increase greed and become slaves of slaves? For the more we need, the more of your freedom you undo. For true freedom is that one should need nothing, and next to it is that one should need little, which belongs rather to the angels. But if anyone should achieve this in these mortal bodies, that is a great thing, for necessities were given to us for our relief [?] and not to enslave us. For if we seek to multiply them, we no longer possess them, but they have possessed us [?]. Let us then escape from such slavery, let us then acquire that true freedom. Why do we procure for ourselves myriads of bonds? Is that bond of nature not enough for us? Yet we acquire others as well.

Let us at last press on toward those good things of heaven. For would that, even when we have broken all these bonds, we might thus be able to reach that heavenly city, for many are the things that hinder us! Let us then loosen these bonds, that thus we may find eternal life by the grace and love for mankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 81

This saying: "I have manifested your name to the men whom you gave me; they were of this world and you gave them to me. And they have kept your word." The Son of God is called "Angel of Great Counsel" on account of all the teachings that he taught, and first of all because he preached the Father to men, which he now speaks of, saying: "I have manifested your name to men." For when he had said, "I have accomplished your work," he now says: "What is this work?"

"I have manifested the name of God." Was it itself known? Understand that it was known only by the Jews, and not completely even by them, while the pagans did not know it at all; and the Jews, although they knew it, did not know him as Father. But Christ manifested his name both by word and by deed.
Gospel: "Those whom you gave me out of this world."

Commentary: Just as he said above, "No one can come to me unless it has been given to him from heaven, unless the Father brings him," so also here he says, "those whom you gave me," and again he himself calls himself the Way. For this reason he shows two things here: first, that he is not opposed to the Father; and second, that the Father wills that all should believe in the Son.
Gospel: "They were yours, and you gave them to me."

Commentary: Here he makes known the love that he had toward the Father, for otherwise it was not that he needed them to be given to him, since he created them and he himself provided for them; how, then, would they have been given? But, as I said, he makes known the unity that he has with the Father. If anyone should understand these words in a human way, that understanding will prove to be evil. For if, when the Father had them, they were not the Son's, but afterward he gave them to the Son, then it is clear that when he gave them to the Son, he himself withdrew from his authority over them. And this again is another, still more evil statement, for it would then appear that when they were with the Father they were not perfect, and when they came to the Son they became perfect. But these words are the devil's; what the Lord signifies is this, that the Father greatly wills that all should believe.
Gospel: "And they have kept your word, and now they have known that all whom you gave me are yours."

Commentary: What does this mean, "they have kept your word"? It means this: that they believed me and did not listen to the Jews. For it says, "Whoever believes him has set his seal that God is true." "And now they have known that everything I say is from you and that they are your words, and not only this, but also this,
that I came forth from you," for he strove above all to convince them of this.
Gospel: "I pray for them."

Commentary: What is this? Does he teach the Father this way, as though the Father did not know the matter, like a man who did not know? What, then, is this distinction? Do you see, then, that his prayer was for no other reason than that they might know what love he has toward them? For he who not only gave his own help but also made a show of entreating another on their behalf was showing that he has great love for them. "I pray for them," he says, "and not for the world, but for those whom you gave me." He says this repeatedly so that they may know that the Father also wills the same. And then, since he had said repeatedly, "They were yours and you gave them to me," in order to dispel the evil suspicion of those who were going to say that what is the Father's is somehow separated from the Son, and that his authority is new, for this reason he added and said:

Gospel: "And all that is mine is yours, and what is yours is mine, and I am glorified among them." Have you seen this faith? It is so that when you hear "you gave them to me," you may not think that they have been removed far from the Father's authority and that before this they were strangers to the Son.

Therefore he resolved both of these suspicions by his word, as if to say: "Do not, when you hear 'You gave them to me,' suppose that they had become strangers to the Father, for 'all that is mine is his.' Nor, when you hear 'they were yours,' suppose that they were strangers to the Father, for 'all that is his is mine.'" But this saying, 'You gave them to me,' was said for the sake of the hearers, for all that the Father has is the Son's, and all that the Son has is the Father's, as he says in another place: "All that is the Father's is mine." And this saying, 'You gave them to me,' and others of this kind he spoke because he is showing: "It is not as strangers that I received them, but they were mine and I received them." And then he also stated the reason and the proof: "I am glorified in them," that is, "I have authority over them," and "they will glorify me," when they believe in me and in you equally. For so it came about: all of them died for the Father and the Son, and they preached the Father and the Son equally,
just as they did everything in his name, so also in his name.
Gospel: "And I am no longer in this world, and these are in the world."
Commentary: That is: "Although I do not appear in the flesh, yet I am glorified by them."
But why does he say repeatedly: "I am not in the world, and I entrust them to you, and when I was with them, I guarded them"?
For if anyone understands these words in this way, many evils will befall him. For if it were so, that he had withdrawn from them completely, how could he have entrusted them to another?
For these are human matters. Rather, he said all this for their sake and for the sake of their understanding, so as to make them expect greater help, since he was going away.

Therefore he says: "When I was there, I protected them," and again he said to them: "I am coming to you, and I will be with you until the end of the world." And how could he have spoken these words if he himself were going to abandon them?
But, as I said, he was speaking according to their suspicion, so that they might rejoice a little, and so that he might comfort their sorrow when they heard that he was entrusting them to the Father.
For since they had heard many words of consolation from him and had not believed, he therefore now speaks to the Father about them, in order to show them his love for them.

It is as if he were saying: "Since you have called me to yourself, keep these, for I am coming to you!" What are you saying: "And are you not able to keep them?" "Yes, I am able," he says. "And why do you speak these words?" "For this reason," he says,
"that they may have my joy in full among them and may not be afraid, for they have not yet been made perfect."
Now the Lord said all this for the sake of their joy and rest, for he said:
"I am not in the world, and these are in the world."
And they supposed the same thing, and he said this because of their suspicion; and if he had said, "I protect them," they would not have believed. Therefore he also said:
Gospel: "Holy Father, keep these in your name."
Commentary: Again he speaks as a man and as a prophet, for nowhere does it appear that he ever said anywhere: "Let these things be done in my name." But here he says this:
Gospel: "Those whom you gave me, I kept, and none of them perished except the son of perdition, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled."

Commentary: And in another place he says: "Of all that you have given me, I will lose none." Yet not only Judas perished, but many others also afterward. How then does he say, "I will not lose"? But this is what he means: "For my part, I will not lose them." As he said in another place: "I will not cast out; but if anyone willingly hastens to perish, I will not hold him by force."
Gospel: "But now I am coming to you, and I say this in the world, so that they may have my joy in full."

Commentary: Do you see how many of these words are spoken in human fashion? And whoever is senseless and darkened, and belittles the Son on account of these words, would belittle the Father too. For see from the beginning how some speech belongs to teaching and some to command. It belongs to teaching when he says: "I do not pray for the world,"

but to command: "I have kept them until now, and none has perished, and now you too keep them." But the explanation of all these is this: he spoke in this way because of their weakness. And when he said, "None has perished except the son of perdition," he added: "so that the Scripture might be fulfilled" — the Scripture which says [?], but that which speaks many times of him [?], and because he was perishing. For this reason the Scripture spoke, and I have said this elsewhere too: this is a manner peculiar to Scripture, for it sets down as though it were a cause that which was coming to pass of itself. And it is necessary to understand everything precisely, both the mind of the speaker and the aspect of the matter and the customs of Scripture, so that we may not err, for the Apostle says: "Brothers, do not become children in mind."

Homily 81: That one must seek heavenly glory and not earthly glory, and on mercy. Now this must be read not only for the understanding of the Scriptures, but also for our deeds. For little children do not long for great things, but for play they desire worthless things, vain things and things of no account. For they make kings of clay, and thrones and horses, while they count the true king as nothing. So too are people who do such things: they hear of the good things of heaven and do not care at all, but for these vain things of clay they are as eager as children. They love wealth and glory and everything of the world, which is children's play, but they do not seek that true heavenly glory and kingdom. Instead, like children, they weep over these vain things, while they do not call those true things to mind at all. For this reason the Apostle says: "Do not be children in mind." O man, do you long for things that pass away and not seek the things that do not pass away? And you, if you should see someone throwing away a drachma of gold and choosing one of lead, would strongly condemn his ignorance.

But you gather what is more worthless even than this and suppose that you have wealth. I, however, call rich the one who has come to despise the things of the world. And no one despises those worthless things unless he has a desire for that higher desire, just as no one disregards lead,
...if he does not recognize gold. So you too, if you see a person who passes by the whole world, know that the longing for the eternal age dwells within him.
Likewise the farmer disregards a small amount of wheat when he expects a greater harvest. And if this is so where it is [only] to be known [?] whether we shall receive the harvest or not,
and we thus disregard our possessions, should we not all the more sow the seed where the receiving of the harvest is sure and beyond doubt?
Therefore I beg you, let us not deprive ourselves of those heavenly good things. Whatever he wishes,
let anyone say about us, and let whoever wishes be angry again and again over this teaching and call us long-winded. But I will not cease teaching and speaking that word of the prophet:
"Wipe away your sins by almsgiving." But not in such a way that you do it today and stop tomorrow.

For just as these bodies need food every day, so it is with the soul, and it needs it even more. If we do not give it, it grows weak. So let us not neglect it, for it is constantly being choked in affliction, since many wounds come upon it from lusts, from anger, from evil speech, from negligence [?], from bearing grudges, and from envy. We must therefore apply medicines to it, and the medicine of almsgiving is no small one for all wounds, for: "Give alms, and everything will be clean for you." Lay alms upon yourselves and do not lay greed upon yourselves, for alms must be free of all injustice. Otherwise alms made through greed are of no use. But alms that are pure are good, and better than anything they enlighten the soul, make it beautiful, and fatten it.

Let us therefore rub this oil on our hands, so that we may be well able to resist the devil, for every passion is dissolved by almsgiving. For just as a physician who spends every day among the sick is humbled if he reflects on human misery, so we, if we spend time among the poor and always show them mercy, will gain great wisdom from this work, will despise the whole world, will rise up to heaven, and will easily attain those eternal good things by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
Chapter 22
This saying: "I have given them your words, and the world hated them, because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world."

For when we are persecuted by the lawless because of virtue and reproached by them, let us not be grieved, for such is the nature of this matter, and virtue always brings a person to perfection by means of the wicked,
for the wicked hate those who strive, and they think
that they are doing themselves some good, and they hasten to bring shame upon the life of those who strive. But let us not be grieved, for this is the sign of endurance.
For this reason the Lord also said: "If you were of the world, the world would love its own." And again he says: "Woe to you when people speak well of you."
For this reason he says here too: "I have given them your words, and the world hated them," and he further states the reason,
For this reason they are worthy of great care from the Father: "For they were hated for your sake and for the sake of your word." Therefore they are worthy of every honor.
Gospel: "I do not say that you should take them out of the world, but that you should keep them from the evil one."

Commentary: Again he makes his statement still clearer, which he did for no other reason than to show that he cares greatly for them, since he speaks on their behalf with such earnestness. And he himself used to say: "Whatever you ask, the Father will give you." And how is it that here he entreats on their behalf? It is for no other reason, as I said, than to demonstrate his love.
Gospel: "They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world."

Commentary: And as he said in another place, "Those whom you gave me from the world were yours," there he was speaking about nature, for by nature the apostles were of the world; but here he speaks about evil deeds, and he speaks great praise of them: first, that they are not of the world; next, that that One gave them to this One; and again, that they kept his word, and that they were hated for his sake. And if he says, "As I am not of the world," do not be surprised, for he does not use this expression "as I" of true likeness. For when he speaks about the Father, saying, "As I and the Father," he is speaking of complete likeness, but when he says it about us, he shows our great distance from him.

For if he committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth, how could the apostles be equal to him? But what he is saying is this: "They are not lovers of this world, but they look toward other things; they have no share in the affairs of this world, but have become citizens of heaven." And by this too he shows his love, since he praises them in this way before the Father and entrusts them to him. And when he said:
"Keep them," he speaks not only of bodily trials, but also of being strengthened in the faith. For this reason he added and said:
Gospel: "Sanctify them by your truth."
Commentary: That is to say: "Sanctify them by the giving of the Holy Spirit and through right teachings," just as when he said to them:
"You are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you." And now too he says the same thing, namely:

"Teach them the truth." And he also designates the Holy Spirit as the teacher of truth. And how is it that he now asks that this be done by the Father? It is so that you may again recognize the unity,
for when right words are spoken about God, they sanctify the soul. And after this he said:
Gospel: "Your word is truth."
Commentary: That is to say, there is no falsehood at all in it, nor any type or shadow, but all of it is truth, as Paul says about the Church:
"He sanctified it by the word, for the word of God too knows how to sanctify." And I think that this saying also signifies something else, namely:
"Sanctify them," that is: "And set them apart for the preaching and the word." And this is evident from the words that follow, where he said: "As you sent me into the world";
as Paul too says:
"He has placed among us the word of reconciliation, for that for which Christ came is the very thing for which they too traversed the world."
But, as here also, this is not a likeness between the apostles and the Lord.
And it is the custom of the Lord himself to speak of what is coming as of what is to be [?]; therefore he says:
Gospel: "For my sake [?] I sanctify myself, that they too may be holy in truth."
Interpretation: What does this mean: "I sanctify myself"? "I offer myself as a sacrifice to you," he says, for a sacrifice offered to God

is all holy. And since under the old covenant holiness came through the offering of a sheep, in type and shadow, now it is no longer in type but in truth. Therefore he says, "that they may be holy in your truth,"
"for I offer them too to you as an offering," he says. Or else it is for this reason: since the Lord and leader does this, so they also should do it, for they too are offered, for he says:
"Present your members as a living, holy sacrifice," and, "We were counted as sheep for slaughter." And without death he makes them a sacrifice and an offering.
But since he was going to his death, he said:
"For these I sanctify myself." So that no one might say, "He says this only about the apostles," he therefore added and said:
Gospel: "I do not ask for them, but for all who believe in me through their word."
Interpretation: With this saying he again strengthened their souls, showing that many are going to become their disciples,

for since he revealed that what they possessed in greater measure was shared with others, he comforted them again, indicating that they would be the cause of salvation for many others. And since he had spoken about their offering and salvation,

and that they might be holy in truth, he again begins to speak about unity, and with this he concludes his discourse. With the very thing with which he began, with that he finishes, for at the beginning of the discourse he said, "I give you a new commandment." And now he again begins to speak about the same thing:
Gospel: "That all may be one, as you, Father, in me, and I in you, that they too may be in us."
Interpretation: Again this word "as" does not denote true likeness, for such a likeness was not possible for them,

but rather as far as lies within human power, as when he says, "Be merciful, as your Father is merciful." And what does the saying "in us" mean, by faith in us? For since nothing causes many to stumble so much as disunity, he therefore says this, that they may be one. And such benefit came of that deed, for as many as believed through the apostles are now all one; though some have separated, they have perished. For this too he himself foretold, and he showed that this comes about through human negligence.
Gospel: "That the world may believe that you sent me."

Commentary: Just as he said at the beginning, "By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another," so now too he says, "that the world may believe." And what is it to believe? That you are the God of peace and that you sent me. For if these keep unity, all will recognize the teacher through the disciples. Do you see how, right up to the end, he shows his unity with his Father?
Gospel: "And the glory that you gave me, I have given to them."

Commentary: He speaks of the glory of miracles and of teaching, and of their being of one mind, for this is even higher than miracles, since by this deed they became radiant. How then does he ask this of the Father, when he himself was giving it, whether his word concerns miracles, or unity, or peace? It is apparent that he himself has given them everything, and from this it is evident that the request was made only for their consolation.
Gospel: "I in them and you with me."
Commentary: See what glory he gave them, for he had the Father in himself, and in this way he dwelt in them.

But in another place he does not speak in this way, but says, "The Father will come through me," and "I and the Father will come," and "we will make our dwelling with him." But there he stops the mouth of Sabellius, and here that of Arius.
Gospel: "That they may be perfect in unity, and that the world may know that you sent me."
Commentary: He says this repeatedly and shows openly that peace is more capable than even miracles of converting the nations.
Gospel: "And I have loved them as you have loved me."

Commentary: Here again this word "as" means as far as love is possible for a human being, and the sign of that love is that he laid down his own life as a pattern. And having said that they should be without error and be holy, that many should believe through them and that they should receive great glory, and that not only he but the Father also loves them, he now speaks again of the crowns and gifts that will be given to them after their departure from here.
Gospel: Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me.

Commentary: Behold, this is what they were always asking: "Where are you going?" But how is it that he himself told them, "You will sit on twelve thrones," and promised many other such things, and now asks it of the Father as though he himself were unable? Do you not see that he said all this in this way for their full assurance? Otherwise, did he himself not earlier say to Peter, "Afterward you will follow me," and many other such things?
Gospel: "That they may behold my glory, which you gave me, because you loved me before the creation of the world."

Commentary: Again, this is a sign of his unity with the Father, higher than those earlier ones, for he says, "before the creation of the world." Yet this too contains an expression of lowliness, for he says, "which you gave me." Do you see his being without beginning? For "you gave me before everything" means "you begot me before all the ages," since glory was not given to him at some later time, but he always had it from that essence.
And he did not say, "that they may have my glory," but "that they may behold my glory."
For this is the whole of that rest: that they should behold the glory of the Son of God,
as the apostle Paul says: "With unveiled face let us behold the glory of God,"
just as those who look at the sun receive light by that very looking, so also, and far more surpassingly, will that light be then. And at the same time he said this for this reason too,
to show that what they behold is not the nature of his divinity, but some essence that can be received.
Gospel: "Righteous Father, the world too did not know you."
Commentary: What does this saying mean? For he shows here that no one has known the Father except only those who know the Son alone.
But this saying amounts to this: "I wished that all should know you, but they did not know you, and that without any excuse." For this is why he said:

"Righteous Father, for you are truly righteous, and no one has any cause against you, and yet they did not know you," he says. But in this place, I think, he spoke with sorrow, that one so good and righteous [?] they did not know.
For since the Jews were saying, "We know God, and you do not know him," for this reason he says:
"You loved me before the ages, and how could I, who am so beloved by you and have received glory from you, be opposed to you?
So then it is not as the Jews say, that they know you and I do not know you; rather, it is the opposite, for I know you, but they did not know you."
Gospel: "And these too knew that you sent me."
Commentary: Do you see that he was alluding to the Jews, who said that he was opposed to God, and from whom he separated the apostles, and brought it about that they knew him?
Gospel: "And I made your name known to them, and I will make it known."
Commentary: The perfect understanding that he said would come about through the Spirit, he now says is given by himself, in order to show that oneness.
Gospel: "And may the love with which you loved me be among them and with them."
Commentary: This means: "If they know who you are, then they will know that I am not separated from you, but am the beloved Son, who shares the throne with you.
And when they know this, then they will love you as is fitting. And when they love you in this way as is fitting, then I will abide with them."
Do you see what a good ending this was? For he brought his speech to its end upon the mother of all the virtues, which is love.

Homily 82, on virtue and on the affairs of the world. Therefore let us too believe and love God, both in deed and in mind, so that it may not be said of us too that they believe in God in word and deny him in deed.

But when unbelievers show mercy even to strangers, and we not even to our own, what hope of salvation will there be for us, when God is blasphemed through us? See how many occasions for doing good God has given us, so that we should show mercy to one as a relative, to another as a friend, to another as an acquaintance, and to another as a man of our own nature. But if we despise all of these, we shall hear from Paul: "You are worse than the pagans, for those who have heard nothing of mercy and the kingdom have surpassed you in mercy.

But you, who have been taught to love even your enemies, do you regard even your friends as enemies, and have more pity on gold than on people? Where has such great mercilessness and wickedness come from? For if someone were to sit in a high place to observe human affairs, how much he would weep and grieve, and how severely he would condemn them!

For we do things that deserve laughter and scorn. One man raises dogs to hunt wild beasts and himself becomes more senseless than the beasts. Another raises hawks and falcons and spends a great deal of gold on such things, yet does not look at people dying of hunger. Another again collects gold [?] and marbles and applies them to his walls, yet does not give even a small garment to the naked poor; such people have countless garments, while the poor do not have even one.
And in the law courts one man swallows up and devours one thing, another squanders his wealth on prostitutes, and another on jesters and minstrels,

on building great houses and buying estates. Another counts interest and interest upon interest, while another writes letters of denunciation to deliver others into the hands of death. Some go about to steal, some to fornicate, and others to one evil or another. There is so much zeal for evil things, but not even a little for good things. And judges have the name of judges, but the deeds of robbers.

Or if anyone were to look at their judgments, or at the records they have written, he would find much injustice. All the striving is for such things, while no one cares for what is spiritual, and they go to church only to look around and not to pray to God. And perhaps someone may say a few words, but deeds appear nowhere, and words without deeds obtain forgiveness for no one. Look, O man, at the naked, the hungry, the many who are afflicted: God has given us ways of life. Let us therefore not deceive ourselves by living in vanity, and let us not think that death is far off, for death is always at the door.

Therefore let us turn from evil to do good. For behold, the judges are like beasts, the merchants like foxes, and even the poor pass their days in vanity. All seek sin, and no one hates it. All this I say every day and I will not cease speaking. If anyone listens, it will be to his benefit; if he does not listen, I have done my part. You will listen only when the benefit will be mine and yours will be nothing, and you will blame yourselves. But may it not happen so. Rather, may we have you as our boast before the throne of Christ, so that together we may attain the eternal good things by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
Chapter 83
The text: When Jesus had said this, he went out with his disciples across the Ravine of the Firs, where there was a garden, and he and his disciples entered it.
Death is very terrible, but it is not terrible to those who have learned heavenly wisdom,
for the one who does not know heavenly things, but considers death to be only destruction and annihilation, rightly fears it, as one going into nonexistence.
But we, who by the grace of God have learned the hidden mysteries of his wisdom, ought not to tremble at it,
but ought to rejoice and be glad, for we are leaving this corruptible life and passing over to one far higher and better,
which Christ also teaches us by his deed, for he goes to his passion not under compulsion but willingly.
Gospel: Having said this, Jesus went out with his disciples across the ravine of the cedars, where there was a garden, which he himself and his disciples entered.
Judas also, the betrayer, knew that place, for he had many times gone in there with his disciples.
Commentary: At midnight he goes, crosses the river, and comes to the place
