known to the betrayer, so as to spare those who were to seize him much labor, and to show the disciples that he goes to his passion willingly, which was enough to comfort them; and so he entered the garden. For this reason the Evangelist says, "Jesus said this." What are you saying, O blessed one?

For that was a prayer, so why did you not say, "When he had ceased from prayer, he went there"? But it was not a prayer; rather, it was a discourse that he was making for the sake of the disciples, and he entered the garden with the disciples. In this way he strengthened them, for they were no longer afraid as they had been before, and they even entered the garden. And as for how Judas came there, from this it is evident that he mostly used to spend his time in deserted places, and if he had been in a house, Judas would not have come there. And so that, when you hear "garden," you may not think that he was hiding, he added that Judas also knew that place, for he had many times gone in there with his disciples; and many times he would spend time apart with them in deserted places and speak to them about mysteries that others ought not to hear.
Gospel: Then Judas took a band of men from the chief priests and servants of the Pharisees and came there.

Commentary: The Jews had many times wished to do this and could not, and from this it is evident that they seized him at the time when he willingly gave himself up; otherwise they could not have seized him, just as they had many times wished to and could not. And where did that band come from? They were hired pagans.
Gospel: But Jesus, knowing all that was coming upon him, came out and said to them, "Whom do you seek?"

Commentary: That is, it was not that he needed to learn of their coming, but he himself knew everything from the beginning. Therefore he acted and said everything without being disturbed. And why did they come with weapons?
Because they were afraid of the crowds who followed him, and for this reason they came at an untimely hour, at night.
Gospel: He went out and said to them, "Whom do you seek?" And they said to him, "Jesus of Nazareth."

Commentary: Do you see the invincible power, how it was among them and darkened their eyes, for the night was not the cause? For this reason the Evangelist pointed it out and said, "They had torches." Even if they had not had torches, he ought to have been recognized by his voice. And if they did not recognize him, how did Judas not recognize him, since he who had always been with him was with them? Yet he too did not recognize him, but fell on his face. Jesus did this to show us that not only were they unable to seize him, but they could not even have recognized him, had he himself not permitted it.
Gospel: "Then again he asked them: 'Whom do you seek?'"
Commentary: O, what senselessness! That first word threw them down on their faces, and still they did not take heed, so as to recognize his power.
But the Lord, since he had done what it was fitting for him to do and they did not understand, therefore hands himself over and says to them:
Gospel: "'I told you that I am he.' Judas the betrayer was also standing there"

Commentary: Do you see the calmness of the evangelist? How he does not revile the betrayer, but simply relates what was done, and is eager for one thing only: to show that everything came about through his peaceableness. And so that no one could say, "He brought them to this deed," since he had said, "I am he," he therefore did everything that would restrain them, and when they persisted in their wickedness and had no excuse at all, then he handed himself over to them and said to them:
Gospel: "If you seek me, let these men go"
Commentary: Even to the very last moment he showed them his love for humankind, for he says, "If you seek me, I give myself over to you, and let these men go."
Gospel: "So that the word which Jesus had spoken might be fulfilled: 'Of those whom you gave me, I will not lose even one'"

Commentary: Now by "losing" he does not mean this death here, but that eternal one; yet the evangelist applied that saying to this also. And how is it that they did not seize them along with him and kill them too, especially since Peter had enraged them? Who was restraining them? It was no one else but that power which threw them down on their faces, on account of which the evangelist said, "So that the word which Jesus had spoken might be fulfilled: 'I will not lose even one of them.'" And Peter, trusting in this word and in the deeds that were being done, armed himself against those opponents. And if anyone should say, "How is it that he who had been commanded not to have a staff had a sword?", I think that he had prepared it beforehand for this very purpose. And if you should say, "How does he who had been commanded not even to give a slap become one who wounds a man?", understand that he did not take that vengeance for his own sake but for the Teacher's, and also that he did not yet have complete perfection, nor were they yet at that measure which they reached later. But if you wish to see Peter's endurance, see after this how many afflictions came upon him, and how even unto death he bore everything with endurance. And Jesus performed a miracle here, at once so that he might teach us to do good to evildoers, and so that he might show his own power, for he healed the man's ear, and he said to Peter, "Those who take up the sword will also die by the sword." And in this way he calmed him. For the evangelist also gives the name of that servant, so that people of that time could truly know that it was so. But see how he [?] struck at the man's head and cut off his right ear, and had the Lord not rebuked him, he would have killed him outright. But the Lord not only restrained him, but also spoke words of consolation to him and said to him:
Gospel: "The cup which the Father has given me, shall I not drink it?"
Commentary: He said this in order to show Peter that his arrest does not come from their power but from his own permission, and that he is obedient to the Father unto death.
Gospel: "Then they seized Jesus and bound him and led him first to Annas. And Annas was the father-in-law of Caiaphas.
Now Caiaphas was the one who had advised the Jews, saying: "It is better that one man should die for the people."

Commentary: They led him to Annas because in their joy they were going about and proclaiming it, as though they had won some great victory. But why did the Evangelist mention that prophecy? So that when you hear of the seizing and binding of Jesus you would not be troubled, but would know that it truly was for the life of the world, and that this was so true that even his enemies prophesied it.
Gospel: And Peter and that other disciple followed him.

Commentary: Who is that other disciple? None other than the Evangelist himself, who has said this. But why did he not give his own name, just as at the time of the supper he said "another disciple" and did not give his own name? At that time he rightly concealed himself, because that matter was great; but why here? Understand that it is for the same reason, for this deed too was very great: all the others scattered and he alone followed. For this reason he did not give his own name, but only Peter's, and he mentioned himself briefly, so that you would know that he says everything truthfully, since he was there, standing by. And see what he does, so that no one should be amazed that all the others went away and Peter too remained outside, and he alone went in with the Lord. For this reason he says that "he was known to the high priest," so that no one should say, "He did it out of his own courage and fearlessness." And it was not as something praiseworthy that he said, "He was known to the high priest" (may it not be so!), but, as I said, he said it for that reason, so that no one should marvel at his courage, for his conduct was always adorned with humility. And of Peter he said that "they did not allow him to enter"; otherwise he too would have gone in with him. But Peter's deed is also great, for all abandoned the Lord, yet he did not abandon him, even though he could not go inside until John came out and told the doorkeeper to bring him in. But why did John not bring him in himself, rather than speaking to the doorkeeper? Because he himself was hastening to be with Christ. See, then, what that doorkeeper woman did:
Gospel: The maidservant said to Peter: "Surely you too are not one of this man's disciples?" Peter said: "I am not."
Commentary: What are you saying, O Peter? Did you not say, "I will lay down my life for you"? And what has happened, that you cannot bear even the word of a doorkeeper?
It was not a soldier who questioned you, but a contemptible maidservant, and even her words were not harsh and wrathful, but rather gentle.
But perhaps you too will say on this account: "John was inside, and she asked so sweetly, and yet could Peter not bear even that?"
And they sent Jesus bound to Caiaphas, and Peter stood outside and warmed himself.
Alas, with what heaviness was that fervent man seized, who before, when they seized Jesus, was blazing like fire in his heart! But now he did not stir at all, but sat and warmed himself.
And so that you may know how great the weakness of human nature is when God abandons someone: they questioned him, and again he denied.
And then that kinsman of the servant whose ear Peter had cut off accused him, saying: "Did I not see you in the garden with him?"
And when he mentioned the garden, Peter was still not moved to compunction, but denied again.
But why did all four evangelists alike speak about Peter? Not in order to accuse him, far from it!
Rather, it was to show how evil it is not to trust in God, but in oneself.
But as for you, marvel at the goodness of the Teacher: how, though bound and being judged, he took care for him in all of this, and by his look moved him to compunction and stirred him to tears.
Gospel: They led him from Caiaphas to Pilate.
Commentary: All this took place so that the multitude of judges might reveal the truth of the matter.
And it was dawn, for they brought him to Caiaphas before the cock crowed, and to Pilate at dawn.
For through so many hours of the night he was being judged by Caiaphas, and they could convict him of nothing. But you, behold the blindness of the Jews,
for they seized the innocent one with weapons and wanted to kill him, and they did not shrink from this, yet they would not enter the judgment hall, so that they might not be defiled.
Those who swallowed the camel and strained out the gnat did not count the unjust killing of the Lord as a sin, yet they reckoned coming into the judgment hall as a sin.
But why did they not kill him themselves, but sent him to Pilate?
Because their great authority had been dissolved, since affairs were under the authority of the Romans, and they were afraid that they might be brought to judgment by them.
Gospel: Pilate came out to them and said: "What accusation do you bring against this man?"
Commentary: Do you see how radiant the truth is? For even he realized that they were accusing him groundlessly.
For this reason he questioned them, for it seemed wrong to him to carry out their judgment and to hand him over to punishment. But hear also their words:
Gospel: "If this man were not an evildoer, we would not have handed him over to you."
Commentary: O folly! Why do you not prove the evil, but only say:
"He is an evildoer," and yet cannot charge him with the evil deed? Do you see that they could find nothing anywhere?
Annas questioned him about his teaching and found no fault, and sent him to Caiaphas; and Caiaphas likewise found nothing, and brought him to Pilate.
And Pilate says to them: "What accusation do you bring against this man?" And they can say nothing true. For this reason Pilate said to them:
Gospel: "Take him and judge him according to your law!" The Jews said to him:
"It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death," so that the word of Jesus might be fulfilled, which he spoke when he made known by what death he was to die.
Commentary: The evangelist says this because it was necessary that he die not for the Jews only, but for the Gentiles as well.
And for this reason they said: "It is not lawful for us to kill anyone, or to crucify."
And the Jews did not crucify, but killed by other means, as they stoned Stephen and did not crucify him; yet they wanted this man to be crucified.
But Pilate did not hold a thorough trial, but brought him inside and said to Jesus:
Gospel: "'Are you the king of the Jews?' Jesus said to him: 'Do you say this of your own accord, or did others tell you about me?'"
Commentary: Why did the Lord ask this, except to expose that wicked mind of the Jews,
for Pilate had heard this from many people, and since at that moment the Jews had nothing they could say to him?
So that there would not be a long investigation of this matter, he brought into the open what he was always hearing, and since he had said to them:
"Judge according to your law," and they had said to him: "It is not lawful for us," so that they might show that the offense was not a Jewish matter but one against everyone.
And for this reason Pilate asked: "Are you the king of the Jews?" And it was not that Christ did not know whether he was saying it of his own accord or others had told him,
but he wished that Pilate too should come to know the doings of the Jews, and for this reason he said to him: "Did others tell you?" On account of which Pilate said:
Gospel: "Am I a Jew? Your own kinsmen and the chief priests handed you over to me. What have you done?"
Commentary: He wished to show himself innocent, but since he had said: "Are you the king of the Jews?"
for this reason Jesus reproved him and said to him: "Did you hear this from the Jews? Why then do you not conduct a proper trial with careful scrutiny?
For they said: 'He is an evildoer'? Ask [?] what evil I have done.
But you do not do this; instead you vainly gather pretexts. Do you say this of yourself, or did others tell you?" For he could not say:

"They have told me just now," but he merely went along with the talk of the people, which he had heard earlier, saying: "They have handed you over into my hands; what have you done?" But the Lord said to him:
Gospel: "My kingdom is not of this world"
Commentary: Pilate was not like them in wickedness.
For this reason he speaks these words to him, so that he might make him understand that he is not a mere man, but God and the Son of God, and he says to him:
Gospel: "If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would fight for me, so that I would not be handed over to the Jews"
Commentary: Pilate was afraid of this, that he might perhaps be seeking kingship and the wrath of Caesar might come upon him.
But Jesus, behold, has removed that suspicion. But what does this saying mean?
Is his kingdom not also of this world? Yes, he is king of all; but the Lord did not say:
"I am not lord of the world," but that the beginning of his kingdom is from heaven, while here he gave himself up willingly; but he does not yet say this.
And he said: "My servants would fight for me"; here he shows the weakness of earthly kingship, that it relies on servants.
But the heavenly kingdom is not like this; rather, he is Lord of all things in his own right. Yet the heretics have seized on this saying:
"My kingdom is not of this world," and in this way they make him a stranger to the work of creation, and they refuse to lift up their eyes and see the truth.
But what then will they say about the saying, "He came to his own, and his own did not receive him"? For just as he says about the apostles:
"They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world," so also he speaks about the kingdom, not to show
that the world is not in his power, but that his kingdom is not earthly and corruptible in this way. Hear, then, what Pilate says:
Gospel: "Pilate said to him, 'So then, are you a king?' Jesus said to him, 'You say that I am a king. For this I was born.'"
Commentary: See now, since he was born a king, he also has everything else from his birth. So then, when you hear:
"As the Father has life, so also he has given it to the Son," understand nothing other than birth, and not that something was given to him afterward.
And "For this I have come, that I may bear witness to the truth" means "that I may teach this very thing to everyone, so that they may recognize that I am a king."
Homily 83, on patience and vengeance. But you, O man, when you hear all this, that the King of all was judged in bonds,
let the affairs of this world count as nothing to you. For how is it not evil if Christ endured so much for you, and you have not endured even a word for him?
He endures being spat upon, while you adorn yourself with beautiful clothing and make your hands glitter with rings.
He was reproached and reviled and beaten, but you will not endure even a small hardship; instead you seek honor.
When someone insults you, remember how they insulted Christ. If anyone holds you in contempt, remember
that they bowed down to him in mockery and laughed at him, and not only did he do them no harm, but he also endured everything with meekness and gentleness.
Let us imitate him, then, O brothers. What he endured for us, shall we not endure for our own sake?
For why do you grow angry at the one who insults you? If he has insulted you unjustly, you should not be angry,
but should rather have mercy on him, for he has gone astray. If he has done so justly, then you should bear it patiently in quiet, for he is speaking the truth.
And if you were rich and someone called you poor, why would you take any account of that word?
Or if you are poor and they call you poor, should you not likewise refrain from anger? For it is the truth. So understand everything in this way, and you will bear it well.
If he insults you in front of others and you feel ashamed, consider in light of all those people that it is all the better that they should all see your patience and praise you, and blame him.
And if no wise person is there, then rejoice all the more, for God and the holy angels see your patience and praise you there.
For the praise of one angel is better than that of the whole world. And why do I speak of angels? God himself will praise you.
Let us reflect on such thoughts as these, for it is not evil if someone insults us, but it is evil if we seek vengeance on him.
And if it were not good to bear this matter in silence, Christ would not have said: "If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also."
But the evil among us comes from this, that we seek after human things and not the things of God.
Rather, let us learn to remember our own sins, and so pass through this life contrite, so that we may reach heaven little by little,
as by a ladder; for that ladder of Jacob signified this: the ascent from virtue to virtue. Let us therefore climb that ladder,
so that we may reach heaven and find those eternal good things, by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong glory and might forever and ever. Amen.
Chapter 84
This saying: "For this I was born, and for this I was sent into the world, that I may bear witness to the truth, and everyone who is of the truth
will hear my voice." Long-suffering is a wonderful thing: it brings the soul to calm as if to a harbor, and frees it from the waves and from evil winds.
And Christ taught us this in many places, but most of all when the Jews arrested him, for he answered Annas too with great calm, and to that servant
who struck him on the cheek he spoke words of great long-suffering and freedom from anger.
And again he went to Caiaphas and then to Pilate, and through all that time he showed great meekness.
And they kept saying, "He is an evildoer," yet they could not prove it, and he remained silent.
But when Pilate asked him about the kingship, then he spoke to him, in order to teach him and raise his mind to the heights.
But why does Pilate take him inside by himself and not question him in their presence?
Because he had some great thought about him, and so that their tumult would not spoil it for him, he questioned him by himself, in order to learn the whole truth.
And when he asked him, "What have you done?" he answered nothing; but when he asked about the kingship, which he wished to learn about, he himself said to him:
"My kingdom is not of this world," that is to say: "I am a king, but not such a one as you suppose,
but one far more splendid and greater; and for this I was born and have come, to bear witness to the truth."
By this he shows him and makes him understand that he has done no evil, for since he was born and had come for the sake of the truth, how could he have done any evil?
"But whoever is of the truth will hear my voice," that is to say:
"Whoever loves and desires the truth, I know that he will hear me." And so he won him over with a few words, until he said:
"What is truth?" And he realized that learning that word needed a long time.
Therefore he went outside, in order to rescue him from the hands of the Jews, and said to them: "I find no guilt in him."
And see how knowingly he acted: first he questioned him and learned what the charge was, and only then does he speak to them about releasing him, saying:
"Even if you do not wish to release him as innocent, yet as one guilty, grant him to this feast." For this reason he also said to them:
Gospel: "It is your custom that I release one man to you at this Passover.
Do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?" They all cried out: "Not this one, but Barabbas!" And Barabbas was a robber.
Commentary: O wicked folly! They ask for a murderer like themselves and hand the innocent one over to death,
for this has been their custom from the beginning. But you, in all of this, take note of the Master's love for humankind.
After this Pilate scourged him, perhaps for this reason: so that he might dissolve the anger of the Jews and they would no longer kill him.
And for this reason he tormented him and allowed the soldiers to clothe him in the purple robe and to put the crown of thorns on him, and then he led him out to them wearing the crown,
so that their anger might subside and, when they saw his humiliation, they might cast the venom out of their hearts and calm down.
But the Lord remained silent through all of this, just as he had earlier when they were judging him. But you, do not only listen to these words,
but take them into your mind as well, and see the King of all creation, how those soldiers mocked him in word and deed,
and he bore everything in silence. And you too, imitate him in deed. For since Pilate had said:
"King of the Jews," they also clothed him in a costume of derision. And then he led him out and said: "I find no cause at all in him."
Gospel: Jesus came outside, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe. And Pilate said to them: "Behold, the man!"
And when the chief priests and the attendants saw him, they cried out: "Crucify him, crucify him!"
Pilate said to them: "You take him and crucify him, for I have found no guilt in him."
Commentary: From this it is evident that the judge did all the earlier things as well because of their demonic frenzy, for he says: "I have found no guilt at all in him."
See how repeatedly the judge clears himself of blame. But those men, who had come to resemble the nature of dogs, could not be swayed by anything that was done.
For they had brought him so that his death might come about through the ruler's deliberation, and the opposite happened: by his judgment there came instead a release.
But since they were ashamed, for this reason they said to him:
Gospel: "We have a law, and according to our law he deserves death, for he made himself the Son of God."

Commentary: How then, when the judge said to you, "Take him away and judge him according to your law," did you say, "It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death," and now you flee to the law? And see that accusation: "He made himself the Son of God." Is this a crime? For he was the Son of God, and he did the works of the Son of God, and he said, "I am the Son of God"! But while they were saying all this, Christ remained silent, to fulfill the word of the prophet: "He does not open his mouth; in his humiliation his judgment was taken away." But Pilate became afraid when he heard, "He makes himself the Son of God," lest it should truly be so and he should commit an injustice. Yet those who had come to know the truth by deeds and by words, that it is so, were not afraid, but brought in the argument: "Whoever makes himself king speaks against Caesar." For this reason Pilate questioned him again, but Jesus answered nothing. For the man to whom he had said, "For this I was born, and for this I have come, and my kingdom is not of this world," and who after all this again believed the Jews, why should he answer him further? And since Pilate ought to have investigated carefully when he had ever shown tyranny against Caesar, and did not investigate truthfully, for this reason the Lord answered nothing, for he knew that Pilate was asking everything in vain. And also for this reason: since the deeds were bearing witness, he did not wish to prevail by words, and he also shows that he goes willingly to his passion. But when he kept silent and said nothing more, Pilate said to him:
Gospel: "Will you not speak to me? Do you not know that I have authority to crucify you and I have authority to release you?"

Commentary: Do you see how he condemned himself by his own words? For if you have all authority, wretched and vain man, and you find no cause at all, why do you not release him? Since, then, you yourself have condemned yourself, for this reason Jesus said to him: "The one who hands me over to you has the greater sin," to show him that he too had great sin, even though those who handed him over had more. And further, he humbled his mind and said to him: "You have no authority over me at all, unless it had been given to you from above," showing that this matter is a great mystery and not something done just simply in this way. But lest, on hearing "it has been given from above," he should think that he was free of guilt, for this reason he said to him: "They have the greater sin." For here by "giving" he means nothing other than permitting, that is, that this deed has been allowed to be done, but "not for that reason are you free of guilt"; he frightened him with these words. For this reason too he wished to release him, but they cried out: "If you release this man, you are no friend of Caesar, for everyone who makes himself king speaks against Caesar." And where has his tyranny appeared, O unbelievers? Or from what do you convict him of this: from a purple robe, or a crown, or horsemen? Did he not always go about in the wilderness with twelve disciples? But O folly and vain fear! For this reason Pilate was afraid, and he came out and sat down to judge, and he did not judge but handed him over to be crucified. And he also thought that perhaps they might relent, and for this reason he said to them:
Gospel: "'Behold, your king!' But they cried out: 'Take him away and crucify him!' Pilate said to them: 'Shall I crucify your king?'
The chief priests answered and said to him: 'We have no king but Caesar.'"
Commentary: See now, of their own will and with their own mouth, they fell away from the kingship of God and chose Caesar as king.
And for this reason the Lord, according to their own word, gave them over to Caesar, and, since they had denied his kingship, he abandoned them,
those who were crying out for his crucifixion. For that death by crucifixion was an evil one and under a curse, and for this reason they wished to kill him by it,
so that they might entirely blot out his memory; and they did not understand how the truth and that glory of his would be revealed.
Homily 84, on love and on doing good to enemies. But let us not merely read all this, but let us also plant in our minds the crown of thorns,
that robe of contempt, the reed and the slaps on the face, the spitting and the mockery. For if we reflect on these things,
we shall gain great benefit and shall not be angered, whatever evil anyone may bring upon us, "for a servant is not greater than his lord."
As the Jews said to him: "You are a Samaritan and have a demon," and many other such things; and for this reason he endured all this,
so that we too might follow in his footsteps, for he taught this same thing to the apostles. And so let all of us acquire this practice,
for nothing makes God so merciful toward us as love and patience and not doing evil to enemies.
When someone harms you, do not blame him but the devil who led him astray, and show him all the more mercy. For Christ too, it says, was troubled over Judas. Why was he troubled?
He became sorrowful over his perdition. Let us too imitate all of this. But if we do not imitate him and do not carry out his commandments, it would be better
if we had not been born, for faith alone without works is not enough to bring us into the kingdom, but instead becomes a cause of condemnation.
For the servant who knows the will of his lord and does not do it will be severely beaten.
What answer, then, shall we give, we who have been brought inside the kingdom, who have seen invisible things and have been made partakers of those high mysteries, and yet are worse than the pagans?
For if they showed such striving for the sake of vain glory, shall we not show it for the sake of the kingdom and of God?

For they often held even their own lives in contempt for the sake of men, but we destroy our soul for a little gold and do not hold it in contempt for Christ's sake; and we are wrathful and love abominable deeds.
Therefore I am ashamed and I tremble when I see the pagans striving and our own people not. And this comes about for this reason:
that we neither listen to God's commandments nor carry them out, but listen to God's words for a short time and then turn for a long time to the cares of the world.
And in this way that seed of the word is choked. But let us look up to heaven and look down into the graves, for we too are hastening toward the same end.
And may that creditor [?] not come upon us before then?
Let us therefore prepare for that hour, for we need abundant provisions, because the long road is waterless and hard, and we must travel all of it,
and there is no lodging for strangers and no market along the road where we might buy anything, if we do not have everything with us from here.
Listen to what those wise virgins say to the foolish ones: "Go and buy," but they did not find any.
Listen to what the prophet Ezekiel says about that day:
"Noah and Job and Daniel could not rescue their sons." But may we not hear these words; let us take provisions from here that will suffice for eternal life,
and let us see with confidence our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 85
This passage: Then Pilate handed him over to them to be crucified, and they led him away. And his cross was laid on him, and he went up to the place of the Skull.
Benefits become harmful to the wicked and the foolish, for the Jews too formerly had the grace and help of God,
yet they sought servitude to the pagans, and in the wilderness their heart longed for garlic instead of manna; and now they denied the kingship of Christ and placed Caesar's over themselves.
For this reason the Lord gave them a king according to their word. And when Pilate heard this, he handed him over to be crucified, most improperly.
For he ought to have asked when he had ever desired that kingship, since Christ had already declared:
"My kingdom is not of this world." But that wretched man did not wish to use even a little wisdom, even in view of his wife's vision,
Though this was enough to frighten him, he was not moved by any of it, nor did he lift his eyes to heaven, but handed him over to them.
And they laid the cross on him, as on a condemned man, for they [?] to touch the wood; that is why they laid it on him himself.
And as they went on, they found Simon of Cyrene, of whom the other evangelists speak, and then they took it from the Lord and laid it on him.
But here John speaks of the Lord, saying that the cross was laid on him when they led him out of the judgment hall. So it was also in the type, for then too Isaac carried the wood.
But there the deed was done according to the father's will, for it was a type, whereas here it was fulfilled in truth, for it was the truth and not a figure.
Gospel: And they came to the place of the Skull, where they crucified him.
Commentary: For some say: "Adam was buried there, and the Lord Jesus, in the place where death received the beginning of its reign,
there Christ raised up his trophy, for the cross hung as a trophy against the devil."
And they crucified him between robbers, so that here too they unwittingly fulfilled prophecy, for the prophet said this from the beginning:
"He was reckoned among the lawless." And the devil wanted to conceal the matter by this deed, but he could not, for three were crucified,
yet Jesus alone shone forth, so that you may know that it was his power that did everything. For when all three were hanging on the wood,
it was then that those miracles took place, yet no one attributed a single wonder to anyone else, but only to the Lord.
Thus the tyranny of the devil was made void and his evil plot turned back on his own head. For not only was he unable to harm the glory of the Lord, but even more,

the one robber was converted and saved, and the devil was ruined. For the conversion of the robber on the cross and his being brought into paradise was no lesser thing than the splitting of the rocks.
Gospel: And Pilate wrote a board.
Commentary: First, in order to put the Jews to shame, and again, he was also justifying himself, for them,
since they had condemned him as an evildoer and wanted to confirm this by joining him with the robbers,
he therefore did this to shut their mouths, so that all who read it might know that they had risen up against their own king.
And for this reason he set up that inscription, which proclaimed their wickedness and his kingship, though not completely and as was fitting.
And that inscription was not in Hebrew only, but in three languages, for since many others were also there because of the feast,
he therefore did this so that all might know the matter, and he exposed the wickedness of the Jews.
But they grew angry at this, for they envied him even when crucified. But, O lawless ones, how did that inscription harm you?
For if he is mortal and weak, how do those letters harm you, and why are you afraid because they say "King of the Jews"?
But the matter was not without purpose. Rather, since the crosses were to be buried, and they were to be sought and found after many ages, and all three would be together,
therefore, so that the cross of the King might not go unrecognized, the board remained in place by divine providence, so that by it they might recognize it, for the robbers had no boards with them.
And for this reason Pilate did not listen to those who were saying: "Do not write him down as king of the Jews, but rather that he said: 'I am king of the Jews.'"
See their wickedness: they wanted that inscription to be more of an accusation against him, because he said [?]:
"I am king." But the men of the host divided his garments, and they did not divide the tunic.
See how the prophecies were being fulfilled in every respect; and this too had been foretold from the beginning.
And you, marvel at how the prophet wisely told of everything: not only that "they divided," but also that "they cast lots for the tunic."
Now the phrase "woven from above" is not there to no purpose, but I think that it is a figure, signifying that the crucified one was not merely a simple man,
but also had divinity from heaven; for the nature of the divinity remained impassible and undivided, while the nature of the flesh suffered and was wounded.
And again, some say that the evangelist is indicating the actual form of the garment,
for in Palestine they join two pieces of cloth and weave them together as one, and make that into a tunic, and they call it "woven from above."
And the evangelist said this in order to indicate his lowly state, for such a tunic is a poor thing,
which was a figure of the word spoken earlier, which we discussed concerning this "woven from above."
And the soldiers were doing these things, while he himself, even on the cross, was entrusting his mother to the beloved disciple, so that he might teach us too the service owed to parents.
But John again conceals himself out of humility, for if he had not kept silent out of his great humility,
he would also have stated the reason for which the Lord loved him; for the reason was great and wonderful, had he told it.
But why does he not speak some other word of consolation to John, who was standing there grieving?
First, because it was not the time to say many words; and second, because this too was no small honor and consolation, that he entrusted his own mother to him.
And see how, while crucified, he did and said everything without being troubled:
he spoke to the disciple about his mother, he fulfilled the prophecies, he saved the thief, he who before the crucifixion had been distressed and afraid.
But there he acted so in order to show his human nature, while here he displayed the power of the divinity, and did so in order to teach us
that, even if we fear afflictions, we should still not flee from them, for once we have entered into them, everything is easy.
Let us therefore not tremble at death, when it is required to die for God's sake.
For although our nature has fear of it, yet if we wish, we weaken that fear, and if we wish, we magnify it.
Only let us neither rush to death of our own will, nor, if the time comes, be terrified and honor this passing world more than eternal life.
Gospel: Now there stood by the cross his mother, and his mother's sister, Mary of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.
Commentary: For Mary of Clopas was the brother's wife of Joseph, to whom the Mother of God was betrothed, and she was a friend of the holy Mother of God.
And for this reason he gave her the name of her sister, because she was her friend and also her kinswoman.
But see how that weak nature of women stood there so fearlessly, and they were braver than the men.
Thus everything was being changed. And the Lord Jesus entrusted his mother to that beloved disciple and said to him:
Gospel: "Woman, behold, your son!" Then he said to that disciple: "Behold, your mother!"
Commentary: Oh, what honor! With what great honor he honored that disciple! For since he was departing, he entrusted her to the disciple in his own place and said to him:
"Behold, your mother," on account of which he took her to his own home. And he did this to teach us care for our parents above all things.
But if they should destroy the benefit of our soul, we ought not to take them into account; yet if they do not harm our soul, we ought to care for them above all things.
Gospel: "After this Jesus saw that everything had been accomplished, and so that the Scripture might be fulfilled, he said: 'I thirst.'"

Commentary: He saw that his whole dispensation had been accomplished, for death and not dying were within his own power. And for this reason, until the time had been fulfilled, he did not wish to taste death. And he said, "I thirst," so that he might fulfill that prophecy as well. But you, look at their foulness! For even if we have countless enemies, when we see them in death we relent. But they did not relent in spite of all this; rather, they grew more savage and increased their mockery. They held up vinegar to him with a sponge, and they put hyssop on a reed and held it up to him in this way, for they themselves did not wish even to touch him, as though he were something evil, but held it up to him with a reed and hyssop. And he himself, when he had received that vinegar, said: "The Scripture has been fulfilled." Do you see how he does everything with authority? Hear also what follows: how, when he saw that all Scripture had been fulfilled, he bowed his head and gave up the spirit. See here his authority! For when we give up the spirit, it is then that the head droops. But here, when he himself willed it, he bowed his head and gave up the spirit. And by all this the evangelist shows that he was Lord of all. But the Jews, in turn, who swallowed a camel and strained out a gnat, having done such a terrible deed, were making inquiry about the day and being scrupulous over it.

Gospel: But the Jews, so that those bodies might not remain on the cross until the Sabbath, for the day of that Sabbath was a great one, asked Pilate that their legs might be broken and that they might be taken away.

Commentary: See how strong the truth is, for the prophecy was being fulfilled through the very deeds they were so eager to do. For when the soldiers came, they broke the legs of the other two, but not those of Jesus; instead, to gratify the Jews, they pierced his side with a lance and went on abusing that dead body. O defiled and foul mind! But do not be troubled, do not be grieved, beloved, for all that they did with a wicked mind was aiding the truth. For this too was a prophecy, which said: "They shall look on him whom they pierced." And after this it became a cause of faith for the unbelieving, as for Thomas. And again a fearsome mystery was being accomplished, for "blood and water came out." And these two streams did not come forth simply and to no purpose, but because the mystery of the church comes from these two; and the faithful know that they are born by water and nourished by the blood and flesh of the Lord. For this reason we also mix water with the wine and so offer it at the holy liturgy, so that when we approach the holy chalice, it may be reckoned to us as though we were drawing near to the very side of the King and receiving from it; and let us approach with such a thought.
Gospel: And he who saw has testified, and his testimony is true.
Commentary: That is to say: "I did not hear this from others, but I myself was there, and I saw, and this is true."
For the evangelist wished to stop the mouths of the heretics who were going to appear after him.
For this reason he confirms the saying: "And here too the prophecy was fulfilled: 'His bone shall not be broken.'"
For this saying, although it was spoken about the lamb slaughtered by the Jews, was nevertheless a type of this truth.
Do you see how he strives to confirm these words and to make that contemptible deed credible?
For the wounding of that dead body was a greater insult than the crucifixion.
But the evangelist says: "I have said all this earnestly so that you may believe."
So let no one be unbelieving, nor be ashamed of these things of ours and conceal them, for rather,
the things that appear to be a cause of contempt and reproach are our good things and our honors.
Gospel: After this Joseph of Arimathea asked Pilate, for he too was a disciple of Jesus.

Commentary: He was a disciple, one of the Seventy, and he asked Pilate for the body of the Lord, and Pilate gave it, for why should he have begrudged it, since he had already killed him? And Nicodemus also helped Joseph, and they buried him with honor, for they regarded him as a mere man; for this reason they had brought these spices, which preserve the body of a dead person from decay for a long time. And from this it is evident that they looked on him as a man, and they showed him great love and honor, even though they did not look on him as perfect God. See how none of the Twelve came, neither Peter, nor John, nor any other of the eminent ones, and the evangelist does not conceal even this; for if anyone should say it was from fear of the Jews, these men too were afraid, and yet they came. And John was standing there when he gave up the spirit, and he did nothing of this kind. But I think that this came about because these men were very prominent, and Joseph was also known to Pilate, and he made his request of him and took the body away, and they buried him not as one condemned, but according to the custom of the Jews, as someone great and wonderful. And since it was evening, they laid him in that nearby tomb. And this too came about by divine providence, that he was laid in a new tomb, so that the resurrection might not be supposed to be that of anyone else, but his, and so that the disciples might come easily, for the place was close by, and so that not only they, but even the enemies themselves might be witnesses of the burial, so that no one could say, "He was not buried."
Gospel: On the first day of the week Mary Magdalene came to the tomb at dawn, while it was still dark, and she saw the stone taken away from the door of the tomb.

Commentary: On the first day of the week, which is Sunday, she came. Now Jesus had risen while the stone still lay on the tomb and the seals were upon it; and since it was necessary that all the others too should see this, the stone was taken away after his resurrection. For this reason, when the Sabbath had passed, Mary came there, for she had great zeal for the Lord; and when she saw the stone taken away, she ran to tell the disciples, so that she might learn where his body was. For this is why she said: "They have taken my Lord from the tomb, and I do not know where they have laid him." Do you see that she did not yet know anything for certain about the resurrection? For she supposed he had been moved to another place, and that is why she went and told the disciples. And they arrived there in haste and saw the linen cloths and the napkin, which was a sign of the resurrection. For if someone had moved him to another place, why would his body have been stripped? And if someone had stolen him, why would he have left all this there? Or why would he have taken the trouble to fold up the napkin and lay it apart by itself, rather than taking him just as he found him? For this is why the evangelist said beforehand: "They brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, a hundred pounds," which binds linen and body together more firmly than lead, so that when you hear, "The linen cloths lay by themselves," you may not listen to those who say, "They stole him." For who would be so foolish a thief as to undertake so much labor, stripping off what was glued on with myrrh? Or how would he have remained hidden while he was doing all that? And why did the linen cloths lie to one side and the napkin folded by itself? So that you may know that the thing was not done hastily or in fear, for so calmly was the one placed by itself and the other folded by itself and laid in order. For this reason the disciples saw all this and knew that he had neither been stolen nor laid in another place, and they believed in the resurrection. But see here too the humility of the evangelist, how he says of himself: "He came first, yet he did not search, nor did he go inside." But Peter, more fervent, went in and searched everything, and only then did he too go in; and they saw the wrappings set apart by themselves, from which they knew that no one had done this in haste or in fear, and they believed.

Moral Teaching 85: That one must not bury the dead in costly wrappings, but do acts of mercy for them.

As for you, when you hear that the Lord rose naked, cease from those costly wrappings. For what is this great and vain expense, which profits the departed nothing? Indeed, if you will allow it, let me say that it even does harm, for the costliness of wrappings has often given thieves cause to dig up the grave, and they cast the body aside naked. But oh, vainglory! For even in the time of mourning it displays its tyranny, for many even pour fragrant ointment into the wrappings and bury the dead that way. Are these not, then, the deeds of madmen? And if someone says, "Then why did they bury Christ in this way?" I say: do not put his affairs on a level with those of men. For a harlot too poured ointment on those holy feet of his. And let me say this as well: "They did not know at that time the word of the resurrection," and so they did this according to the custom of the Jews. So that you may know that Christ had no need of this, he says: "You saw me hungry and fed me, and thirsty and gave me drink." And nowhere does he say: "You saw me dead and buried me in expensive clothing." For it is not that I am keeping you from burial and wrappings — God forbid! — but from that vain excess. And if you say, "Love of the departed persuades us to do this," this is not love. But if you love the departed, I will show you the work of love: clothe him in garments that never decay and that no one will steal; that is, mercy. He will rise with it and be glorified, for those to whom he will say, "I was hungry and you fed me," will shine in that garment. But these present adornments are nothing but a table for worms. For one should wrap the dead in due measure, but what need is there of that vain thing? Those who are commanded to pass even this life with a single garment, why after death do you clothe them in costly garments and gold and silver? Let us cease from this vanity, and let us wrap the departed as is fitting and do acts of mercy for them. Let us send along with them a good companion, for this is what delivers the soul from torment. This has even raised the dead, as with Tabitha. Such wrappings are good. If we bury ourselves in this way, we shall be fair and radiant at the time of the resurrection; but if we adorn the flesh and do not labor for the soul, much evil and great disgrace will then come upon us, for it is no small evil when the soul is naked of virtues. Let us adorn it all the days of our life; and if we have been negligent here, let us hasten at the time of our end to do acts of mercy, so that in this way we may find boldness before our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and ever and to the ages of ages, amen.
Chapter 86
This saying: "Then the disciples went away again to their own homes, but Mary stood outside by the tomb and wept." The nature of women is tender and easily moved to mourning.

And I have said this so that you may not wonder how Mary stood and wept while the disciples went away to their homes. For she was mournful by nature, and she also did not know the word of the resurrection in the way
that those did who had seen the linen cloths and went away in wonder. But she stood there and wept, and looked down into the tomb where the body of the Lord had been.
For this reason she received no small reward for her eagerness, for what the disciples had not seen,
the woman saw: angels clothed in white, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of the Lord had lain.
For since the woman's mind was not so lofty that she would believe in the resurrection from the linen cloths and the napkin, she therefore saw radiant angels,
so that they might comfort her. Yet they said nothing to her about the resurrection, but she came to understanding by herself, for they said only this to her: "Woman, why are you weeping?"
And in this way they opened to her the door of understanding, and the manner of their sitting led her to ask questions. For since she did not dare to ask, they therefore began to speak first.

But when she said to them, "They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him," what are you saying, Mary? Do you not yet understand the resurrection? Do you see how they were still ignorant?
Gospel: When she had said this, she turned around.
Commentary: And why did she do this, since she had asked them and turned around before they had answered?
But I think that while she was saying this, Christ suddenly appeared behind her and the angels were afraid; when they saw the King, they showed their fear in their appearance and in their faces.
And when Mary saw them like this, she turned around, for the Lord appeared awesome to the angels,
but not so to her, so that she might not be afraid, for one who was so lowly could not yet bear this matter.
Therefore he appeared in another form, so that she took him for the gardener, and the Lord asked her: "Woman, whom are you seeking?"
And when she perceived, "He knows whom I am seeking," she therefore said to him: "Lord, if you have taken him away, tell me."
And when the Lord saw her eagerness, he revealed himself to her, for when he himself wishes he is recognized, and when he wishes he is hidden.
And here too, when he said to her, "Mary!" she immediately recognized the Lord and turned around to look.
But how did she turn around to look, since he was speaking to her? I think that when she asked,
"Lord, if you have taken him away, tell me," she immediately turned toward the angels to ask them why they were so amazed, and then the Lord said to her: "Mary!"
And when she heard and recognized his voice, she turned back to him, for she recognized him by his voice.
And if anyone should say, "And how is it known that she turned toward the angels?" then how is this known, that she touched him?
But just as this is known from the fact that the Lord said, "Do not touch me,"
so that is likewise known from the fact that it says, "She turned around to look." But why did the Lord say, "Do not touch me"?
I think that she wished to be with him in the same way as before the crucifixion, and in her joy she was running to meet him,
and she did not understand that it is no longer proper to touch him in that way, and for this reason Jesus said to her, "Do not touch me."
And if he had said, "Do not approach me so boldly as before, for things are no longer as they were, and I no longer intend to be with you in that way,"
it would have been a stumbling block to her weakness, for this saying, namely:
"I have not yet ascended to my Father" — this was better, for when he said, "I have not yet ascended to my Father," he was indicating this:
"I am going up there and will no longer be among men, and it is not fitting that you should see me in the same way as before." And then he said to her:
Gospel: "Go and say to my brothers: 'I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.'"
Commentary: He was not going to ascend immediately, but after forty days. Why then did he say this to her now?
Because he wished to assure her that he was going up to heaven. And this saying, namely:
"my Father and your Father, my God and your God" — this belongs to his human nature, and the ascent to heaven is on account of the nature of the flesh,
for these words were addressed to her, who could understand nothing lofty. But he is his Father in one way and ours in another,
for if God is God of righteous men in one way and of other men in another, then how could he not be God of the Son and of us in different ways?
For he is his Father by nature, but ours by the grace of being Creator; and again, he is our God by nature, but his by the dispensation of the nature of the flesh.
And even according to the nature of the flesh he is not Father to him in the same way as he is to us, just as he is not God equally of the righteous and of other men,
for although by the nature of the flesh he became our brother, there was nevertheless a great difference, for he was to sit on the paternal thrones, while they were to stand before him.
Gospel: "Mary Magdalene came to tell the disciples that she had seen the Lord and that he had said these things to her."
Commentary: She recounted to them his appearance and his words and how she had seen him. And when the disciples heard, they were likely either to disbelieve her,
or to be distressed because he had not deemed them worthy of seeing him, though he had promised them that they would see him after the resurrection.
Therefore, so that they might not grieve, when evening came he appeared to them with great wonder,
with the doors shut and at evening. This was because at evening it was more wondrous, and because the grief of those who grieve increases more at night, whereas by day the doors were open.
And so in the evening he stood before them as they sat inside behind shut doors. He did not knock at the door, nor did he make any commotion,
but in an instant he stood before them and showed them his hands and his side. With words, too, he calmed their troubled minds, saying to them:
"Peace be with you", which means "Do not be troubled". And he reminded them of the word that he had spoken to them before the crucifixion:
"My peace I leave with you." And again: "In me may you have peace."
Gospel: The disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord.
Commentary: Do you see how words are fulfilled in deeds?
For what he had said to them before the crucifixion, "I will see you, and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you", has now been fulfilled in deed.
Since they were engaged in an unending war with the Jews, he says to them again and again:
"Peace be with you", so that he might give them peace as a means of overcoming that war and as a consolation. For he had said this word first of all, as soon as he rose.
For this reason the apostle Paul always says, "Grace and peace to you." But to the women the Lord announced joy first of all,
for that sex was in sorrow. So, to suit the men's warfare, he announced peace,
but because of the women's sorrow he announced joy. And since he had accomplished everything, he now speaks of the work of the cross: "Peace be with you!"
Since every obstacle had been removed and the victory had become glorious, he then said to them:
Gospel: "As the Father has sent me, so I also send you."
Commentary: That is: "There is no longer any difficulty before you, since I have conquered, and I am sending you."
At this point he gladdens their souls and makes them joyful, when they heard that they were to do the work of the Lord himself.
He no longer prays to the Father, but by his own authority gives them grace and power. For the evangelist says:
Gospel: And when he had said this, he breathed on them and said: "Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven; and if you retain the sins of any, they are retained."
Commentary: When a king sends out his governors, he gives them authority to cast into prison and to release.
In the same way, when the Lord sent out the disciples, he gave them this kind of authority. But how?
For he had said earlier, "If I do not go away, he will not come," and yet here he now gives the Spirit. Some say:
"He did not give the Holy Spirit, but by that breathing he made them ready and fit to receive him when he came." For if Daniel, when he saw an angel,
was struck with terror and became afraid, how could they have borne that awesome grace if they had not been prepared beforehand?
That is why he did not say, "You have received the Holy Spirit," but "Receive the Holy Spirit." Yet it is also not unfitting for us to say:
"Even then they received spiritual power and authority. It was not the power to raise the dead and work miracles, but to forgive sins to those
[?] who would turn to God and repent of their sins," for the graces of the Holy Spirit are many, and here they received the grace of this one work only,
but after the day of Pentecost they received the grace of all signs and powers and tongues, for the grace of the Holy Spirit is incomprehensible and his gifts are manifold.
And this was done so that you may know that the gift of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit is one, for whatever might be thought
to belong to the Father only is found to belong also to the Son and to the Holy Spirit, except for unbegottenness and begottenness and procession,
For being unbegotten belongs to the Father, being begotten to the Son, and procession to the Holy Spirit, but everything else of theirs is one.
Whatever is the Father's is also the Son's and the Holy Spirit's, for it says: "No one comes to the Son unless the Father brings him."
But it is found that the Son also has this same power, for he says: "I am the way, and no one comes to the Father except through me";
and again the same belongs to the Holy Spirit as well, for no one can say "Lord Jesus" except by the Holy Spirit;
and again, they say that the apostles were given to the Church by grace, sometimes by the Father, sometimes by the Son, and sometimes by the Holy Spirit.
Homily 86: That priests must be honored. Therefore let us all strive that the grace of the Holy Spirit may be with us, and let us honor priests with great honor,
for great is the honor of priests, and they have the grace of the Holy Spirit, as the Apostle says: "Obey your teachers."
For you care for yourself, and if you do your own deeds well, you have no care to bear for others,
but a priest, even if he himself is pleasing to God, if he does not manage your life well, goes away to Gehenna with the wicked;
and often he is himself good and yet perishes on account of your sins, if he does not do with diligence everything that it is his duty to do.
Therefore you must honor priests, for the Apostle indicated this, that they keep watch over your souls, since they have to give an account.
Therefore you must honor them, for in this way they are all the more able to exert diligence on your behalf; if you despise them,
your affairs will go badly, and they too will slacken in helping you. Hear what the Lord says:
"The scribes and Pharisees have sat down on the seat of Moses; so whatever they tell you to do, do it." But now no one can say:
"The priests have sat down on the seat of Moses," but rather on that of Christ, for they hold his teaching, and therefore honor is due to them.
Do you not see that all obey the rulers of this world, even if they themselves are better than those rulers?
And if it is so with one whom a man appoints, is not honor due all the more to those appointed by God?
What word of defense, then, can they have, those who have been commanded not to judge a neighbor, and yet revile and denounce priests?
Yet I do not say this as though those who approach the priesthood unworthily were good;
on the contrary, they are greatly to be pitied and worthy of weeping, but their flocks ought not to despise them.
For if you are good, you will suffer no harm from his evil; and,
if God showed teaching through a donkey and poured out a blessing through a magus, would he not give you grace through priests and bestow the Holy Spirit on you?
For not even a holy man brings that grace by his own holiness, but it is grace that does everything; for not only does a human priest do nothing, but neither does an angel
or an archangel do anything in these gifts of God; rather, it is the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit who administers everything,
and the priest lends his tongue and gives his hand; for how could that grace upon the believers be harmed by that priest?
Therefore, then, let us who know these things both fear God and honor the priests,
so that in this way we may receive a reward from God by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 87
This saying: "But Thomas, one of the twelve, who was called the Twin, was not with them
when the Lord came." Just as believing idly and hastily in this way is not good, so too investigating the truth beyond measure is improper.
For this reason Thomas became pitiable, because he did not believe the disciples: not that he considered them liars, but the matter of resurrection from the dead seemed impossible to him.
But how was it that they were all together, and Thomas was not there?
Evidently, after the scattering that took place at the Lord's arrest, he had not yet come back to them from that time on.
But you, see the Lord's love for humankind, how for the sake of that one soul he hastened to save it and showed him his wounds, in order to make that man of dull mind understand.
And why did he appear after eight days? So that during the days that passed in between he might keep hearing from the disciples and come to long for it.
And how did he know that his side had been pierced? He had heard it from his companions themselves. And how is it, then, that he believed that but not this?
Because this was an exceedingly fearful matter. See, then, the truthfulness of the apostles, how they truthfully tell every shortcoming of their own and of their companions.
Then Christ appeared, and he did not wait to hear anything from him, but himself anticipated him and called him, in order to show that when he was saying,
"I do not believe," he heard him, for nothing was hidden from him. And he said to him: "Bring your fingers and see my hands, and put your hand in my side."
Do you see how weak they were before receiving the Holy Spirit? But from then on they truly became perfect.
And when he believed and said, "My Lord and my God," the Lord said to him: "You have seen me and you believe; blessed are those who have not seen and have believed."
For this is faith: when one who has not seen him believes. And here he calls blessed not only the disciples but all believers.
For the disciples too believed in the resurrection without seeing it, when they saw only the linen cloths and the shroud lying by themselves.
And now, if anyone should say, "Oh, if only I had lived in those days and had seen Christ's miracles,"
let him hear this word which he speaks: "Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed."
Now it is right for us to wonder how the marks of the wounds were on that incorruptible body and how it could be touched by mortal hands,
but understand that this was a matter of divine dispensation, for he who was so subtle and fine
that he entered through closed doors did this to confirm his resurrection, and so that they might know that he is the one who was crucified.
And for this same reason he also ate and showed his wounds. It was not that there was any grossness in his flesh at that time; rather, he did all this then for the sake of that disciple.
Gospel: Jesus also did many other signs
Commentary: For, since this one said less than those other evangelists, he now says that the others too have not told everything, but told only a little,
only as much as was enough to bring people to faith; otherwise the world itself could not have contained those books. But let us also say this:
if anyone believes all this, he needs nothing else; if he does not believe this, then even if he should hear something else, he would still not believe.
But here he speaks of these signs done after the resurrection, for he said, "in the presence of his disciples," and, just as before the crucifixion
signs were necessary so that it might be believed that he is the Son of God, so likewise after the resurrection it was necessary to perform signs, so that it might be believed that he had risen.
Gospel: "After this he again revealed himself to his disciples at the Sea of Tiberias."

Commentary: Do you see that he did not dwell with them continually, as he had before? For he appeared in the evening and vanished, and again after eight days, and again at the sea. But what does "he manifested himself" mean? From this it is clear that his incorruptible and intangible body was invisible, and that it was impossible to see him unless he himself manifested himself. And why did he mention the place? He shows that their fear had passed, and that they went about wherever they wished and went out to fish; for since he himself was not with them and they had not yet received the Holy Spirit, they had nothing to do, and so they fished, plying their trade. And there were Peter and Thomas and Nathanael, who had been called by Philip, and the sons of Zebedee and two others, and the other disciples followed along, and they were toiling in hardship. And then the Lord came and said to them: "Do you perhaps have anything to eat?" Is he not speaking to them in a human way? And when they said, "We have nothing," he commanded them to cast the net on the right side, and when they cast it, they came upon fish. Then they recognized him, and then the disciples Peter and John again showed their own characters; for Peter was the more ardent and John the more lofty, Peter the quicker and John the more perceptive. For this reason John was the first to recognize the Lord and Peter was the first to come to him. For the marvels were not small: the catching of so many fish, the net not tearing, and the finding of coals and fish on the seashore, for wood was no longer needed for the fire. And when they had come out, the Lord said, "Come and let us dine," and no one dared to question him, for they no longer had such boldness, nor did they speak to him, but they sat in silence and fear and looked on, since they knew that it was the Lord. For they knew this, that it was he, but they saw that other form and awesome appearance, and they wished to ask about it and did not dare, but they ate what he had miraculously given them. For here he does not look up to heaven, nor does he do human actions, so that he might make them understand that all those things too were done by dispensation. And he commanded them to bring also some of those fish that they had caught, so as to show that the event was not an illusion. Here, then, it does not say that he ate with them, but Luke says, "He ate with them." But how he ate, it is not for us to say, for it came about in some strange manner, not because his nature still needed food, but he did it by dispensation for their sake.

Homily 87, on patience and sufferings. Now when you hear these things, are you perhaps moved to compunction, and do you call blessed those who were with him and those who will be with him on that day?
Let us hasten to see that radiant face of his with delight on that day.
I beseech you, then, let us not fall away from such glory, for this matter is not difficult, nor is it heavy,
if only we are willing and endure all things for his sake, so that we may reign with him, and walk here on that narrow way.
For although it appears narrow, yet it becomes for us the cause of great spaciousness.

Let us then lift up our eyes to heaven and think on the good things that are there, and in this way let us bear every affliction of the world with joy, and no affair of the world will be able to enslave us,
If we love Christ, we will not even pay attention to the affairs of the world, for great is the power of love.
Let us too say: "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ: tribulation, or distress, and what follows?"
For see how the apostle did not speak of wealth, or desire, or any other such thing, for all of this is contemptible, but he spoke of those hard things:
of death and persecutions and fire and sword, and he counted all these heavy things as nothing,
but we, for the sake of wealth and foul desires, fall away from life and light.
Paul counted death and life and this passing world and the world to come and everything else as nothing beside the love of Christ,
but in our case a small desire makes us forget all of that, and we swear oaths and plunder and lend at interest and seek the taking of flesh [?] and
we do not call to mind those eternal good things, and we do not call to mind those eternal torments, nor those good things of which we are being deprived.
For if, according to the word of the Lord, our righteousness does not exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees, we go to Gehenna; what answer shall we give if it is not even as great as theirs?
But no, beloved, let us not be like this, but let us strive to love Christ as he loved us,
so that we may find eternal rest by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong glory and power, now and always and to the ages of ages, amen.
Chapter 88
This saying: "And when they had dined, Jesus said to Simon Peter: 'Simon son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?'
Peter said to him: 'Yes, Lord, you know that I love you.'" There are many things that God seeks from us, but more than everything he seeks love of neighbor.
And for this reason too the Lord says to Peter: "If you love me, feed my lambs." But why did he pass over the others and ask this one?
Because he was the head of all the disciples, and because he also wished to assure him that the stain of that denial had been wiped away.
So then, when he had asked him once and twice, Peter brought that very Examiner of minds as his witness, and he asked him yet again, a third time.
Then he became afraid that some further trial might be coming upon him. Do you see how he had learned no longer to trust in himself?
But the Lord asked a third time and said the same thing to him three times, to show how precious he holds the care of his sheep, so much so that he continually made it [?] the sign of his love.
And when he had said this, he next tells him of his martyrdom, to show that he does not distrust his words. Therefore he says to him:

Gospel: "Amen, amen, I say to you, when you were young, you girded yourself and went wherever you wished, but when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands and others will gird you, and you will be where you do not wish."
Commentary: He too longed for this, for he used to say: "I will lay down my life for you." And for this reason he here fulfilled his longing. But what does "where you do not wish" mean?
He is speaking of what belongs to nature and of the suffering of the flesh, that the soul is separated from the body under compulsion, for his mind was eager,
but even so he was opposed by nature, for no one leaves the body unfeelingly, since God has so ordained it.
And here too this saying, "where you do not wish," signifies the natural condition, while the saying "when you were young"
indicated his former life, as if he were saying: "In the affairs of the world a young man is vigorous, but my affairs are not like this;
rather, when old age comes, then your courage and virtue will appear all the more, and age will not be a hindrance to them."
He said this not to frighten him but to strengthen him, for he knew his desire, that from the beginning he had set his heart on this good; and he was also indicating the manner of his death.
Having said this, the Evangelist immediately says: "He said this to indicate by what death he would glorify God."
Not "he would die," but "he would glorify God," for death for Christ's sake is the glory of the one who suffers.
Gospel: "Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved, who had also leaned on his breast at the supper, and he said: 'Lord, what about this one?'"
Commentary: Why did he remind us of that leaning? Not idly, but in order to show
how much boldness had been given to Peter after his denial, for he who at that time did not dare to ask now asks even about John.
And here he also shows the love that he had for John, for Peter loved him greatly, and this is evident throughout the Gospel and in the Acts of the Apostles.
And since the Lord had given him the flock of the world, had foretold his martyrdom, and had accepted his love,
he then asked about John: "Will this one not be likewise?" And the Lord said to him:
Gospel: "If I wish him to remain until I come, what is that to you?"
Commentary: Since Peter was speaking out of great love and did not want to be separated from him, Christ shows
that however much he may love him, he cannot match his love, and he said: "If I wish him to remain until I come, what is that to you?"
Gospel: And this saying spread among the brothers, that that disciple would not die; yet Jesus did not say to him:
'He will not die,' but: 'If I wish him to remain until my coming.'"
Commentary: See here the humility of mind of the Evangelist, for he stated the thought of the disciples and then corrects it,
as if they had not understood that saying, for he did not say, "He will not die," but: "If I wish him to remain until my coming."
Gospel: This is the disciple who testifies about this and who wrote this, and I know that his testimony is true.
Commentary: Why is it that none of the other Evangelists did this, yet this one, behold, has said this even twice?
But they say that he began writing the Gospel last of all, because Christ commanded him to do this.
For this reason he speaks repeatedly of his love and cries out: "The words of God are true"; and whoever does not believe, let him hear the following saying and believe:
Gospel: "And there is also much else that Jesus did; if it were written down one by one, the world itself could not contain the books written."
Commentary: From this it would be known that everything is true.
For he who, out of so many marvels, did not even tell of others, but told only the disputes with the Jews and their insults, how would he have told any lie?
And since he wrote with great zeal, for this reason he does not shrink from bringing in his own testimony as well, for he is truthful; and we too,
when we speak the truth, are not afraid to bring forward our own testimony as well. And if we act in this way, would he not have done so all the more,
he who wrote by the Holy Spirit, and was present through all things, and stood there at the crucifixion, and to whom the mother of the Lord was entrusted, all of which was a sign of love?
But as for his saying, "Not even the world itself could contain them," do not marvel at this, nor be unbelieving, but call to mind the inexpressible power of the Lord and accept this in faith,
for just as it is easy for us to speak a word, so it is far easier for him to do whatever he wishes, for merely willing was enough, and everything came to be.
Homily 88. On the divine and the devilish way of life and on avarice. Let us then listen to these things that have been well said,
so that in this way we may be able to make our life pure, in this way we may be able to root out the thorns of the passions,
for such are sin and the care of the world, fruitless and evil, and like a caltrop, from whatever side one holds it, it wounds.
So too the care of the world, from whatever side you approach it, harms you; but spiritual deeds are not like this, rather they are like a pearl, and,
whichever way you turn it, it is delightful and lovely. For if someone shows mercy, or [?] something else [?].
But if we have sinned, let us shed tears, let us mourn as is fitting, let us strip away our sins, as Zacchaeus did, so let us also do.
And just as with a wound or a disease, if you do not first stop the cause of the disease and draw out the discharge [?], then even if you pour on many medicines, it is of no benefit,
so with us: if we do not restrain our hands from avarice, everything is vain, for even if we give alms,
or do some other good thing, and then remain in avarice again, we are defiled by it again and become worse than before.
Let us therefore cease from avarice and robbery, and in this way let us give alms.
For if someone were falling from a great height, and one person were holding him from above while another dragged him from below, nothing would result
except the tearing apart of that man. So then, lest this befall us too, and lest almsgiving let go of us because of the weight of avarice,

for this reason let us be on our guard and hasten to depart from evil things, so that by good deeds we may be made perfect and may attain those eternal good things, by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ,
to whom belong glory and honor, worship and might, glory and great splendor, together with the Father who is without beginning and the all-holy,
good and life-giving Spirit, now and always and in the endless ages to come, unto ages of ages. Amen.
