Colophon of Saint Euthymius the Athonite. Glory to you, O Holy Trinity. The commentary on the chapters of the Gospel of John has been completed with the help of Christ. Amen.
He who was from the beginning with God, the Word of God.
who shares the throne of the Father and the Holy Spirit, all things were made through him, as John the Theologian says, and the blessed Paul proclaims:
"Through him all things in the heavens and on earth were created, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities
or powers; all things were created through him and for him, and he himself is before all things, and all things were established through him."
For in his great goodness he created all things out of nothing, in wisdom, and over this visible world he stretched out the firmament of heaven
like a vault, and in it he set the luminaries, to shine upon the earth and to assist the affairs of human beings.
And he made man in his own image and likeness, and placed him in the paradise of delight, with free will
and with honor, and he gave him a commandment as the material and exercise of his free will, as Scripture says.

But through the envy of the devil and the deception of the woman, he forgot the commandment given to him and was overcome into eating from the tree, and for this reason he fell out of paradise and became an exile in this world.
And from then on death reigned, and sin multiplied among the human race, and lawlessness took hold of the whole world.

But in the last times the only-begotten Son and Word of God resolved upon the salvation of human beings, and by the counsel of the Father he came down from heaven and put on flesh from the Holy Spirit and from the Virgin Mary,
and he became man, like us in all respects except for sin, and he purchased us with his precious blood and prepared for us a second, spiritual firmament,
which is the holy Church, and in it he set shining luminaries: the holy apostles, prophets, teachers, martyrs and fathers,
through whom he enlightens the human race and brings their minds to the understanding of the Holy Trinity by the guidance of his grace; and those who follow him
he makes children of God and heirs of this unshadowed light. And "this visible firmament of heaven," as Scripture says,
"will be rolled up like a scroll on the day of the Second Coming, and its stars will fall like leaves";
but this spiritual heaven, which he prepared for us by his incarnation, he himself will then make shine forth all the more, and he will reveal its luminaries as far more brilliant than the sun.
Concerning this spiritual firmament the prophet David said by the Spirit:
"The heavens declare the glory of God, the created thing, the work of his hands — the firmament," for truly this came to pass.
For after the resurrection Christ commanded the holy apostles:
"Go, make disciples of all the Gentiles," and then on the day of Pentecost he sent them the Holy Spirit and filled them with grace.
They went out and made disciples of all the Gentiles, and they recounted the glory of God and the indescribable works of his dispensation.
And they fulfilled their preaching not by word alone, but by the grace of the Holy Spirit they also left us the mystery of salvation in writing,
for the all-praised evangelists, whom the Holy Spirit commanded to write, wrote down the holy Gospel and taught us those glorious wonders,
which our Lord Jesus Christ accomplished while he lived in the world among men, and everything that he took upon himself for our salvation:
the crucifixion, the burial and the resurrection, and the ascension into heaven in glory, and his glorious second coming.
And they called this book the Gospel, because the good news of every good thing is written in it, as Saint John Chrysostom says.
Then again the blessed Paul and the other apostles strengthened the believers by their epistles and gave us all the teaching of the service of God.
But since in the writings of the evangelists and apostles there was much that was hard to understand, and certain unlearned and unstable people were twisting it, to their own destruction,
as the apostle Peter says in the Catholic Epistle, therefore after the apostles the Lord brought forth other luminaries as well for that firmament of the church,
the holy hierarchs, who, according to the grace given to them, explained to us everything in the Scriptures that is hard to comprehend, and
they anathematized those heretics, the perverters of the truth, and drove them in disgrace from the church, and they enlightened the people of the believers.
But above all others the grace of teaching and of interpreting the Scriptures was given to the holy and God-clad John Chrysostom,
who was archbishop in Constantinople. For before him [?] there were great luminaries: Saint Athanasius of Alexandria, and Saint Gregory the Wonderworker
of Neocaesarea, and Saint Basil of Caesarea in Cappadocia, and Saint Gregory the Theologian, and Saint Gregory of Nyssa, and others like these. However,
since in their days the error of the idol-worshippers and of the heretics was very great, Arius and Eunomius, Sabellius and Macedonius and Apollinaris and many others,
those holy fathers were occupied with battling and opposing them, and with many struggles and labors they established the true faith.
For their combat was also against heretical emperors, and for this reason they had no leisure to interpret the Scriptures,
but all their writing was on behalf of the true faith and in opposition to the heretics,
except only that Saint Basil wrote some interpretations of the Scriptures and divine teachings, full of spiritual wisdom. But,

when, by the grace of the Lord and the struggles of those blessed fathers, that fog of the heretics had been dispersed, and orthodox emperors reigned, and the church had been made firm upon the preaching of the apostles,
then the Lord brought forth another great luminary of the church, Saint John Chrysostom, and he filled the world with divine teaching and explained all the Scriptures by his interpretation.
Likewise he undertook to interpret the holy Gospel by the grace of the Holy Spirit, for it is written
that in the days of the great emperor Theodosius, when Saint Gregory the Theologian was in Constantinople, Emperor Theodosius entreated him
to write an interpretation of the holy Gospel, for he saw that spring of wisdom that flowed from his mouth.
So the blessed Gregory complied and wished to set about interpreting the Gospel, but one night he stood in prayer,
so that God might reveal to him whether he willed this undertaking, for the God-clad fathers did nothing without prayer.
And as he was praying, he heard a voice saying to him: "Gregory, Gregory, the commentary on the Gospel has been commanded to John of Antioch."
For in those days, when Gregory the Theologian was archbishop in Constantinople, Saint John Chrysostom was archdeacon in Antioch.
And when the blessed man heard this voice, he told the vision to the emperor and did not undertake the commentary any further.
A short time afterward the people of Antioch had a certain petition to present to Emperor Theodosius, and the blessed John wrote it, and,

when that letter came before the emperor, the emperor marveled at the wisdom of its writer and showed the letter to Saint Gregory. He read it, perceived the matter by the Spirit, and said to the emperor:
"The one who has written this letter, O emperor, is the one about whom God informed me that the commentary on the Gospel has been commanded to him."
And this prophecy of his was fulfilled, for truly the God-clad John Chrysostom wrote a commentary on the holy Gospel of Matthew and
of John, and in these he gathered together most of what was written by Mark and Luke, and he laid up in the church abundant treasures, full of spiritual grace.
For they taught the proclaimed truths with divine knowledge and speech, and through their instruction we confess the uncreated Trinity, who in wisdom created all beings,
which is above all thoughts and all utterances of fleshly lips: a Godhead, a Trinity in persons and a Trinity equal in nature;
the Father, without beginning and without end, light immaterial in nature, a luminary among living bodies, equal in the will and governance of sovereign self-rule;
and the Son without beginning, the only one, only-begotten from the Only One, life from life, light from light, on which eyes cannot gaze,
who by the property of his authority abides unchangeably with the Father and the Spirit in complete likeness, apart from sonship; and the Spirit, without beginning,
life-giving, who fills all with the riches of the knowledge of God, and abides with those two, co-essential, in the kingdom of immortality.
Thus in orthodoxy we confess the true Godhead, revealed in three living persons, and yet one of the Trinity,
the only Son, in two natures, one person without confusion, who before the ages was with the Father in that uncontainable nature of the Godhead.
As that pipe of theology sounds forth, and that vessel of purity, recounting that timeless Being, says:
"In the beginning was the Word," so he raises our minds toward that beginning, which is impossible to reach,
for however high the mind ascends toward the height of the ages, that beginning is found to be higher still.
But let us bring the mind back to its proper station and listen to this same divine evangelist,
for first he tells us of that incomprehensible and boundless Being, and then he proclaims that unknowable mystery and cause of our salvation,
full of all awe, and says: "And the Word became flesh."
This is the Word who from the beginning was with the unbegotten Begetter, and at the end of the ages became akin to the likeness of men,
so that we might see his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth,
And from the fullness of his divinity let us receive grace for grace, that is, law for law.
For he changed the form of those former ordinances and made the light, the truth, shine forth to those near and those far off,
who are the peoples of heaven and of earth, whom he made one flock on account of his love for humankind, as he said:
"Let them be one flock and one shepherd." For he united the earthly with the heavenly and made known to all alike the manifold incomprehensibility of his dispensation,
for he who appointed the limit of nature for the times was found subject to the count of the times through that nature.
For he took from us, and in the temple of the nature of flesh he concealed the fullness of his divinity, whose beauty covered the heavens.
For that uncomposed firebrand was blended with material composition in the furnace of purity, which is his immaculate mother,
in whom, by his mysterious indwelling, he without change fulfilled the proclamations of those who had been informed beforehand by the Spirit,
who longingly awaited and desired to see the one they proclaimed, of whom the Word of God has now in his goodness made us worthy,
this new people, whom he called to me from foreign worship, and he built for me a spiritual house on the foundation of the apostles and prophets,
whose foundations stand unshaken against the assault of the winds and rivers of unbelief,
for the head of its corners is the only-begotten Son of God, who sprinkled it with the blood of the new covenant and adorned it as if with purple.
Therefore she who was formerly called barren, her courts have been filled with a multitude of offspring, among whom she rejoices with a ten-stringed instrument of praise,
like a mother gladdened by her children, for she has received the good tidings of Isaiah the loud-voiced, who said:
"Rejoice, you barren one who do not bear; lift up your voice and cry out, you who have not been in labor."
For this reason also streams of divine milk and of living water flow within the dwellings of Zion,
which are the proclamations of the apostles and prophets and holy hierarchs, among whom the only-begotten Son of God has made his abode together with the Father and the Holy Spirit.
Therefore it is not fitting to call them equals of men, but they made their minds winged toward the height of the firmament, as fellow-choristers of the bodiless ones of heaven,
who like the eagle and like clouds made the dew of the knowledge of God flow over the world, and the fruit of the true faith flourished more than before.
For from its midst they separated out, like tares, that plant of bitterness, the belief of the heretics grown wicked as wild beasts, who went mad in the wisdom of this world,
and in the wantonness of their evil did not submit in obedience to the teaching of the apostles, but brought in a foreign and manifold doctrine.
Therefore they became strangers to that spiritual second birth, and thus, seized by the darkness of ignorance, they were arrayed against the face of the light.
But the holy teachers of the true faith, as with fire,
with their tongues burned up the thorns of their heresy, and that meadow of Orthodoxy, the assembly of believing peoples, rejoices in the dew flowing down
by his mouth, and, drawn up in ranks, they sound forth amid the surging streams of the Church in glorification of the awesome Trinity, who is glorified forever.
By true faith in this holy Trinity, and by the intercession before it of our Lady, the all-holy Virgin Mary,
who, beyond nature, contained in her womb the One of the Trinity, the Son, equal in nature to the Father,
and she is the intercessor of all Christians before her Son and our God; and by the power of the life-giving, precious Cross, and by the grace of Saint John the Baptist,
by the intercession of the holy hierarchs, martyrs and fathers,
who by their valiant spiritual struggle parted the depths of the abysses of unbelief and led the people of God, the new Israel, out into the promised Jerusalem,
for they prepared the ship of their teachings, not one that carries from land to land,
but one that carries up from earth to heaven the soul and mind of the orthodox, by the intercession and assistance of all these.
